en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Itivuttaka in the Khuddakanikāya.
Introduction to the Work:
I pay homage to the Lord of Great Compassion, who has reached the further shore of the ocean of all that is to be known, and who teaches through methods that are skillful, profound, and diverse.
I pay homage to that supreme Dhamma, honored by the Fully Enlightened One, endowed with true knowledge and conduct, by which people are led out from the world;
it is perfected in qualities such as virtue and is established in the paths and fruits.
I pay homage to that Noble Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit.
By the power of whatever merit has arisen from this homage to the Triple Gem,
may I be free from obstacles everywhere.
The discourses taught by the Great Seer according to their divisions,
such as the *Ekaka* and others— which specifically illuminate the abandonments of greed and the other [defilements]—
have been brought together here along with the words and syllables of the *Itivuttaka*.
The Elder Dhammasaṅgāhakas, those of great wisdom,
compiled this work known by the name Itivuttaka in former times— this which,
within the Khuddaka Nikāya, follows a sequence of words of profound meaning.
Because it must be plunged into by means of profound knowledge,
although this commentary on the meaning was difficult for me to compose,
I have nonetheless undertaken it; for together with this commentary, it sustains the Teacher’s dispensation.
The exposition of the lions among former teachers remains established.
Therefore, relying upon that, having plunged into all five Nikāyas,
and depending on the method of the ancient commentaries—
Relying upon the path of recitation— well-purified and unconfused—
the precise determination of the meaning by the residents of the Mahāvihāra;
having carefully avoided meanings that have been repeated over and over again.
"I shall compose, according to my ability,
a commentary on the *Itivuttaka*. Therefore, O virtuous ones,
listen as I analyze its meaning for one who desires the long endurance of the True Dharma."
Therein, the *Itivuttaka* consists of a collection of four sections: the Ekaka-nipāta, Duka-nipāta, Tika-nipāta, and Catukka-nipāta.
It is included within the Sutta Piṭaka among the three Piṭakas—namely, the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Sutta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—and is further contained within the five Nikāyas:
the Dīgha Nikāya, Majjhima Nikāya, Saṃyutta Nikāya, Aṅguttara Nikāya, and Khuddaka Nikāya.

Among the Nikāyas, it is included in the Khuddakanikāya; among the nine branches of the Teaching (sāsanaṅga), it belongs to the Itivuttaka branch—consisting of Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla.
“I received eighty-two [verses] from the Buddha, and two thousand from the Bhikkhus.”
“There are eighty-four thousand teachings that have been set forth by me.
Thus, regarding the compilation of a certain number of Dhamma aggregates (*dhammakkhandha*) out of the eighty-four thousand Dhamma aggregates acknowledged by the Dhamma-treasurer:
first, from the perspective of the *Sutta* [collection], there are twenty-seven suttas in the *Ekakanipāta*, twenty-two in the *Dukanipāta*, and fifty in the *Tikanipāta*.
The *Catukkanipāta* consists of thirteen [sections], comprising one hundred and twelve suttas in total.
Among its chapters (*nipātas*), the *Ekakanipāta* is the first; among its groups (*vagga*), the *Pāṭibhogavagga*; and among its suttas, the *Lobhasutta*.

Furthermore, the introduction (*nidāna*) beginning with "This was said by the Blessed One" was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council (*paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāla*). Now, as for this First Great Council:

These [introductory stories] are indeed included in the Vinaya Piṭaka. Furthermore, the method of discourse that ought to be stated here for the sake of proficiency regarding the introductory narratives (*nidāna*) has already been explained in detail in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya;
therefore, it should be understood according to the method set forth therein. The Explanation of the Introductory Narratives (*Nidānavaṇṇanā*).
Now, that which was stated as "Thus it was said by the Blessed One," and so forth, is the *nidāna* (introduction). "Bhikkhus, abandon one thing," and so forth, is the *sutta* (discourse).
Therein, "It was said by the Blessed One" and so on are noun-words (*nāmapada*). "Iti" is a particle-word (*nipātapada*).
In the phrase "abandon" (*pajahatha*), "pa-" is a prefix-word (*upasaggapada*) and "jahatha" is a verb-word (*ākhyātapada*). By this method, the analysis of words is to be understood everywhere.
As for its meaning, the word *vutta*— whether with or without a prefix— is seen in such senses as sowing, making equal through planting,
the removal of hair, the maintenance of life, the state of being spoken, that which is set forth by way of the teaching,
an exhortation, and speaking; for instance:—
In such passages as, “Cattle are born for him, what is sown in his field grows;
he eats the fruit of what was sown, who does not deceive his friends,” it occurs in the sense of sowing.
In such passages as, “But it has not yet been reaped,” it refers to the act of leveling the ground for sowing with ivory pegs and so forth.

In such passages as “The young brahmin student Kāpaṭika with shorn hair,” it refers to the plucking out of hair. In such passages as “With hair fallen out, subsisting on what is given by others, he dwells with a mind become like that of a deer,” it refers to the mode of livelihood.
In such passages as “Just as a withered leaf, detached from its stem, is incapable of becoming green again,” it refers to the state of having been detached from its bond.
In such passages as “Of those [who possess this], O brahmins, at present... [it refers to the present].
In such passages as "The ancient mantra-word, sung, uttered, and intended," it occurs in the sense of being set forth as the Word of the Buddha (*pāvacana*).
In common usage, however, it occurs in the sense of recitation, as in "the *gaṇa* has been recited" or "the *pārāyana* has been recited. In such passages as "This was indeed said by the Blessed One:
'Bhikkhus, be my heirs in the Dhamma, not my heirs in material things,'" it occurs in the sense of speaking. Here too, it occurs in the sense of speaking.
It should be understood as "spoken. Therefore, the meaning is: "said," "uttered," or "declared.
However, the second occurrence of the word *vutta* should be understood in the sense of "speech" and "the state of having been practiced.
The particle *hi* is used in the sense of "indeed" or "certainly" (*jātu vibyattaṃ*). It illuminates the clear and distinct manner in which the Blessed One spoke this sutta that is now being recited.
For particles (nipāta) employed in proximity to a word that expresses meaning illuminate the sense to be expressed by them. This particle *etaṃ*—
that is, this word *etaṃ*— "He who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha,
sees the Four Noble Truths with right wisdom."
“Suffering, the origin of suffering, and the transcendence of suffering;
and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the stilling of suffering—
this indeed is the secure refuge, this is the supreme refuge.”
“Having come to this refuge, one is liberated from all suffering”— in such passages as these,
it is used in the sense of what has been previously stated, that which is near and directly perceived. However, in such passages as, “But this, monks,
is a mere trifle, a mere pittance, a mere matter of virtue, by which an ordinary person might speak in praise of the Tathāgata,” it is used in the sense of what will be stated hereafter.
"Near at hand" (*āsannapaccakkhe*). Here too, it should be understood as referring to exactly what will be stated below.
For the discourse that is to be recited by way of the communal chanting was placed in the mind of the Dharma-treasurer (Ānanda) and then referred to as "this" (*etaṃ*) at that time.

Regarding the term "by the Blessed One" (*bhagavatā*): here, "Blessed One" (*bhagavā*) is a term of respect. For in the world, one who is venerable is called "Blessed One. And the Tathāgata is venerable to all beings because he is distinguished by every excellence; therefore, he should be understood as "the Blessed One. It has also been said by the Ancients:
“‘Bhagavā’ is the best word; ‘Bhagavā’ is the supreme word.
He is venerable and worthy of honor; therefore he is called ‘Bhagavā.
For the word that expresses excellence is called “excellent” because it is accompanied by excellent qualities. Alternatively, it is said: “He is called [Bhagavā]...”
The word and its meaning. Therefore, "the Blessed One" (*bhagavā*) means that the meaning which is to be expressed by this word "Blessed One" is the most excellent;
such is the sense. The same method applies here to the phrase "the word 'Blessed One' is supreme.

"Worthy of reverence" (*gāravayutta*) means endowed with a state of weightiness due to being possessed of weighty qualities; or, he is "worthy of reverence" because he deserves to be highly honored. Thus, he is one who possesses reverence.
This is the meaning. Thus, this term "Bhagavā" is a designation for one who possesses supreme reverence for the most excellent beings distinguished by such qualities. Furthermore:
"He possesses [the qualities], he frequents [them], he shares in them, he has analyzed them;
He has broken [the defilements], he is venerable, he is fortunate."
“He whose self is well-developed through many methods,
he who has reached the end of existence— he is called the Blessed One.”—
according to the method handed down in the Niddesa.
“Fortunate (bhāgyavā), one who has destroyed (bhaggavā), one who is endowed (yutto), one who possesses excellences (bhagehi vibhattavā);
one who has enjoyed (bhattavā), one who has gone beyond (vantagamano) existences (bhavesu)—therefore he is the Blessed One (bhagavā).

The meaning of the term *bhagavā* should be explained according to this verse. Furthermore, this meaning has been stated in its entirety in the *Visuddhimagga*, in the section on the Recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati-niddesa*). It should be understood there exactly according to the method set forth therein.

Another method: He is the Blessed One (bhagavā) because he possesses fortune (bhāga); he is the Blessed One because he has nourished (bhatava); he is the Blessed One because he desires fortune (bhāge vani); he is the Blessed One because he desires excellence (bhage vani); he is the Blessed One because he has conquered (bhattava);

he is the Blessed One because he vomits out excellence (bhage vamī); he is the Blessed One because he vomits out fortune (bhāge vamī). “Possessor of fortune, nourisher, desirer of fortune, And desirer of excellence, conqueror of excellence, Likewise, vomiter of excellence and fortune— Thus the Victor is called the Blessed One.”

In this context, how is he "Bhagavā" (the Blessed One)? Those aggregates of Dhamma consisting of virtue and so forth, which are portions of qualities, exist and are found in the Tathāgata as unique and unsurpassed.

For his virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, knowledge and vision of liberation, moral shame, moral dread, faith, energy, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and purification of virtue [belong to him alone].
Purification of mind, purification of view, serenity, insight, the three roots of wholesome merit, the three types of good conduct, the three right thoughts,
the three blameless perceptions, the three elements, the four foundations of mindfulness,
the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the four noble paths, the four noble fruits, the four [bases of accomplishment]...
The analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*); the knowledges that delimit the four modes of birth; the four noble lineages (*ariyavaṃsa*); the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*);
the five factors of striving (*padhāniyaṅga*); right concentration with five factors; right concentration with five knowledges;

the five faculties (*indriya*); the five powers (*bala*); the five elements leading to escape (*nissāraṇīyā dhātu*); the five knowledges of the bases of liberation (*vimuttāyatana*); the five things that ripen liberation...
perceptions, the six bases of recollection, the six respects, the six elements leading to deliverance,
the six constant abidings, the six unsurpassed states, the six perceptions partaking of penetration, the six direct knowledges, the six unique types of knowledge,
the seven qualities that prevent decline, the seven treasures of the noble ones, the seven factors of enlightenment, the seven qualities of a true person, the seven...
The bases for the wearing away [of kamma], the seven perceptions, the teaching on the seven persons worthy of offerings, the teaching on the seven powers of one whose taints are destroyed,

the teaching on the eight causes for the acquisition of wisdom, the eight rightnesses, the transcendence of the eight worldly conditions, the eight bases for exertion, the teaching on the eight inopportune moments,
the eight thoughts of a great person, the teaching on the eight bases of mastery, and the eight liberations.
The nine states rooted in appropriate attention; the nine factors of exertion for complete purification; the teaching on the nine abodes of beings; the nine ways of removing resentment;
the nine perceptions; the nine diversities; the nine successive dwellings; the ten qualities that make one a protector;
the ten bases of totality; the ten courses of wholesome action; the ten rightnesses; and the ten noble abodes.
The ten qualities of one beyond training (*asekha*), the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the eleven benefits of loving-kindness (*mettā*), the twelve aspects of the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*),
the thirteen ascetic virtues (*dhutaguṇa*), the fourteen knowledges of a Buddha, the fifteen qualities that ripen liberation, the sixteenfold mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*),
the sixteen qualities that burn away the future, the eighteen qualities of a Buddha, and the nineteen knowledges of reflection.
These include: the forty-four bases of knowledge; the fifty knowledges of arising and passing away; the more than fifty wholesome states; the seventy-seven bases of knowledge;

the great diamond-like knowledge that moves through twenty-four hundred thousand million meditative attainments; the knowledges of teaching, reviewing, and analyzing the *Paṭṭhāna* according to its infinite methods;
and likewise, the knowledges that discern the inclinations and other traits of infinite beings in infinite world-systems—and such as these.
Infinite, of immeasurable varieties, unique, unsurpassed, portions of qualities (*guṇabhāga*), and divisions of qualities (*guṇakoṭṭhāsa*) exist and are found.

Therefore, because he possesses these aforementioned divided portions of qualities, although he should be called "possessor of portions" (*bhāgavā*), by shortening the vowel *ā* [to *a*], he is called "Bhagavā.
Thus, first of all, he is "Bhagavā" in the sense of being a possessor of portions.
“Because all the factors of virtue, beginning with morality, exist without exception in the Sugata, he is therefore called ‘Bhagavā.

How is he ‘Bhagavā’ in the sense of being ‘possessed of’ (bhatavā)? Those [qualities] which were attained by those who exerted themselves for the welfare of the entire world, starting from human birth and so forth—eight [of these]...”
Having synthesized these qualities, the perfection of giving (dānapāramī) must be fulfilled by Great Beings (mahābodhisatta) through their great resolves for perfect enlightenment;
namely, the ten perfections (pāramī)— giving, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity—
the ten secondary perfections (upapāramī), and the ten ultimate perfections (paramatthapāramī), making thirty perfections in total, beginning with giving and the rest.
The four bases of sympathy, the four foundations, the sacrifice of oneself, and the sacrifice of one’s eyes, wealth, kingdom, sons, and wife— these are the five great sacrifices;
the prior application, the prior conduct, the proclamation of the Dhamma, the conduct for the welfare of the world, the conduct for the welfare of kinsmen,
and the conduct for the welfare of Buddhahood— such as these, in brief, are the requisites of merit and the requisites of knowledge, the qualities that produce a Buddha.

From the time of their great resolution (*mahābhinīhāra*) onwards, for four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) plus a hundred thousand aeons, they do not become partaking of decline (*hānabhāgiya*), partaking of defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*), or partaking of stagnation (*ṭhitibhāgiya*); rather, they become exclusively partaking of ever-higher distinction (*uttaruttara-visesabhāgiya*).
Thus, because he has performed, accumulated, and possesses [these qualities] thoroughly, continuously, and without remainder, he is called "one who has performed" (*bhata-vā*).
“Bhagavā”: by way of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), the letter *ta* is changed to *ga*. Alternatively, “he has nourished” (*bhatavā*):
the meaning is that he has nurtured (*bhari*) and fulfilled (*sambhari*) those very qualities that produce Buddhahood, in the manner already described. Thus too he is “Bhagavā.
Because, through perfect enlightenment, [he has fulfilled] all the perfections, beginning with giving...
“Having fulfilled the requisites, he is therefore considered the Blessed One (Bhagavā).

How does he “possess” (bhajati) the portions? Those portions consisting of the twenty-four hundred thousand millions of attainments that are utilized daily—he possesses them entirely for the sake of the welfare of the world and for his own dwelling in happiness in this very life throughout the entire aeon.
He has enjoyed and cultivated [the path] extensively, thus he is the Blessed One (*bhagavā*).

Alternatively, among the things to be directly known—such as the wholesome states and the aggregates—there are those fourfold portions of direct realization categorized as "to be fully understood" (*pariññeyya*) and so forth in brief;
but in detail, there are many portions to be fully understood, such as: "The eye is to be fully understood... up to ... aging-and-death is to be fully understood."
The portion to be abandoned, such as: “The origin of the eye is to be abandoned... [and so on] ...the origin of aging-and-death is to be abandoned”;
the portion to be realized, such as: “The cessation of the eye is to be realized... [and so on] ...the cessation of aging-and-death is to be realized”; and the portion to be developed, such as:
“The practice leading to the cessation of the eye is to be developed... [and so on] ...the four foundations of mindfulness.”

Furthermore, by the words "should be developed" and so forth, there are various categories of phenomena (*dhamma*) that are to be developed; he frequented all of them as portions (*bhāga*), having cultivated them according to their suitability through the practice of the proper range of objects (*gocara*) and meditative development (*bhāvanā*).

Thus, because he frequented these portions, he is the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*). Alternatively, those aggregates of the Dhamma (*dhammakhandha*) such as virtue (*sīla*) and the rest, which are common to disciples—those portions of qualities, those segments of excellence—how indeed might they [be established] within the mental continuums of those to be trained? [He acted so that they might be. Thus, because he caused those portions to be [established], he is the Blessed One.
"May he establish [me]"—thus he aspired to the forest of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). And that aspiration of his brought about the fruit exactly as intended.
Thus, because he has "gone to the portion," he is called the Blessed One (*bhagavā*).
"Because the Tathāgata has gone to the portion of the qualities of the attainments regarding the knowable..."
"Therefore, for the welfare of beings, the Blessed One (Bhagavā) then set forth.

How is he "Blessed" (bhagavā)? Briefly stated, those who have performed merit and are endowed with skillful means possess "blessings" (bhagā)—that is, mundane and supramundane attainments—according to their respective wealth.
Among these, first, regarding the mundane: from his full enlightenment, the Tathāgata...

Formerly, when he was a Bodhisatta, he frequented and resorted to forests that had reached the highest excellence, where, by establishing himself, he brought to full maturity the qualities of a Buddha while perfecting all the factors that constitute Buddhahood.
But when he had become a Buddha, he likewise frequented and resorted to forests that were free from blame, endowed with bliss, and supramundane, being shared by no other.
In detail, however, this refers to his mastery over regional sovereignty, universal sovereignty as a Cakkavatti, the attainment of celestial kingship, and so forth.

And because he resorted to, frequented, and enjoyed manifold, unique blessings (*bhaga*) consisting of the higher human states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), such as knowledge and vision regarding the meditations (*jhāna*), liberations (*vimokkha*), concentrations (*samādhi*), attainments (*samāpatti*), the development of the path (*magga-bhāvanā*), and the realization of the fruits (*phala-sacchikiriyā*), he is called the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*). Thus, "one who resorts to blessings" is the Blessed One.
"Those various prosperities in the world, and those many supramundane ones..."
The Fully Enlightened One has abandoned them all; therefore, too, he is called the Blessed One (Bhagavā).
How is he the Blessed One by virtue of being a Master (bhattava)? Because he has many devoted followers who possess firm devotion, he is the Blessed One.
For the Tathāgata is the supreme among all beings due to his possession of immeasurable and incomparable distinctions of power and qualities, such as Great Compassion and Omniscient Knowledge.
By virtue of his unsurpassed perfection of practice— which is preceded by the avoidance of all that is harmful and intent solely upon the provision of every benefit and happiness without exception—

and by virtue of his physical body being adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor characteristics, the fathom-wide aura, and other distinguished qualities not shared by any other, he is of ultimate benefit to the world of devas and humans; thus,
through the attainment of such qualities as they truly are, [he is known as] "Itipi..."
Because he is endowed with a vast and perfectly pure sound of praise that pervades the three worlds,
proceeding in the manner beginning with “So bhagavā,” and because he is firmly established in such qualities as fewness of desires and contentment which have reached the highest perfection,

and because he possesses the most excellent and unsurpassed special qualities such as the ten powers and the four grounds of self-confidence, he is immeasurable in form and inspires confidence in form.
"Measured by fame, confident in fame; measured by austerity, confident in austerity;

measured by the Dhamma, confident in the Dhamma"—thus, because it is beautiful on all sides through its quality of inspiring confidence in every way within this world-system characterized by these four measures, it is the supreme object of love and devotion for immeasurable beings, including devas and humans, as a source of respect, esteem, and reverence.

And those who are established in his instruction and endowed with verified confidence (aveccappasāda) possess a friendship that cannot be diverted by anyone—whether by a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, or Brahmā.
For even at the sacrifice of their own lives, they do not abandon their confidence therein, because of the firm nature of their devotion to his command. Therefore it was said:
“He who is grateful and mindful of what has been done, wise, a friend of virtue, and firm in devotion.
“Just as, monks, the great ocean is stable in its nature and does not overstep its shore, even so, monks,”
“Whatever training rule has been laid down by me for my disciples, my disciples do not transgress it even for the sake of their lives.

Thus he is called *Bhattava* (the One Honored) by the Blessed One through the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), having elided one *ta*-sound and changed the other to a *ga*-sound. [As it is said:
“Because he is endowed with preeminent virtues and seeks the welfare of the world...”
“Because many have partaken [of his teaching], the Blessed One is called ‘Bhagavā’.

How is it that he vomits out fortune (*bhaga*), thus being “Bhagavā”? Because even while he was a Bodhisatta, fulfilling the perfections (*pāramitā*) in previous births, the Tathāgata vomited forth—cast up and disgorged like a globule of spittle—the glory, sovereignty, and fame designated as *bhaga*, without any longing for them.

He renounced it. For instance, during his births as the youth Somanassa, the youth Hatthipāla, the wise Ayoghara, the wise Mūgapakkha, and Cūḷasutasoma, and so forth, there is no limit to the number of times he sacrificed his own person—possessing royal glory equal to that of the gods—in order to fulfill the perfection of renunciation.
Even in his final existence, that which had come into his hands...

Having renounced—without regarding even as a blade of grass—the glory of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*), which is like sovereignty over the realm of the gods, the lordship over the four continents, the splendor based on the fortune of a wheel-turner, and fame radiant with the seven treasures;

and having gone forth without attachment, he awakened to perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*). Therefore, he is called the Blessed One (*bhagavā*) because he has vomited out (*vamati*) these fortunes such as glory and the rest. Alternatively, *bhāni*...
The *bhagas* are those [beauties] that go along with and proceed together with the lunar mansions (*nakkhattāni*).

They are splendors based on specific features of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), such as Sineru, Yugandhara, Uttarakuru, and the Himalayas, because they endure for the duration of an eon (*kappa*). The Blessed One vomited these out—that is, he abandoned them—by transcending the abodes of beings dwelling therein and by relinquishing the desire and lust (*chandarāga*) bound to them.
Thus, too, he is the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*) because he has vomited out the *bhagas*.
“Because the Sugata, the Blessed One, has abandoned the glory of a wheel-turning monarch, as well as fame, sovereignty, happiness, and the worldly mind, he is therefore ‘Bhagavā.
How does he vomit out his portions (bhāga)? ‘Portions’ (bhāgā) means parts. These [are classified] by way of the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), and so forth.”
There too, they are manifold, categorized by way of form, feeling, and so forth, as well as by way of the past, and so on.
And the Blessed One, having utterly severed all proliferation (*papañca*), all bondage (*yoga*), all ties (*gantha*), and all fetters (*saṃyojana*), attained the deathless element;
he vomited them up, cast them out, and, being without regard for them, abandoned them and did not return to them. For in this way, he [abandoned] the earth everywhere.
Water, fire, air; the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena;
eye-consciousness … pe … mind-consciousness; eye-contact … pe … mind-contact;
feeling born of eye-contact … pe … feeling born of mind-contact; that which is born of eye-contact … pe … [feeling born of] mind-contact.
Perception... [and so on] ...perception born of mind-contact; volition born of eye-contact... [and so on] ...volition born of mind-contact;
craving for forms... [and so on] ...craving for mental phenomena; thought concerning forms... [and so on] ...thought concerning mental phenomena; examination of forms...
[and so on] ...examination of mental phenomena—and thus, by way of the analysis of phenomena one by one (*anupadadhammavibhāga*), all categories of phenomena (*dhammakotthāsa*) without exception.
Having vomited it up, he discarded it through the relinquishment of non-attachment. For this has been said:

“Ānanda, that which has been cast off, vomited out, released, abandoned, and relinquished—that the Tathāgata would take back again: such a possibility does not exist. Thus, too, he vomits up what belongs to him;
or alternatively, “he vomits up what belongs to him” means all things—both wholesome and unwholesome, blameworthy and blameless.
Through the gateway of knowledge of the Noble Path, he vomited up, disgorged, and renounced—without regard for them—the low and the sublime, the dark and the bright, mutually opposed phenomena;
he abandoned them and taught the Dhamma to others so that they might become like him. And this has been said:

“Bhikkhus, even phenomena are to be abandoned, let alone non-phenomena. Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma as similar to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping,” and so forth.
"Thus too, the Blessed One vomits out a portion," [it is said].
"Since the Great Seer has vomited out the various phenomena— such as the aggregates, bases, and elements—
which are black and white, for that reason also he is considered 'Bhagavā'."
Therefore it was said:
“He has attained the portions (bhāga), he has fulfilled his duties (bhata), he has conquered the portions (bhaga);
he has vomited out the portions (bhaga) and likewise the portions (bhāga)—thus the Conqueror is called the Blessed One (Bhagavā).”

By that Blessed One: he is called an *arahant* for these reasons: because he has gone far away (*ārakatta*) from the defilements; because he has slain (*hatattā*) all enemies that are the defilements;

because he has slain the spokes (*arā*) of the wheel of saṃsāra; because he is worthy (*arahattā*) of requisites and so forth; and because there is an absence of secrecy (*rahābhāva*) regarding his evil deeds. This is the summary here.
The detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
And here, by the term "Bhagavā," through the indication of his blessedness and so forth, there is revealed the excellence of his physical body—
which is not shared by others— adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor characteristics, the fathom-wide aura, the jewel-garland, and so on,
owing to his having accumulated a store of merit over many incalculable eons. By the term "Arahant,"...
By this indication of the abandonment of all defilements without remainder, which demonstrates the attainment of omniscient knowledge— the proximate cause for the destruction of the taints (*āsava*)—

there is revealed the perfection of his inconceivable and immeasurable Dhamma-body, consisting of the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the six unique knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and so forth. By both of these,
his status as one highly esteemed by those similar to him in the world— both householders and those gone forth— is shown.
It is proclaimed that [the Blessed One] is worthy of being approached; likewise, he possesses the capacity to remove the bodily and mental suffering of those who have approached him;
he is a benefactor through both the giving of material gifts and the giving of the Dhamma; and he is capable of endowing others with mundane and supramundane virtues.

Furthermore, by the term "Blessed One" (*bhagavā*), there is an illumination of his possession of the distinguished dwellings, such as the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), which stand at the pinnacle among the qualities of conduct.

By the phrase "accomplished in conduct" (*caraṇasampadā*), the perfection of conduct (*caraṇasampadā*) is illuminated. By the word "Arahant," through the indication of the attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*) which has reached the pinnacle of all forms of true knowledge (*vijjā*), the perfection of true knowledge (*vijjāsampadā*) is illuminated.

Alternatively, by the former [phrase], there is the conjunction with the latter two grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*) through the illumination of the unerring exposition of the factors conducive to obstacles and those leading to liberation;
and by the latter [word], there is the illumination of the abandonment of the defilements (*kilesa*) together with their underlying tendencies (*vāsana*) without remainder.
The conjunction with the first two kinds of self-confidence is thus elucidated.

Likewise, by means of the former [section], there is the fulfillment of the foundation of truth through the Tathāgata’s demonstration of the truth of his promise, the truth of his words, and the truth of his knowledge;

and the fulfillment of the foundation of relinquishment through the demonstration of his renunciation of the strands of sensual pleasure, worldly sovereignty, gains, honor, and so forth, as well as his renunciation of all defilements and volitional formations without exception.

It is thus revealed: by the second [section], which illustrates the attainment of the complete stilling of all conditioned phenomena and the illumination of perfect enlightenment, the fulfillment of the foundation of tranquility (*upasama*) and the foundation of wisdom (*paññā*) is revealed.

For it was through the application of great compassion that the Blessed One, while still a Bodhisatta who had made his resolution toward supramundane qualities, fulfilled all the perfections (*pāramitā*) exactly as he had promised.
The foundation of truth (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*); the foundation of generosity (*cāgādhiṭṭhāna*) through the relinquishing of that which is opposed to the perfections;

the foundation of peace (*upasamādhiṭṭhāna*) through the tranquility of the mind by means of the qualities of the perfections; and the foundation of wisdom (*paññādhiṭṭhāna*), brought to completion through skill in the means for the welfare of others by means of the perfections themselves.
Likewise, [this is achieved] through giving after having made a promise by saying, "I will give without deceiving the person who asks."

The foundation of truth (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*) is fulfilled through the relinquishing of what is to be given; the foundation of generosity (*cāgādhiṭṭhāna*) through the giving away of what is to be given;
the foundation of peace (*upasamādhiṭṭhāna*) through the subsiding of greed, hatred, delusion, and fear regarding the recipient, the act of giving, and the exhaustion of the gift;

and the foundation of wisdom (*paññādhiṭṭhāna*) through the preeminence of wisdom in giving according to what is appropriate, at the right time, and by the correct method. By this same principle, [it should be understood] for the remaining perfections (*pāramī*) as well.
The fulfillment of the four foundations should be understood. For all the perfections are manifested by truth, expressed through generosity, reinforced by tranquility, and purified by wisdom.
Thus, for the Tathāgata who has fully realized the four foundations, there is the foundation of truth;
and through the realization of the foundation of truth comes the purification of virtue, and through the realization of the foundation of generosity...
Purity of livelihood; purity of mind through the realization of the foundation of tranquility; and purity of view through the realization of the foundation of wisdom.
Likewise, his virtue is to be known by association with one who has realized the foundation of truth;

his integrity is to be known by dealing with one who has realized the foundation of generosity; and his fortitude in times of adversity is to be known by association with one who has realized the foundation of tranquility.
Wisdom is to be known through discussion by means of the accomplishment of the foundation of wisdom.
Likewise, through the accomplishment of the foundation of truth, one endures without malice; through the accomplishment of the foundation of generosity, one partakes without greed;
through the accomplishment of the foundation of peace, one avoids with fearlessness; and through the accomplishment of the foundation of wisdom—
Being undeluded, he dispels [the hindrances]. Thus, by the accomplishment of the foundation of truth (saccādhiṭṭhāna), his attainment of the happiness of renunciation (nekkhammasukha) is illustrated;

by the accomplishment of the foundation of generosity (cāgādhiṭṭhāna), the attainment of the happiness of seclusion (pavivekasukha); by the accomplishment of the foundation of peace (upasamādhiṭṭhāna), the attainment of the happiness of peace (upasamasukha);

and by the accomplishment of the foundation of wisdom (paññādhiṭṭhāna), the attainment of the happiness of full enlightenment (sambodhisukha) is illustrated. Or alternatively, by the accomplishment of the foundation of truth, there is the attainment of the rapture and happiness born of seclusion (vivekaja-pīti-sukha).
Through the accomplishment of the foundation of relinquishment (*cāgādhiṭṭhāna*), there is the attainment of the rapture and happiness born of concentration (*samādhi*);

through the accomplishment of the foundation of tranquility (*upasama*), there is the attainment of bodily happiness not accompanied by rapture; and through the accomplishment of the foundation of wisdom (*paññā*), there is the attainment of the happiness of equanimity born of the purity of mindfulness (*satipārisuddhi*).
Likewise, through the accomplishment of the foundation of truth (*sacca*), the association with the happiness of conditions characterized by the perfection of retinue is illustrated.

It exists through non-deception; through the accomplishment of the foundation of generosity (*cāgādhiṭṭhāna*), there is a conjunction with the happiness of the essential nature characterized by contentment, due to the state of non-greed (*alobha*);

through the accomplishment of the foundation of tranquility (*upasamādhiṭṭhāna*), there is a conjunction with the happiness of the cause characterized by the state of having performed merit, due to being unconquered by defilements;
and through the accomplishment of the foundation of wisdom (*paññādhiṭṭhāna*), there is a conjunction with the happiness of the subsiding of suffering, characterized by the attainment of liberation.
It is fully illuminated because, through the attainment of knowledge, one reaches Nibbāna.
Likewise, through the accomplishment of the foundation of truth, there is the achievement of the awakening to and penetration of the Noble Aggregate of Virtue;
through the accomplishment of the foundation of generosity, that of the Noble Aggregate of Concentration; and through the accomplishment of the foundation of wisdom...

By means of the accomplishment of the noble aggregate of wisdom through the attainment of the foundation of tranquility, the success of the awakening to and penetration of the noble aggregate of liberation is illustrated.
Furthermore, by the fulfillment of the foundation of truth, the success of austerity is shown; by the fulfillment of the foundation of generosity, the success of relinquishing everything;
by the fulfillment of the foundation of tranquility, the success of restraint of the faculties; and by the fulfillment of the foundation of wisdom—

Through that, the accomplishment of wisdom is achieved, and by that, the accomplishment of Nibbāna. Likewise, it is shown that through the fulfillment of the foundation of truth, there is the attainment of the realization of the Four Noble Truths;

through the fulfillment of the foundation of generosity, there is the attainment of the four noble lineages; through the fulfillment of the foundation of tranquility, there is the attainment of the four noble abidings;
and through the fulfillment of the foundation of wisdom, there is the attainment of the four noble modes of conduct.

Another method: by the term "Bhagavā," the Tathāgata’s great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is revealed through the indication of his longing for the mundane and supramundane prosperity of sentient beings.
By the term "Arahant," the wisdom of abandonment (*pahānapaññā*) is revealed through the indication of his perfection in relinquishment.
In this regard, through wisdom he attained sovereignty over the Dhamma, and through compassion he shared the Dhamma. Through wisdom...

Through wisdom there is revulsion toward the suffering of saṃsāra; through compassion, the endurance of the suffering of saṃsāra. Through wisdom, there is full understanding of the suffering of others;
through compassion, the undertaking of the remedy for the suffering of others. Through wisdom, there is the state of being directed toward parinibbāna;

through compassion, its attainment. Through wisdom, there is one’s own crossing over; through compassion, the crossing over of others. Through wisdom, the accomplishment of the state of a Buddha; through compassion...
The accomplishment of the Buddha’s work. Alternatively, through compassion there is the inclination toward *saṃsāra* on the bodhisattva stage, while through wisdom there is lack of delight therein.
Likewise, through compassion there is non-harming of others, and through wisdom there is fearlessness for oneself from others;
protecting another through compassion, one protects oneself, and protecting oneself through wisdom, one protects another. Thus it is said:

Through compassion, he does not torment others; through wisdom, he does not torment himself. By this, his status as the fourth type of person among those practicing for their own benefit and so forth is established.

Likewise, through compassion he is a lord of the world, and through wisdom he is a lord of himself; through compassion he possesses the quality of being inclined [toward others], and through wisdom he possesses the quality of being free from arrogance.
Similarly, through compassion he generates assistance toward all beings, and because it is accompanied by wisdom, he is not lacking in anything.

His mind is dispassionate; his mind is dispassionate toward all phenomena through wisdom (*paññā*), yet because it is accompanied by compassion (*karuṇā*), it does not fail to proceed toward the assistance of all beings.
For just as the Tathāgata’s compassion is devoid of affection and sorrow, so too is his wisdom free from the notions of "I" and "mine";
thus they should be seen as mutually purified and supremely pure. In this regard, the field of wisdom consists of the powers (*bala*), while the field of compassion consists of...

The grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajjāni*). Among these, through the conjunction with the powers (*bala*), one is not overcome by others; through the conjunction with the grounds of self-confidence, one overcomes others. By means of the powers, the perfection of the Teacher is accomplished;
by means of the grounds of self-confidence, the perfection of the Dispensation is accomplished. Likewise, by means of the powers, the perfection of the Buddha-jewel is accomplished;
by means of the grounds of self-confidence, the perfection of the Dhamma-jewel is accomplished. This is what is meant here by the phrase "by the Blessed One, the Worthy One."
This is merely a demonstration of the general meaning of the two phrases.
But why, after stating here, “For this was said by the Blessed One,” is it stated again, “It was said”? It is for the purpose of showing a restriction by way of rejecting mere hearsay.
For even if something has been said by someone else after hearing it from another, and even if it was said by one who knows [the truth], [it may still not be the word of the Buddha].
It was not spoken by him alone, because it was also spoken by another; nor was it spoken by him alone, but was also heard [from others]. However, it is not so in this case.
For the Blessed One spoke that which he himself had attained through his own self-existent knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*), without having heard it from another.
To show this distinction, the word "spoken" (*vutta*) is stated twice. This is what is meant: "For this has been spoken..."
“By the Blessed One”: this was spoken by the Blessed One himself, not by another; and it was spoken, not merely heard.
For an additional statement (adhikavacana) makes known another meaning, and thus there is no fault of redundancy (punaruttadosa). This same method applies to what follows as well.
Likewise, the word "spoken" is stated twice in order to show that this is not a prior composition (pubbaracanā). For the Blessed One, by virtue of his Perfect Enlightenment (sammāsambuddhatā)—
With spontaneous eloquence, he teaches the Dhamma in accordance with the inclinations of the assembled company;
for this reason, there is no need for him to perform preliminary composition, as is the case with giving and other such acts. By this, he shows:
"For this was spoken by the Blessed One, and it was not hammered out by logic nor followed by mere inquiry, but rather in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained."
“It was stated right on the spot.
Or, it is stated twice as “it was stated” in order to show that the words are irrefutable. For whatever has been spoken by the Blessed One has indeed been stated;
it cannot be rejected by anyone because of its perfection of phrasing and its perfection of meaning. For this has been said:
“This unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma has been set in motion by the Blessed One at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana; it cannot be turned back by any ascetic or brahmin,” and so forth.
Furthermore, it is said:
“In this case, monks, some ascetic or brahmin might come and say: ‘This is not the Noble Truth of Suffering...’”
‘Setting aside this Noble Truth of Suffering proclaimed by the ascetic Gotama, I shall proclaim another Noble Truth of Suffering’—
this is impossible,” and so forth. Therefore, it is stated twice that “it was said” in order to demonstrate the state of his words being irrefutable.
Alternatively, the word "spoken" (*vutta*) is stated twice for the purpose of showing that it brings about the welfare of the listeners.

For if something were spoken by one who is not omniscient—without knowing the dispositions and so forth of others, or at an improper place or time—even though it is true, it would be as if it were "not spoken" because of its inability to accomplish the welfare of the listeners, let alone if it were untrue. [This applies] to what was spoken by the Blessed One.
However, because he is a Perfectly Enlightened One, knowing correctly the dispositions and so forth of others, as well as the place, time, and the accomplishment of their welfare, he has spoken;
since he invariably brings about for the listeners the very purpose intended, what he has spoken is indeed [the truth], and there is no way in which it could be considered unsaid.
Therefore, it is stated twice that "it was spoken" in order to demonstrate its quality of producing benefit for the listeners. Furthermore—
Just as there is no such thing as a "son" who has not understood the meaning and has not practiced for suchness, so too there is no such thing as "spoken" that has not been correctly received.
However, the four assemblies, having correctly received the word of the Blessed One, practice for suchness.
Therefore, it is also for the purpose of showing that it has been correctly received [that this is said].
It is stated twice that "it was said.
Alternatively, it is stated twice that "it was said" in order to demonstrate that the words are not in conflict with those of the Noble Ones (ariya).

For just as the Blessed One [taught] the phenomena (dhamma) distinguished as wholesome and unwholesome, blameworthy and blameless, and as the engagement and withdrawal in terms of conventional and ultimate truth—

And he speaks without contradicting [the truth]. Thus, noble ones such as the Dhamma-Senāpati (Sāriputta) and others, both while the Blessed One was still living and after his Parinibbāna, speak by following his very teaching; there is no diversity of doctrine therein.

Therefore, it was said by the Arahant [Mahākaccāna] that "thereafter, by the Arahant Saṅgha of Noble Ones" as well—this was stated for the purpose of showing that the words of the Noble Ones are not contradictory.
Alternatively, the word "stated" is repeated twice for the purpose of showing that the manner and nature [of the teaching] were stated by the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones as well.

For even though there are differences among Buddhas regarding birth, lineage, lifespan, stature, and so forth, there is no difference in their teaching of the Dhamma, just as there is none in their possession of the ten powers and other qualities;
they speak to one another and to themselves in a way that is entirely consistent from beginning to end.
Therefore, this was said: "Just as it was stated by the Buddhas themselves in the past, so too has it been stated now by our Blessed One, the Arahant.
Thus, the word "stated" is repeated twice in order to show that the method [of teaching] exists in both the previous Buddhas and in himself within other discourses (*suttanta*).
By this, the absence of contradiction in the teaching of the Buddhas in all respects is illustrated.
Alternatively, regarding the word “spoken” (*vutta*): that second term should be understood as a statement concerning the state of having been spoken by the Arahant.

This is what is meant: “For this was spoken by the Blessed One, and it was also spoken by the Arahant”—namely, the speech now being stated, beginning with “Bhikkhus, there is one thing,” and so forth.
Or else, the word “spoken” (*vutta*), which is this second term, does not have the meaning of speech.
Rather, it should be understood as being for the purpose of sowing. By this he shows: "For this was spoken by the Blessed One;
and it was not merely spoken, nor merely told; rather, the root of merit has been sown in those to be trained"—this is the meaning.
Alternatively, that second word, "spoken" (*vutta*), is for the purpose of establishing [the fact]. For this is its meaning:
—for this was said by the Blessed One, the Arahant; and it was not merely spoken, but rather that which constitutes its meaning was spoken as a practice.
By this, he shows that "the Blessed One acts exactly as he speaks. Alternatively, the meaning is: it was spoken by the Blessed One, and the spoken word is fit to be uttered by the Arahant.
Alternatively, the first "said" (*vutta*) is stated with reference to the pointing out of a brief exposition, while the second "said" indicates a detailed exposition;

for the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma both briefly and in detail. Alternatively, after stating "for this was said by the Blessed One" in order to show the absence of any ill-spoken words from the Blessed One, it is stated again as "said. This is because his speech and action are always accompanied by knowledge (*ñāṇānugata*).

Indeed, for the Blessed One—who has abandoned all faults along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*) and whose mode of speech is never faltering—there is never such a thing as a poorly spoken word.

Just as some people in the world, having said something through forgetfulness, or in jest, or out of haste, and then having regained their mindfulness, either do what was previously said or undo it, or else reflect upon it;
the Blessed One does not act in this way. Rather, the Blessed One...
Always composed, possessing the nature of non-forgetfulness and the nature of non-delusion,

he brings forth the meaning conveyed by the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*), which is built upon the knowledge of omniscience. For those who hear it— [a teaching] that serves as a tonic for the sense-base of the ear—

he does so through his extraordinary faculties, which are exceptionally clear and pure, not shared by others, and brought about by an immeasurable accumulation of the equipment of merit over a vast period of time.

Like one raining down the rain of the Deathless, he proclaims the Four Truths—the essence of what is to be heard and the unsurpassed excellence of listening—with a voice as melodious as the song of the karavīka bird.
Speaking in his own natural language, he utters words that accord with the inclinations of those to be trained;
therein there is not even a hair’s breadth of error, so how could there be any occasion for a mispronunciation? Therefore, "whatever was spoken by the Blessed One, that is indeed spoken."
In order to show that "nothing is ever spoken that is ill-spoken," it was stated, "For this was said by the Blessed One";

and then, by stating again, "It was said by the Arahant," there is no fault of redundancy here. In this way, the purposefulness of the word "redundancy" (punarutta) in this context should be understood.
Regarding the phrase *iti me sutaṃ* (“thus have I heard”), here the word *iti* has many distinct meanings, such as cause, completion, reversal of meaning, manner, indication, and restriction.
For instance, it is seen in the sense of cause in such passages as: “It is deformed (*ruppati*), monks, therefore it is called ‘form’ (*rūpa*). Likewise, in the passage:
“Therefore, monks, be my heirs to the Dhamma, not my heirs to material things. I have [the Dhamma] for you... it is used in the sense of cause.
In such passages as “Out of compassion: ‘How might my disciples become heirs to the Dhamma, not heirs to material things’,” it has the sense of concluding a discourse.
In such passages as “Thus, or in this way, he abstains from such frivolous spectacles,” it has the sense of “beginning with. [And in the passage:
“‘Māgaṇḍiya’—this was the designation, the appellation, the description, the conventional usage, the name, the naming, the denomination, the linguistic expression, the phrasing for that brahmin.”
In such passages as “expression,” etc., it refers to the reversal of the meaning of the terms. In such passages as “Thus, monks, the fool is full of fear, while the wise man is free from fear;
the fool is beset by calamity, while the wise man is free from calamity; the fool is beset by misfortune, while the wise man is free from misfortune,” it refers to a manner or mode.
In such passages as “‘Everything exists,’ Kaccāna, is one extreme; ‘everything does not exist,’ Kaccāna, is [the other]…” it refers to a position.
In such passages as "this is the second extreme," it has the sense of illustration (*nidassana*). In such passages as "When asked, 'Is there aging-and-death with this specific condition?
one should answer, 'There is. And if he should ask, 'With what condition is there aging-and-death?
one should answer, 'With birth as condition there is aging-and-death,'" it has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), meaning a definitive conclusion (*sanniṭṭhāna*). This [particle] here—
The particle *iti* should be understood in the senses of manner, indication, and restriction.
Therein, by the sense of manner, he illuminates this meaning with the word *iti*:

[the teaching] which is skilled in various methods, originated from manifold inclinations, endowed with both meaning and phrasing, possessing manifold wonders, and profound in its penetration of the Dhamma, the meaning, the teaching, and realization—for all sentient beings.
Who is capable of understanding in every way the word of that Blessed One as it comes within the range of hearing according to each person's own particular language?
Nevertheless, having generated a desire to hear with all one's might, one thinks: "Thus have I heard;
I too have heard it in one particular way."

And here, the various methods (*naya*)— categorized by way of their objects and so forth— are manifold, being designated as "unity," "diversity," "inactivity," and "suchness of phenomena" (the *nandiyāvatta*,

*tipukkhalo*, *sīhavikkīḷita*, *disālocana*, and *aṅkusa* methods). Alternatively, "methods" are the courses of the text (*pāḷigatiyo*), and these are classified by way of formal rule (*paññatti*) and supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*),

by way of the categories such as "partaking of defilement" (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*), "worldly" (*lokiya*), and their mixture, by way of the wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth, and by way of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth.
The "various methods" (nānānaya) are those of various kinds, such as by way of the means of attraction (saṅgaha), etc.; by way of those liberated by occasion (samayavimutta), etc.;

by way of setting aside (ṭhapanā), etc.; by way of the roots of the wholesome (kusalamūla), etc.; and by way of the threefold matrix (tikapaṭṭhāna), etc. That which is "subtle, delicate, and refined" through these is "refined by various methods.

"Inclination" (ajjhāsaya) is simply "disposition" (āsaya); and that is of many kinds, distinguished by such categories as eternalism (sassata) and so forth, and by such categories as having little dust in one's eyes (apparajakkha) and so forth.

Or, "anekajjhāsaya" means many inclinations (*ajjhāsaya*), such as one's own personal inclination (*attajjhāsaya*) and so forth. That which has this as its source (*samuṭṭhāna*)—that is, its cause of arising—is "arising from many inclinations" (*anekajjhāsayasamuṭṭhāna*).

[It is explained] by way of the attainment of the meaning of the wholesome and so forth, and the attainment of the phrasing that clarifies it, through the methods of indicating, manifesting, explaining, analyzing, making plain, and describing.
It is "endowed with meaning and phrasing" because it is possessed of six bases of meaning— by way of the exposition of letters, words, phonemes, grammar, and etymology— and six bases of phrasing.

It is "various and manifold" through its divisions into supernormal power (*iddhi*), direct teaching (*ādesanā*), and instruction (*anusāsani*), and further through the various distinctions of their respective objects and so forth.
Or, it is "various wonders" (*vividhapāṭihāriya*) because these [powers] have wonders as their nature.

In this context, since "wonder" (*paṭihāriya*) means "removal of the opposite" (*paṭipakkhaharaṇa*), that is, the removal of defilements such as lust, there are no opposites such as lust in the Blessed One that need to be removed;
for even in ordinary persons, when the mind is free from corruption, endowed with the eight qualities, and has destroyed its opposites, the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) come forth.
Therefore, it cannot be called a "pāṭihāriya" (miracle) here by way of the conventional usage current in that context.

However, because the defilements residing in those to be converted are the adversaries of the Blessed One, who is possessed of great compassion, it is called a *pāṭihāriya* because of the removal (*haraṇa*) of them.
Alternatively, the sectarians are the adversaries of the Blessed One’s teaching; it is called a *pāṭihāriya* because of the removal of them. For they—

By way of removing wrong views and by being incapable of manifesting [such] views, they are "carried away" (*harita*)—that is, removed—by means of psychic power (*iddhi*), direct teaching (*ādesanā*), and instruction (*anusāsanī*).

Alternatively, *paṭi* has the sense of "afterwards. Therefore, it is called a "display" (*paṭihāriya*) because, when the mind is concentrated, free from defilements, and the task is accomplished, it is to be carried away—that is, put into operation—subsequently. Or, regarding one's own defilements, by means of the fourth jhāna and the paths...
The subsequent removal among those things that have been removed is a marvel (*paṭihāriya*).

Furthermore, the supernormal power (*iddhi*), the instruction by demonstration (*ādesanā*), and the instruction by advice (*anusāsani*) should be performed again for the benefit of beings by one who is free from defilements and has completed his task;

and because they remove the defilements within their own continuums as well as the defilements in the continuums of others among those things already removed, they are called "marvels" (*paṭihāriya*). A marvel itself is a "miracle" (*pāṭihāriya*); [this applies] to the marvel...
Alternatively, that which exists within the collection of supernormal power (*iddhi*), mind-reading (*ādesanā*), and instruction (*anusāsanī*) is called each a "wonder" (*pāṭihāriya*).

Or, the fourth jhāna and the Path are "wonderful" (*paṭihāriya*) because they remove opposing factors; that which is born therein, or that which has that [fourth jhāna or Path] as its sign, or that which has come from that, is thus a "wonder" (*pāṭihāriya*).

However, because the penetration of the Dhamma, the meaning, the teaching, and the realization—comprising respectively the teaching on the Thread, the teaching on the meaning, the designation, and the convergence—or alternatively, the penetration of the designation of cause, cause-and-effect, and both—is profound;
and because it is difficult to plunge into and provides no foothold for those who have not accumulated the necessary requisites, like the great ocean for frogs and the like;
therefore, it is endowed with these four kinds of profundity.
Profound in its penetration of the teaching on the nature of phenomena (dhammattha).
Even the single sound of the Blessed One’s Dhamma-teaching, occurring at one moment,
becomes accessible for simultaneous comprehension by beings of various languages according to each being’s own tongue, leading to the realization of the meaning.
For the spiritual power of the Buddhas is inconceivable; thus it should be understood that [the Dhamma] comes within the range of hearing for all beings according to their respective languages.

In the sense of illustration—liberating himself by saying, "I am not self-become, nor have I realized this myself"—he indicates the entire Sutta to be spoken now with the words, "Thus have I heard, I too have heard thus.
In the sense of emphasis—as in: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who are learned... (Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.23).
"Namely, Ānanda, among those who possess [noble] destiny, mindfulness, and fortitude, he is the attendant— namely, Ānanda. Thus,

in accordance with his state of being praised by the Blessed One and likewise by the General of the Dhamma, who said, "The Venerable Ānanda is skilled in the goal, skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in the phrasing, skilled in terminology,
and skilled in what precedes and follows," [he displayed] his own power of retention.
By presenting [the teaching], he generates in beings a desire to hear it, thinking: "Thus have I heard;
and that should be regarded as neither deficient nor redundant in meaning or phrasing, exactly so and not otherwise.

"Otherwise" means other than the manner in which it was heard in the presence of the Blessed One, but not other than the manner in which it was taught by the Blessed One; for the power of the Blessed One is inconceivable.

This meaning has already been stated: that the teaching cannot be fully understood in every aspect. For the power of retention consists precisely in not contradicting the manner in which it was heard.
Here, there is no need to avoid the charge of redundancy, because both meanings refer to the same subject matter;
otherwise, one would have to conclude that the Elder was either capable or incapable of receiving the Blessed One’s teaching in its entirety.
The word *me* is seen in three senses. For instance, in such passages as “Gāthābhigītaṃ me abhojaneyyaṃ,” the meaning is “by me.
In such passages as “Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetū,” the meaning is “to me.
In such passages as “Dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave, bhavathā,” the meaning is “my. But here, [it means] “by me.”
The two meanings, "heard" and "heard by me," are both applicable here. Furthermore,

since that which is not another is called "self" (*atta*), and because the word *me*— whether it be of the three types designated as "one's own" (*niyaka*) or "internal" (*ajjhatta*)— is used in reference to one's own continuum (*sakasantāna*),
even though it appears in only a single sense [in this context], the distinctions such as the instrumental case (*karaṇa*) or the dative case (*sampadāna*) are [implied].
Since this distinction of meaning does indeed exist for it, he says: "The word *me* is seen in three meanings.

As for the word *suta*, this term *suta*—whether with a prefix (*sa-upasagga*) or without a prefix (*an-upasagga*)—is divided into many meanings, such as going, renowned, moistened, accumulated, application, cognizable by the ear, and that which is cognized following the ear-door.
For although a prefix is a specifier of action, nevertheless, because it functions as an indicator (*jotaka*), even when that prefix is present, it remains simply the word *suta*.
In the extraction of the meaning of the word *suta* when it is without a prefix, it is cited even with a prefix as follows: "it expresses such and such a meaning.
In that regard, in phrases such as *senāya pasuto*, the meaning is "going. In phrases such as *sutadhammassa passato*, the meaning is "of one who has heard the Dhamma" (*vissutadhammassa*).
In phrases such as *avassutā avassutassā*, the meaning is "the lustful [desiring] the lustful" (*kilinnā kilinnassa*). [And in the phrase] *tumhehi puññaṃ*...
In such passages as “pasutaṃ anappakaṃ,” the meaning is “accumulated. In such passages as “ye jhānappasutā dhīrā,” the meaning is “devoted to jhāna.

In such passages as “diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ,” the meaning is “to be cognized by the ear. In such passages as “sutadharo sutasannicayo,” the meaning is “one who retains what is cognized through the channel of the ear.
Here, however, it means “ascertained by way of the channel of the ear.”
Or rather, the meaning is "retention" (*upadhāraṇa*). For when the word *me* has the sense of *mayā* ("by me"), the meaning is: "Thus have I heard;
it was retained by me following the path of the ear-door. When it has the sense of *mama* ("my"), the meaning is: "Thus have I heard;
it is my retention following the path of the ear-door."

Thus, regarding these three terms, since the word *iti* used in conjunction with the word *suta* must be one that indicates the act of hearing, therefore *iti* is a demonstration of the function of consciousness such as ear-consciousness (*sotaviññāṇa*).

*Me* is a demonstration of the person possessing the aforementioned consciousness. Furthermore, all sentences are indeed accompanied by the sense of the particle *eva*, because they have the result of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
Therefore, "heard" (*suta*) is [so called] by way of the negation of the state of not having heard.

This is an illustration of grasping that is neither deficient nor erroneous. For just as that which has been heard deserves to be called "heard," so too that which is rightly heard constitutes a grasp that is neither deficient nor erroneous.

Alternatively, since a word expresses its meaning by way of excluding the meanings of other words, the meaning of the term *suta* (heard) is that it is not *asuta* (unheard); therefore, it is called *suta*.
This is a demonstration of grasping [the teaching] without deficiency or distortion by way of rejecting its state of not being heard. This is what is meant:
"Thus have I heard"—it was not seen, nor realized through self-dependent knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*), nor apprehended otherwise;
rather, it was indeed heard, and that too correctly. Or, when the word *iti* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), this is the application of the meaning for that which depends upon it.

Since the sense of necessity (*niyama*) is possible for the word *suta*, it should be understood as a negation of the state of not having heard, as well as an indication of grasping [the teaching] without omission or error.
Thus, the application of the meaning of the three terms should be seen as having been made by way of the cause of hearing, the act of hearing, and the excellence of hearing.
Likewise, the word *iti* [is used] because of the grasping of various meanings and phrases by the cognitive process (*viññāṇavīthi*) proceeding through the ear-door.
The word *iti* has the sense of "mode" (*ākāra*), because it signifies the state of occurring with respect to various kinds of objects.
*Me* signifies the self. *Sutaṃ* signifies the Dhamma, because the aforementioned cognitive process (*viññāṇa-vīthi*) has the Dhamma of the scriptures as its object.
This is the summary here: by me, who am the cause for the cognitive process occurring with respect to various kinds of objects...
"This was done, but this was done instead; this Dhamma has been heard.
Likewise, the word *iti* is used in the sense of "indicating," as it clarifies that which is to be indicated.

Since there is no absence of that which is to be indicated by what is to be indicated, it should be understood that by means of the word *iti*, the entirety of what has been heard (*suta*) is referred back.
“Meti” (Thus) is the designation of the person. “Suttaṃ” (Discourse) is the designation of the person’s function.
For the act of hearing, which is obtained through the word “sutta,” is bound up with a continuity of auditory consciousness; and therein lies the conventional designation of a “person.

Indeed, the act of hearing is not found in a mere continuity of phenomena (dhamma) devoid of the conventional designation of a person. This is its summary meaning: the discourse that I shall point out—
"That was by me" means "thus. Likewise, regarding the word "iti":

since there is a grasping of various meanings and phonemes due to the occurrence of various objects within a particular stream of consciousness, the word *iti* has the sense of "aspect," as it is a designation of that aspect. For this *iti* is a designation of aspect (*ākāra-panñatti*).
This is because it has a nature that must be designated based on the various modes of occurrence of phenomena (*dhamma*). "Me" (*meti*) is a designation for the agent;

"suta" (*sutam*) is a designation for the object. For a phenomenon that is to be heard becomes the locus of occurrence for the person who is the agent of the act of hearing, by way of that act of hearing.
To this extent, by means of a mental continuum proceeding in various ways, [the object] belongs to the agent who possesses it.
The conclusion of the apprehension of the object has thus been shown.

Alternatively, "iti" is a designation for the function of a person (*puggala-kicca-niddesa*). For, by means of the word *iti*, which functions as an indicator, a determiner, or an elucidator of the mode in which the heard teachings (*dhamma*) have been grasped, there occurs the state of a person’s conventional expression (*puggala-vohāra*) through the undertaking of the activity of those phenomena (*dhamma*) that maintain that mode and so forth.

"The function of the person" (puggalakicca) is thus indicated. "Hearing" (suta) is a description of the function of consciousness (viññāṇakicca), for even for a proponent of the person (puggalavādin), the act of hearing does not exist independently of consciousness. "Me" (meti) is a description of the person as endowed with both functions;
for the occurrence of the word "me" refers exclusively to a particular sentient being, and the function of consciousness must be subsumed within that very [person].

This, however, is the summary here: "It was heard" (*suta*) refers to the function of hearing obtained by me, a person endowed with the consciousness that performs the act of hearing, by way of that consciousness;
this is a designation for what does not exist in the sense of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), using the terms "thus" (*iti*) and "by me" (*me*). For everything...
Since one must proceed by way of the description (paññatti-mukha) alone regarding the meaning that is to be attained through words,
and since all descriptions are subsumed within the six types of description beginning with "existent" (vijjamāna), therefore, that which is an unreal object— like an illusion or a mirage—

and which is not the unsurpassed object to be grasped through hearsay and so forth, is [merely] the category of form, sound, and so on, characterized by being affected (ruppana), experiencing (anubhavana), and so forth.
Furthermore, the ultimate intrinsic nature exists by way of the true and ultimate sense.

However, that which is called "this" (*iti*) and "mine" (*me*), having an intrinsic nature consisting of forms and so forth that is not ultimate, is unapprehendable by way of the true and ultimate sense;
this is what is called a "concept of the non-existent. What is there here that exists ultimately such that it could receive the designation "this" or "mine"? [The word] *sutaṃ* (heard).
It is a designation of what exists (*vijjamānapaññatti*). For that which is apprehended by the ear exists in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).

Likewise, the term "thus" (*iti*) is a designation by way of grasping (*upādāpaññatti*), because it refers back to the specific modes and so forth determined in relation to those phenomena that have come within the range of hearing.

The term "I" (*me*) is also a designation by way of grasping, because it must be spoken in reference to the aggregates included within one's own continuity (*sasantati*), as distinguished by such particularities as the agent and so forth.
"Learned" (*suta*) is a designation by way of comparison (*upanidhā-paññatti*), because it is spoken of in relation to what is seen (*diṭṭha*) and so forth.

Although the conventional usage of "learned" occurs even with respect to the sense-base of sound—which is devoid of the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of being seen and so on—it is nevertheless to be understood as "that which is not dependent on what is seen, heard, or cognized is learned," in reliance upon the first category [the seen] and so forth, just like the second or third [categories]. Thus, it is a designation by way of comparison with what is seen and so forth.
It must be said: "What has not been heard is not [so]. For this meaning is declared by the word "heard" (*suta*).
And here, by the word "thus" (*iti*), he illuminates non-delusion. For the specific modes of the penetrated meaning are what were here referred to by the Venerable Ānanda with the word "thus";
thus his non-delusion is illuminated. Indeed, one who is deluded is not capable of penetrating the various modes [of the Dhamma].
The meanings of the Suttas—which are manifold in their aspects, such as the abandoning of greed, and which are difficult to penetrate—are here pointed out.
By the word "heard" (*suta*), non-confusion is indicated, because the mode of hearing is shown exactly as it is.
For one whose hearing has been forgotten does not claim at a later time, "I heard this. Thus, by means of non-delusion—that is, the absence of confusion—[the meaning is established].

Or rather, the perfection of wisdom at a later time is established precisely through that wisdom which arose at the time of hearing; likewise, the perfection of mindfulness is established through non-forgetfulness.
In this context, it is the capacity to grasp the phrasing (byañjana) by means of mindfulness preceded by wisdom.

For the mode to be penetrated in the case of phrases is not exceedingly profound; since what is to be done there is simply the retention of what has been heard as it was, the function of mindfulness is predominant.
In that context, wisdom (*paññā*) is subordinate because it is preceded by mindfulness (*sati*).
It is the capacity of wisdom—preceded by mindfulness—to penetrate the meaning (*attha*). Since the mode in which the meaning is to be penetrated is profound, the function of wisdom is predominant;
thus, mindfulness is subordinate there because it is preceded by wisdom. Through the conjunction of the capacity for both of these, [the path is established].
The status of being the "Dharma-treasurer" (dhammabhaṇḍāgārika) is established by virtue of his capacity to preserve the treasury of the Dhamma, which is perfect in both meaning and phrasing.
According to another method: by the word "iti," he illuminates wise attention (yonisomanasikāra).

This is because the various modes of penetration that will be explained below—which possess the functions of indicating manner, pointing out, and determining—have as their object the unerring True Dhamma (saddhamma) as expressed by that [word]. Not...

For indeed, for one who attends to things in an improper manner (*ayoniso manasikaroto*), various kinds of penetration (*nānappakārappaṭivedha*) are not possible. By the word "heard" (*suta*), he indicates non-distraction (*avikkhepa*).

Hearing the discourse (*sutta*) that is about to be explained—having reached its formal presentation by way of the introduction and the inquiry—is not possible without concentration (*samādhi*), because hearing is absent for one whose mind is distracted. For it is said that a person with a distracted mind [is deprived] of all success.
Even when being told [the teaching], he says, "I have not heard it; say it again.

Herein, through wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), one accomplishes right self-application and the merit previously performed, because these are absent in one who is wrongly applied or has not performed merit in the past.

Through non-distraction (*avikkhepa*), one accomplishes hearing the true Dhamma and reliance upon a true person (*sappurisūpanissaya*), because these are absent in the unlearned person who lacks reliance upon a true person.
And because of the absence of that [state]. For one whose mind is distracted is not able to hear the true Dhamma, nor is there hearing for one who does not attend upon a true person (sappurisa).

Another method: it is said, "The description of various aspects applies to that continuum of consciousness wherein there is the grasping of various meanings and phrasing due to the occurrence of various modes.
And because he [the Buddha] [possesses] the discernment of the distinctions between the meaning and the phrasing of the Blessed One’s word—
Such a fortunate form, which serves as the cause for the complete fulfillment of the welfare of others through the immersion in the entirety of the dispensation (*sāsana*),
does not belong to one who has not previously performed merit or whose self is not rightly directed toward the unconditioned (*appaṇihita*). Therefore, by the word "thus" (*iti*),

he illustrates his own attainment of the latter two wheels [of the Dhamma], and by the word "heard" (*suta*), he illustrates the attainment of the former two wheels through the application of hearing.
For one dwelling in an unsuitable place and lacking the support of virtuous friends, there can be no hearing [of the Dhamma].
Thus, through the accomplishment of the latter two wheels, his purity of disposition (*āsayasuddhi*) is established;

he is one whose self is rightly directed, who has performed merit in the past, and whose disposition is purified because the defilements that cause its impurity have been distanced. For it is said: "Rightly..."
“A well-directed mind will make him even better than before,” and, “You have performed merit, Ānanda;
apply yourself to striving, and you will soon be free from the taints. Through the accomplishment of the first two wheels, there is purity of application.
For indeed, through dwelling in a suitable locality, relying upon virtuous friends, and following the example of the good, one’s application becomes purified.
