Through that purity of disposition (*āsaya*), there is the accomplishment of proficiency in realization (*adhigama*); through purity of practice (*payoga*), which has already purified the defilements of craving and views even previously, there is the accomplishment of proficiency in the scriptures (*āgama*).
For one whose bodily and verbal application is perfectly pure, being free from remorse, possesses an undistracted mind, and is confident in the scriptures.
Thus, for one who is pure in both practice and disposition, and endowed with both scripture and realization—

The word "thus" (*iti*) is worthy of being the precursor to the Blessed One’s speech, just as the rising of dawn is to the sun’s emergence, or as wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) is to wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*).
Thus, establishing the introduction (*nidāna*) in its proper place, he said: “Thus have I heard,” and so forth.

According to another method: by the word “thus,” which indicates the various modes of penetration in the manner previously described, [the author] demonstrates the presence of his own perfection in the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) of meaning (*attha*) and eloquence (*paṭibhāna*).

It illuminates. By the word "Suta" (heard), through its association with the particle *iti*, or by its indication of the penetration of the various things to be heard, it illuminates the presence of the attainment of the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma and of language (*dhammaniruttipaṭisambhidā*).

And the word *iti*—spoken in this manner as a statement that illuminates wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*)—illuminates: "These phenomena have been examined by me with the mind and well-penetrated by insight."
For the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyattidhammā), when examined by the mind according to such methods as "here virtue is taught, here concentration, here wisdom;

there are so many connections here," and when—accompanied by reflection in the form of oral tradition and having become an acceptance of the contemplation of the Dhamma (dhammanijjhānakkhanti)—they are understood through the type of full comprehension known as "comprehension by knowing" (ñātapariññā), then the material and immaterial phenomena taught in various places are seen as: "This is material form; this much is..."
Having well-defined [the aggregates] by way of the method beginning with "form," they become the bringers of welfare and happiness for oneself and others once they have been penetrated.
"Sutta" is a term that illustrates the application of hearing; by speaking it, one demonstrates: "Many teachings have been heard, memorized, and mastered by me through speech.
For the hearing, retention, and mastery of the Dhamma of the scriptures are dependent upon the act of listening with attentive ears.
By both of these [qualities], he demonstrates the perfection of both the meaning and the phrasing through the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma, thereby generating respect for its hearing.
For one who does not listen with respect to a Dhamma that is perfect in meaning and phrasing is excluded from great benefit;
therefore, having generated respect, the Dhamma should be heard with careful attention.
By this entire statement, "Thus have I heard," the Venerable Ānanda, by placing the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata upon himself, transcends the plane of the unworthy person;
by professing discipleship, he enters the plane of the worthy person.
Likewise, he withdraws his mind from what is not the True Dhamma and establishes it in the True Dhamma. "Only..."
By declaring, "This has indeed been heard by me, and it is the word of that very Blessed One," he liberates himself;
he refers back to the Teacher, he anchors the word of the Conqueror, and he establishes the guide of the Dhamma.
Furthermore, by saying "Thus have I heard," he does not claim the state of having produced [the teaching] himself, but rather reveals his prior hearing of it.
This was received by me in the presence of that Blessed One, who is confident in the four grounds of self-confidence, who possesses the ten powers,
who stands in the place of the bull, who roars the lion’s roar, who is the supreme among all beings, the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Sovereign of Dhamma,
the Island of Dhamma, the Refuge of Dhamma, the Wheel-turner of the sublime True Dhamma, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"No doubt or uncertainty should be entertained here regarding the meaning, the doctrine, the phrases, or the syllables.
Thus, it destroys lack of faith in this Dhamma and Vinaya among all gods and humans and generates the perfection of faith. Therefore, this is said:
"It destroys lack of faith and increases faith in the Teaching; ... [and so forth] ..."
"Thus have I heard"—thus speaks this disciple of Gotama.

Here it may be asked: "But why is the introduction (nidāna) not stated here in the same way as in other suttas, where after specifying time and place by saying 'Thus have I heard, at one time the Blessed One,' and so forth? Others first say: "No."
However, this was spoken by the Elder. For this introduction was not first spoken by the Venerable Ānanda;

rather, it was first spoken by the noble female disciple Khujjuttarā—an Ariyan disciple who had been established by the Blessed One among the laywomen as foremost for great learning and who had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) of those still in training—among the five hundred women headed by Sāmāvatī.
In this regard, the sequential account is as follows: It is said that one hundred thousand aeons ago, the Perfectly Enlightened One named Padumuttara appeared in the world.
Having set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, he was dwelling in Haṃsavatī.
Then one day, a daughter of a noble family went to the monastery in Haṃsavatī together with laywomen who were going to hear the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma.
Seeing the Teacher designate a certain female lay disciple as the foremost among those who are "learned" (bahussuta), she performed acts of merit and aspired to that position.

The Teacher also prophesied of her: "In the future, she will become the foremost among the female lay disciples who are learned under the Perfectly Enlightened One named Gotama. Having performed wholesome deeds throughout her life, she—
Having been reborn in the world of the devas and then again among humans—in this way, as she transmigrated through the realms of devas and humans, one hundred thousand aeons passed.

Then, during this auspicious aeon (bhaddakappa) at the time of our Blessed One, she passed away from the world of the devas and took conception in the womb of a maidservant in the house of the merchant Ghosaka; they gave her the name Uttarā.
Because she was hunchbacked at birth, she became known as Khujjuttarā.
Later, when she was given by the merchant Ghosaka to Queen Sāmāvatī of King Udena, she entered the service of the queen and lived in King Udena’s inner palace.
At that time, in Kosambī, the merchants Ghosaka, Kukkuṭa, and Pāvārika were [honoring] the Blessed One.
Having had three monasteries built for the purpose, while the Tathāgata was wandering on tour through the countryside, they reached the city of Kosambī.
They offered the monasteries to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha and provided great almsgivings for a period of about a month.
Then it occurred to them: “The Buddhas are indeed compassionate toward the entire world; let there be space for others as well.”
“We shall give,” they said, and they granted permission to the people living in the city of Kosambī as well.

From that time on, the citizens gave great alms according to their respective streets and social groups. Then one day, the Teacher, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, sat down in the house of the chief florist.
At that moment, Khujjuttarā took eight kahāpaṇas from Sāmāvatī to fetch flowers.
Taking it, she went to her home. Seeing her, the head gardener said, "Sister Uttara, today you have no time to give flowers;
I am serving the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. You too should be a helper in the distribution of food;
in this way, you will be released from having to perform services for others hereafter. Then Khujjuttarā—
She performed services for the Buddhas in the dining hall. She mastered every single teaching spoken by the Teacher during the course of his informal discourses;
moreover, having heard the expression of gratitude (*anumodanā*), she was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
On other days she would go after taking four *kahāpaṇa* coins and flowers, but on that [day], however—
On that day, having seen the truth for himself, he did not set his mind upon the property of others;
instead, he gave eight kahāpaṇas, filled a basket with flowers, and went into the presence of Sāmāvatī.
Then she asked him, "Lady Uttarā, you do not bring many flowers on other days, yet today there are many; has the King given us something?"
"Are you more devoted? Because she was incapable of speaking a lie, she did not conceal what she had done in the past and told everything.
Then, when asked, "Why have you brought so much today?", she said, "Today, having heard the Dhamma from the Sammasambuddha, I realized the Deathless;
therefore, I do not deceive you. Having heard this, [the husband said], "O wicked slave!"

“Give me back the kahāpaṇas you have held for all this time,” she said. Without being intimidated, and urged by her former cause, the mother said, “Mother, you have drunk the Deathless; let us drink it too.

When she replied, “In that case, bathe me first,” she had her bathed with sixteen jars of scented water and gave her two fine cotton garments. She put on one as an undergarment and the other as an upper robe.

Having prepared a seat and sat down upon it, she took up a variegated fan and, addressing the five hundred women seated on low seats, she—standing at the level of one possessing the analytical knowledges of a trainee (*sekha*)—taught them the Dhamma according to the very method taught by the Teacher.
At the conclusion of the teaching, they all became established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). All of them [then addressed] Khujjuttarā...

Having paid homage, they said, "Mother, from this day forward, do not perform defiled work; establish yourself in the position of our mother and our teacher," and thus they placed her in a position of honor.
But why was she reborn as a slave? It is said that during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, in Bārāṇasī...

She was reborn as the daughter of a merchant. When a certain elder nun who had destroyed the taints went to the family where she was a devotee, [the girl] performed a service for her, saying, "Noble lady, please give me this jewelry box. The elder nun thought, "If she does not give it, she will conceive resentment toward me and be reborn in hell;
if she gives it, she will be reborn as a slave to others. Rather than the torment of hell..."
Thinking, "Being a slave is better," he acted upon her words out of compassion. Because of that deed, she was reborn as a slave to others for five hundred births.
But why was she hunchbacked? It is said that before the Buddha had appeared, while she was living in the household of the King of Bārāṇasī, one...

Seeing a Paccekabuddha who was slightly hunchbacked visiting the royal palace, she mocked him in front of the women living with her, assuming a hunchbacked form as a joke according to his actual appearance; therefore, she was reborn as a hunchback.
But what did she do to be born so wise? It is said that before the Buddha had appeared, she lived in the household of the King of Bārāṇasī.

Seeing eight Paccekabuddhas repeatedly turning over and taking the bowls filled with warm milk-rice from the royal palace, he gave his own eight ivory bracelets, saying, "Take these, having placed them here.
They did so and looked at them. He said, "These were given to you alone; take them and go."
They went to the Nandamūlaka cave. Even today, those bracelets remain perfectly intact. By the power of that merit, she was born endowed with wisdom.
Then, five hundred women headed by Sāmāvatī said to her, "Dear lady, go every day into the presence of the Teacher;
having heard the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, please teach it to us. She did accordingly.
In later years, she became a bearer of the Tipiṭaka. Therefore, the Teacher placed her in the foremost position, saying: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my female lay disciples who are learned:

namely, Khujjuttarā. Thus, the noble female disciple Khujjuttarā, who had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and was ranked by the Teacher as foremost among the female lay disciples for her great learning, [was present] when the Teacher was at Kosambī.

Dwelling thus, she would go from time to time into the presence of the Teacher; having heard the Dhamma, she would return to the inner palace and, according to the method taught by the Teacher, speak the Dhamma as she had heard it to the five hundred noble female disciples headed by Sāmāvatī.
Thus liberating herself, she would proclaim the fact that she had heard [the Dhamma] in the presence of the Teacher, for this was said by the Blessed One:
He established the introduction with the words, "Thus have I heard said by the Venerable Arahant.
However, because she had heard this very teaching from the Blessed One’s own presence in that same city and repeated their conversation on that very day,
there was indeed a purpose for specifying the time and place by saying, "At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī."
[The introduction] was not [included] because it was already well-known. Furthermore, the bhikkhunīs received these suttas from her.
Thus, through this lineage, the introduction as established by her became well-known even among the bhikkhus.
Then, after the Parinibbāna of the Tathāgata, the Venerable Ānanda, in the Saddhamma-maṇḍapa constructed by Ajātasattu at Sattapaṇṇi-guhā, [delivered them].

Sitting in the midst of the company of masters headed by Mahākassapa, while rehearsing the Dhamma and avoiding any ambiguity regarding the introduction (*nidāna*) of these suttas, he established the introduction precisely according to the sequence she had set forth.
However, some here elaborate upon this in many ways; what is the use of them? Moreover, the compilers of the Dhamma and Vinaya [established it] through various methods.
They recited [the texts]. For the Great Theras who compiled the Dhamma were those who had realized it;

knowing perfectly the manner of compiling the Dhamma and Vinaya, they established the introductory narratives (nidāna) in some places by way of "Thus have I heard" and so forth, in some places by way of "At that time" and so forth, in some places by way of composing verses, and in some places by omitting the introductory narrative entirely, according to the arrangement into chapters (vagga) and so on.
They recited the Dhamma and Vinaya. Therein, they recited them by establishing the *nidāna* (introductions) with the words "In this case, it was said thus," and so forth.
This word of the Buddha consists of nine divisions, such as the Suttas, Geyyas, and others.
And just as it is for this [Buddha], so it is for all the Perfectly Enlightened Ones. For this has been said: "And their Suttas and Geyyas were few," and so forth. Therein...
Nothing else is discernible as a constituent of the *Itivuttaka* apart from its defining characteristic, namely this statement: “For this was said... [etc.

...thus have I heard. Therefore, the teachers of the commentaries said: “The *Itivuttaka* consists of one hundred and twelve discourses proceeding according to the method beginning with ‘For this was said by the Blessed One.
Consequently, by the compilers of the Dhamma who understood the Teacher’s intention—

It should be understood that the introduction (nidāna) was established by this very method for the purpose of making known that these discourses constitute a limb of the Itivuttaka, whether [spoken] by the Blessed One or by a noble female disciple.

But what is the purpose of including the introductory statement when the compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya is being performed? Is it not [already established] by the fact that it is the word spoken by the Blessed One?
"Should a compendium be made? It is said: for the purpose of ensuring the stability, non-confusion, and credibility of the teaching.

For a teaching established by being bound together through the factors of time, place, teacher, and audience remains stable for a long time, possesses the quality of being free from confusion, and is credible—just as a legal decision is reliable when it is bound together by the factors of the speaker, the time, the agent, the cause, and the motive. Therefore...
And when the Venerable Mahākassapa had posed questions regarding the location and other details of the *Brahmajāla*,
*Mūlapariyāya*, and other discourses, the Dharma-treasurer, providing the answers to those questions, spoke the introductory formula beginning with "Thus have I heard.
However, the reason for not specifying the location and time in this particular case has already been stated.

Furthermore, the introductory statement (*nidāna*) is for the purpose of manifesting the perfections of the Teacher. For the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the establishment of his status as a Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*) follows from the absence of prior composition, inference, scripture, or reasoning.

Indeed, there is no need for prior composition and the like for a Perfectly Enlightened One, because his range of knowledge is unimpeded in all respects and he possesses a single measure regarding all knowable phenomena.
Likewise, this is due to the absence of the "teacher’s fist" (secretiveness), stinginess regarding the Dhamma, or favoritism toward disciples in the dispensation.
The accomplishment of the state of one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*). For those [defilements] do not occur at all in one whose taints are entirely exhausted;

thus, there is the engagement in benefiting others by one who is perfectly pure. In this way, through the states of purity of the Fully Enlightened One—which indicate the absolute absence of ignorance and craving (the defilements of the teacher that corrupt the perfection of view and conduct) and which manifest the perfection of knowledge and the perfection of abandonment—the first two grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajjā*) are established.
Furthermore, because the state of non-delusion regarding the obstructive and emancipating factors is established, the latter two grounds of self-confidence are also established;
thus, by means of the introductory statement, the Blessed One’s possession of the four grounds of self-confidence and his practice for the benefit of himself and others are made manifest,
since he illuminates the teaching of the Dhamma through spontaneous eloquence appropriate to the inclinations of the assembled audiences in each particular instance.
Furthermore, it should be connected [to the previous point] by way of establishing the teaching through the complete abandonment of the faults of sensual desire (*kāmadosa*).
Therefore, it was said: "The words of the introduction are for the purpose of manifesting the excellence of the Teacher.
And here, the manifestation of the meaning as previously stated by means of these two phrases, "by the Blessed One" and "by the Worthy One," has already been shown above.
Likewise, there is the introductory statement (nidāna) for the purpose of demonstrating the excellence of the Dispensation.
For the Blessed One, whose every action is encompassed by wisdom and compassion, there is no practice that is purposeless or intended for his own benefit alone.

Therefore, when the entire bodily, verbal, and mental activity of the Perfectly Enlightened One—which proceeds solely for the sake of others—is described according to its occurrence, it is shown to possess both mundane and supramundane benefits for this present life and for future lives.
It is called "teaching" (*sāsana*) in the sense of instructing beings according to what is appropriate for them; it is not a mere literary composition.
This conduct of the Teacher is manifested, as the case may be, through various introductory statements (*nidāna*) by way of the time, the place, the teacher, and the assembly.

However, in this instance, it should be connected with the place and the assembly. Therefore it was said: "The introductory statement is for the purpose of manifesting the excellence of the teaching."
Furthermore, the introductory statement (nidāna-vacana) is for the purpose of demonstrating that the Dispensation (sāsana) is authoritative by way of demonstrating that the Teacher is authoritative.
That demonstration of its authority should be understood as being clarified by the words "by the Blessed One, the Worthy One" (bhagavatā arahatā), according to the method explained below.
This is merely a brief indication of the purpose of the introductory statement here.
The commentary on the Nidāna is finished.
1. The First Chapter of the Single-Verse Collection (Ekakanipāta). 1. The First Section.
1. Commentary on the Lobha Sutta:
Now, the occasion has arrived for the commentary on the discourse set forth by the Blessed One in the manner beginning with, "Bhikkhus, abandon one thing.
Furthermore, this commentary on the meaning [is presented] after having investigated the setting-forth of the discourse.
When being spoken, it becomes manifest; therefore, we shall first examine the presentation of the discourses (*suttanikkhepa*). There are four such presentations:

those arising from one’s own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*), those arising from another’s inclination (*parajjhāsaya*), those occasioned by a question (*pucchāvasika*), and those arising from a particular incident (*aṭṭhuppattika*).

For just as the discourses—though divided into many hundreds and thousands of types—do not exceed sixteenfold variety according to the method of the *Saṃkilesabhāgiya* and other *Paṭṭhāna* categories, so too [they are classified] by way of the presentation of the discourses, such as those arising from one’s own inclination.

"They do not exceed fourfoldness. In this regard, just as a distinction in association can occur between one's own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*) and an occasion for discourse (*aṭṭhuppatti*), on the one hand, and another's inclination and an occasion for inquiry (*pucchāvasika*), on the other—namely:
one's own inclination together with another's inclination; one's own inclination together with an occasion for inquiry;
an occasion for discourse together with another's inclination; and an occasion for discourse together with an occasion for inquiry—[so it is here].

This is because the connection [of the discourse] arises through a question concerning the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*). Thus, although a division of the connection by way of an occasion for a teaching (*aṭṭhuppatti*) or by one's own underlying intention is possible, there is no connection with an occasion for a teaching when one's own underlying intention and so forth stand before it;

therefore, the method of the *Paṭṭhāna* (the Book of Causal Relations) is not possible in its entirety. Or rather, [it is said that] those [connections] that are possible are included within that [method].
It should be understood that four types of sutta-depositions (suttanikkhepa) have been stated by way of the root-deposition (mūlanikkhepa) among the various types of depositions.
Herein, this is the etymological explanation: it is deposited (*nikkhipīyati*), thus it is a "deposition" (*nikkhepa*); the sutta itself is the deposition, hence "sutta-deposition.
Alternatively, the act of depositing is "deposition"; the deposition of a sutta is "sutta-deposition," which means the teaching of a sutta.

"One's own inclination" (*attajjhāsaya*) means: that which has one's own inclination as its cause is "one whose inclination is one's own"; or, one who possesses his own inclination is "one whose inclination is one's own.
The same method applies to "another's inclination" (*parajjhāsaya*). "By way of a question" (*pucchāvasa*) means:

that which possesses this [question] is "dependent on a question" (*pucchāvasika*). The arising of the meaning that serves as the basis for the teaching of the discourse is "the arising of the meaning" (*atthuppatti*).
*Atthuppatti* is the same as *aṭṭhuppatti*, having changed the letter *tha* to *ṭha*; that which possesses this [occasion] is called *aṭṭhuppattika*.
Alternatively, it is a *nikkhepa* because the Sutta is deposited (*nikkhipīyati*) by means of it; this refers specifically to one's own intention (*attajjhāsaya*) and so forth.
In this interpretation, however, "one's own intention" is *attajjhāsaya*, while "the intention of others" is *parajjhāsaya*. That which is questioned is a *pucchā*.
The matter is to be asked; the speech of those who receive the Dhamma, which proceeds by way of a question, is "question-based" (*pucchāvasa*).

That very term is stated in the masculine gender as *pucchāvasika* with reference to the word used for its formal presentation (*nikkhepa-sadda*). Likewise, "occasioning-arising" (*aṭṭhuppatti*) itself is "occasioning-arising" (*aṭṭhuppattika*);
in this way, the meaning here should be understood.
Furthermore, it is appropriate that discourses delivered according to one's own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*) are established as independent suttas,
because they do not depend on causes such as the ripening of the faculties of others, but proceed solely for the purpose of establishing the lineage of the Dhamma through one's own inclination.

However, regarding those [discourses] that arise when questions based on the inclinations of others— questions posed by others that serve as the cause for the delivery of the teaching— are put forward, [they are classified differently].

How is there no restriction in the case of *aṭṭhuppatti* (occasions for teaching)? Or how is there no restriction regarding the inclinations of others in the case of those *aṭṭhuppattis* that arise from a question or are prompted by the inclinations of others?

This need not be questioned; for the occurrence of a cause for the teaching of a Sutta that is entirely free from the formal proposal (*abhinīhāra*) or inquiry (*paripucchā*) of others is itself accepted as the nature of an *aṭṭhuppatti*.
Thus, even those [teachings] arising from the questions or inclinations of others [are included].

There is a separate mention [of this]. For instance, the "occasion for the teaching" (*aṭṭhuppatti*) is said to be the cause for the teaching of such things as praise or blame, or the acquisition of material gifts, as seen in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*, the *Dhammadāyāda Sutta*, and others. That which is taught by taking the inclination of others as the motive, even without their having asked a question, is "according to the inclination of others" (*parajjhāsayo*);
that which is taught by means of a question is "based on a question" (*pucchāvasiko*). This meaning is evident.

Those discourses that the Blessed One speaks solely out of his own inclination, without being requested by others—such as the *Ākaṅkheyya Sutta*, the *Tuvaṭṭaka Sutta*, and so forth—their presentation is "by his own inclination" (*attajjhāsayo nikkhepo*). However, those [discourses] where he considers the inclination, the receptivity, the aspiration, and the capacity for awakening of others, such as:
"Rāhula’s qualities conducive to the ripening of liberation have indeed matured;
what if I were now to train Rāhula further in the destruction of the taints?"—[these are presented by the inclination of others].
Having observed others, [the discourses] were spoken according to their inclinations (*adhyāśaya*), such as the *Rāhulovāda-sutta*, the *Dhammacakkappavattana-sutta*, and so forth;
for these, the "deposit" (*nikkhepa*) is the inclination of others.
Furthermore, having approached the Blessed One, gods, humans, the four assemblies, and the four castes likewise [spoke].
Likewise, they ask questions such as, "Venerable sir, it is said 'factors of enlightenment,' and it is said 'hindrances,'" and so forth;
the discourses on the factors of enlightenment and others spoken by the Blessed One when thus questioned constitute a teaching based on a question.

However, those discourses spoken in dependence on a specific occasion that has arisen—such as the *Dhammadāyāda*, the *Puttamaṃsūpama*, the *Dārukkhandhūpama*, and so forth—have an "occasional" (aṭṭhuppattika) placement.
Thus, among these four ways of placing a discourse, this sutta has a placement based on the inclination of others (*parajjhāsayo*).
For it was placed by way of the inclination of others. By whose inclination? By the inclination of persons who see the danger in greed. But some...
They say [it means] "one's own intention.

In that context, in such passages as "Bhikkhus, regarding a single dhamma," the word *eka* (one) has the sense of "another" (*aññattha*), as in: "Some assert thus: 'The self and the world are eternal;
this alone is true, all else is false. It also has the sense of "best" (*seṭṭha*), as in: "Of the mind..."
In such passages as "state of being unified" (*ekodibhāva*), it has the sense of being alone, as in "alone, secluded" (*eko vūpakaṭṭho*).

It has the sense of a number, as in "Indeed, monks, there is only one moment and one occasion for living the holy life" (*ekova kho, bhikkhave, khaṇo ca samayo ca brahmacariyavāsāya*). Here too, it should be understood in the sense of a number.
The word *dhamma* is seen in the senses of the scriptures, the truths, concentration, wisdom, nature, merit, attainment, emptiness, the knowable, intrinsic nature, and so forth.
For instance, in such passages as "Here, a bhikkhu masters the Dhamma," the meaning is the scriptures (pariyatti).
In "one who has seen the Dhamma" and so forth, it refers to the Truths (saccāni). In "those Blessed Ones were of such a nature," it refers to concentration (samādhi).

In "Truth, Dhamma, fortitude, and generosity—one does not grieve either here or after death," it refers to wisdom (paññā). And in "Bhikkhus, for beings subject to birth, this desire... [it refers to the underlying tendency].
In such passages as “it arises,” it refers to *pakati* (nature). In such passages as “The Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives by the Dhamma,” it refers to merit (*puñña*).
In such passages as “One might charge [another] with any one of three offenses: either a *pārājika*, a *saṅghādisesa*, or a *pācittiya*,” it refers to an offense (*āpatti*).
In such passages as “At that time, there were states (*dhammā*) present,” it refers to emptiness (*suññatā*). “All phenomena (*sabbe dhammā*) in all their aspects...”

It should be understood [in this sense] in such passages as, "They come within the range of the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One. In such passages as, "Wholesome states, unwholesome states," the meaning is "intrinsic nature" (*sabhāva*).
Here too, it is "intrinsic nature. Therefore, "a single state" (*ekadhamma*) means "a single thing whose intrinsic nature is defilement"—this is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, it is a single thing and it is a state; thus, it is a "single state" (*ekadhamma*), and that is "that single state" (*taṃ ekadhammaṃ*).
"Bhikkhus" is how he addresses the bhikkhus. But why does the Blessed One address the bhikkhus when teaching the Dhamma instead of teaching the Dhamma alone?

It is for the purpose of arousing mindfulness. For the bhikkhus may be sitting there thinking of something else, reflecting on the Dhamma, or attending to their meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). If the Dhamma were taught without first addressing them, [they might miss it].
They were unable to discern, "What is the source of this teaching? What is its condition? However, when addressed, they were able to establish mindfulness and discern it;
therefore, he addresses them as "Bhikkhus" for the purpose of generating mindfulness.

And by that word, which is established through their possession of qualities such as the habit of begging (bhikkhana-sīla), he [indicates] the mode of livelihood practiced by those of inferior and superior persons.

By explaining [this], he effects a restraint against states such as restlessness and dejection. With the address “Monks,” preceded by a glance from eyes that are gentle with the expansion of compassion, he brings them face-to-face with his own countenance;
and by that speech which indicates a desire to speak, he generates in them a desire to listen. Furthermore, by that very sense of addressing them, he ensures their careful listening and attention.
He directs [them]. For the success of the Dispensation depends upon diligent practice and mental attention.
Although other gods and humans were present and included within the assembly, why did he address the bhikkhus alone?
Because they are the eldest, the most excellent, and because of their constant proximity and attendance. Indeed, the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma is common to the entire assembly.

They are the elders of the assembly because they were the first to arise [in the dispensation]; they are the best because, starting from their state of homelessness, they followed the Teacher’s conduct and received the entire teaching;
they are "near" because they dwell close to those seated there; and they are "always in attendance" because they move within the presence of the Teacher.
Moreover, they are the vessels for the teaching of the Dhamma, according to the instructions.
Because of the existence of practice and for the sake of certain specific bhikkhus, this teaching was addressed to them alone. Regarding the word "abandon" (*pajahatha*):

here, "abandoning" (*pahāna*) is fivefold—namely, abandoning by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-pahāna*), abandoning by suppression (*vikkhambhana-pahāna*), abandoning by eradication (*samuccheda-pahāna*), abandoning by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi-pahāna*), and abandoning by escape (*nissaraṇa-pahāna*). Among these, that which is [abandoned] by means of a lamp’s light...

The abandoning of greed and so forth by means of non-greed and so forth—because they are their opposites—and the abandoning of various evils by means of the insight-knowledges such as the discernment of name-and-form, are as follows:
the abandoning of the stain of greed and so forth by means of relinquishment; the abandoning of misconduct such as killing living beings by means of virtue;
the abandoning of lack of faith and so forth by means of faith and so forth; and the abandoning of the view of a self-existent body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) by means of the definition of name-and-form.
By the discernment of conditions, the views of no-cause and irregular cause are abandoned; subsequently, by the overcoming of doubt, the state of being a sceptic is abandoned;

by the comprehension of groups, the grasping at "I" and "mine" is abandoned; by the definition of what is the path and what is not the path, the perception of a path where there is no path is abandoned;
by the vision of arising, the view of annihilationism is abandoned; and by the vision of passing away, the view of eternalism is abandoned.

By seeing fear, there is the perception of fearlessness regarding things that are fearful; by seeing danger, there is the perception of gratification; by the contemplation of disenchantment, there is the perception of delight;
by the knowledge of desire for deliverance, there is the lack of desire for deliverance; by the knowledge of equanimity, there is the lack of equanimity;
by conformity, there is the stability of phenomena; by Nibbāna, there is the state of opposition; and by the change-of-lineage, there is the grasping of the sign of formations.
This is what is called abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*).

However, that abandonment of various states such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), which occurs through concentration— distinguished as access and absorption— by way of obstructing the occurrence [of those states],
just as the removal of moss from the surface of water by striking it with a jar, is called abandonment by suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*).
The absolute non-occurrence and eradication, within the personal continuum of one who has cultivated the four noble paths,
of the collection of defilements belonging to the side of origination— described by the method beginning with "for the abandoning of the various views"—
is called abandonment by cutting off (*samucchedappahāna*). Furthermore, that which is the state of subsidence at the moment of the fruition (*phala-kkhaṇa*)...

This is called the abandonment by subsiding of the defilements. However, that which is Nibbāna—having abandoned all conditioned things because it has escaped from all the conditioned—is called the abandonment by escape.

Thus, since among these five kinds of abandonment it is the abandonment that constitutes the state of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) which is intended here, it should be understood as "abandonment by eradication" (*samucchedappahāna*). Therefore, "abandon" means "renounce."
The meaning is "you should completely cut off.

The Blessed One points to himself with the word *ahaṃ* (I). As for *vo*, this particle *vosadda* is seen in the functions of the direct object (*paccatta*), the instrumental (*upayoga*), the agent (*karaṇa*), the genitive (*sāmivacana*), the verse-filler (*padapūraṇa*), and the dative (*sampadāna*).
For instance, in such passages as "But are you, Anuruddhas, living in harmony and in mutual affection? it is used in the sense of the direct object (*paccatta*).

In such instances as “He has come; go, monks, I dismiss you,” it is used in the sense of the object (*upayoga*). In such instances as “You must not dwell in my presence,” it is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*).

In such instances as “All of you, Sāriputta, have spoken well,” it is used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmivacana*). In such instances as “Those noble ones, monks, whose bodily actions are entirely purified,” it is used for the sake of completing the phrase (*padapūraṇa*).
In such instances as “I shall teach you, monks, the discourse on forest retreats (*vanapattha*”), it is used in the sense of the recipient (*sampadāna*). Here, too, [it is used in the same way].

It should be understood as referring specifically to the recipient (sampadāna). "Surety" (pāṭibhoga) means a guarantor (paṭibhū). For he is a representative (paṭinidhi) of the debtor with respect to the creditor, and of the creditor with respect to the debtor;
he is a "surety" (paṭibhoga) because he is the "enjoyment" (bhoga) consisting of the taking, etc., of the creditor's property from that [debtor].
*Paṭibhoga* itself is *pāṭibhoga*. "For the state of non-returning" (*anāgāmitāya*) means for the sake of the condition of being a non-returner (*anāgāmi*).

For one is called a non-returner because, by way of taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), they do not return to the sensual existence (*kāmabhava*). That third path, together with its fruit, by the attainment of which one is called a non-returner, is what is known as "non-returning.
Thus the Blessed One, skilled in taming those to be trained, [spoke] in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained.
He demonstrated that the attainment of the third path is made firm by merely fulfilling a single factor through a simple means,

just as the Perfectly Enlightened One did. For even those defilements such as the fetter of aversion (paṭigha-saṃyojana) which belong to a different plane and are to be abandoned by the third path do not exceed the abandonment of sensual lust (kāmarāga).
But why did the Blessed One place himself in the position of a guarantor here?
It was for the purpose of generating enthusiasm in those bhikkhus for the attainment of the path of non-returning. For the Blessed One saw:
"When I say, 'Bhikkhus, abandon one thing; I am your guarantor for non-returning,' these bhikkhus will certainly be able to abandon that one thing and reach the third stage."
"In order that they might attain it, the Lord of Dhamma first said, 'I am the guarantor,' so that they would conceive the aspiration and think,
'We must practice for that purpose. Therefore, in order to generate such aspiration, he established himself as the guarantor for those bhikkhus regarding their non-returning."
Regarding the phrase "What is the one dhamma?": here, *katamaṃ* is a word of inquiry. This inquiry is fivefold:

an inquiry for the illumination of what has not been seen, an inquiry for the verification of what has been seen, an inquiry for the cutting off of doubt, an inquiry for assent, and an inquiry out of a desire to speak.
Among these, the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) is by nature unknown, unseen, unmeasured, and so forth.

When something has not been crossed over, not made manifest, and not clearly discerned, one asks a question for the sake of knowing it, seeing it, weighing it, examining it, making its meaning manifest, and clearly discerning it—

this is a question for the purpose of clarifying what has not been seen. When the characteristic is naturally known, seen, weighed, examined, made manifest, and clearly discerned, one [asks] for the purpose of reconciling it with other wise people.
He asks a question; this is a question for the purpose of correlating what has been seen. He is by nature prone to doubt, prone to perplexity, and full of uncertainty, thinking:
"Is it thus? Is it not thus? What is it? How is it? He asks a question for the purpose of cutting through that uncertainty;
this is a question for the purpose of cutting through uncertainty. For the Blessed One asks a question for the purpose of obtaining consent.
He asks: “What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent? and so forth; this is an inquiry for assent.
The Blessed One asks a question because of his desire to speak to the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have come to be, or for the assistance of those seeking existence. Which four?”
"Cattāro" (four) is a question expressing a desire to speak.

Among those, the first three questions do not exist for Buddhas. Why? Because in the three periods of time, there is nothing—whether conditioned, unconditioned, or independent of time—that has not been seen, weighed, scrutinized, or fully manifested by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
There is nothing that has not been fully realized. Therefore, for them, there is no inquiry for the purpose of revealing what has not yet been seen.
Furthermore, regarding that which they have penetrated by their own knowledge, there is no need to verify it with another ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā;
therefore, for them, there is also no inquiry for the purpose of verifying what has already been seen. Because...
However, the Blessed Buddhas are free from indecision, have crossed over doubt, and are devoid of uncertainty regarding all phenomena;
therefore, they have no need for a question to sever their own doubts. But there are two other types of questions, among which this should be understood as a question out of a desire to speak.
Now, in order to show the meaning asked in that question in its true form, he said: “Lobha, bhikkhus, is a single dhamma,” and so forth.
Therein, it is called *lobha* because they are greedy by means of it, or it itself is greedy, or it is merely the act of greed.
This greed has the characteristic of grasping at an object, like the salivation of a monkey; its function is clinging, like a piece of meat placed in a hot pan.

It should be understood as follows: it has non-renunciation as its manifestation, like the redness of oil-based collyrium; it has the perception of gratification in things that lead to fettering as its proximate cause;

and as it increases through the state of craving, it should be seen as carrying away the being wherever it has arisen—just as a river with a swift current flows toward the great ocean, the place of misery.
Although this word "greed" (lobha) is a general term for all forms of greed, [it refers here specifically to sensual greed].
But here it should be understood as a term for sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), for that is to be abandoned by the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*).
Again, the address "O monks" is intended to generate reverence toward that [teaching] in those who have turned their attention toward it as recipients of the Dhamma.

By the word "abandon," the realization of abandonment (*pahānābhisamaya*) is established; and this [realization] occurs together with the realizations of full understanding (*pariññā*), realization through direct experience (*sacchikiriyā*), and development (*bhāvanā*).
They occur together and not separately; thus, all four foundations of the Four Noble Truths are indeed established as the functions of right view.

And just as when it is said, "Abandon greed," the abandonment of hatred and the rest is also effectively stated by implication because they share the same state of being abandoned, so too, regarding the function of right view concerning the truth of the origin, in the realization of abandonment—

When this has been stated, it should be understood that the function of the remaining path-factors—right intention and so forth—which serve as the cooperative causes for that [factor], regarding the object of the truth of origination, is also effectively explained by implication; thus, the complete operation of the Noble Path is described here.

In this same manner, the fact that the operations of the factors conducive to enlightenment, such as the foundations of mindfulness and so on, are also described here should be elaborated upon as appropriate.
Furthermore, by the words "abandon greed here," the full understanding of abandoning (*pahānapariññā*) is stated.

That [full understanding] is based upon the full understanding of scrutinization (*tīraṇapariññā*), and the full understanding of scrutinization is based upon the full understanding of the known (*ñātapariññā*); thus, by their inseparable connection, all three types of full understanding are indicated.
In this way, it should be understood that the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths has been explained here in its entirety, together with its fruit.

Alternatively, by the instruction "Abandon greed," the purification of knowledge and vision together with its fruit is taught. And that [purification] is dependent upon the purification of knowledge and vision of the way...

[and so on] ...dependent upon the purification of mind and the purification of virtue; thus it should be understood that all seven purifications, together with their fruits, have been elucidated without any omission.
Thus, by means of this development of the stages of purification and the accomplishment of the three kinds of full understanding, one who desires to abandon greed should reflect:
“Greed gives rise to harm; greed agitates the mind.
Fear born from within—people do not understand it.”
“The greedy one does not know the goal; the greedy one does not see the Dhamma.
It is utter darkness then for the man whom greed overcomes.
Indeed, friend, one who is lustful, overcome by lust, and whose mind is consumed by it, kills living beings, takes what is not given, and so forth.
They break into houses, they carry off plunder, they commit burglary, they stand as highwaymen, they commit adultery,
and they speak falsehoods. Even that is merely the agitation and the vacillation of those venerable recluses and brahmins who do not know,
who do not see, who do not feel, and who are pursued by craving.
“With craving as his companion, a person wanders through the long course of existence;
from this state of being to another state of being, he does not transcend the cycle of saṃsāra.
“There is no fire equal to passion; there is no ill luck equal to hatred.”
“I am burning with sensual lust; my mind is consumed by fire.
And: “Those who are stained by passion fall into the stream, like a spider into its own web.
Following such passages from the Suttas, one should contemplate the danger of greed through various methods and proceed toward its abandonment.

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sensual lust: the apprehension of the sign of the unattractive, devotion to the development of the meditation on the unattractive, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, having virtuous friends, and appropriate discourse.

For sensual lust is abandoned even by one who is apprehending the tenfold sign of the unattractive; and by means of the development of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*), [lust for] that which possesses consciousness...
This applies even to one who is devoted to the practice of meditation on the foul by means of the bloated corpse and so forth;
even to one whose doors are bolted with the door-bolt of mindfulness by way of restraint over the six sense faculties, including the mind;
and even to one who knows the proper measure in eating, having the habit of drinking water and sustaining himself when there is space for four or five morsels. For this very reason it was said:
“Having eaten only four or five mouthfuls, one should drink water;
this is sufficient for the comfortable dwelling of a bhikkhu who is resolute.

Even for one who serves virtuous friends who delight in the cultivation of the meditation subject of foulness, and who engages in appropriate talk concerning the ten kinds of foulness while standing, sitting, and so forth, [craving] is abandoned. For this very reason it was said:

“Bhikkhus, there is the sign of the unattractive; frequent and thorough attention directed toward it is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen sensual desire, or for the abandoning of arisen sensual desire.

Thus, one who has practiced for the abandoning of greed—known as lust for sense pleasures—in the prior stage, having intensified insight, eradicates it completely by means of the third path. Therefore it was said: “Bhikkhus, greed is a single dhamma...”
“Abandon it; I guarantee you non-returning.
Here one might ask: “But what kind of greed is abandoned here—is it past, or future, or present?
Now, in this matter, past greed cannot be abandoned, nor can future greed, because they do not exist [at that time]. For that which has ceased...
If it were unarisen, it would be called "existent," and effort would become fruitless.

Or, if it were present, even then effort would be fruitless because of its inherent momentary destruction; furthermore, the cultivation of the Path would result in being defiled, or greed would have to be dissociated from consciousness, and this mode [of existence] is not accepted.
It is said in reply: [Greed] is not past, future, or present in the manner stated.

Greed is abandoned. Just as if there were a young tree here that had not yet borne fruit, and a man were to cut it down at the root with an axe—since that tree has been cut down, those fruits which would have been produced will not be born, for they are unborn because the tree has been severed;
even so, when the Noble Path has not been attained, that which was liable to arise [does not arise].

Greed does not arise because the destruction of its conditions has been accomplished through the attainment of the Noble Path. For this [greed] is called "arisen from the ground acquired" (*bhūmiladdhuppanna*) in the Commentaries.
Indeed, the five aggregates, which serve as the object for insight (*vipassanā*), are called the "ground" because they are the locus of its arising.
Since that ground has been acquired by him, it is "arisen from the ground acquired. It is also "arisen from the apprehension of the object" (*ārammaṇādhiggahituppanna*).
This very thing is called "arisen but not suppressed" and "arisen but not eradicated.
"Therein" means in that sutta. "This" refers to this collection of meanings. "Now being stated by way of verse composition" means it is now being expressed in metrical form.
By whom, then, is it said "it is thus said"? It is by the Blessed One himself. For in such other instances, [the words] are supplied by the compilers of the Council.

These are verses of summary; however, in this instance, the Blessed One, having condensed the very same meaning already spoken according to the disposition of those individuals who delight in verse, spoke it in the form of verses.
Therein, "by which greed they are greedy, beings go to a bad destination" refers to that [greed] characterized by the grasping of an object.
For that very reason, being greedy through greed characterized by attachment, they are lustful and infatuated with the internal and external sense bases.
*Se* is merely an indeclinable particle; however, etymologists maintain that the letter *se* is inserted in such instances.
Likewise, because of that very greed, having failed to perform any good conduct of body and so forth, they engage in misconduct of body and so forth.
Having accumulated [kamma], living beings— who have acquired the name "satta" because they are attached and bound to form and the other aggregates—

go to and are reborn in hell, the animal realm, and the sphere of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya), which are designated as "duggati" because they are the places where suffering arises, by way of taking rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).

"Having fully understood that greed, Vipassī abandons it": having fully understood—that is, having known through the wisdom consisting of the full comprehension by way of knowing and scrutinizing—that greed as previously described, correctly and without error, by means of these aspects:

its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), its origin (*samudaya*), its passing away (*atthaṅgama*), its gratification (*assāda*), its danger (*ādīnava*), and the escape from it (*nissaraṇa*)—[he abandons] the five aggregates of clinging, beginning with form.

Because they see [the aggregates] through various aspects such as impermanence (*anicca*), the wise ones abandon the remaining defilements by means of the wisdom of the path (*magga-paññā*) preceded by the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*), through their total eradication;
they do not allow them to arise again within their own continuum.

Having abandoned them, they "never return to this world"—thus, by means of those [defilements] that are abandoned simultaneously with birth (*sahaja-ekaṭṭha*) and those abandoned by effort (*pajahana-ekaṭṭha*).
Having abandoned that greed, together with the remaining defilements, by means of the path of non-returning,
they never again come to this world— known as the sense-sphere realm— in the manner of taking rebirth-linking,
because the lower fetters have been thoroughly abandoned. Thus, the Blessed One concluded the teaching with the fruit of non-returning.
"This meaning too" refers to the meaning elucidated by this sutta from the beginning of the introduction (nidāna) up to the conclusion of the verses.
The word "api" (too/also) serves to include the meaning of the sutta that will now be explained. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

In this sutta, the truth of the origin (samudayasacca) is presented in its own form, while the truth of the path (maggasacca) is presented by way of its abandonment. The other two truths are likewise included.

This should be determined by way of being the cause for both. In the verse, however, the truths of suffering, origin, and the path are understood according to their literal meaning, while the other [the truth of cessation] must be determined.
This same method applies to the suttas that follow as well.
(From the *Paramatthadīpanī*, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya.)
The commentary on the first sutta of the *Itivuttaka* is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Sutta on Hatred (Dosa-sutta).
2. For this has been said... [etc. ...the second sutta is "Hatred. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not previously explained. Just as here...
In this way, for all subsequent sections as well, we shall provide only the commentary on the words not previously explained.
Since this sutta was taught by observing the disposition of persons abounding in hatred, for the purpose of pacifying that hatred, it says:

"Bhikkhus, abandon the one thing that is hatred. Therein, "hatred" (dosa) refers to [the mental state] described by such passages as: "The thought 'he has done me harm' gives rise to resentment," and so forth.
By way of method, there are nine stated in the Sutta, and another nine established as their opposites, such as "he did not act for my welfare" and so forth;
thus, together with the eighteen [grounds] beginning with stumps and thorns, there is resentment arising from any one of these nineteen grounds of resentment.
For it is by means of this that one becomes corrupted, or one is oneself corrupted, or it is merely the state of being corrupted—hence it is called *dosa* (hatred).
It is so called. It has the characteristic of ferocity like a struck viper; the function of spreading [poison] like the application of venom;
or the function of burning its own support like a forest fire. Its manifestation is resentment when it has gained an opportunity, like an enemy who has found an opening.
Its proximate cause is the aforementioned grounds for malice, and it should be regarded as like putrid urine mixed with poison. "Abandon it" means:
Cut them off completely.
In this regard, there are these five ways of removing resentment, wherein any resentment that has arisen in a bhikkhu must be removed entirely.
What are the five? Bhikkhus, toward whatever person resentment might arise, loving-kindness should be cultivated toward that person... [and so on].
Compassion... [and so on] ...equanimity, or lack of mindfulness and lack of attention toward that person should be applied;
in this way, resentment toward that person is to be removed. Monks, toward whichever person resentment might arise, one should resolve upon that person’s ownership of kamma:
“This venerable one is the owner of his kamma, the heir to his kamma... [and so on] ...he will become [the result of his deeds]. Thus should resentment be removed.
Thus, the five ways of removing resentment have already been stated.
“Friends, there are these five ways of removing resentment, wherein any resentment that has arisen in a bhikkhu should be removed entirely.
What are the five? Here, friends, a certain person is impure in bodily conduct but pure in verbal conduct;”
“Friend, ill will should be removed even toward such a person.
In this manner, five methods for removing ill will have been taught; having reflected upon them by means of whichever method for removing ill will one chooses, one should proceed.

Furthermore, there is the Teacher’s admonition: “Monks, even if bandits with saws that have teeth on both sides were to hack away at your limbs and members one by one, whoever should allow their mind to become corrupted thereby would not be following my instruction.”
“Worse than that is he who, being provoked, provokes in return;
he who does not provoke in return when provoked wins the battle that is hard to win.
He acts for the benefit of both, his own self and the other.”
But he who, knowing the other is provoked, remains composed with mindfulness.
“Monks, these seven things, which are pleasing to an enemy and bring about enmity, come upon a woman or a man who is prone to anger.
What are the seven? Here, monks, an enemy desires this of his enemy: ‘Oh, may he be angry!’”
‘Alas, this person is ill-favored! Why is that? Monks, an enemy does not rejoice in the beauty of his enemy.

Monks, when a person is angry, overcome by anger, and possessed by anger, even though he may be well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, and clothed in white garments, he is nonetheless ill-favored.
“He becomes overcome by anger. This, monks, is the first thing that is pleasing to an enemy and conducive to an enemy’s purpose that comes upon an angry woman or man.
“Furthermore, monks, an enemy wishes this for an enemy: ‘Oh, may this person sleep in discomfort! … [and so on] …”
"He would not have abundant wealth... he would not have riches... he would not have fame... he would not have friends...
and with the breakup of the body, after death, he might be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell. Why is that?
Because, monks, an enemy does not rejoice at an enemy’s going to a good destination. This person, monks, is prone to anger."
“A person overcome by anger, possessed by anger, engages in misconduct by body,
misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind. Having engaged in misconduct by body,
misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death… he reappears in hell, being overcome by anger.”
“One who is angry does not know the goal; one who is angry does not see the Dhamma...
[etc. ... One should abandon anger, relinquish conceit, and transcend all fetters.
Anger gives rise to misfortune; anger agitates the mind... [etc. ...”
“Having cut off anger, one sleeps happily; having cut off anger, one does not grieve.
O Brahmins, [this is the way] for anger, which has poison as its root and sweetness as its tip.
“Forgive this one offense, O you of vast wisdom.”
"The wise do not become powerful through anger.
Having reflected in this manner on the faults and dangers [of anger], and on the benefits of abandoning anger by means of their opposites as previously described,

one abandons anger in the preliminary stage through methods such as abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-ppahāna*), and having intensified insight (*vipassanā*), [one abandons it] by means of the third path.
"Completely cut off hatred; abandon it"—this is the exhortation to those bhikkhus in that regard. Therefore it was said:
"Bhikkhus, abandon the one thing, hatred. "Hateful" means corrupted by resentment, having a mind defiled by ill-will.
Whatever else needs to be said here follows the same method as explained in the commentary on the first sutta.
The commentary on the second sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Mōha Sutta:
In the third [sutta], "delusion" (mōha) means ignorance. For that is ignorance regarding suffering, ignorance regarding the origin of suffering, and ignorance regarding the cessation of suffering.

Although it is divided into many varieties according to the method beginning with "ignorance regarding suffering" and "ignorance regarding the way leading to the cessation of suffering," they are deluded.
Because of that, whether one is oneself deluded or the state is merely the act of being deluded, it is called "delusion" (*moha*).
It has the characteristic of blindness of the mind, or the characteristic of non-knowing; its function is non-penetration, and its function is the obscuring of the true nature of the object.

Or rather, it should be regarded as having wrong practice as its manifestation, or darkness as its manifestation, with improper attention as its proximate cause, and as the root of all unwholesome states.
Here too, regarding the word "abandon" (*pajahatha*), [it is said]:
"The deluded one does not know the goal; the deluded one does not see the Dhamma."
“Then there is blinding darkness for the person whom delusion overcomes.
“Delusion is the producer of what is harmful…” “Bhikkhus,
ignorance is the precursor to the attainment of unwholesome states.”
“The world is bound by delusion, yet it appears as if it were real”;
“Delusion is the source for the arising of kamma”;

and, “Deluded, O Brahmin, overcome by delusion and with mind consumed by it, one produces fear and enmity pertaining to this present life, and one produces fear and enmity pertaining to future lives.”

In this manner, having reflected upon the danger in delusion and the benefit in abandoning it by way of its opposite— considering that "whatever phenomenon is to be produced by defilements such as sensual desire, all of them in their actual sense have delusion as their cause"—

those who abandon delusion during the preliminary stage by means of the "partial abandonment" method and so forth, following the very sequence for abandoning sensual desire and the rest, [attain it] with the third path.
The meaning should be understood as: "Abandon delusion—which is driven by the faults of greed as previously described—by means of its total eradication.

For it is specifically the delusion that is to be abandoned by the path of the Non-returner (anāgāmimagga) which is intended here. "Deluded" (mūḷhāse) means those who are utterly confused regarding their own welfare and harm, such as the distinctions between the wholesome and unwholesome, the blameworthy and blameless, and so forth.
The remainder is exactly as explained in the method already stated.
The commentary on the Third Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Kodha Sutta:
In the fourth [sutta], "anger" (*kodha*) refers to hatred (*dosa*). For indeed, it is hatred itself that is expressed by the synonym "anger" for those individuals who understand it in that way.
It was stated thus according to the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*). Therefore, the meaning here should be understood in the very same manner as explained in the second sutta.

Furthermore, anger (*kodha*) should be regarded as having the characteristic of being angry, the function of causing resentment (*āghāta*), the manifestation of a state of mental hostility, and the essence of a putrid state of the mind;
this too should be understood as a distinction.
The commentary on the fourth sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Makkha Sutta:
In the fifth [sutta], "makkha" means the smearing over of another's virtues. For even if one were to take excrement and strike another with it, [it would not be as harmful as this].
Although it first smears one’s own hand, nevertheless,
because it must be practiced with the intention of smearing over the virtues of others, it is called "the smearing of others' virtues.

For just as a water-wiping cloth wipes away the water on the body of one who has bathed, it smears over— that is, wipes away and destroys— the virtues of others, or even those great virtues performed by others.
Because it smears and defiles, it is called "makkha" (sycophancy). It has the characteristic of smearing over the virtues of others; its function is their destruction;

its manifestation is concealing those [virtues]. As for its meaning, it should be understood as an arising of consciousness accompanied by displeasure that proceeds in the manner of smearing over the virtues of others. "Abandon it"—referring to the various types mentioned therein.

The meaning is: having reflected upon hatred (*dosa*), the method described regarding hatred, its danger (*ādīnava*), and the benefit (*ānisaṃsa*) in its abandonment, those who abandon it in the preliminary stage by means of "overcoming through substitution" (*tadaṅga*) and so forth, should further intensify their insight (*vipassanā*) and eradicate it completely with the third path.
*Makkhāse* means those who are defiled; they are those whose own virtues are defiled, or rather, those who smear the virtues of others; for that very reason...
The meaning is "even one's own virtues have been destroyed. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Māna-sutta.
6. In the sixth [chapter], *māna* (conceit) is the loftiness of the mind based on such factors as birth and so forth.

For by means of that, one conceives in the manner of "I am superior," and so on; or it itself conceives, or it is called *māna* because it is the act of conceiving (*mānana*) or the grasping (*sampaggaha*).
This [conceit] is threefold: the conceit "I am superior," the conceit "I am equal," and the conceit "I am inferior. Furthermore...

The conceit "I am superior" in one who is superior; [the conceit] "I am equal" in one who is superior, or "I am inferior" in one who is superior; "I am superior" in one who is equal, "I am equal" in one who is equal, or "I am inferior" in one who is equal;

"I am superior" in one who is inferior, "I am equal" in one who is inferior, or "I am inferior" in one who is inferior—thus, even this ninefold [conceit] has the characteristic of inflation, the essence of the "I-making" (ahaṃkāra), or the essence of grasping, and it is manifested as a state of swelling up.
It should be understood as being manifested by the desire for preeminence, or as resembling madness, having greed dissociated from wrong view as its proximate cause.

"Abandon it" means that all of this has the characteristic of self-exaltation and disparaging others; it is the cause for the non-performance of such acts as saluting, joining the palms, and respectful service toward those worthy of reverence;
and it is the cause for falling into negligence through states such as pride of birth and pride of personhood—such are its various divisions.

The meaning is: having reflected upon the danger [of pride] by way of its opposite and the benefit of being free from conceit, one who has entered the royal assembly should maintain a humble mind toward their fellow practitioners like an outcaste;

then, abandoning that [pride] in the preliminary stage through the method of "substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅga*) and so forth, and increasing insight, one should eradicate it by means of the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*). This is what is to be abandoned by the path of non-returning.

For it is precisely this kind of conceit that is intended here. "Intoxicated" means those who, intoxicated by conceit—such as pride in birth or pride in being a man—and having grasped themselves with such conceit which is a cause for falling into negligence, continue to wander. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
In these six successive suttas or verses, however, the teaching is brought to its conclusion by reaching the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
In this context, there are five types of non-returners according to their mode of rebirth: the Avihas, Atappas, Sudassas, Sudassīs, and Akaniṭṭhas.
Among them, those reborn in the Aviha realm are called the Avihas.

They are of five kinds: those who attain final nibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyī), those who attain final nibbāna upon arrival (upahaccaparinibbāyī), those who attain final nibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī), those who attain final nibbāna with exertion (sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī), and those who go upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm (uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī).
Likewise, there are the Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassin [heavens]. However, among the Akaniṭṭha [deities], one who is an "upstreamer bound for the Akaniṭṭha" may fall away.

In that regard, one who is reborn in the Aviha and other [heavens] and attains Arahantship without exceeding the midpoint of the lifespan, attaining final Nibbāna through the extinction of defilements, is called an "antarā-parinibbāyin" (one who attains Nibbāna in the interval). Furthermore, one who [is reborn] in the Aviha and other [heavens] for a duration such as five hundred kappas from the beginning...
One who attains final nibbāna after having passed through the middle of the lifespan is called one who attains final nibbāna after having "climbed" (upahacca-parinibbāyī).

One who attains final nibbāna without volitional effort, without excessive exertion, and without pain or difficulty is called one who attains final nibbāna without volitional effort (asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī).
However, one who attains final nibbāna with volitional effort, having performed excessive exertion, and with pain, hardship, and difficulty—
This one is called "one who attains Parinibbāna with exertion.

As for the other, because his stream of craving, his stream of the round of existence, and indeed his stream of the Path flow upwards by way of being carried upward through the Aviha and other realms, he is an "Upstreamer" (uddhaṃsota).

Being unable to reach Arahantship after having been reborn in the Aviha and other realms, he remains there for the full duration of his lifespan and, by way of taking rebirth-linking, [proceeds] to the Akaniṭṭha realm.

One who goes [there] is called "one bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm. In this context, a fourfold classification should be understood: one who is an upstream-goer and bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm; one who is an upstream-goer but not bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm; one who is not an upstream-goer but bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm;
and one who is neither an upstream-goer nor bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm. How so? Starting from the Aviha heaven...
Having purified the four divine worlds and gone to the Akaniṭṭha realm, one attains final nibbāna; this is called an "upstreamer bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm.
However, one who purifies the three lower divine worlds, remains in the Sudassī divine world, and there attains final nibbāna is an "upstreamer" but not "bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm.
And one who goes from here directly to the Akaniṭṭha realm itself and attains final nibbāna—

This one is called "one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm. However, he who attains final nibbāna right there in each of the four lower deva-worlds is called neither "one who goes upstream" nor "one who goes to the Akaniṭṭha realm.
In that regard, having been reborn among the Aviha devas, one who attains final nibbāna after more than a hundred kappas [is of the first type]; after two hundred kappas...

There are three types of those who attain final nibbāna in the interval (*antarāparinibbāyino*): one who attains final nibbāna at the head [of the life-span], and one who attains final nibbāna before five hundred kappas have elapsed.
For this has been said: "Either immediately upon being reborn, or before reaching the middle. By the word "or" (*vā*), even those who have merely reached [the middle] are included.

Thus there are three who attain final nibbāna in the interval, one who attains final nibbāna after having passed away (*upahaccaparinibbāyī*), and one who is a stream-winner heading upstream (*uddhaṃsota*).
Among those, there are five who attain final nibbāna without exertion (*asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyin*) and five who attain final nibbāna with exertion (*sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyin*), making ten.
Likewise, there are four decads for the Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī realms, totaling forty.

However, in the Akaniṭṭha realm, because there is no one who goes upstream (*uddhaṃsota*), there are three types of those who attain final nibbāna in the interval (*antarā-parinibbāyin*) and one who attains final nibbāna after landing (*upahacca-parinibbāyin*); thus, there are four who attain final nibbāna without exertion.

There are four who attain final nibbāna with exertion; thus, there are eight. In this way, these forty-eight non-returners (anāgāmin) should be understood as all being included in these discourses by means of the expression used without distinction.
The commentary on the sixth discourse is finished.
7. Commentary on the Sabbapariññā Sutta In the seventh [sutta], "all" (*sabba*) means without remainder. For this word "all" is a term denoting non-remainder.
Whatever it is connected with, it illuminates that very thing as being without remainder; just as in the case of "all form," "all [feeling]," and so forth.
“Feeling [is included] among all phenomena comprised within the entire personal aggregate (sakkāya). Now, this term *sabba* (all) is twofold, according to whether its scope is limited or unlimited.

For it is seen to be employed in four distinct spheres: the all-of-all (*sabbasabba*), the partial-all (*padesasabba*), the all-of-the-bases (*āyatanasabba*), and the all-of-the-personal-aggregate (*sakkāyasabba*).
Among these, [it is said]: “All phenomena in every aspect [are known] at the door of knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One.”
In such passages as “coming within range,” it refers to the *sabbasabba* (the all-inclusive).

In such passages as “Sariputta, all of you have spoken well by way of exposition,” it refers to the *padesasabba* (the partial all). In the passage, “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the ‘all’: the eye and forms... [etc. ...
the mind and mental objects,” it refers to the *āyatanasabba* (the all of the sense bases). [And so on regarding] “The Exposition of the Root of All Phenomena.”

In such passages as "I will teach you, bhikkhus, all of existence-body (sakkāya)," [the term "all"] refers to the entirety of existence-body. Therein, when it occurs in the phrase "all of all," its scope is universal;
when it occurs in the other three [phrases], its scope is partial. However, here it should be understood as referring to the entirety of existence-body.
For here, the phenomena of the three planes that have become the object of insight (vipassanā) are taken in their entirety, without exception, as "all."
They do not recognize all the phenomena to be directly known— such as "these phenomena are wholesome, these are unwholesome," "these are blameworthy, these are blameless," and so forth;

nor do they recognize them according to their non-perverted nature as "these are the five aggregates, these are the twelve bases, these are the eighteen elements, this is the noble truth of suffering, this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering," and so on.
"Not fully understanding" means not knowing by means of distinguished knowledge. "Not fully comprehending" means not comprehending thoroughly.
For whoever fully comprehends the entire collection of phenomena belonging to the three planes, he comprehends it through three kinds of full comprehension:

full comprehension as the known (*ñātapariññā*), full comprehension as investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*), and full comprehension as abandonment (*pahānapariññā*). In that regard, what is full comprehension as the known? It is all name-and-form belonging to the three planes.
“This is form; this much is form, not more than this. This is name; this much is name, not more than this.

Thus one defines form—classified as the primary elements and the sensitive matter—and name—classified as contact and so forth—from the standpoint of their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), functions (*rasa*), manifestations (*paccupaṭṭhāna*), and proximate causes (*padaṭṭhāna*).
One also comprehends its conditions, beginning with ignorance. This is full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*). What is it?
What is full understanding by scrutinization? Having thus known [all things], one scrutinizes them all in forty-two aspects as impermanent, as suffering, and as a disease.

This is full understanding by scrutinization. What is full understanding by abandoning? Having thus scrutinized, one abandons all desire and lust through the supreme path. This is full understanding by abandoning.
The purification by overcoming doubt and the purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path constitute full understanding as the full understanding of the known (*ñāta-pariññā*).
Alternatively, the wisdom beginning with the comprehension of aggregates up to the end of conformity constitutes full understanding as investigative full understanding (*tīraṇa-pariññā*).

Abandoning by means of the Noble Path is full understanding as abandoning (*pahāna-pariññā*). Whoever fully understands everything does so by means of these three kinds of full understanding. Now, here—
