Because dispassion (*virāga*) and abandoning (*pahāna*) have been taken separately by way of their negation, thorough understanding (*parijānanā*) should be understood by way of both the full understanding through knowledge (*ñāta-pariññā*) and the full understanding through investigation (*tīraṇa-pariññā*).
However, with reference to one who does not thoroughly understand in this way, it is said: "not thoroughly understanding" (*aparijāna*).
In that context, they do not cause their own mental continuum to become dispassionate toward that specific object of direct higher knowledge (*abhiññeyya-visesa*) which is to be fully understood.
"Not becoming dispassionate" means not giving rise to the contemplation of dispassion (*virāgānupassanā*) in such a way that passion (*rāga*) does not cease therein.

"Not abandoning" means not abandoning, without remainder, the cycle of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*) to be abandoned therein by means of the wisdom of the path (*maggapaññā*) accompanied by the wisdom of insight (*vipassanāpaññā*).
And just as this is so, so too are "directly knowing" (*abhijānanā*) and the others [to be understood] by way of the mixed path (*missakamagga*).

It should be understood as follows: in the preliminary stage, having successively accomplished higher knowledge and so forth through the various types of consciousness by means of the full understandings of knowing, scrutinizing, and abandoning, at the time of the Path, a single moment of knowledge arises that simultaneously brings all of that to fruition through its functional activity.
"Unable to reach the destruction of suffering" means unable to attain Nibbāna, which is the casting off of the entire round of suffering.
“Not capable” means not fit or not competent.
In the phrase “and all indeed” (*sabbañca kho*), the word *ca* (and) indicates distinction, while the word *kho* (indeed) functions as an emphatic particle.

By the combination of these two, it illuminates the specific excellence to be attained through higher knowledge (*abhijānana*) and so forth, as well as the absolute cause for the destruction of suffering. Regarding what is to be said concerning higher knowledge and the others:
That has already been stated. However, it was stated there by way of negation, whereas here it should be understood by way of affirmation.

This is the only difference. Furthermore, they "directly know" (abhijānanti) the entirety of personal existence (sakkāya), which is comprised of the five aggregates of clinging, by way of making it manifest to knowledge through its essential nature and its conditions; having thus directly known it, they comprehend it through aspects such as non-existence.
Fully understanding that [object] by way of delimiting it through its characteristics such as impermanence;

making one’s own mind dispassionate toward it by means of the power of the knowledge of fear, disadvantage, and disenchantment, which arise through the correct realization of its impermanence and so forth;
and abandoning even the slightest attachment toward it without producing it again, by means of insight associated with the path leading to emergence.

Abandoning and cutting off the cycle of defilements that belongs to the side of origination by means of the wisdom of the path— one is "capable of the destruction of suffering. Thus, through the very abandonment of the stain of defilements,

because the entire cycle of kamma has been exhausted, one is capable of the Nibbāna-element without residue, which consists in the casting off of the entire cycle of resultant rebirth and the total destruction of the suffering of the whole cycle of saṃsāra.
"It is to be attained exclusively"—this is how the meaning should be understood here. "He who, having known all from every aspect" means:

he who is devoted to yoga and has commenced insight (vipassanā) knows "all," that is, the entire collection of phenomena belonging to the three planes, "from every aspect," that is, by way of all their modes, such as the classification into the aggregates beginning with the wholesome, and the classification into suffering, oppression, and so forth. Then...
Or, having understood "in every way" (*sabbato*)— that is, having known from every aspect, such as the characteristics of hardness,
contact, and so forth, as well as impermanence and so on— and having penetrated it through path-knowledge preceded by insight, or else for the reason of knowing by means of insight-knowledge itself;

he "does not delight in any things" (*sabbatthesu na rajjati*), that is, in all phenomena of personal existence (*sakkāya-dhamma*) which are divided into many categories according to the past and other periods.
He does not lust; through the attainment of the Noble Path, he does not generate passion (*rāga*).

By this, showing the absence of his grasping at craving (*taṇhā-gāha*), he shows—by way of that [craving] being the cause for the grasping at views (*diṭṭhi-māna-gāha*)—the absence of these three types of wrong grasping: "This is mine," "I am this," and "This is my self.
In the phrase *sa ve*, *sa* is merely a particle. *Ve* means "clearly" or "categorically."
In this context, it is a particle used for emphasis. "Complete full understanding" (*sabbapariññā*) means from the perspective of knowing everything;

that is, from the perspective of fully understanding, by way of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), all that has been previously mentioned. "He" refers to the practitioner (*yogāvacara*) as previously described, or indeed the Noble One (*ariya*).
"He has transcended all suffering" means he has gone beyond, surpassed, and completely overcome all the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
The commentary on the Seventh Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Mānapariññā Sutta:
In the eighth [sutta], there is nothing new; the teaching proceeds solely by way of conceit (*māna*). However, in the verses, they are accompanied by conceit.

These beings, who have received the name "pajā" because they are born (*pajāyati*) from the defilements of karma, are possessed of and approached by *māna*, which has the characteristic of conceiving.

Bound by the fetters of pride (*mānaganthā*), they delight in existence (*bhave ratā*); even in the forms of existence such as worms, insects, and moths, they are bound by pride and fettered by the fetter of pride. For that very reason, by virtue of the long-term cultivation of the conceit of "I,"...

Because they are full of attachment toward volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*)—thinking “this is mine”—and because of the perversion (*vipallāsa*) regarding permanence, pleasure, and self, they delight in existence through sensual desire and the like.
“Not fully understanding conceit” means not fully understanding conceit by means of the three kinds of full understanding (*pariññā*).

Alternatively, it means not transcending it by means of the knowledge of the path of Arahantship; some read the text as “not having fully understood conceit. “Comers to renewed existence” means [coming] again...

"Future existence" (*āyatim upapattibhavam*) means that because they undergo existence again and again, they go toward and approach the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), which is termed "renewed existence" (*punabbhava*), by way of revolving from one state to another; the meaning is that they are not liberated from existence.

But those who, having abandoned conceit, are liberated through the destruction of conceit—meaning those who have completely abandoned conceit by means of the path of Arhatship—[they do not go to renewed existence].

They are "well-liberated" (vimuttā) because they are liberated from all defilements associated with conceit—whether in Nibbāna, which is the fruit of Arahantship that is the absolute destruction of conceit, or in the liberation itself. Having overcome the fetters of conceit, they have transcended all suffering.

These Arahants, whose fetters of existence are completely exhausted, stand having utterly overcome the fetter of conceit and the fetter of conceit through its abandonment by means of total eradication.
The meaning is that they transcended the suffering of saṃsāra without remainder. Thus, in this seventh sutta, arahantship is explained.
The commentary on the eighth sutta is finished.
9–10. Commentary on the two suttas on the full understanding of greed and hatred.

9–10. There is nothing new in the ninth and tenth [suttas]. It should be understood that they were taught in such a manner either by way of the Teacher’s skill in exposition or in accordance with the inclinations of those disciples who would understand them thus.
The commentary on the ninth and tenth suttas is concluded.
The commentary on the first chapter is concluded.
2. Second Chapter: 1–3. Commentary on the Discourses on the Full Understanding of Delusion, etc. (Suttas 11–13).
In the second chapter as well, the first three discourses follow the same method already explained; likewise, the reason for the teaching has already been stated.
4. Commentary on the *Avijjānīvaraṇa-sutta* 14.
Regarding the fourth [sutta], in the passage beginning with “I do not, monks,” the word “not” (*na*) has the sense of negation. “I” (*ahaṃ*) is the Blessed One’s designation for himself.

“Another” (*aññaṃ*) means other than the obscuration of ignorance (*avijjānīvaraṇa*) which is to be discussed now. “Even a single obscuration” (*ekanīvaraṇampi*) means even a single factor that constitutes an obscuration.
“I contemplate” refers to two kinds of contemplation: contemplation by way of view (*diṭṭhi-samanupassanā*) and contemplation by way of knowledge (*ñāṇa-samanupassanā*).
Therein, that which comes in such passages as “he contemplates form as self” is called contemplation by way of view.
However, that which comes in such passages as “he contemplates it as impermanent, not as permanent” is called contemplation by way of knowledge. Here too, [it is the latter].
Only the contemplation by means of knowledge (ñāṇasamanupassanā) is intended here. Furthermore, the word "samanupassāmi" is connected with the negative particle *na*.

This is what is meant: "Monks, although I survey all phenomena with the universal eye (samantacakkhu), which is to say the knowledge of omniscience, as if they were an amala fruit in the palm of my hand, I do not perceive even a single other hindrance."

"By which hindrance beings are shrouded, wandering and transmigrating for a long time"—this means that because it has the nature of a hindrance, it prevents one from knowing, seeing, or penetrating the true nature of phenomena;
by concealing, enveloping, and standing as a darkness in its place, beings shrouded by it wander through the beginningless cycle of existence for immeasurable eons, both in great... [and so forth].
And in the minor states of existence and so forth, they both run away and wander about by way of repeated rebirth.
Alternatively, "running" refers to the transition from one object to another, while "wandering" refers to the transition from one state of existence to another.
Or else, "running" occurs through the power of the defilements, while "wandering" occurs through their weakness. This is by way of momentary death.
Or, "running" (sandhāvana) refers to wandering through many births by way of conventional death and rebirth;
or, "running" is by way of the mind—as it is said, "his mind runs about"—while "wandering" (saṃsaraṇa) is by way of karma.
In this way, the distinction between running and wandering should be understood.
*Yathā idam* means "just as this. The letter *ya* serves to join words (*padasandhikara*); by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), it is shortened. Regarding the term *avijjānīvaraṇa*:
here, bodily misconduct and so forth are called "unfound" (*avindiya*) in the sense that they are unfit to be fulfilled; the meaning is that they are not to be obtained.
Ignorance (*avijjā*) is so called because it finds (*vindati*) that which is unfound (*avindiya*). Conversely, bodily good conduct and so forth are called "founded" (*vindiya*); that founded thing...

It is called *avijjā* (ignorance) because it does not find [the truth]. It is ignorance because it makes unknown the fourfold meaning of the aggregates as a "heap," the sense bases as "bases," the elements as "emptiness," and the faculties as "predominance";
and because it makes unknown the meaning of the truths as "suchness" and their fourfold aspect—suffering and so forth—as stated by way of oppression and so on.
It is ignorance because it causes sentient beings to run about in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

Or, it is called ignorance (*avijjā*) because it stirs up and proceeds toward things that do not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), such as "woman" or "man," while it does not stir up or proceed toward things that do exist, such as the aggregates (*khandha*).

Furthermore, it is ignorance because it conceals the bases and objects of eye-consciousness and so forth, as well as the phenomena of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) and dependently arisen phenomena (*paṭiccasamuppanna-dhamma*). Ignorance itself is an obstruction; thus, it is the "obstruction of ignorance" (*avijjā-nīvaraṇa*).
"Monks, shrouded by the hindrance of ignorance, beings wander and transmigrate for a long time"—this was said for the purpose of strengthening what was stated previously.

Or rather, the previous statement—"Monks, just as this is the hindrance of ignorance"—was spoken by way of showing a simile, whereas this [present statement] is by way of showing the power of the hindrances. But why is this so?
Is it ignorance alone that is spoken of in this way, and not other phenomena? Because, by concealing its disadvantage, it serves as a specific condition for sensual desire and the rest.
For indeed, when the disadvantage of an object is concealed by it, sensual desire and the like arise.
The verse beginning with "There is nothing else" was spoken to summarize the meaning both of what has been stated and of what has not yet been stated.
In this context, *nivutā* means covered, obstructed, or concealed; the sense is that they are hidden. *Ahorattaṃ* means by day and by night—that is, at all times.

Just as by delusion (*moha*)—meaning by that which is called the veil of ignorance (*avijjānīvaraṇa*)—the people are covered and concealed, and thus, even though things are easy to understand, they do not know them and wander through the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), such is the nature [of that delusion].
It should be understood that there is not even a single phenomenon or a single hindrance [other than this]. As for those noble disciples who, having abandoned delusion, shatter the mass of darkness:

these noble disciples, having first abandoned delusion—which is to be abandoned by each respective path—either through the abandonment of its factors (*tadaṅga*) and so forth during the preliminary stage, or by means of the lower paths, subsequently abandon that which is called delusion itself by means of the supreme path, with knowledge resembling a thunderbolt.
They have demolished the mass of darkness and cut it off without remainder. They do not wander in saṃsāra again; thus they are Arahants.
For: "The uninterrupted succession of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases as they proceed is called 'saṃsāra.'"
When this has been said, they do not wander, they do not roam about in this saṃsāra. For what reason?

Because the cause for them does not exist; since ignorance is the cause, the root-cause of saṃsāra, that [ignorance] does not exist for them—it is entirely non-existent because it has been utterly eradicated.
The commentary on the fourth sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Taṇhāsaṃyojana Sutta (Sutta 15).

In the fifth [verse], "for whomsoever it exists"—that person is bound by sufferings, or by karma through its results, to existence, birth, destiny, stations of consciousness, and the abodes of beings.
It is called a *saṃyojana* (fetter) because it yokes one to future existence and so forth. It is *taṇhā* (craving) in the sense of craving;
it craves (*tasati*) and is distressed itself, or else it is that by which beings crave, thus it is *taṇhā*. "Bound" means bound to the bases for misapprehension, such as the eye and so forth.
The rest is exactly as previously explained. Granted, in this context, ignorance also possesses the nature of a fetter, and craving also possesses the nature of an obscuration (*nīvaraṇa*).

Nevertheless, in order to show this specific distinction—that craving binds beings to existences whose dangers are concealed by ignorance—ignorance was stated in the previous sutta by way of being an *nīvaraṇa* (hindrance), whereas here craving is stated specifically by way of being a *saṃyojana* (fetter).
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of showing the predominance of hindrances and fetters. For just as by way of being a hindrance...
Ignorance (*avijjā*) is the primary and forerunner of the defiled phenomena (*saṃkilesadhamma*);
thus, in order to show that craving (*taṇhā*) is subordinate to it by way of their nature as fetters (*saṃyojana*), these phenomena are described in this manner in the two suttas.
Furthermore, ignorance is specifically called an "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*) because it obstructs the bliss of Nibbāna, whereas craving [binds] sentient beings with the suffering of *saṃsāra*.
It is called "fetter" (*saṃyojana*) because it fetters.
Alternatively, the two [types] are stated as twofold because they create obstacles to seeing and proceeding, and because they are the opposites of true knowledge (*vijjā*) and conduct (*caraṇa*).
For ignorance (*avijjā*), which is the direct antithesis of true knowledge, is specifically an obstacle to the vision of Nibbāna and to unerring vision.
Craving, being the direct opposite of the factors conducive to progress, acts as an obstacle to going—that is, to the right practice.

Thus, this uninstructed worldling, the ordinary person, who is shrouded by ignorance, blinded, enclosed by craving, and bound—like one who is blind and bound—does not cross over the great wilderness, the wilderness of saṃsāra.
This is also for the purpose of showing the two causes for the arising of misfortune.

The dyad is stated in two ways. For a person who has fallen into ignorance, by virtue of his foolishness, he lets go of what is beneficial and brings about what is harmful for himself, like an unskilled patient performing unsuitable actions.

Even though he knows, the fool lets go of what is beneficial and brings about what is harmful by virtue of his foolishness, like a knowledgeable patient who indulges in what is unsuitable. This is the Simile of the Monkey’s Salve Sutta.
It is the accomplisher of the mind’s welfare.
Furthermore, two factors are stated here in a twofold manner for the purpose of showing the root causes of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).
Specifically, because delusion is predominant, the past time is the field of ignorance (avijjā); because aspiration is predominant, [the future] is the field of craving (taṇhā).

The future time-period (*anāgato addhā*). For in this way, a foolish person, being full of delusion, grieves over the past; for him, "with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations"—all [of this] should be applied.
Being full of longing, he hankers after the future; for him, "with craving as condition there is clinging," and so forth—all [of this] should be applied.
Precisely because of that, by bringing back the past and connecting it with the future, [the continuity of suffering is established].
It should be understood that its status as the primary cause has been shown in due order.
In the verses, "having craving as his companion" (*taṇhādutiyo*) means having craving as his associate.

For craving performs the function of a companion by showing a gratification to a being who—like one overcome by thirst in a waterless desert through the perception of a mirage—is themselves overwhelmed by suffering that cannot be remedied.
By producing non-disenchantment with existence and so forth, it causes one to wander; therefore, craving is called the "second" for a person.
But are not other defilements and so forth also conditions for the production of existence? True, this is so; however, they are not such specific conditions as craving is.
For indeed, [craving] exists even without wholesome states, and among unwholesome states, it exists even without those wholesome states belonging to the sense-sphere and so forth.

And there is no specific condition for the production of existence apart from wholesome states of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and so forth, which is why it is called the Truth of Origin (*samudayasacca*).
"This state and another state" (*itthabhāvaññathābhāva*): this refers to both "this state" (*itthabhāva*) and "another state" (*aññathābhāva*).
That which possesses these is "this state and another state," namely, *saṃsāra*. Within that, "this state" is human existence.

"Otherwise-ness" (*aññathābhāva*) refers to the remaining abodes of beings. Alternatively, "thus-ness" (*itthabhāva*) is the present individual existence (*attabhāva*) of various beings, while "otherwise-ness" is their future individual existence.
Or, such a kind of individual existence is "thus-ness," and that which is not of such a kind is "otherwise-ness.
This cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), consisting of the succession of aggregates (*khandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), is this very "thus-ness and otherwise-ness."
It does not transcend, it does not go beyond.

"Having known this danger" means having known craving—the origin, the source of all the suffering of the entire cycle of existence—as a danger from the perspective of its being a danger. Alternatively, "having known this danger" refers to this...

Having understood the danger and defect of not transcending the aforementioned saṃsāra; and having understood craving as the origin of suffering—that is, craving as the primary cause of the suffering of the round according to the method already stated;

and thus comprehending by means of the three types of full understanding, "The bhikkhu who is free from craving, without clinging, mindful, goes forth," he increases insight and proceeds through the sequence of the paths.
With the fading away of craving by means of the supreme path, being entirely free from craving and devoid of thirst,
and for that very reason being without grasping due to the absence of any of the four types of clinging— or rather, due to the absence of future grasping known as rebirth-linking— the bhikkhu,
having attained fullness of mindfulness and thus acting with constant awareness in all things, should wander about, his defilements shattered, through the final nibbāna of the aggregates.
The meaning is that one would depart from the occurrence of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).
The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the First Sutta on the Trainee (*sekhā*).
16. Regarding the sixth [term], *sekha* (the trainee): in what sense is one a *sekha* here? One is a *sekha* by virtue of having attained the qualities of training (*sekkhadhamma*).

For this has been said: “To what extent, venerable sir, is one a *sekha*? Here, bhikkhu, one is endowed with right view that is in training... [and so on] ...one is endowed with right concentration that is in training. To this extent, bhikkhu, one is a *sekha*.
Furthermore, one is a *sekha* because one trains (*sikkhati*). And this too has been said:
“‘He trains,’ bhikkhu, therefore he is called a ‘trainee’ (*sekha*). And what does he train in?
He trains in higher virtue, he trains in higher mind, and he trains in higher wisdom. ‘He trains,’ bhikkhu, therefore he is called a ‘trainee.
Even that noble ordinary person (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) who fulfills the practice in accordance with the truth, who is perfected in virtue, and who guards the doors of the sense faculties...

One who is moderate in eating, devoted to the practice of wakefulness, and during the first and last watches of the night remains devoted to the development of the states conducive to enlightenment, thinking:
"Today or tomorrow I shall attain one of the fruits of recluseship"—he too is called a trainee (*sekha*) because he trains.
In this sense, it is one who has not yet fully penetrated [the goal] who is intended by the term "trainee."
Now, there is also the "virtuous worldling" (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*). He is called *appattamānaso* because his mind (*mānasa*) has not reached [its goal]. Regarding the term *mānasa*:

in the passage, “The snare that moves through the sky, which wanders as the mind,” it is lust (*rāga*) that is called *mānasa*. In the passage, “Mind (*citta*), intellect (*mano*), and consciousness (*mānasa*),” it is the mind (*citta*) itself.
In the passage, “The trainee (*sekha*) who has not attained his mind may pass away while listening to the teaching,” it refers to *arahatta* (Arahatship). Here, too, it is the same.
Only *arahatta* (perfected state) is intended here. By this, it is meant "for one who has not yet attained *arahatta*.
*Anuttara* means supreme; the sense is that it is peerless. *Yogakkhema* means secure from the four *yogas* (bonds), being unafflicted;
only *arahatta* is intended here. Regarding "of one who desires": there are two kinds of desire—desire as craving (*taṇhā-patthanā*) and desire as wholesome aspiration (*kusalacchanda-patthanā*).
And: “For one who yearns, there are indeed utterances of longing, or even trembling over what has been planned”—here, it is the yearning of craving (*taṇhāpatthanā*).
Also: “The stream of the Evil One is cut off, scattered and destroyed;
be full of gladness, O monks, and aspire for safety.”
Here, it is precisely the wholesome desire and aspiration characterized by the wish-to-act that is intended.
"By one who aspires" means by one desiring to go to that security from bondage, one who is inclined toward it, leaning toward it, and bent toward it.
"Dwells" means having interrupted the suffering of one posture with another posture, he maintains his personal existence without letting it fall away.

*Harato*. Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood according to the method of exposition (niddesa) as follows: "One dwells in faith, resolving that 'all conditioned phenomena are impermanent,'" and so forth. *Ajjhattikaṃ* means that which exists within the internal (*ajjhatta*), which is defined as one's own internal state. *Aṅgaṃ* means a cause or factor. *Iti karitvā* means having made it thus. Regarding the phrase "I do not see even a single factor other than this": [The remainder of the passage continues: ...in this context, the Blessed One has stated that there is no other single factor—whether among those conducive to decline or conducive to distinction—that is more effective for the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage than the faculty of faith. This is because faith is the foundation for all wholesome qualities; it is the root of the tree of the Dhamma, the seed of all wholesome states, and the precursor to all noble attainments.

Therefore, by means of faith, one gains confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and subsequently develops the factors of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Thus, faith is the primary basis for the entire path to liberation. For one who possesses faith, the other faculties follow in due order, leading to the realization of the ultimate goal. Hence, the Blessed One emphasizes that faith is the most essential factor for spiritual progress. [End of excerpt]
This is the summarized meaning: "Monks, considering it as a cause arisen within one's own internal continuum,
I do not perceive any other single cause that is so very beneficial as this, namely, wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*)— that is, attention as a means, attention as a path,
attention in the manner of impermanence and so forth regarding the impermanent and so on, and attention in conformity with impermanence."
Or it is the turning toward, the repeated turning toward, the inclination, the attention, and the mental engagement of the mind.
This is wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*). Now, in order to demonstrate the power of wise attention, it is said:
"Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu attends wisely, he abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome. In this context, "attending wisely" means:

“‘This is the noble truth of suffering, this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering, this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, this is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—thus one applies systematic attention to the four noble truths.
Herein, this is the exposition of the meaning: although this discourse has come down without distinction concerning persons who are still in training (sekkha), [it applies to them all].

However, we shall explain the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) in brief by way of its commonality with the four paths. A practitioner (yogāvacara) who takes the four truths as his meditation subject is one who has previously mastered the meditation subject of the four truths under a teacher, [understanding it] thus:
"The aggregates of the three planes, excluding craving, are suffering; craving is the origin; the non-occurrence of both is cessation;
and the path is that which leads to the attainment of cessation."
Then, at a later time, having ascended the path of insight (vipassanā-magga), he attends wisely to the aggregates belonging to the three planes as "this is suffering" (dukkha);
he both directs his attention and contemplates them by means of the appropriate method and path. For here, "insight" (vipassanā) is spoken of under the heading of "attention" (manasikāra).
Furthermore, that which gives rise to this suffering—the [craving] belonging to a previous existence—[is also abandoned].

He applies appropriate attention, thinking: "Craving is the origin of suffering. Furthermore, because this suffering and this origin cease and do not proceed once they reach this state, he applies appropriate attention, thinking: "That which is called Nibbāna is the cessation of suffering.
[And he applies appropriate attention to] the Eightfold Path that brings about cessation.
“He attends wisely, ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’; he both directs his mind and sees with insight by means of the method and the path.
Herein, this is the method: adherence occurs regarding the aggregates, not regarding the turning away from them. Therefore, the meaning is this:
by way of the formula beginning, “In this body there is the earth element, the water element,” and so forth, one [contemplates] the four great elements and, following that, the derived forms.

Having grasped it, one defines it as “this is the aggregate of form. As one defines that, one defines the mental states and mental factors that have arisen with that as their object as “these are the four immaterial aggregates.
Thereafter, one defines “these five aggregates are suffering. These, in brief, constitute two portions: name and form. And this—

Name-and-form arises with a cause and with conditions; he defines its cause as ignorance, existence, craving, and so forth, and its condition as nutriment and so forth, thus determining the cause and the condition.
Having determined the specific characteristics of those conditions and the phenomena arisen from those conditions according to their true nature, he discerns:
"These phenomena, having not been, come to be; having been, they cease."

Therefore, by saying "they are impermanent," he applies the characteristic of impermanence; by saying "they are suffering because they are oppressed by arising and passing away," he applies the characteristic of suffering;
by saying "they are non-self because they do not exercise mastery over themselves," he applies the characteristic of non-self.

Having thus applied the three characteristics, while practicing insight, [he encounters] the defilements of insight such as the "aura" (obhāsa) that arise with the emergence of the knowledge of arising and passing away.

Regarding the phrase "the non-path": having defined the path and the non-path by determining that the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*) alone is the "preliminary path" serving as the means (*upāya*) for the Noble Path, one then successively produces the knowledge of dissolution (*bhaṅga-ñāṇa*) and the others, thereby reaching the paths of stream-entry and so forth.
At that moment, one penetrates the Four Truths through a single penetration (*ekappaṭivedha*) and a single clear realization (*ekābhisamaya*).
He realizes it. Therein, penetrating suffering through the penetration of full understanding, and penetrating the origin through the penetration of abandonment, he abandons all that is unwholesome;

penetrating cessation through the penetration of realization, and penetrating the path through the penetration of development, he develops all that is wholesome. For the Noble Path is, in the ultimate sense, [the means].

It is "skillful" (*kusala*) in the sense of being free from what is blameworthy, such as the faults of the womb; and when that [mindfulness] is cultivated, all skillful states—those factors conducive to enlightenment that are blameless—reach the fulfillment of their cultivation.
Thus, by attending to things thoroughly (*yoniso*), one abandons the unskillful and cultivates the skillful.
For it has been said: "One attends thoroughly, thinking, 'This is suffering'; 'This is the origin of suffering'..."
“He attends wisely,” and so forth. Furthermore, it is said: “For a bhikkhu, bhikkhus, who is endowed with wise attention, this is to be expected:
he will develop the Noble Eightfold Path; he will cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path.”
The summary meaning of the verse beginning with "Yoniso manasikāro" (Proper attention) is as follows:
One who trains, or for whom there are training rules, or whose nature is to train, is a *sekha* (trainee). One who sees fear in *saṃsāra* is a *bhikkhu*.
For that *sekha* bhikkhu, proper attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) is of great benefit for the attainment and realization of the supreme goal, which is *arahantship*.

There is no other state that is so greatly beneficial. Why? Because if one exerts oneself by placing systematic attention (yoniso manasikāra) at the forefront through skillful means, exerting oneself by way of the fourfold right striving (sammappadhāna), one would reach the destruction of suffering;
one would reach the complete exhaustion and the end of the suffering of the cycle of defilements—that is, one would attain and realize Nibbāna. Therefore, systematic attention is of great benefit.
The commentary on the sixth sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the second Sekha-sutta. 17.

In the seventh [sutta], "external" means existing outside of one's own internal continuum. "Good friendship" (kalyāṇamittatā) refers to one who is endowed with qualities such as virtue (sīla) and so forth.
One who destroys evil, provides for welfare, and is a benefactor in every way is a friend; such a person is a "good friend" (*kalyāṇamitta*).

The state of being such a person is "good friendship" (*kalyāṇamittatā*). In this regard, such a good friend is by nature endowed with faith, endowed with virtue, endowed with learning, endowed with generosity, endowed with energy, endowed with mindfulness, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom.

Therein, through the perfection of faith, one has conviction in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata; by that means, one does not abandon the desire for the welfare and happiness of sentient beings, which is the cause of perfect self-enlightenment (sammāsambodhi).

Through the perfection of virtue (sīla), one becomes dear to fellow practitioners of the holy life, respected, worthy of esteem, an admonisher, a censurer of evil, one who speaks appropriately, and one who is patient with what is said.
Through the perfection of learning (suta), [one gains knowledge] of the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), truths (sacca), dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), and so forth.
He is a speaker of profound discourses; through the perfection of generosity, he is of few desires, contented, secluded, and unattached;
through the perfection of energy, he is one who has aroused energy in the practice of his own welfare and that of others;
and through the perfection of mindfulness, he is one whose mindfulness is established, endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection, [remembering] even what was done long ago.
He recollects what was spoken long ago; through the perfection of concentration, he is undistracted, composed, and one-pointed in mind;

through the perfection of wisdom, he understands things without error. Seeking out the courses of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena by means of mindfulness, and having understood the welfare and happiness of beings as they truly are by means of wisdom, he remains with an undisturbed mind therein by means of concentration.
By means of energy, he restrains beings from what is harmful and enjoins them solely to what is beneficial. Therefore it was said:
“He is dear, respected, and worthy of honor; he speaks and is patient with being spoken to;
he delivers profound discourse and does not enjoin one to what is improper.”
“Monks, a monk who has a virtuous friend abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome.
Thus, a person with a virtuous friend, relying upon that virtuous friend, gives rise to the knowledge of being the owner of one’s own kamma; he increases the faith already arisen;
having become endowed with faith, he approaches [the Teacher]; having approached, he listens to the Dhamma. Having heard that Dhamma from the Tathāgata...
He acquires faith; by that acquisition of faith, he abandons the household life and undertakes the going-forth;
he fulfills the fourfold purity of virtue (*sīla*); he undertakes and practices the ascetic qualities (*dhutadhamma*) according to his strength; he becomes a possessor of the ten topics of discourse;
and he dwells with energy aroused, mindfulness established, and clearly comprehending, throughout the first and last watches of the night, [devoted] to the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Devoted to the practice of developing the qualities (dhammas), before long he brings insight (vipassanā) to its peak;
through the attainment of the Noble Path, he eradicates all unwholesome states and increases all wholesome states as they reach full maturity through development. For it has been said:
“Meghiya, for a bhikkhu who has a good friend, a good companion, and a good associate, this is to be expected…”
‘That he will be virtuous, dwelling restrained by the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, seeing fear in even the slightest faults,
and training himself by undertaking the rules of training’—

this is for one who has a good friend... [and so on] ...for one who is devoted to what is excellent, that this discourse which is conducive to effacement and favorable to the opening of the mind [should be heard].”
It leads to utter disenchantment... [and] to Nibbāna. That is to say:

talk on fewness of desires, talk on contentment, talk on seclusion, talk on non-association, talk on the arousal of energy, talk on virtue, talk on concentration... [and] talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation.
He will obtain such talk as he desires, without difficulty and without hardship.”

“For one who has a good friend... for one who is well-supported by the virtuous, it is to be expected that they will dwell with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states—steadfast, firm in effort, not casting off the burden regarding wholesome states. “For one who has a good friend...

for one who is well-supported by the virtuous, it is to be expected that they will be wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, noble, penetrative, and leading to the complete destruction of suffering.”
Thus, it should be understood that a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitta) is the means for liberation from all the suffering of saṃsāra. For this very reason, it was said:
“For, Ānanda, by coming to me as a virtuous friend, beings subject to birth are liberated from birth; beings subject to aging are liberated from aging,” and so forth.
Therefore it was said: “Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has a virtuous friend abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome.”
"Sappatissa" means "one who is with *paṭissava*," that is, one who is accompanied by *paṭissava*.

The meaning is: one who receives the exhortation of a good friend (*kalyāṇamitta*) upon the head, being easy to speak to. Alternatively, he is a *paṭissa* because he honors (*isati*) [the teacher] by establishing him in welfare and happiness;
thus, he is the giver of exhortation. One who conducts himself together with that *paṭissa* through the application of reverence for the venerable is *sappatissa*.
"Abounding in respectful service toward teachers": one who is endowed with the sixfold reverence. "Acting upon the word of friends":
practicing according to the instruction of virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitta), following their advice as given.

"Possessed of clear comprehension": endowed with the sevenfold clear comprehension (sampajañña). "Mindful": by means of mindfulness capable of bringing the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) to full development.
"Mindful" means acting with mindfulness. "Gradually" refers to the sequence of purification beginning with virtue (*sīla*) and so forth;
therein it refers both to the sequence of insight (*vipassanā*) and the sequence of the paths (*magga*).

"The destruction of all fetters" means that which constitutes the culmination of the Noble Path, so called because it exhausts all fetters, such as the fetter of sensual lust (*kāmarāga-saṃyojana*) and the rest.
It means that one would reach or attain either Arahantship itself or Nibbāna, which is its object.
Thus, it should be understood that in these two suttas, the Teacher has taken up what is called the "factor of striving" for the attainment of the Noble Path.
The commentary on the seventh sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Saṅghabhedasutta 18.
Regarding the eighth [sutta], what is the occasion for the delivery of this discourse? It is an *aṭṭhuppattika* (occasion-based) discourse. Herein is the brief account:
Devadatta, having caused Ajātasattu to form a wrongful attachment, [incited him] against his father, King Bimbisāra.
Although he had caused [the Elder] to be killed, had employed assassins, and had committed the offense of drawing blood by striking him with a stone, he did not yet become publicly known for it;
however, after releasing Nāḷāgiri, he became widely known.
Then the great multitude raised a clamor, saying, "The king even wanders about committing such evil as this! and there was a great outcry. Hearing this, the king—
He caused five hundred pots of rice-meat (*thālipāka*) that were being offered by himself to be withheld, and even his own attendance did not come to him.
Even when he entered the families of the city-dwellers, they would not give him even a spoonful of food.
With his gains and honor thus diminished, wishing to live by means of hypocrisy, he approached the Teacher and requested five points; [the Teacher replied], "Enough, Devadatta! Whoever wishes—"
Having been rejected by the Blessed One with the words, “Let him be a forest-dweller,” and so forth, he—
persuading the foolish people who were devoted to austerity by means of those five points— had the five hundred Vajjiputta monks take voting tickets,

split the Saṅgha, and taking them with him, went to Gayāsīsa. Then, the two Chief Disciples, having gone there at the Teacher’s command and taught the Dhamma, [established the monks in the higher training].
Having established them in the fruits of the noble ones (ariyaphala), they brought them back. However, those who, while he was striving for a schism in the Saṅgha,
approved of his doctrine and remained having adopted it, and who were compliant with the Saṅgha both while it was being split and after it had been split—
for them that resulted in harm and suffering for a long time.
Not long after, Devadatta too was overcome by disease and fell gravely ill. At the time of his death, thinking, "I shall pay homage to the Teacher," he was being carried on a palanquin litter;
when he was stopped at the edge of the Jetavana lotus pond, a fissure opened in the earth, and falling into it, he was reborn in the Avīci hell.
His physical form there was a hundred yojanas in height and remained for an eon, with a girth equal to the trunk of a palm tree.
He was pierced by iron spikes. About five hundred families belonging to Devadatta’s faction, who had adhered to his doctrine along with their kinsmen, were reborn in hell.
One day, the monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Dharma, saying, “Friends, Devadatta committed a grave deed when he caused a schism in the Saṅgha. Then—
The Teacher, having approached the Dhamma Hall, asked, "Monks, with what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "With this very one," he spoke this Sutta, demonstrating the danger of schism in the Saṅgha.
Some, however, say that he spoke it after seeing how Devadatta and those on his side had been reborn in hell in such a manner.
"Showing the danger in a schism in the Saṅgha, the Blessed One taught this sutta solely out of his own inclination.
In that context, "one thing" means one unwholesome state that is a great offense. "In the world" refers to the world of sentient beings. Regarding the phrase "when it arises, it arises":
even when disputes and so forth conducive to a schism have arisen in the Saṅgha, [it arises] in regard to such matters as "this is Dhamma" or "this is non-Dhamma."
Among the eighteen grounds for schism, even when people speak by way of illustrating any one of them,

or when they cause a proclamation to be made there in order to generate consent, or even when a voting ticket has been distributed after such a proclamation, a schism in the Saṅgha is said to arise; however, when four or more [monks] have taken up the voting tickets,
if they perform a separate recitation or a formal act (saṅghakamma) [of their own], [the schism is established].
When they do so, it is said that a schism in the Saṅgha arises. But once that has been performed, how is it said that a schism in the Saṅgha has arisen?

For among these five causes of schism in the Saṅgha—namely, formal act (*kamma*), recitation (*uddesa*), designation (*vohāra*), proclamation (*anussāvanā*), and the drawing of lots (*salākaggāha*)—the formal act or the recitation is the decisive factor;
however, the designation, the proclamation, and the drawing of lots are merely preliminary stages.

Regarding the phrase "for the harm of many people" (*bahujanāhitāya*) and so forth: it is for the harm (*ahitāya*) of the great multitude by obstructing their attainment of meditative absorption (*jhāna*), the Path (*magga*), and so on;

for their lack of happiness (*asukhāya*) by obstructing their attainment of heaven (*sagga*); and for their disadvantage (*anatthāya*) by serving as a cause for rebirth in the states of misery (*apāya*). Alternatively, it is for their harm through unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*);

and because even a mere benefit is absent, the connection is that [such a person] arises with bodily and mental suffering even in a happy destination (*sugati*). "Of gods and humans" (*devamanussānaṃ*)—
This is the description of the superior person among those referred to by the phrase "of many people. Another method of explanation:
"for the harm of many people" means for the sake of the harm of many people—that is, for the great mass of beings—and for their disadvantage in both the present life and the future life;
"for their unhappiness" means for the sake of unhappiness in both the present life and the future life, that is, for the sake of the two kinds of suffering.
“For no good” means for the sake of rejecting the ultimate goal (*paramattha*). For Nibbāna is the ultimate goal; there is no goal higher than that.
“For harm” means for the sake of rejecting the Path. For there is no benefit higher than the Path that leads to the attainment of Nibbāna.

“For suffering” means, by way of the loss of noble happiness, because of the state of suffering within the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*). For those who have missed out on noble happiness [experience] that...
They are incapable of attaining [liberation] and wander through the suffering of saṃsāra; indeed, there is no happiness higher than the happiness of the Noble Ones (ariya).
For it has been said: "This concentration is pleasant in the present and results in happiness in the future.
Now, having shown "schism in the Saṅgha" by its own nature, [the text proceeds] to demonstrate its status as the absolute cause of harm and so forth.
“Now, monks, when the Saṅgha is split,” he said, beginning with these words.

In this context, “split” (*bhinne*) is the locative case used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*), as in the expression “when wealth is not being bestowed upon the poor”; the meaning is “due to a schism.
“Mutual quarrels” (*aññamaññaṃ bhaṇḍanāni*) refers to the mutual disputations among the four assemblies and their respective factions, such as “This is the Dhamma; that is not the Dhamma.”
For *bhaṇḍana* (quarreling) is the preliminary stage of *kala-ha* (strife). *Paribhāsā* (reviling) is the act of threatening by instilling fear, saying, "We shall do this and that harm to you.
*Parikkhepā* (slandering) is the casting about [of blame] on all sides by way of birth and so forth; it is the censuring and insulting by means of the ten grounds for abuse.
*Pariccajanā* (expulsion) is the removal [from the community] by means of performing the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepaniya-kamma*) and so forth. *Tattha* (therein):
Regarding that schism in the Saṅgha, or its causes such as quarrels and the like: "Lacking confidence" means not being acquainted with the qualities of the Triple Gem.

"They do not have confidence" means they do not develop the form of confidence toward the monks that arises from [the thought], "They are practitioners of the Dhamma, practitioners of the right way," and so forth;
or else, they do not consider those [monks] to be worthy of being heard or trusted. And likewise regarding the Dhamma and the Teacher...
And they become indeed non-devout. "The change of state in some" refers to the alteration of the confidence of worldlings (*puthujjana*) whose faith has not yet matured.
In the verse, regarding the terms *āpāyika* and so forth: one is called *āpāyika* because of being subject to rebirth in a state of misery (*apāya*).

Furthermore, because one arises in the great hell known as Avīci, one is called *nerayika*. Because one remains there for the full duration of one intermediate eon (*antarakappa*), one is so designated.

One who stands for an eon is a *kappaṭṭha*. One who delights in a faction known as a schism in the Saṅgha is one who "delights in factions" (*vaggarata*). That which is contrary to the Dhamma is "unrighteousness" (*adhamma*).
And because he stands in that very unrighteousness known as a schism in the Saṅgha through the grounds for causing division, he is one who "stands in unrighteousness" (*adhammaṭṭha*).

"He falls away from security from bondage" means he falls away and declines from what is beneficial—the security from bondage—or, alternatively, from Arahantship, which is called "security from bondage" because it is free from affliction by the four bonds (*yoga*).

And as for Nibbāna, there is nothing whatsoever to be said regarding its loss. Because of the commonality of their view and virtue, in the sense of being united, he [the schismatic] splits the Saṅgha;
and because of that very unity, it is harmonious and concordant through the application of the formal acts (*ekakamma*) and so forth.

"Having split" means having divided by means of a schism in the Saṅgha characterized as previously described. "An aeon" (*kappa*) refers here to a life-span aeon (*āyukappa*), but in this context, it is specifically an intermediate aeon (*antarakappa*). "In hell" means in the Great Avīci Hell.
The commentary on the eighth sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Saṅghasāmaggī Sutta. 19.
In the ninth [sutta], "one thing" (*ekadhamma*) means one wholesome thing, a blameless thing. [It is taught] by such passages as, "This is the Dhamma; this is not the Dhamma. etc.
If a dispute should arise in the Saṅgha, one who is wise and desires the Dhamma should reflect thus:
"It is indeed possible that this dispute, as it increases, may lead to a schism in the Saṅgha or even to a formal split in the Saṅgha.
If one stands upholding that legal issue oneself, like one who has stepped into a fire—

One must suddenly retreat from there as if in fear. Then, if others have taken up that dispute and one is personally able to settle it, one should become resolute and go even a great distance to act in such a way that it is settled.
However, if one is not personally able to do so, and that dispute continues to increase further and further without being settled, those who are there—
There are fellow practitioners who are worthy and desirous of training;
having encouraged them, that legal issue should be settled in such a way that it is resolved according to the Dhamma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Teacher’s instruction.
For one who settles it in this manner, that skillful quality which brings about harmony in the Saṅgha is intended here as "the one quality. Indeed, it belongs to both sides.
For the monks who have become full of doubt, for the nuns who stand following them, for the laymen and laywomen,
and for their protective deities— even up to the Brahmās— it serves as the cause for a great mass of merit and a flow of wholesome results by removing that which is harmful,
painful, and subject to defilement, and thus it is worthy of arising even among the Brahmās throughout the world with its devas.
He brings benefit and happiness to the world. Therefore it was said: “Bhikkhus, one thing, when it arises in the world, arises for the welfare of many people,” and so forth.
Its meaning should be understood by way of the reverse of what was stated in the immediately preceding sutta.
“Harmony in the Saṅgha” (saṅghasāmaggī) means the state of being united in the Saṅgha, the absence of schism, and the commonality of action and the commonality of recitation.
In this verse, "harmony in the Saṅgha is happiness" is said because harmony is a condition for happiness, just as it is said, "The arising of Buddhas is happiness.
"Favoring those who are harmonious" means supporting those who are in harmony by rejoicing in their harmony;
it is an act of favoring that accords with harmony, a holding and establishing them in such a way that they do not abandon their harmony.

The meaning is "granting further support. "Having made the Saṅgha harmonious" means having made the divided Saṅgha—whether it had reached a state of schism or was merely discordant—unified and reconciled.

"For an aeon" refers specifically to the full span of a lifespan. "He rejoices in heaven" means that in the world of the devas of the sense-sphere, having surpassed other gods in ten respects, he experiences divine bliss through the very fulfillment of his wishes.
"He rejoices, exults, dallies, and plays.
The commentary on the ninth sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Paduṭṭhacitta-sutta*.
20. What is the origin of the tenth chapter? It is indeed an occasion for instruction (*aṭṭhuppatti*). One day, it is said, the monks sat together in the Hall of Dharma and raised this discussion:

"Friends, here some person performs much meritorious karma, another performs much evil karma, and another performs both mixed together. In that case, what is the future destiny of one who performs the mixed kind?"
Then the Teacher, having approached the Hall of Dharma and sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared for him, heard that conversation.
Perceiving that "monks, at the time of death, one with a defiled mind may expect a miserable rebirth," he taught this discourse on this occasion.
In this context, *idha* is a particle used as a designation for a location. Sometimes it is used with reference to a specific place, as in such passages as:
“While I was standing right here, having become a deva. Sometimes it is used with reference to the Teaching (*sāsana*), as in:
“Right here, monks, is the ascetic; right here is the second ascetic. And sometimes it is used merely to fill out the meter, as in: “Here, monks, I...”
In such passages as "he would have eaten and been invited," it refers to the world; for example, in "here a Tathāgata arises in the world," and so forth.
Here too, it should be understood as referring to the world alone. "Ekaccaṃ" means one; the sense is "one or another. "Puggalaṃ" means a being (*satta*).
For he [the person] is so called because, according to conditions, he fills (*pūraṇa*) wholesome and unwholesome states and their respective results through the process of dying.
And because of his lapse, he is called a "person. "With a corrupted mind" means a mind corrupted by malice (*padosa*) or resentment (*āghāta*).
Alternatively, "with a corrupted mind" means a mind defiled by hatred (*dosa*) or by lust (*rāga*) and so forth.
And here, the term "certain one" (*ekacca*) is an epithet for the person with the corrupted mind; for he is so described as one whose rebirth-giving karma has found its opportunity.
And for one whose mind cannot be turned back from the occurrence of unwholesome states and brought down toward the wholesome—such is one whose death is imminent.
The word "evam" (thus) shows the manner that is now to be described. "Cetasā" means by one's own mind, by means of the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*).

"Ceto" means the mind of that person. "Paricca" means having delimited [it], I understand it. But is this not [the domain] of the knowledge of the destination according to deeds (*yathākammupaga-ñāṇa*)?
"Is it an object? Yes, this is true; however, this was said with reference to the unwholesome consciousness occurring at that time.

"And at this time" means at this moment, or within this assembly of conditions; the meaning is that this person might pass away after the stage of the impulsion (javana) process. For there is no passing away during the moment of impulsion itself. "As carried" (yathābhataṃ)...
"Cast thus into hell" means that just as something is placed there after being brought from elsewhere, so too one is cast into hell and established therein by one's own karma;
this is the meaning. "With the breaking up of the body" means with the relinquishing of the aggregates that have been grasped.
"After death" means immediately thereafter, upon the seizing of the newly produced aggregates. Alternatively, "with the breaking up of the body" [is explained as follows:]...
"By the cutting off of the life-faculty. "Beyond death" means after the moment of death (*cuti*).
"The states of loss" (*apāya*) and so forth are all synonyms for hell (*niraya*). For hell is called "the state of loss" (*apāya*) because it is devoid of the pleasure known as "gain" (*aya*);

or alternatively, it is called "the state of loss" because it is devoid of "gains" (*aya*)—that is, merit—which are the causes for heaven and liberation. It is "the destination of suffering" and "the refuge of suffering."
It is a "bad destination" (*duggati*). Alternatively, it is a "bad destination" because it is a state produced by defiled action due to an abundance of hatred.
It is a "fall into ruin" (*vinipāta*) because those who have committed evil deeds fall into it helplessly, or because they fall into it while their limbs and members are being shattered.

It is a "hell" (*niraya*) in the sense of being devoid of enjoyment (*nirassāda*), for there is no "essence" (*āya*) here that can be termed a gratification. Or else, by the inclusion of the term "state of deprivation" (*apāya*):
The animal realm (*tiracchānayoni*) is so called because it is a state of loss (*apāya*) due to being departed from a happy destination (*sugati*);

however, it is not a miserable destination (*duggati*), since beings such as powerful nāga kings can be born there. By the term "miserable destination," the sphere of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*) is meant;

for that is both a state of loss and a miserable destination because it is departed from a happy destination and is a place of suffering. Yet it is not a downfall (*vinipāta*), because it does not share the same nature of downfall as the asura realm.
By the inclusion of "the states of ruin" (vinipāta), the host of asuras is meant. For that, in the sense already described, is both a state of loss (apāya) and an unhappy destination (duggati);
and because it has fallen away from all heights of excellence, it is called "ruin" (vinipāta). By the inclusion of "hell" (niraya), various types of hell such as Avīci and others are meant.
However, here, by all the terms used, only hell is intended. "They are reborn" (upapajjanti) means they take rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
Among the verses, the first verse was established by the Elders of the Dhamma Council at the time of the First Council. *Ñatvāna* (having known) denotes an action occurring in the past.
For an explanation is preceded by knowledge. Alternatively, the suffix *-tvā* has the sense of a cause (*hetu*), as in the expression "fear arises upon seeing a lion," meaning "because of knowing.
*Buddho bhikkhūnaṃ santike*: the Buddha, the Blessed One, [spoke] in the presence of the bhikkhus.
He explained the meaning of this as it was being spoken in the two following verses. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the tenth sutta is finished.
The commentary on the second chapter is finished.
3. Third Chapter. 1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Serene Mind (Pasannacittasutta). 21.
In the first [discourse] of the third chapter, "serene mind" means [a mind serene] through faith in the Triple Gem and faith in the results of kamma.
And with a mind full of confidence. *Sugatiṃ* means a beautiful destination (*sundaraṃ gatiṃ*), or the destination of happiness (*sukhassa vā gatiṃ*).

*Saggaṃ* means a supreme place (*suṭṭhu aggaṃ*) due to its excellence in forms and other qualities. *Lokaṃ* refers to that wherein the fruits of merit and demerit are experienced (*lokīyanti*), or it is called *loka* in the sense of being subject to destruction (*lujjanaṭṭhena*).
And here, by the mention of "a happy destination" (*sugatiggahaṇena*), the human destination is also included; by the mention of "heaven" (*saggaggahaṇena*), [the celestial realms are included].
The destiny is indeed that of the gods. The remainder is exactly as explained in the method stated below.
The commentary on the first sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Mettā-sutta.
22. In the second [instance], "Do not, monks, [say] 'merits'" (*mā, bhikkhave, puññānan*): here, *mā* is a particle used as a prohibition.
The word *puñña* occurs in reference to the fruit of merit in such passages as, "Monks, it is because of undertaking wholesome states that this merit increases.
It also occurs in such passages as, "Monks, when a person immersed in ignorance performs a meritorious formation (*puñña-saṅkhāra*)."

In such passages as “consciousness leads to merit,” it refers to the rebirth-existence (upapattibhava) that constitutes a specific form of a happy destination within the realms of sense-sphere and fine-material sphere.

In such passages as “Monks, there are these three bases for meritorious action: the basis for meritorious action consisting in giving, the basis for meritorious action consisting in virtue, and the basis for meritorious action consisting in meditation,” it refers to wholesome volition (kusalacetanā). But here, however—

It should be understood as wholesome states belonging to the three planes. Regarding the phrase "he was afraid," there are two kinds of fear here: the fear of knowledge (*ñāṇabhaya*) and the fear of trepidation (*sārajjabhaya*).

In this context: "Bhikkhus, even those gods who are long-lived, beautiful, abundant in happiness, and dwell for a long time in lofty palaces—even they, upon hearing the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, for the most part experience fear, agitation, and terror..."

The fear of knowledge (*ñāṇabhaya*) is that which appears in such passages as "falling into [fear]"; the fear of trepidation (*sārajjabhaya*) is that which appears in such passages as "there was indeed fear, there was trembling, there was horripilation.

Here too, it is precisely the fear of trepidation. This is the meaning here: "Monks, for a long time you have practiced restraint of body and speech, fulfilled the duties of conduct and counter-conduct, observed the single seat, the single bed, the taming of the sense faculties, and the ascetic virtues (*dhutadhamma*)."

"Do not fear, do not fall into terror or dread, because of the fear that some pleasant state in this very life might be obstructed by those merits which must be practiced continuously by a bhikkhu— such as the restraint of the mind, mindfulness and clear comprehension,
and the exertion of energy through application to the meditation subject— which bestow the bliss of Nibbāna in the future world."
"Do not fear on account of merits. Here, this is the genitive case used in the sense of the ablative (*nissakka*).
Now, showing the reason why one should not fear from that [merit], he says, "Of this happiness," and so forth.

In that context, the word *sukha* occurs in the sense of the root of happiness, as in such passages as, "The arising of Buddhas is a happiness; dispassion toward the world is a happiness. And because...
In such passages as, "Mahāli, form is pleasant, followed by pleasure, immersed in pleasure," it refers to a pleasant object (*sukhārammaṇa*).
In such passages as, "To this extent, monks, it is not easy to reach by description how far the heavens are pleasant," it refers to the state of being a condition for pleasure (*sukhapaccayaṭṭhāna*).

In such passages as, "The accumulation of merit is pleasant," it refers to the cause of pleasure (*sukhahetu*). In such passages as, "These states are dwellings pleasant in the present life," it refers to...
In the phrase "free from affliction" (*abyāpajje*), it refers to non-affliction. In passages such as "Nirvana is the supreme happiness," it refers to Nirvana.

In passages such as "With the abandoning of pleasure," it refers to pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*). In passages such as "Neither-painful-nor-pleasant, being peaceful, is indeed spoken of as happiness," it refers to the feeling of equanimity (*upekkhāvedanā*).
In passages such as "Ānanda, both feelings have been described by me in a figurative sense as pleasant feeling and painful feeling," [it refers to those two].

“In desirable pleasure”: in such passages as “The result of merit is pleasant,” it refers to a pleasant ripening (*vipāka*). Here too, it should be understood as referring specifically to a desirable ripening.
Regarding the phrases beginning with “of the desirable” (*iṭṭhassa*): it is “desirable” because it is to be sought after and because it is the opposite of the undesirable;

it is “lovely” (*kantassa*) because it is desirable, because it is desired by the mind, and because it enters [the mind]; it is “dear” (*piyassa*) because it is to be cherished and because it brings satisfaction; it is [“pleasing”] because it is to be honored by the mind...
The meaning should be understood as "because it increases what is agreeable. Regarding the phrase "these are merits" (*puññāni*):
this expression "merits" is a designation and a name for pleasant, desirable fruition;

he speaks of the cause by means of its effect through the metaphorical identification of the fruit with the cause when he says, "that which is merit is indeed happiness. Thus, the fruit of merits performed and accumulated is necessarily certain to occur.
Having heard this, he exhorts them to perform meritorious deeds with diligence and respect, and inspires in them a sense of earnestness toward such merit-making.
Now, [he reveals] that which was experienced for a long time through the meritorious deed performed by himself during the time of Sunetta, though concealed by the interval between existences.
Having described the most exalted ripening of merit (*puññavipāka*), he spoke the passage beginning with “I recall indeed” in order to make that matter clear.
Therein, “I recall” (*abhijānāmi*) means I know by means of distinguished knowledge; I realize it through direct experience.
“For a long time” (*dīgharattaṃ*) means for a long period. “Of merits” (*puññānaṃ*) refers to wholesome states such as giving and so forth. “Seven years” (*satta vassāni*) means seven full years.

*Mettā* means that which is "moistened" (*mijjati*) by a mind of loving-kindness; the meaning is that it "becomes smooth" (*siniyhati*). It is called *mettā* because it exists in a friend (*mitte bhavā*), or because it is the activity of a friend (*mittassa esā pavatti*).

From the perspective of its characteristics and so forth, however, its characteristic is the manifestation in the mode of welfare (*hitākārappavatti-lakkhaṇā*). Its function is the promotion of welfare (*hitūpasaṃhāra-rasā*). Its manifestation is the removal of ill-will (*āghātavinaya-paccupaṭṭhānā*).

Its proximate cause is the perception of beings as being agreeable (*manāpabhāva-dassana-padaṭṭhānā*). The perfection of this [virtue] is the pacification of ill-will (*byāpādūpasama*). Its non-occurrence is the absence of affection (*sinehāsambhava*).

"Vipatti" means failure. That which possesses this [failure] is "mettā-citta" (the mind of loving-kindness). "Having developed" means having both produced and increased the mind accompanied by loving-kindness;
here, "concentration" is expressed by the term "mind," thus it refers to the concentration of loving-kindness, the divine abode of loving-kindness (*mettā-brahmavihāra*).

"Seven eons of dissolution and evolution" refers to seven great eons (*mahākappa*). By the mention of dissolution and evolution, the periods of stability during dissolution and the periods of stability during evolution are also included.
“Seized. “This world” means the world of sense-desire (*kāmaloka*). “While it is collapsing, indeed” means while it is being destroyed;
*suda* is merely a particle, meaning “while it is perishing. Some also read “*saṃvattamāne sudaṃ*. “In an aeon” means in time;
for by the term “aeon,” time is expressed. When time is exhausted, the aeon itself is exhausted as well. As it has been said:
“Time devours all beings, including itself.
Because it was said, “May I go to the Ābhassara realm,” the emergence of the eon here should be understood by way of the fire dissolution.
“May I go to the Ābhassara realm” means: may I go to the Ābhassara Brahmā-world by way of taking rebirth-linking there.
"I go to the Abhassara realm. "Vivaṭṭamāne" means while it is being established; the meaning is "while it is being born. "I am reborn in the empty Brahma-palace":
it is "empty" because of the absence of any other being who has been reborn there.

That Brahma-palace, which is designated as the plane of the first jhāna and was produced at the very beginning, is that which I "approach" (upapajjāmi) or reach by way of taking rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). "Brahmā" [means...]

He is a *brahmā* in the sense that his qualities have been developed in various ways to the highest degree among beings of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), and in the sense that he has arisen from the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
He is a "Great Brahmā" (*mahābrahmā*) because he is greater than the Brahma-parisajja and Brahma-purohita deities.

For that very reason, because he stands having overcome them, he is "the Overcomer" (*abhibhū*). Because he is not overcome by any quality whatsoever on their part, he is "Unconquered" (*anabhibhūta*).
*Aññadatthu* is a particle used for emphasis. *Daso* means one who has the habit of seeing; he is capable of seeing the past, future, and present. The meaning is:
"By means of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), I see that which is to be seen. Regarding the remaining Brahmās, it should be connected thus:
"By the power of the development of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), I bring my own mind under my control; thus I am a 'controller' (*vasavattī*). At that time, it is said, the Bodhisatta...

Although he was an attainer of the eight meditative absorptions (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*), observing the welfare of beings and the fulfillment of his own perfections (*pāramī*), he conceived a preference for those two specific levels of jhāna and wandered from one existence to another by way of the divine abode of loving-kindness (*mettā-brahmavihāra*).
Therefore it is said: "For seven years... [and so on]... a master of his own will."

Having thus demonstrated the greatness of the ripening of merit pertaining to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), the Blessed One now spoke the words beginning with “thirty-six times” in order to show that same quality of the merit pertaining to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).

Therein, “he was Sakka” means that for thirty-six successive occasions, without being reborn elsewhere, he was continuously Sakka, the Lord of the Devas, the king of the Tāvatiṃsa gods. Regarding the phrases “he was a king,” and so forth:
He is called a *rājā* (king) because he delights the world with four wonderful qualities and the four bases of sympathy.

He is a *cakkavattī* (wheel-turning monarch) because he sets the wheel-treasure in motion, he himself proceeds by means of the four wheels of prosperity, he causes others to proceed by those same means, and because in him there is the turning of the wheels of postures for the benefit of others.
Here, "king" (*rājā*) is the general term, while "wheel-turner" (*cakkavattī*) is the specific one. By righteousness (*dhammena*).

"He acts according to the Dhamma" means he conducts himself by way of the right method and justice; thus the meaning is "one who acts according to the Dhamma. Having obtained sovereignty through the Dhamma alone, he has become a king;

thus he is a "Dhamma-king" (dhammarāja). Alternatively, he is "righteous" (dhammika) because of his practice of the Dhamma for the welfare of others, and a "Dhamma-king" because of his practice of the Dhamma for his own welfare.
He is "ruler of the four quarters" (cāturanta) because he is the lord over the earth bounded by the four oceans and adorned with the four kinds of islands.
The meaning is "lord. He is a conqueror (*vijitāvī*) because he has conquered his internal adversaries, such as anger, and all external kings, by means that are neither punitive nor violent.
He has attained stability and steadfastness in his kingdom; it is not possible for anyone to shake him from that state.
Or, the kingdom has attained stability under him—it is firmly established, devoted to its own duties, intent on its work, immovable, and unshakable.

Having attained sovereignty over the realm, he is "endowed with the seven treasures" because he is possessed of these seven treasures: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure. Among these:
For indeed, O King, a wheel-turning monarch conquers what is unconquered by means of the Wheel-treasure; he traverses the conquered realm with ease by means of the Elephant and Horse-treasures;
he protects the conquered territory by means of the Counsellor-treasure; and he enjoys the pleasure of luxury by means of the remaining treasures.

Of these, the first involves the application of the power of energy, while the last involves the application of the power of counsel; [the others involve] the Elephant, Horse, and Householder-treasures.
The application of the three types of power is perfectly fulfilled; this is the fruit of the application of the three powers through women, gems, and jewels.

He experiences the pleasure of enjoyment (*paribhogasukha*) by means of women, gems, and jewels, and the pleasure of utility (*upabhogasukha*) by means of the remaining [possessions]. Specifically, for him, the first three succeed through the influence of kamma produced by the wholesome root of non-hatred (*adosa*);

the middle three through the influence of kamma produced by the wholesome root of non-greed (*alobha*); and the final one through the influence of kamma produced by the wholesome root of non-delusion (*amoha*).
"It should be understood as 'of regional sovereignty' means of a minor kingdom.
"This occurred" refers to what occurred during his final period as a wheel-turning monarch while he was reflecting upon his own successes, beginning with:
"Of what deed of mine is this the fruit? This happened throughout every single existence.
This was indeed so. Herein, this is the application according to the time of a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti*).

"Possessing such great psychic power" means he is thus powerful by virtue of his excellence in the transport of treasures—headed by the jewel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, and so forth—and by his attainment of stability over the realm.

"Possessing such great majesty" means that through his possession of the wheel-treasure and the rest, without causing affliction to anyone, his commands are received with bowed heads by all kings, and he travels with great splendor.
Thus it is of great power. "Of giving" means of the relinquishing of objects fit for donation, such as food and so forth.
"Of self-control" means both the taming of the sense faculties, such as the eye, and the taming of the defilements such as lust by means of concentration.

"Of restraint" means restraint of body and speech. In that context, the taming of the defilements by means of concentration is merit consisting of mental development (*bhāvanāmaya*); and that specifically takes the form of the divine abode of loving-kindness (*mettā-brahmavihāra*).

This is what is intended here. And regarding that [meditative attainment] which is twofold—distinguished as access (upacāra) and absorption (appanā)—it was by means of that which had reached absorption that his rebirth occurred in the two aforementioned planes of jhāna.
By the other threefold [attainment], however, he attained, as appropriate, the status of a Wheel-turning Monarch and so forth; this should be understood.
Thus, having made himself a personal witness and demonstrated the greatness of the ripening of merits, the Blessed One now [expounds] that very same matter...
Showing this by means of a verse, he said, “Puññameva...,” and so forth. Therein, “He should train only in merit”:

the meaning is that a clansman who desires his own welfare should train in, establish, accumulate, and generate only the threefold wholesome—what is called “merit” because it produces the fruit of merit and because it purifies (punati) one’s own continuum. “Āyataggaṃ” [means...]
It is "the foremost in its course" (*āyatagga*) because it has vast fruit and sublime fruit; or, because its fruit is pleasant and agreeable, it is "foremost in the future" (*āyati*);
or, because of the most sublime course—namely, the conditions such as wise attention—it is "the summit" (*agga*). The letter *ta* serves to facilitate the euphonic junction (*sandhi*) of words.
