take cessation as their object, and perform, respectively, the functions of correctly placing, embracing, originating, purifying, exerting, establishing, and concentrating the co-nascent states.

And they perform [their functions]—thus it is according to the analysis of their functions. Right View, which in the preliminary stage occurs at different moments and has suffering and so forth as its respective objects, becomes at the time of the Path a single-moment state;
having Nibbāna alone as its object, it receives the four names beginning with "knowledge of suffering" according to its function.
Right Intention and the others also, which in the preliminary stage occur at different moments and have various objects, [become so at the time of the Path].
They share a single moment and a single object; among them, right intention receives three names—“intention of renunciation,” and so forth—by way of its function.

The three beginning with right speech, which in the prior stage consist of both abstinence (virati) and volition (cetanā) according to their divisions such as “abstaining from false speech,” at the moment of the Path become abstinences alone. Right effort and right mindfulness [receive their names] by way of their functions as the right exertions and the foundations of mindfulness.
They receive four names. Right concentration, however, is different at the moment of the path according to the first jhāna and so forth;

thus it is distinguished by its occurrence in the prior and subsequent stages. Furthermore, it is distinguished by the method of development, as in: “Here, monks, a monk develops right view dependent on seclusion,” and so forth. In this regard, what is the eightfold path? Here—
“Bhikkhu, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna... [as before] ...difficult in practice and slow in direct knowledge, at that time there is the eightfold path:
right view, right intention,” and so forth—thus, through eighty-four thousand divisions of methods, the Blessed One’s knowledges for elucidating the noble path proceed in manifold ways.

Because he does not deceive regarding the goal (*attha*), all [his words] are suchness (*tatha*), non-false, and not otherwise; thus, because the Blessed One has come (*āgata*) as suchness, he is the Tathāgata.

Likewise, with respect to the attainment of the first *jhāna* and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), in the sense that one should dwell and enter these in successive order, and by way of accomplishing and reviewing the attainments of successive dwellings (*anupubbavihārasamāpatti*), etc.
The knowledges of the Blessed One that proceed by way of appropriate conjunctions are, for the sake of accomplishing that purpose, such, not otherwise, and not different.
Thus also, because the Blessed One has come (āgata) to what is such (tathā), he is the Tathāgata.
Likewise, there is his unerring knowledge of the cause and non-cause of various fruits, [knowing] "this is the proper occasion for this, this is not the proper occasion. Of these...
It is the knowledge, exactly as it is, of the ripening of the undertaking of kamma—divided into past and other periods—of those beings without exception;
the knowledge, at the very moment of accumulation, of the distinction between kamma with and without taints for each respective being, such that one knows truly: "This is the path leading to hell...
[and so on]... this is the path leading to Nibbāna"; and the knowledge of the manifold natures of the aggregates and bases, whether clung-to or not clung-to.

And as for the diversity of that world: it is the knowledge, according to reality, of the diversity of elements (*dhātu-nānatta*) by way of such principles as, "Because this particular element is predominant, this specific distinction arises in this continuity of phenomena (*dhamma-pabandha*)," etc.; the knowledge of the sharpness and flexibility of the faculties such as faith;

the knowledge of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), liberations (*vimokkha*), and so forth, together with their defilements (*saṃkilesa*) and other factors; and [the knowledge] of beings within immeasurable...
These ten powers of knowledge of the Blessed One consist of: (1) the complete knowledge of the continuity of aggregates in previous existences together with their connections across births;

(2) the knowledge of death and rebirth along with the distinctions of inferiority and so forth; and (3) the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths according to the method explained below, beginning with "This is suffering.
These are so called because they penetrate their respective objects without fail and accomplish the intended purpose.
And because of his conduct in accordance with reality, those things are such, not otherwise, and not different. For it has been said:
“Here, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible,” and so forth.
Thus also, the Blessed One is the Tathāgata because he has come (āgata) to that which is such (tathā).

And just as by way of these knowledges, so too, because the Blessed One has come to— that is, attained— those such knowledges consisting of the specific types of wisdom that are unique to him and not shared with others,
such as the knowledge that analyzes the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, and so forth, which have the aforementioned infinite and immeasurable divisions,
he is therefore called the Tathāgata; thus, "he has come to those things as they truly are" (tathāni āgato), and for this reason he is the Tathāgata.

How is he a *Tathāgata* because he has "thus gone" (*tathā-gata*)? Those things of the Blessed One—namely, his noble birth, his full enlightenment, his proclamation of the Dhamma and Vinaya, and the element of Nibbāna without residue—are "thus" (*tathā*).

What is meant by this? Because they are not deceptive due to the absolute accomplishment of that purpose for which they were aspired to and set in motion by the Lord of the World, and because they function with an unerring meaning, they are thus, not otherwise, and not different. Thus...
For this Blessed One, while still a bodhisatta, having fulfilled all the causes for Buddhahood described above—

beginning with the perfection of the thirty pāramīs— while dwelling in the Tusita heaven, heard the "uproar of the Buddhas" as the devas of the ten thousand world-systems gathered together and approached him.
“The time has come for you, Great Hero, to arise in a mother’s womb;
crossing over the world including the devas, awaken to the deathless state.
Thus entreated, he who had previously manifested the signs of his arising performed the five great observations, and [considered]: “Now, in the human womb...”
Having conceived the thought, "I shall arise and attain full enlightenment," he took rebirth on the full moon of Āsāḷha in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā within the Sakyan royal family.
After being nurtured with great honor by gods and humans for ten months,
he reached his birth at dawn on the full moon of Visākha.
At the moment of his noble birth, however, just as at the moment of his conception, thirty-two omens appeared;
this ten-thousandfold world system quaked, trembled, and shook violently; an immeasurable radiance pervaded ten thousand world-systems;
and the blind, as if desiring to behold that glory, regained their sight.
The deaf heard sounds, the mute spoke, the hunchbacked became straight-limbed, the lame regained the power of walking on their feet,
all beings who were in bondage were released from their fetters and bonds, the fires in all the hells were extinguished,
hunger and thirst were stilled in the realm of the hungry ghosts (pettivisaya), and fear ceased for the animals; thus it was for all sentient beings.
Disease was stilled; all beings became pleasant-spoken; horses neighed with sweet tones, elephants trumpeted, and all musical instruments emitted their respective sounds without being struck;
even the hand-ornaments and other jewelry of human beings emitted sweet sounds without being struck; and all directions became serene for sentient beings.
As he was producing bliss, a soft, cool breeze blew; unseasonable clouds rained down; water burst forth from the earth and overflowed;
birds abandoned their flight through the sky; rivers stood still without flowing; the waters of the great ocean became sweet;
and while the sun shone free from all impurities, all the luminaries in the sky likewise blazed forth.
There was light; with the exception of the gods of the formless realm (*arūpāvacara*), all other gods and all those in the hells became visible in form.
Trees, walls, doors, mountains, and so forth became non-obstructive. There was no passing away or rebirth among sentient beings.
Overpowering all unpleasant odors, a divine fragrance wafted abroad, and all fruit-bearing trees were laden with fruit.
They blossomed, and the great ocean became entirely covered over by five-colored lotuses;
all flowers, both land-born and water-born, bloomed; on the trunks of trees, trunk-lotuses; on the branches, branch-lotuses;
and on the creepers, creeper-lotuses bloomed; and having split open the surface of the earth and the surfaces of rocks, [they appeared] one above another.
Seven by seven, stalks of lotuses named Daṇḍapaduma emerged; hanging lotuses appeared suspended in the sky;
a rain of flowers fell on all sides; and divine musical instruments resounded in the air.

The entire ten-thousandfold world system was like a mass of garlands cast down after being wound around, or like a cluster of garlands spread out after being pressed together, fully adorned and prepared.
Like a garland-seat, it was adorned with a single garland, fanned by waving yak-tail whisks, perfumed with flowers, incense, and scents, and attained the highest excellence of beauty;
and those portents were indeed signs of the many distinguished attainments that would subsequently be achieved.
Thus, this birth was accompanied by the manifestation of many wonders for the purpose for which it occurred.
That which was aspired for, for the sake of the absolute accomplishment of his perfect enlightenment, occurred exactly so—true, not false, and not otherwise.
Likewise, all those who were to be disciplined by a Buddha, the kinsmen among those to be awakened, were themselves entirely disciplined by the Blessed One without exception.
And those who were to be disciplined by disciples or by the Dhamma, they too, being disciplined by the disciples and others, come to be disciplined.
"And they will go" means that for the sake of which the Blessed One aspired to full enlightenment, the attainment of that goal was through his full enlightenment exactly as it is,
not otherwise, and not differently. Moreover,
whatever intrinsic nature of each knowable phenomenon (ñeyyadhamma) was to be awakened to, each of those was like an *āmalaka* fruit placed in the palm of the hand.
Furthermore, it is "thus" because the Blessed One has perfectly awakened to all things without error, by means of his own knowledge which is connected merely to the act of adverting [the mind]. Thus,
the manner in which those various phenomena are to be taught in their respective ways, and for those various beings— [that too is thus].

Having correctly observed the underlying tendencies (*āsaya*), latent dispositions (*anusaya*), conduct (*cariyā*), and inclinations (*adhimutti*), and having—without deviating from the nature of phenomena (*dhammatā*) nor overstepping the mere conventional mode of designation (*paññatti-naya*)—clarified that very nature of phenomena, the Blessed One instructed according to the offense, according to the disposition, and according to the Dhamma;
thus were those to be trained (*veneyya*) disciplined and brought to the plane of the Noble Ones (*ariya-bhūmi*). This is his wisdom in the proclamation of the Dhamma and Vinaya.
It is "thus" (tathā) because it is accomplished for that purpose and functions according to reality; thus it is non-false and non-otherwise.

That which was attained by the Blessed One—the contact, feeling, and so forth, pertaining to earth and the rest, which is free from the nature of both the material and the immaterial, transcends the worldly nature due to the absence of the state of breaking up and dissolving, and because it is dissociated from darkness, it cannot be illuminated by anything, precisely because of the absence of worldly nature.
The great deathless element of Nibbāna, which is devoid of the states of existence such as the realms of rebirth, is without foundation and without object;
because there is not even a trace of the clinging known as the aggregates, it is also called "without residue" (*anupādisesa*). With reference to this, it was said:
"Bhikkhus, there is that base where there is neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air, nor the base of infinite space..."
“Neither the base of infinite consciousness, nor the base of nothingness, nor the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
neither this world nor the other world, nor both the moon and the sun. Of that, monks, I say there is no coming, no going, no staying, no passing away, and no arising.
It is without foundation, without occurrence, and without an object; this indeed is the end of suffering.”
It is the subsiding of all aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), the stilling of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), the relinquishing of all acquisitions (*upadhi*),
the pacification of all suffering, the eradication of all attachments (*ālaya*), the cutting off of all rounds of existence (*vaṭṭa*), and it has the characteristic of absolute peace.
Because it never fails to correspond to the aforementioned intrinsic nature, it is "thus" (*tathā*) and "not otherwise" (*avitathā*).
Not otherwise. Thus, because he has gone to, approached, attained, practiced, and reached these [states] beginning with the higher births (*abhijāti*), he is the Tathāgata.
In this way, the Blessed One is the Tathāgata as one who has "gone thus" (*tathā gata*).
How is he the Tathāgata as one who is "of such a kind" (*tathāvidha*)? Just as the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones were of such a kind, so too is this Blessed One.
"Of such a kind. What is meant? Just as those Blessed Ones were endowed with the virtue of the path, the virtue of the fruit, and all mundane and supramundane virtue;
with the concentration of the path, the concentration of the fruit, and all mundane and supramundane concentration;
with the wisdom of the path, the wisdom of the fruit, and all mundane and supramundane wisdom—[to be] utilized daily...
In brief, by means of the twenty-four hundred thousand millions of abidings in meditative attainments, and by way of liberation through that factor (*tadaṅga-vimutti*),

suppression-liberation (*vikkhambhana-vimutti*), eradication-liberation (*samuccheda-vimutti*), subsidence-liberation (*paṭippassaddhi-vimutti*), and escape-liberation (*nissaraṇa-vimutti*); and in detail,
by means of all the qualities of omniscience with their inconceivable power and infinite, immeasurable divisions— this too is our [refuge].
The Blessed One was such as this. For among all the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, there may be variation due to these five variations:
variation in lifespan, variation in the size of the physical body, variation in lineage, variation in the practice of austerities, and variation in the radiance of rays;
however, there is no variation in their purity regarding the purification of virtue and so forth, nor in their practice of serenity and insight.
Furthermore, there is no difference whatsoever among the qualities they have penetrated;

rather, like gold broken into pieces, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are indistinguishable from one another. Therefore, just as the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones were, so too is this Blessed One.
Because he is "thus" (tathā), he is the Tathāgata. And here, the word *gata* has the sense of "being" (*vidha*).
For indeed, worldly people explain the word *vidhūta* as having the sense of "manner" (*pakāra*).

How is he the Tathāgata? Because the Blessed One is endowed with supernatural power (*iddhānubhāva*) that is not shared by others, because he has attained the highest perfection of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) such as the analysis of meaning (*attha*), and because of his acquisition of unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*).
Because there is no obstruction anywhere regarding the activity of the body and so forth, he has gone (gata) in such a way (tathā) according to his wish;
thus, the activity of body, speech, and mind is his, and for this reason he is the Tathāgata. Thus, he is the Tathāgata because he proceeds in such a way.
How is he the Tathāgata because he has not gone (agata) in such ways (tathā)? In the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment, [he has not gone] toward the occurrence of their opposites...

There is no destination for him, thus he is "un-gone" (*agata*). Furthermore, this state of being un-gone is understood through those very knowledges that proceed by way of the correct contemplation of the disadvantages and advantages regarding stinginess, the perfection of giving, and so forth; therefore, he is the "Tathāgata" because he has gone by means of such knowledges.

Alternatively, [he is the Tathāgata] because he has gone to the cessation of the five aggregates—whether characterized as the occurrence of defilements and volitional formations, or simply as the occurrence of the aggregates themselves—in all five [realms].
He is "not gone" (*agata*) because there is no further going for him among the realms of existence (*gati*).

This state of his being "not gone"—due to the attainment of *nibbāna* with remainder and without remainder—is reached by means of the knowledge of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga-ñāṇa*); thus, in this sense also, the Blessed One is a "Tathāgata" because he has come (*āgata*) by means of what is real (*tatha*).
How is he a "Tathāgata" by way of the state of a Tathāgata? "By way of the state of a Tathāgata" means by way of the actual presence (*sabbhāva*) of a Tathāgata.
"Because of his existence" is the meaning. But who is this Tathāgata, because of whose existence the Blessed One is called "Tathāgata"?

It is the True Dhamma (Saddhamma). For as far as the Noble Path (ariyamagga) is concerned, the True Dhamma has "gone" (gata) in the sense of having been traversed by means of abandonment through complete eradication, just as it is to be gone to by one who utterly destroys the faction of all defilements (kilesa) through the power of the yoke-bound pair of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). As for the Dhamma of the Fruit (phala), it has "gone" in the sense of having reached its own...
It is to be gone by means of the path in accordance with its course, through the subsiding and abandoning [of defilements]; thus having gone, it proceeds.
But as for the Dhamma of Nibbāna, when it has been gone to—that is, penetrated by wisdom—it results in the pacification of all the suffering of saṃsāra;

since it was thus gone to and realized by the Buddha and others, he is called the Tathāgata. The Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti) also, just as it was [taught] by previous Buddhas by way of discourses, verses, and so forth...

Furthermore, because he has proceeded in accordance with the dispositions and so forth of those to be trained (*veneyya*), by way of manifesting the modes of existence and so forth, or because he has been spoken of and proceeded by the Blessed One as "Thus-Gone" (*tathāgata*), he is the Tathāgata. Or, because the disciples of the Blessed One have gone to and understood [the Dhamma] exactly as it was taught by the Blessed One, he is the Tathāgata.
In this way, the entire True Dhamma (*saddhamma*) is also the Tathāgata. Therefore, Sakka said:
The Lord of the Devas said: "Let there be well-being as we pay homage to the Dhamma, which the Tathāgata—honored by gods and humans—is.
He is called the Blessed One (Bhagavā) because he possesses that [state] of being a Tathāgata.
And just as it is with the Dhamma, so too it is with the Noble Saṅgha, who are perfectly purified by those practicing for their own benefit and for the benefit of others.
Having placed the practice of serenity and insight in their prior stages before him, he must go by way of this or that path;

thus, because he has gone in such a manner (*tathā-gato*), he is the Tathāgata. Or alternatively, because he has awakened to and spoken accordingly (*tathā-gadanato*) the method taught by the Blessed One—such as the Truths and Dependent Origination—he is the Tathāgata. Therefore, Sakka, king of the gods, said: "The Tathāgata..."
“We pay homage to the Saṅgha, honored by gods and humans; may there be well-being!”—because he has such disciples, the Blessed One is the Tathāgata.
Thus, he is the Tathāgata by virtue of his state as a Tathāgata.
This is merely a brief illustration of the Tathāgata’s state as a Tathāgata; however, in every respect, he is indeed the Tathāgata.
One might describe the state of a Tathāgata. For this term "Tathāgata" has great significance, it is of great scope, and its domain is vast;

thus, one who brings forth even the entire word of the Buddha contained in the Tipiṭaka according to its logical connection and essential meaning—just as one would with that single word for "heedfulness"—cannot be said to be "a preacher of Dhamma who has leaped across before reaching the ford."
Regarding this, it is said:
"Just as in the world the former great seers,
the sages, attained omniscience here;”
In the same way, this Sage of the Śākyas has also come;
therefore, he who possesses the eye is called the Tathāgata.
Having abandoned the stains of sensual desire and the rest without remainder—
Just as the ancient Conquerors, the Sage of the Śākyas, the bearer of splendor, went by means of the knowledges of meditative concentration,
so has he gone; therefore he is considered a Tathāgata.
And thus, regarding the characteristics of the elements, bases, and so forth—
by way of their individual essence, commonality, distinction, and classification—
the Victor has arrived at them through his self-arisen knowledge.
The Bull of the Sakyas is called the Tathāgata.
“With his all-seeing eye, he has seen the truths as they truly are,
and likewise the conditionality of this world in its entirety.”
Not to be led by others, having been discerned through the method;
because he has thus gone, the Victor is the Tathāgata.
Even in world-systems of manifold divisions...
Regarding the Victor’s range of experience,
such as the sense-base of visible forms, his vision is exactly the same toward their various and manifold distinctions;
therefore, the Tathāgata is called Samantalocana (the One with Universal Vision).
But when one speaks of the Dhamma exactly as it is,
and acts in accordance with those words,
they proceed surpassing the world by means of their virtues.
The Tathāgata, the leader of the world,
through that very thorough understanding of suchness,
has known the world and transcended its origin.
Having gone to Nibbāna through the act of direct realization,
and having likewise gone by the Noble Path, he is the Tathāgata.
Because of his suchness in every respect, according to his promise, [he is called the Tathāgata].
Because he has come for the welfare of the world,
and because the Protector always acts out of compassion,
he is therefore called the Jina and the Tathāgata.
“Because his knowledges are such as they truly are, from whence he has come,
through the awakening to objects according to their intrinsic nature;
because of such noble birth and so forth, he is the Tathāgata.”
He is the Tathāgata because he has accomplished that purpose:
“Just as those former Great Seers were,
so am I likewise, according to my own resolve.”
Because his speech is well-restrained and his mind is subtle,
the Tathāgata is called the Supreme Person.
Prior to this, through the ripening of the requisites for full enlightenment...
He has gone, yet he does not go within the cycle of existence;
for the Protector who perceives the end of becoming, there is no such thing as "coming.
Thus, because he has thus come, he is the Tathāgata.
“The Tathāgata, the supreme Dharma, the Great Seer—
just as the impurity that is to be abandoned is abandoned;
so too the Tathāgata, the Noble Assembly, the Guide.”
“The Tathāgata [is so called] because of being endowed with that.
Regarding the phrase “the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One” (*arahantaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ*): here, the meaning of the word *arahā* has already been explained above.

He is the “Perfectly Enlightened One” (*sammāsambuddha*) because of having awakened (*buddhattā*) to all phenomena both correctly (*sammā*) and by himself (*sāmaṃ*). Whatever is known (*ñeyya*), of all that—
It is said that he has fully awakened by himself, in every aspect and without error.

By this, his attainment of omniscient knowledge—known as unobstructed knowledge—is demonstrated; it is a knowledge capable of awakening to all phenomena in every aspect without reliance on the instruction of others, and its operation is independent of desire.
But is it not the case that there is an unobstructed knowledge other than omniscience? Otherwise, the statement that "the six unique knowledges are the Buddha-knowledges" would be contradicted.

It is not contradicted, because that single knowledge is described in two ways for the purpose of showing its uniqueness in relation to others by way of the distinction between its objects and its modes of occurrence. For that very same knowledge, by virtue of having as its object all conditioned and unconditioned conventional phenomena without exception, [is so designated].
Omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) is called "unobstructed knowledge" (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) because it moves without attachment due to the absence of any obscuration therein.
As it is said in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*:

"It is omniscient knowledge because it knows everything—both the conditioned and the unconditioned—without exception. Because there is no obscuration therein, it is unobstructed knowledge," and so forth.
Therefore, there is no difference between them in meaning; this must certainly be accepted in this way.

Otherwise, it would follow that the knowledge of omniscience and the unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa) are identical and have all phenomena as their object. For there is not even the slightest obstruction to the Blessed One’s knowledge;
and if the unobstructed knowledge were not to have all phenomena as its object, there would be a place where it does not occur.

In that case, because of the existence of an obstruction, there could not even be the state of being unobstructed. Alternatively, let it be that "unobstructed" is something other than omniscient knowledge;
however, here, by virtue of its functioning without hindrance everywhere, it is precisely omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) that is intended as "unobstructed knowledge.
It is through the attainment of this alone that the Blessed One is called omniscient (*sabbaññū*), all-knowing (*sabbavidū*), and perfectly enlightened (*sammāsambuddho*).
It is not merely by the simultaneous awakening to all phenomena. Thus it is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*:
"This is the final liberation of the Blessed Buddhas; together with the acquisition of omniscient knowledge at the foot of the Bodhi tree, there is the realization and designation of 'Buddha'.
For through the attainment of the knowledge capable of awakening to all phenomena, the Blessed One possessed the capacity to penetrate all phenomena without exception within his own continuum.
Here it is asked: Does this knowledge, when it occurs, occur all at once regarding its entire object, or does it occur successively?

What of it? If, first of all, it occurs all at once regarding its entire object, then when conditioned phenomena—divided into the distinctions of past, future, present, internal, external, and so forth—as well as unconditioned and conventional phenomena, appear together, [it would be like] a mental cloth from afar...

If it were as if [the Buddha] were merely looking, there would be no comprehension through the differentiation of objects; and if that were so, it would follow that for those practicing insight into "all phenomena are non-self," all phenomena would become objects of the Blessed One’s knowledge in an undifferentiated form, just as they appear in the aspect of non-self.
Furthermore, [it would imply that his knowledge] is at all times free from conceptual construction and has as its object the established characteristics of all knowable phenomena...
The knowledge of the Buddhas proceeds; therefore, they are called "all-knowing" (*sabbavidū*).

And if one were to argue that by this [definition] the statement—"The Nāga is concentrated while walking, and he is also concentrated while standing"—is well-said, even for them the aforementioned fault does not cease, because [their knowledge] has the characteristic of being stationary as its object.
Furthermore, because past and future conventional phenomena do not exist [in the present], the Blessed One’s knowledge would have to have only a partial scope.
Therefore, it is not tenable that his knowledge occurs all at once.

If, on the other hand, it is argued that his knowledge occurs sequentially regarding the entire object, this too is not tenable; for [knowledge] does not [arise] by way of genus, plane, intrinsic nature, and so forth.

Furthermore, when the objects of knowledge—which are divided into many categories according to direction, place, time, and so forth—are apprehended in succession, it is possible to penetrate them without remainder, because the objects of knowledge are limitless.
However, as for those who claim: "The Blessed One is omniscient because he does not deceive regarding the meaning;
having made one portion of the objects of knowledge directly perceived, he resolves that 'it is likewise' in the remainder, and establishes [this] through such determination."
And that knowledge is not inferential because it is free from doubt. For they say that in the world, inferential knowledge is accompanied by doubt;

however, this is not correct for them either. Because if an object were entirely beyond direct perception, it would be impossible to determine it by first making one part of the knowable object directly perceived and then resolving that "it is so" regarding the remainder through non-contradiction.
For that which remains is not directly perceived (*paccakkha*). If even that were directly perceived, its status as "the remainder" would not exist;
therefore, all this [objection] is without reason. Why? Because it concerns an investigation into what is not an object [of such perception].
For this was said by the Blessed One: "The domain of the Buddhas, monks, is inconceivable; it should not be thought about. Whoever should think about it would partake of madness and frustration."

This, however, is the conclusion here: whatever the Blessed One desires to know—whether in its entirety or in part—knowledge regarding that proceeds directly through its unimpeded operation; and because there is no distraction, his concentration is constant.
Since it is not the case that everything he desires to know falls outside the scope [of his knowledge], his mode of operation cannot be dependent upon mere wish.
It must certainly be accepted that "all phenomena are dependent upon the advertence, the desire, the attention, and the arising of consciousness of the Buddha,
the Blessed One," according to the scriptural statement. Furthermore, because the Blessed One’s knowledge regarding objects of the past and future is devoid of inference,
deduction, reasoning, or grasping through logic, it is indeed direct perception (*paccakkha*).

But surely, even on this position, when one wishes to know everything, the Blessed One’s knowledge would have to arise all at once in an undetermined form because its object is the whole; thus, it would not escape the aforementioned fault. No, for that has been cleared away.
For that domain of the Buddha has been established as inconceivable. Otherwise, [the Buddha’s knowledge] would be identical in operation to the knowledge of ordinary people.
The inconceivability of the knowledge of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, would not exist;

therefore, although that [knowledge] has all phenomena as its object, it proceeds having made those phenomena well-defined as if they were the object of a single phenomenon—this is what is inconceivable here.
As much as there is to be known, so much is there knowledge; as much as there is knowledge, so much is there that which is to be known.
Knowledge has its limit in the knowable, and the knowable has its limit in knowledge;

thus, because he has perfectly and independently awakened to all phenomena—whether taken together or separately, simultaneously or successively, according to his wish and through his own direct realization—the Blessed One is the Perfectly Self-Awakened One (Sammāsambuddha).
[I pay homage] to that Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
“Two kinds of thought” means two kinds of right thought. In this context, it is called *vitakka* because by means of it one thinks, or it itself thinks, or it is merely the act of thinking.

This [thought] has the characteristic of directing the mind onto an object; its function is striking and threshing [the mind]; it is manifested as the leading of the mind toward the object. However, having divided it into two according to the difference in its objects, it is said: “two kinds of thought.”
“They practice” (samudācaranti) means they proceed equally and correctly, ever higher, within the bounds of propriety. For this syllable *ā* has the sense of a boundary;
and by virtue of that connection, the word “the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One” is used in the accusative case in the sense of the genitive.
This is what is meant: [they proceed] equally and correctly within the domain of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
And they move and proceed upwards, upwards, frequently, repeatedly, and constantly, without overstepping one another’s boundaries.
But what is their domain, or what is their boundary, and how do they proceed upwards, upwards, frequently, repeatedly, and constantly, without overstepping that [boundary]?
It is said: the thought of security (*khema-vitakka*) and the thought of seclusion (*paviveka-vitakka*). These—

There are two types of applied thought (vitakka). Among them, the thought of security (khema-vitakka) is especially associated with the Blessed One’s compassion (karuṇā), though it is also found associated with loving-kindness (mettā) and sympathetic joy (muditā);
therefore, it should be understood as being both the precursor to and associated with the attainment of great compassion (mahākaruṇā-samāpatti) and the attainments of loving-kindness and the others.

The thought of seclusion (paviveka-vitakka), however, is the precursor to and associated with the attainment of the fruition (phala-samāpatti), and also by way of the divine abodes (dibba-vihāra) and so forth.

It can indeed be obtained. Thus, thought (vitakka) is their domain; therefore, even though they occur frequently within a single continuum, there is no fixed boundary because they move only within their own respective domains from time to time, nor do they function through confusion.

In this regard, the thought of security (khema-vitakka) is to be manifested by the Blessed One’s emergence of compassion and so forth, while the thought of seclusion (paviveka-vitakka) is manifested by the meditative attainments (samāpatti).

Herein, this is the analysis: through such passages as “This world is born of anguish, overcome by suffering,” which show the world’s habitation as being ablaze with the fires of lust and so forth, [this meditation] is to be practiced prior to the attainment of great compassion, and also during the attainment itself, by way of the first jhāna.
For this has been said:
“Great compassion for beings descends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as they perceive them in many ways:
great compassion for beings descends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as they perceive that ‘the world-dwelling is ablaze.
The world is driven forward, set in motion, traveling along a wrong path; the world is being led away, it is unstable, it is without refuge, and it is without a protector.”
“The world is ownerless; having abandoned everything, one must depart. The world is deficient, unsatisfied, and a slave to craving.
The dwelling of the world is without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and has become a place of no refuge. The world is agitated and unpacified;
the dwelling of the world is pierced by many arrows and possessed by a shaft. It is shrouded in the darkness of ignorance and enclosed within the cage of the defilements.”
For those who see that the world-dwelling has entered into ignorance, being like an egg, enveloped, born from a tangled web, born from a cocoon,

and like a reed-thicket, it does not transcend the states of loss, the miserable destinations, the lower realms, and saṃsāra; for they see that it is smeared with the poison of the stain of ignorance,
become a mire of defilements, and entangled in the tangle of lust, hatred, and delusion.

“Ensnared by the net of craving, covered by the web of craving, carried away by the stream of craving, bound by the fetter of craving, permeated by the underlying tendency of craving, tormented by the fever of craving, he is consumed by the burning of craving.

“Ensnared by the net of views, covered by the web of views, carried away by the stream of views, bound by the fetter of views, permeated by the underlying tendency of views, tormented by the fever of views, he is consumed by the burning of views.”
“Followed by birth, pursued by old age, overcome by sickness, struck down by death,
established in suffering. “Entangled by craving, enclosed by the rampart of old age, hemmed in by the snare of death, bound by the great fetters—
the dwelling in the world with the bond of lust, the bond of hatred and delusion, and the bond of pride, views, defilements, and misconduct.”
He is bound; he has entered upon a path of great congestion; he is entangled by a great impediment; he has fallen into a great precipice;
he has entered upon a great wilderness; he has entered upon the great saṃsāra; he revolves in a great thicket; he is mired in a great quagmire. “The world-dwelling is struck down;
the world-dwelling is ablaze with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion, [and] with birth... pe...”
The world-dwelling is led away by anxieties; it is constantly being slain, defenseless, and like one who has committed a crime and received punishment.
Bound by the fetters of fault, it stands at the place of execution. The world-dwelling is without protector, fallen into a state of supreme pitiability;
it is overwhelmed by suffering, oppressed for a long time, perpetually clinging, and eternally thirsty.
“Blind, sightless, with ruined eyes, without a guide, strayed onto a wrong path, missed the straight way, and plunged into a great flood.

‘He is obsessed by two types of views, has practiced wrongly through three kinds of misconduct, is bound by four yokes, fettered by four knots, clings by means of four clingings, and has mounted upon the five destinations. By the five...”
He is stained by the strands of sensual pleasure; he is overwhelmed by the five hindrances; he disputes by means of the six roots of dispute;
he is stained by the six classes of craving; he is obsessed by the six views; he is permeated by the seven underlying tendencies;
he is fettered by the seven fetters; he is puffed up by the seven types of conceit; and he is tossed about by the eight worldly conditions.
He is fixed in eight kinds of wrongness; he is corrupted by eight faults of a man;
he is provoked by nine grounds for resentment; he is puffed up by nine types of conceit; he is stained by nine states rooted in craving;
he is defiled by ten grounds for corruption; he is provoked by ten grounds for resentment; and he is possessed of ten courses of unwholesome action.
To the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who perceive that the world-dwelling is bound by the ten fetters, fixed by the ten forms of wrongness, possessed of views based on ten grounds,
possessed of extreme views based on ten grounds, proliferated by the hundred-and-eight elaborations of craving,
and obsessed by the sixty-two types of speculative views— [this is their perception].
Great compassion descends upon beings:
"I have crossed over, yet the world has not crossed over; I am liberated, yet the world is not liberated; I am tamed, yet the world is untamed;
I am at peace, yet the world is not at peace; I have attained consolation, yet the world has not attained consolation."
“I have attained final Nibbāna, yet the world has not attained final Nibbāna. I am indeed able—having crossed over, to help others cross;

being liberated, to liberate others; being tamed, to tame others; being at peace, to bring others to peace; being comforted, to comfort others; having attained final Nibbāna, to lead others to final Nibbāna.
It is when they see this that great compassion for beings arises in the Blessed Buddhas.
In this same manner, the Blessed One’s entry into loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward sentient beings should be clarified.
For loving-kindness also proceeds by bestowing upon sentient beings that happiness which is the antidote to the suffering that is the object of compassion (*karuṇā*);

thus, here, the thoughts of non-ill will (*avyāpāda*) and non-cruelty (*avihiṃsā*) constitute the thought of security (*khemavitakka*). Furthermore, the thought of seclusion (*pavivekavitakka*) is simply the thought of renunciation (*nekkhammavitakka*).
Its occurrence should be understood by way of the reviewing of the preliminary stage of the first jhāna within the divine abidings (*dibbavihāra*) and the noble abidings (*ariyavihāra*).
In that regard, there are those abidings in attainment numbering twenty-four million four hundred thousand which the Blessed One utilized daily;
their occurrence as a precursor is accompanied by the practice of concentration and the practice of knowledge.
Knowledge is called the "great diamond-like knowledge" that moves through the twenty-four million meditative attainments;
by means of these, the frequent occurrence of the Blessed One’s thought of seclusion should be understood.
This meaning is also to be understood from the Mahāsaccaka Sutta, for it was said there by the Blessed One:
“Thus, Aggivessana, I steadied my mind right within that very same basis for concentration (*samādhinimitta*) from before; I settled it, so that indeed I dwell there constantly.
For the Blessed One [thought]: “The ascetic Gotama is handsome, pleasing, with well-formed lips, a thin tongue, and sweet speech;
he seems to wander about delighting the assembly with these, yet he lacks one-pointedness of mind (*cittassa ekaggatā*).”
When Saccaka the Nigaṇṭhaputta had thus reflected, "He who wanders so full of conciliation," the Blessed One, like one seizing a thief caught with the stolen goods, replied:
"Aggivessana, it is not by seeking to please the assembly that the Tathāgata wanders full of conciliation;

he teaches the Dhamma even to an assembly as vast as the limits of the world-system. Unflagging and unsullied, he possesses the fruit of the attainment of the state of unity and the fruit of the attainment of emptiness."
He brought this up to show that [the Buddha] was "devoted" (*anuyutta*).
For at whatever moment the assembly gives its applause or the Blessed One reviews the Dhamma,
at that very moment he delimits the time by means of the prior stage and enters the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) during both the inhalation and the exhalation.

While the sound of the cry of "Well done! is still unceasing, and at the conclusion of the reflection on the Dhamma, he emerges from attainment and begins his teaching of the Dhamma starting from the very spot where he stood. For the dwelling in the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) of Buddhas is light;
they enter attainments during both the inhalation and the exhalation. Thus, regarding the aforementioned attainments together with their preliminary stages—
By means of this, the frequent occurrence of the Blessed One’s thoughts of security (*khemavitakka*) and thoughts of seclusion (*pavivekavitakka*) should be understood.

In that regard, through the power of his thoughts of non-ill will (*abyāpādavitakka*) and thoughts of non-cruelty (*avihiṃsāvitakka*), which abandon the defilements such as thoughts of ill will and cruelty, he dwells having attained security because there is no fear from any quarter; and from that, of everything...
It is always indeed secure and indeed fearless. Therefore, both kinds [of thoughts] are called "thoughts of security" because they bring security to both.
Furthermore, by the power of the thought of renunciation (*nekkhamma-vitakka*), which abandons the defilements such as the thought of sensual desire (*kāma-vitakka*), there is a threefold seclusion:

seclusion of body, seclusion of mind, and seclusion from acquisitions (*upadhiviveka*); as well as seclusion by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-viveka*), seclusion by suppression (*vikkhambhana-viveka*), and seclusion by eradication (*samuccheda-viveka*).
The fivefold seclusion—seclusion by suppression, seclusion by substitution of opposites, seclusion by removal, seclusion by tranquillization, and seclusion by escape—attains fulfillment.

The thought accompanied by seclusion (*paviveka-sahagata vitakka*) is "thought of seclusion" (*paviveka-vitakka*), which, as appropriate, is associated with seclusion both in terms of its object and its mental concomitants.
Although these two types of thought have thus been analyzed according to their respective domains, they arise for beginners as mutual aids to one another.

For just as the thought of seclusion (*paviveka-vitakka*) leads to the arising of the thought of security (*khema-vitakka*) that has not yet arisen, and to its increase and expansion once it has arisen, so too does the thought of security lead to the thought of seclusion. Indeed, without body and mind being withdrawn (*vūpakata*), dwelling in loving-kindness (*mettā-vihāra*) and the like are impossible;
and without the abandoning of ill-will (*byāpāda*) and so forth, mental seclusion and the rest simply cannot occur.
These states should be seen as being of great mutual assistance to one another.

However, in the case of the Blessed One, who has entirely abandoned all defilements, both the thought of security and the thought of seclusion bring about welfare and happiness even at the mere moment of an inhalation. Thus, it should be connected as:
"the thought of security and the thought of seclusion."
When the two types of thought have thus been announced, he spoke the passage beginning with “one who delights in non-affliction” (*abyāpajjhārāma*) in order to explain them.
Therein, *abyāpajjha* means the non-afflicting of anyone; that which is to be delighted in (*āramitabba*) is the delight (*ārāma*) for him, thus he is “one who delights in non-affliction.

He is “delighting in non-affliction” (*abyāpajjharata*) because he is devoted to it through the practice of cultivation. “This very one” (*eseva*) means this same person. “Of conduct” (*iriya*) means of activity, that is, of bodily and verbal application.

The meaning is as follows: “I do not harm anyone” means that I do not afflict or cause suffering to any being—whether inferior or otherwise—by means of the thirst and craving that lead to trembling (*tasa*), nor do I harm those who are stable (*thāvara*) due to the absence of such trembling because all the fluctuations of the defilements have been abandoned.

The Blessed One, whose disposition is compassion and who frequently enters the attainment of great compassion, spoke thus in accordance with his own supreme inclination toward a compassionate disposition.
By this, he demonstrates thoughts of non-harming and thoughts of non-ill-will. This is what is meant:

"By means of this deportment, by means of this practice, practicing rightly in this way, dwelling in such states of meditative attainment, and enduring in this way the honors, respect, esteem, reverence, salutations, and worship performed by those seeking merit toward beings..."
"I do not harm anyone; rather, I promote for them only that which is beneficial and pleasant, categorized as pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal.
Thus, whatever is unwholesome—namely, the fifteen hundred types of defilements and whatever else is associated with them—is abandoned.
"Unwholesome states are of infinite variety; all of them have been abandoned and uprooted by me right at the foot of the Bodhi tree.

By this, he demonstrates the seclusion of eradication (*samuccheda-viveka*) and the seclusion of subsidence (*paṭippassaddhi-viveka*), together with the seclusion that is the pinnacle among all forms of seclusion, namely the seclusion of escape (*nissaraṇa-viveka*).
Some, however, include here also the seclusion of substitution (*tadaṅga-viveka*) and the seclusion of suppression (*vikkhambhana-viveka*). This is the path leading onward.
For it is stated here that the Blessed One’s own destruction of the defilements (kilesakkhaya) occurred together with [the attainment of] the Blessed One.

Thus, having now brought to its ultimate consummation his own inclination toward seclusion— which had been cultivated over immeasurable eons— along with his inclination toward renunciation, the Blessed One,
having entered the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), [proceeds] by way of reviewing the abandonment of his own defilements.
He causes [them] to be abandoned. Now, showing the purpose for which the Teacher extracted these two types of thought here, he said, "Therefore, monks," and so forth.
For the Blessed One began this teaching in order to establish the monks therein by way of demonstrating his own frequent occurrence of these two types of thought.
In this context, "therefore" (*tasmā*) means: because for me, who delights in non-affliction and seclusion, thoughts of security and seclusion alone prevail frequently;
therefore. "Tihā" is merely a particle. "Dwell delighting in non-affliction" (*abyāpajjhārāmā viharatha*) means:

dwell not delighting in the dwelling of loving-kindness (*mettā*) nor in the dwelling of compassion (*karuṇā*) toward all beings. By this, he speaks of the distancing of ill-will (*byāpāda*) and the defilements associated with it.

In the phrase *tesaṃ vo* here, *vo* is merely a particle. "Dwell delighting in seclusion" means: dwell having made all forms of seclusion—the seclusion of body and so forth, as well as the seclusion by way of its factors (*tadaṅga*) and so on—your place of resort.
The passage beginning with "By this means, for us... is a demonstration of the manner in which their thoughts of safety (*khema-vitakka*) arise;
likewise, the passage beginning with "What is unwholesome? is a demonstration of the manner in which their thoughts of seclusion (*paviveka-vitakka*) arise.

In this context, just as one who desires to fulfill blameless states must become a seeker of what is wholesome and conduct a search for wholesome states, so too must one who desires to abandon blameworthy states conduct a search for the unwholesome;

thus he says, "What is unwholesome? and so forth. For full understanding, abandoning, realization, and development are preceded by direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). In that regard, "what is unwholesome" refers to the unwholesome.

"What is its name? What is its characteristic according to its intrinsic nature? Or what are its function, manifestation, and proximate cause?"—this shows the method of reflection upon the unwholesome state by way of its intrinsic nature, function, and so forth.
This initial thought (vitakka) is introduced from the perspective of a beginner;
the two phrases "What has not been abandoned? What shall we abandon? are addressed from the perspective of one in training (sekkha). Therefore, [the question] "What has not been abandoned?"...
Regarding the unwholesome factors such as the fetter of sensual lust (*kāmarāga-saṃyojana*) and so forth: what unwholesome state has not yet been completely eradicated by our Path?
What shall we abandon? By this, what unwholesome state shall we uproot? Alternatively, "What shall we abandon? means:

among transgressions (*vītikkama*), obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), and underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), which specific portion of the unwholesome shall we now abandon? Some, however, read it as "What has not been abandoned? (*kiṃ appahīnaṃ*).
Among those many varieties of unwholesome states—such as the fetter of views and so forth—it is implied:
"Which unwholesome state is it? By what means, or by which path, has it not been abandoned by us? The rest is according to the method already stated. Regarding the verses:

*Buddham* ("the Buddha") refers to one who has awakened to and penetrated the four noble truths without error through his own independent knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*), because there is no object of knowledge (*ñeyya*) apart from the truths. For it has been said: [The verse continues: "Whatever has been realized by the Perfectly Enlightened One, Whether in the past, future, or present, All that is encompassed within these four truths; Therefore, he is called 'Buddha'. Thus it is stated.
“That which was to be directly known has been directly known; that which was to be developed has been developed;
that which was to be abandoned has been abandoned by me—therefore, O brahmins, I am a Buddha.
Because no one other than the Great Bodhisatta is capable of enduring or bearing the entirety of the insuperable [burden],...
Because it endures and carries the equipment for enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) and the domain of great compassion (mahākaruṇā); because it is difficult for others to endure or overcome;

because it endures and overcomes the five insuperable Māras; and because, through the awakening to the distinctions of dispositions, latent tendencies, conduct, and inclinations, it provides instruction—termed "guidance"—to those to be trained according to their needs by means of the ultimate truths pertaining to this life and the life to come.
Because he bears and carries out the Buddha-activity that is unbearable for others, or because he acts with excellence therein, he is "the bearer of the unbearable" (*asayhasāhī*).
"They act upon" (*samudācaranti*) means they strike; here *naṃ* is a mere particle, or its meaning is "that Tathāgata.

He is "the dispeller of darkness" (*tamonudo*) because he has pushed away and cast off the darkness of delusion, known as *tama*, within his own and others' mental continuums. The further shore is Nibbāna.

"Gone" means gone to the further shore (*pāragata*). Alternatively, he is "gone to the further shore" because he has reached the limit or boundary of the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*)—which proceeds according to the method beginning with "having been liberated, may he liberate others"—or of the entirety of the suffering of *saṃsāra*, or of the qualities of omniscience. Thus, he is the Dispeller of Darkness who has gone to the further shore.

For that very reason, he is the Buddha who has attained what was to be attained; [he is endowed] with the virtues of the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, such as morality and so forth, as well as the ten powers, the knowledge, and so on.

The meaning is that "all that is to be attained has been attained. One who possesses mastery (*vasimā*) is so called because he possesses the supreme state of mastery over application-of-mind (*āvajjanā*) and so forth, which is dependent upon his wish regarding the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and other states, as well as the state of mastery of mind (*cittavasibhāva*) known as noble supernormal power (*ariyiddhi*), which is not shared by others; thus, he is a master (*vasī*), meaning one who possesses such mastery.
It is "taintless" (*anāsava*) due to the absence of all taints (*āsava*), such as the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*). [It is free from] the unevenness of the body and so forth...

Or, because he has vomited out all the stains of the defilements known as "poison" (*visa*), or because he himself has crossed over and causes others to cross over the entire suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*)—which is like poison—he is a "crosser of poison" (*visantaro*);
thus, he is "one who has crossed over poison" (*visantaro*). He is liberated in the exhaustion of craving, in the fruit of Arhatship, or in Nibbāna;
and because he proceeds toward both [of these], he is preeminent through knowledge known as "sagehood" (*mono*), or through bodily sagehood and the rest.
Because he is endowed with these qualities, he is called a *muni*. For "muni" refers to many kinds of sages:

the householder sage (*agāriya-muni*), the homeless sage (*anagāriya-muni*), the training sage (*sekkha-muni*), the one beyond training (*asekkha-muni*), the solitary sage (*pacceka-muni*), and the sage of sages (*munimuni*). Among these, a layperson who has attained the fruit and understood the teaching is a householder sage;
a renunciant of such a nature is a homeless sage; the seven types of trainees (*sekha*) are training sages; and one whose taints are destroyed is a sage beyond training.
The *paccekabuddha* is a solitary sage (*paccekamuni*), and the *sammāsambuddha* is the sage of sages (*munimuni*). It is this [latter] alone who is intended here.
Because there will be no further renewed existence in the future, he bears his final, last body; thus he is the "bearer of the final body" (*antimadehadhārī*), and [the text refers to] him as such.

Because the Māras, beginning with the Māra of the defilements (*kilesamāra*), have been completely abandoned, he is the "conqueror of Māra" (*mārañjaha*). Precisely for that reason, through the total eradication of the cause of aging, [he is so called].
"He has gone beyond all aging, including manifest aging and so forth, by way of attaining Nibbāna without remainder.
It should be understood that here, by means of "aging" as the primary example, the going beyond birth, death, sorrow, and the rest is intended.
The connection is: "I say that two types of thought approach the Tathāgata who has become such."
Thus the Blessed One, having indicated the two types of thought in the first verse and then shown the thought of seclusion in the second verse,
now spoke the third verse, beginning with "As on a crag," in order to show the thought of security (*khema-vitakka*). Therein,
"as one standing on a crag" means as one situated upon the summit of a mountain made of stone, a solid mass of rock.
For one standing there, there is no need for such actions as raising the neck or stretching out the limbs.
"Tathūpamaṃ" means similar to that; it is like the simile of the rocky mountain. This, however, is the summary of the meaning:

just as a man with good eyesight standing on the summit of a rocky mountain would see the people all around him, even so did Sumedha, who possessed beautiful wisdom, by means of his omniscient knowledge.

The Blessed One, the All-Seeing, having ascended the palace made of Dhamma and made of wisdom, himself free from sorrow, gazes upon, sustains, and scrutinizes the multitude of beings—the people plunged in sorrow and overcome by birth and old age.
This, moreover, is the intended meaning here: just as if one were to clear a vast field all around at the foot of a mountain and, within its irrigation banks...
Suppose one were to build huts and kindle a fire at night, and there were a darkness endowed with four factors; then,
as a man with keen vision stood upon the summit of a mountain and surveyed the ground, neither the fields, nor the boundaries of the fields, nor the huts,
nor the people sleeping therein would be discernible, but only the glow of the fires within the huts would be seen.

If it were so perceived, then for the Tathāgata who has ascended the palace made of Dhamma and surveys the world of beings, those beings who have not performed wholesome deeds do not come within the range of the Buddha’s knowledge even when sitting in the same dwelling on his right side;
they are like arrows shot in the night. But those individuals who are vessels for training and have performed wholesome deeds, even if they are far away, [come within his range].
When they come within range, they appear like a fire or like Mount Himavanta. For it has been said:
"The virtuous shine from afar, like Mount Himavanta;
the wicked are not seen here, like arrows shot in the night."
Thus, in this sutta and in its verses, the Blessed One presented himself as if he were another.
The commentary on the first sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Desanā Sutta.

39. Regarding the phrase "by a second method" (*pariyāya*): here the word *pariyāya* occurs in the sense of a "teaching" in such passages as, "Remember this indeed as the 'Honey-Ball Method' (*madhupiṇḍika-pariyāya*).
It occurs in the sense of a "reason" or "ground" in such passages as, "There is, O Brahmin, a method (*pariyāya*) by which one speaking rightly of me might say:
'The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-action'. And it occurs in the sense of "turn" or "opportunity" in such passages as, "Whose turn (*pariyāya*) is it today, Ānanda?"
In such passages as "to exhort the bhikkhunīs," it refers to a turn [of speaking]. However, in this case, it applies both to a turn and to a reason;
therefore, the meaning here is: "Monks, the Tathāgata’s two methods of teaching the Dhamma occur either by way of a reason or by way of a turn.
For the Blessed One, in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained, sometimes says: "These states are wholesome; these states are unwholesome."
“‘These states are blameworthy; these states are blameless. These are to be cultivated;
these are not to be cultivated’—thus, by analyzing wholesome and unwholesome states and pointing out unwholesome states without confusing them with wholesome ones, he teaches the Dhamma, saying:
‘See evil as evil. Sometimes [he says]: ‘Bhikkhus, the taking of life, when practiced...’”

By declaring the danger through such passages as, "When cultivated and frequently practiced, [killing] leads to rebirth in hell, leads to rebirth in the animal realm, and leads to rebirth in the sphere of hungry ghosts;

even the lightest killing of living beings leads to a short lifespan," and so forth, he teaches the Dhamma, urging people toward disenchantment and so on with regard to evil, saying: "Be disenchanted; become dispassionate."
“They come to be” means they arise and proceed. “See evil as evil” means see every unwholesome state as base, because it brings harm and suffering both in this very life and in the future.

“Become disenchanted with that” means become disenchanted with that unwholesome state, [seeing it] as “evil” in the sense of being utterly inferior and base, and as “unwholesome” (akusala) in the sense of being produced by lack of skill.
It is "defiling" because it destroys the luminous nature of the mind which is naturally radiant and clear;
it is "leading to renewed existence" because it repeatedly produces the suffering of becoming; it is "accompanied by distress" because it proceeds together with anxieties and fevers;
it is "having suffering as its result" because it ripens only as suffering; and it is so called because it produces birth, aging, and death in the future for an immeasurable period of time.
"Behold, with right wisdom, the manifold dangers in this way: that it leads to future birth, aging, and death, and is capable of destroying all welfare and happiness.
Seeing both these dangers and the benefits of their abandonment, become disenchanted and attain disenchantment.
And becoming disenchanted, increase your insight and, through the attainment of the Noble Path, become detached from evil and liberated.

And: either become dispassionate by means of the Path through the fading away that consists in complete eradication; then, by means of the Fruit, be liberated through liberation that consists in subsiding.
Alternatively, "evil" (*pāpa*) is evil because it is base. What is meant?

That which is contemptible due to its nature of impermanence, suffering, and so forth, and which is loathsome to the Noble Ones—that cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) which brings one to evil—is "evil. But what is that? It is the class of phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence.

Having seen it as evil in the sense already described, develop insight into it by way of impermanence, suffering, disease, a tumor, an arrow, a calamity, an affliction, and so forth, and become disenchanted.

This is the second: taking the first teaching—which reveals disadvantage and harm as they truly are—as a basis, this subsequent teaching which leads away from that is the second discourse on the Dhamma.

In the verses, "of the Buddha" means of the omniscient Buddha. "Compassionate toward all beings" refers to one whose nature is to feel compassion for all sentient beings through great pity (*mahākaruṇā*).
"Discourse" (*pariyāyavacana*) means speaking or teaching by way of a method or sequence.
"Behold" (*passa*) is an address to the assembly, or it is said with reference to the leader of the assembly. However, some say that the Blessed One spoke this with reference to himself.
‘See,’ he said. “In that regard” means: become dispassionate toward that evil; abandon passion for it—this is the meaning. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the second sutta is finished. 3.
Commentary on the *Vijjā-sutta* (The Knowledge Sutta).
40. "In the third [unwholesome root], they are 'forerunners' (pubbaṅgamā) by way of two modes: as co-nascent (sahajāta) and as decisive support (upanissaya).
They are the forerunners, the precursors, and the primary cause. For there is no arising of the unwholesome without ignorance.

'Of attainment' (samāpattiyā) means of entering into, of acquiring its own nature; the meaning is 'of occurrence. In that regard, it is by concealing the danger (ādīnava) of the occurrence of the unwholesome..."

The state of being a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for unwholesome states is seen both through the conditionality of improper attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*) and through its state of not having been abandoned.
Thus, because they serve as the basis for the suffering of disease, death, and so forth, all realms of existence (*gati*) here are considered "bad destinations" (*duggati*).

Alternatively, "bad destinations" are the courses of activity of body, speech, and mind that have been defiled by the corruptions (*kilesa*) such as lust; that is, the misconduct of body, speech, and mind.
"In this world" means in this world, or in the human realm; "and in the next" means in other realms besides that.
"All have ignorance as their root" means that all those failures of misconduct are rooted in ignorance precisely because they are preceded by ignorance, according to the method already stated.
"The mass of craving and greed" refers to craving, which is characterized by the pursuit of unattained objects, and greed, which is characterized by the clinging to attained objects.
"Accumulated by greed" means built up through desire-greed (*icchālobha*).
"Because" (*yato*) means because, due to the cause of ignorance (*avijjā*), being shrouded by ignorance.

"One of evil desires" (*pāpiccho*): because one's evil desires are concealed by ignorance, one does not see the danger in such desires; thus, by way of concealing one's lack of true virtues, one who practices hypocrisy and the like is "one of evil desires."

It should be understood that even excessive desire (*atricchā*) is grasped by greed itself. "Lack of respect" means being devoid of regard for one's fellow practitioners due to the absence of moral dread (*ottappa*) toward the Lord of the World.
"Therefore" means because of ignorance, evil desire, shamelessness (*ahirika*), and lack of moral dread.
"He produces" means he accumulates evil, consisting of bodily misconduct and so forth. "He goes to a state of misery by means of that" means by means of that which has been thus produced.
Through evil, one goes to and is reborn in the states of misery,
such as the various hells. Therefore, because these— ignorance and the rest— are the roots of all misconduct and the causes of all defilements leading to miserable destinies,
one who desires [liberation] should cause desire, greed, and ignorance— and by the word "and," also shamelessness and lack of moral dread— to fade away.
"I abandon by way of total eradication. How does one cause fading away? He says:

"Arousing true knowledge," meaning that by means of the sequence of insight (*vipassanā*) and the sequence of the path (*magga*), exerting himself, he arouses the true knowledge of the path of Arahantship within his own continuum.
"All miserable destinies" refers to all those states termed misconduct (*duccarita*), or alternatively, because they serve as the basis for the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
"Painful; one should abandon all five destinations, one should relinquish them, one should transcend them.
For by the very abandoning of the cycle of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*), the cycle of kamma and the cycle of result (*vipākavaṭṭa*) are also abandoned.
The commentary on the third sutta is finished.
The commentary on the first recitation section is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Paññāparihīna-sutta* (Sutta on the Loss of Wisdom). 41.
In the fourth [sutta], "well-decayed" (*suparihīnā*) means thoroughly decayed. "Those who have fallen away from noble wisdom" (*ariyāya paññāya parihīnā*) refers to those beings.
Because they have failed to penetrate the arising and passing away of the five aggregates and have failed to penetrate the Four Noble Truths, they remain far from the defilements;
thus, they are destitute of both noble, purified insight-wisdom and path-wisdom.
Being utterly destitute of both mundane and supramundane attainments, they are great losers. Who, then, are they? Those who, by way of the obstruction of karma...
They are thus possessed [of these qualities]. For they are entirely fallen away and incomplete from the state of being fixed in falsehood (*micchattaniyata*), having lost their great lineage.

Therefore he said, "An evil destination is to be expected. Those who possess the obstruction of karmic result (*vipākāvaraṇa*) are also fallen away. Alternatively, on the bright side (*sukkapakkha*), those who are "not fallen away" are of three kinds:
those free from the three obstructions, those possessing right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*), and those endowed with the knowledge that one's own actions are one's own property (*kammassakatañāṇa*).
The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated.
In the verses, "from wisdom" (*paññāya*) is an ablative expression, meaning "due to falling away from insight-knowledge and path-knowledge.
Alternatively, it is a genitive expression, meaning "due to the falling away of the aforementioned knowledge"; and here, "falling away" is simply the non-arising of that which ought to have arisen.

“Established in name-and-form” means that within name-and-form—that is, within the five aggregates of clinging—one is firmly adhered and clings by way of craving and views, thinking “this is mine,” and so forth;
for that very reason, one conceives of it as true, thinking, “This alone is the truth, all else is false.
The case ending in the phrase “in the world with its devas” should be transformed [to the locative].
Having thus shown the side of defilement (*saṃkilesapakkha*) by means of the first verse,

he now uttered the verse beginning with “Wisdom is supreme in the world,” demonstrating the power of wisdom (*paññā*), showing that through the arising of that [wisdom] for which the non-arising of which the cycle of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*) revolves within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) due to conceiving and adherence, there occurs the cutting off of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

In that context, "in the world" means in the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). There is no quality equal to wisdom (*paññā*) among conditioned phenomena, just as there is none equal to the Fully Enlightened One among sentient beings.
For wholesome states have wisdom as their supreme leader; and when wisdom is established, all blameless qualities are necessarily established as well.
Thus it has been said: "For one of right view, right intention arises," and so forth. As for that...
Here, it is wisdom (paññā) that is intended; it is praised as "the best. To show how it functions, the passage beginning with "that which leads to penetration" (yāyaṃ nibbedhagāminī) was stated.

Its meaning is as follows: this wisdom is called "leading to penetration" because it proceeds—that is, it functions—by penetrating and shattering the mass of greed and so forth, which have never before been penetrated or shattered. By means of which...
And in each respective state of existence, birth-place, destiny, station of consciousness, and abode of beings, among the classes of beings,
he correctly and without error knows and realizes Nibbāna— the exhaustion and termination of birth, which is defined as the first manifestation of the aggregates,
and of the kamma-existence that is its cause— as well as Arahantship; this is the wisdom of the Path together with insight, which is supreme in the world.

Now, in order to praise those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) and who are endowed with the power of wisdom as previously described, he spoke the concluding verse beginning with "Of them, both gods and humans.

Its meaning is as follows: of those who are fully awakened (sambuddha) through the awakening to the Four Noble Truths because they have brought to completion the sixteen tasks such as full understanding regarding the Four Noble Truths;
and of those who possess mindfulness (satimanta) due to their attainment of the perfection of mindfulness; [of these, both gods and humans...]
For those who have attained the fullness of wisdom because delusion has been eradicated in the manner described;

or for those possessing "laughter-wisdom" (*hāsa-paññā*) due to the abundance of laughter, joy, satisfaction, and gladness from the time they began fulfilling virtue and the other perfections up until the realization of Nibbāna;
and for the *khīṇāsavas* (those whose taints are destroyed) who bear their final bodies because the fetters of existence have been completely exhausted.
Both gods and humans admire them and hold them dear; they desire to attain that same state, thinking, "Oh, the power of wisdom!
Oh, may we too become like this, having likewise crossed over all suffering.
The commentary on the fourth sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Sukkadhamma Sutta* 42.

In the fifth [sutta], "bright" (*sukka*) does not mean bright by way of the brightness of color; rather, they are "bright" because they lead to a state of purity and supreme cleansing, thus being bright by way of their result.
Furthermore, by their very nature, all wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*) are indeed bright, as they are the opposites of dark states (*kaṇha-bhāva*).
For when these arise, the mind becomes luminous and purified. "Dhammas" refers to wholesome states.

"The world" refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*). "They uphold" means they protect by establishing boundaries through their supporting and sustaining power. Regarding "modesty (*hirī*) and shame (*ottappa*"):
herein, *hirī* is that by which one feels shame (*hiriyati*), or that for which one feels shame (*hiriyanti*); as it has been said: "That by which one feels shame..."
"One feels shame regarding that which is shameful; one feels shame at the undertaking of evil, unwholesome states—this is called *hirī*.
One trembles at what one should tremble at, or that by which one trembles is *ottappa*.
And this has also been said: "That by which one trembles at what one should tremble at, one trembles at the undertaking of evil, unwholesome states..."
"This is called moral dread.
In this context, *hiri* (moral shame) arises from within oneself, while *ottappa* (moral dread) arises from without.

*Hiri* has oneself as its governing principle, whereas *ottappa* has the world as its governing principle. *Hiri* is established on the nature of modesty, while *ottappa* is established on the nature of fear.
*Hirī* has the characteristic of self-respect; *ottappa* has the characteristic of seeing fear in what is blameworthy.
Therein, one arouses *hirī*, which originates from within oneself, by means of four reasons:
by reflecting on birth, by reflecting on age, by reflecting on courage, and by reflecting on great learning. How so?
“Committing evil is not the work of those endowed with noble birth; it is the work of low-born people such as fishermen and the like.
It is not fitting for one like me, who is of noble birth, to do such a deed.
Reflecting on birth in this way, one who refrains from evil deeds such as the taking of life arouses a sense of shame (*hiri*). Likewise: “Committing evil is the work of the young... [and so forth].
Reflecting thus on one’s own age—thinking, "This is an action that ought to be done;

it is not fitting for one established in my stage of life to commit such an act"—one who refrains from evil deeds such as the taking of life arouses a sense of moral shame (*hiri*). Likewise, reflecting:
"The performance of evil is the work of those of weak nature; it is not fitting for one like me, endowed with courage, to commit such an act..."
Reflecting thus on his own courage, thinking, "It is not fitting," he does not commit evil deeds such as the taking of life, thereby arousing a sense of moral shame (*hiri*).
Likewise, reflecting on his great learning, thinking, "This performance of evil is the work of blind fools, not of the wise;
it is not fitting for a wise and learned person like me to do such a deed," he arouses a sense of moral shame.
By refraining from evil deeds such as the taking of life, one arouses *hiri* (moral shame).
In this way, one arouses *hiri* that arises internally through four causes.
Having aroused it and having caused *hiri* to enter one’s own mind, one does not commit an evil deed. Thus, *hiri* is said to be "internally arisen."
How is it that moral dread (*ottappa*) has its origin outside (*bahiddhā*)? It is as follows: “If you commit an evil deed, you will become an object of reproach among the four assemblies.
The wise will revile you, just as they would a filthy city-dweller.
Being shunned by those possessed of virtue, how can you continue as a monk? Thus it is said.
For when reflecting, one does not commit an evil deed out of a sense of dread of others (*ottappa*) arising from the external; thus, *ottappa* is said to have an external origin.
How is it that moral shame (*hirī*) has oneself as its governing principle? Here, a certain son of good family, making himself the ruler and the elder, thinks:
"It is not fitting for one like me—one who has gone forth out of faith, who is learned, and who advocates the ascetic practices—to do an evil deed."
Thinking, "I must not do it," he does not commit an evil deed. In this way, moral shame (*hirī*) is said to have oneself as its dominant influence. Therefore the Blessed One said:
