"Having made himself alone his dominant influence, he abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless; he maintains himself in purity.

How is moral dread (*ottappa*) said to have the world as its dominant influence? Here, a certain clansman makes the world his dominant influence and his chief authority, and thus he does not commit an evil deed. As it has been said:
“Moreover, this world-dwelling is vast. In this vast world-dwelling there are recluses and brahmins who possess psychic power, have the divine eye, and know the minds of others;
they see even from afar, are not seen even when nearby, and understand the mind with their own minds.
They too will know of me thus: ‘Look, sirs, at this clansman!’”
‘Having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, he dwells entangled by evil, unwholesome states.
There are deities who possess psychic power, who have the divine eye, and who understand the minds of others;
they see even from afar, they are not seen even when nearby, and they understand the mind with their own minds. They too will know of me thus: ‘Look!...’
"Sir, this son of good family, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, dwells mired in evil, unwholesome states.
[Thinking thus,] he abandons the unwholesome by making the world itself his authority.
This is moral dread with the world as its governing principle.
Regarding the phrase "established by the nature of shame" (*lajjāsabhāvasaṇṭhitā*): here, "shame" (*lajjā*) refers to the mode of being ashamed; *hiri* is established by that very nature.
"Fear" (*bhaya*) refers to the fear of the states of woe (*apāya*); *ottappa* is established by that very nature. Both of these become manifest in the avoidance of evil.
In this regard, it is as if there were two iron balls: one might be cold but smeared with excrement, while the other is hot and glowing.
Among these, just as a sensible person does not take up the cool [substance] because they are disgusted by its being smeared with excrement,
nor the other because of the fear of burning, so too the wise person does not commit evil out of shame, being disgusted by it, nor do they commit evil out of dread,
fearing the states of misery. Thus, *hirī* is established in the nature of shame, while *ottappa* is established in the nature of dread.
How is it that *hirī* has the characteristic of having a sense of shame, and *ottappa* has the characteristic of seeing fear in what is fearful regarding moral faults?

For a certain person possesses the characteristic of having a sense of shame through a feeling of reverence toward four causes: reflection on the greatness of one’s birth, reflection on the greatness of the Teacher, reflection on the greatness of the inheritance, and reflection on the greatness of one’s fellow practitioners of the holy life.

Having aroused *hiri*, one does not commit evil. Some do not commit evil by arousing *ottappa*—which has the characteristic of seeing fear in what is blameworthy—fearing blame for four reasons: fear of self-reproach, fear of reproach by others, fear of punishment, and fear of an unhappy rebirth.
And herein, *hiri* and *ottappa* have their origin within oneself and so forth.
These are spoken of as being manifest in various instances, yet there is never any mutual dissociation between them.
For there is no lack of shame that is fearless, nor is there any fear of evil that is without shame.
"If, monks, these two bright qualities did not protect the world," monks, refers to these two blameless qualities.
If they did not protect the world, if there were no guardians of the world, then even one's own mother would not be recognized here;
in this world, a biological mother would not be known as "this is my mother" by virtue of being held in high esteem and reverence, nor would she be designated as "mother.
The same principle applies to the remaining terms as well. *Mātucchā* means a mother’s sister. *Mātulānī* means...
The wife of one’s maternal uncle. "Venerable ones" (*garūnaṃ*) refers to those who occupy a position of reverence, such as one’s great-uncle, paternal uncle, elder brother, and so forth.
"Confusion" (*sambhedaṃ*) means a mixture or the breaking of boundaries; he illustrates this with the simile of goats and sheep, and so on.
For these beings do not recognize [their kin] through a sense of reverence and esteem, thinking, "This is my mother," or "This is my maternal aunt," based on whatever object [they encounter].
Having arisen, they even act perversely therein. Therefore, bringing forward a simile, he cited goats, sheep, and so forth.

This is the summarized meaning here: just as goats, sheep, and other such animals—devoid of shame and dread of blame—behave with total promiscuity everywhere, having no sense of mother and so on and having broken all boundaries of propriety;
so too this world of humans [would behave] if the qualities that protect the world...
If these did not exist, everything would proceed with total confusion. But because these qualities of world-guardians protect the world, there is no such confusion.
In the verses, "yesaṃ ce hiri-ottappaṃ" is merely a particle; it means "of those beings for whom there is both moral shame (hiri) and dread of blame (ottappa)."
"Never at any time whatsoever" means it does not exist and is not found.

"Those who have fallen away from the white roots" means that those beings, because they have performed actions that bring about the cutting off of the roots of the wholesome (*kusalamūla*), or because of the absence of moral shame (*hirī*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*)—which serve as the foundation for wholesome deeds—they have fallen away from and retreated from the wholesome;
thus, by remaining [in that state], they are "fallen away from the white roots. Again and again...
The meaning is that, because their nature is subject to birth and decay, they go through birth and death and do not transcend the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
"And for those who possess moral shame (*hirī*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*)," however, means that for those beings of purified intellect,

these two qualities— moral shame and dread of blame— are always and at all times, day and night, throughout the stages of youth, middle age, and old age, firmly established by having correctly approached them.
"Repulsed by evil and fearing it, they abandon evil by means of its various constituent parts.
Having grown in the holy life (*brahmacariya*)," means they have attained growth in both the holy life of the Dispensation and the holy life of the Path.

"Being peaceful" means they are peaceful either through the total pacification of defilements or through the attainment of the supreme qualities via the realization of the highest path. "Having exhausted renewed existence" means that because they have brought an end to further becoming, they are those for whom rebirth is spent.
The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Ajāta Sutta. 43.
Regarding the sixth [sutta], what is the origin of the words "There is, monks"? It is said that one day, by means of many methods, the Blessed One...
Having proclaimed the peril of saṃsāra, when a teaching on the Dhamma connected with Nibbāna was delivered by way of its pacification and so forth, this thought occurred to the bhikkhus:
"This saṃsāra has been described by the Blessed One as having a cause, namely ignorance and other factors;
but no cause whatsoever has been stated for Nibbāna, which is its pacification. How then can this be without a cause?"

“It is found in the sense of a real and ultimate fact. Then the Blessed One, for the purpose of dispelling the doubts of those bhikkhus and [to refute] those who have gone astray like the Lokāyatikas and others—thinking externally that for ascetics and brahmins the term “Nibbāna, Nibbāna” is merely a verbal designation, for in the ultimate sense there is no such thing as Nibbāna because its nature is unfindable—said this: ... [text continues] ... “In this world, the various ascetics and brahmins assert: ‘Nibbāna is the cessation of all formations, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all substrata of existence, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. Now, what do you think, bhikkhus? Is it possible to point out any formation whatsoever that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and that might endure as long as eternity? “No, venerable sir. “Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single formation that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and that might endure as long as eternity. Therefore, bhikkhus, whatever has been formulated, whatever is a formation, whatever is conditioned, whatever is dependently arisen—all that is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. This, bhikkhus, is called the Dhamma that accords with reality, the Dhamma that conforms to the truth, the Dhamma that is in accordance with the Dhamma, the Dhamma that is the true Dhamma, the Dhamma that is the ultimate Dhamma, the Dhamma that is the final goal, the Dhamma that is the supreme good, the Dhamma that is the ultimate good, the Dhamma that is the highest meaning, the Dhamma that is the ultimate meaning, the Dhamma that is the supreme meaning, the Dhamma that is the final meaning, the Dhamma that is the ultimate meaning, the Dhamma that is the unsurpassed meaning, the Dhamma that is the meaning of peace, the Dhamma that is the meaning of bliss, the Dhamma that is the meaning of security, the Dhamma that is the meaning of the deathless, the Dhamma that is the meaning of Nibbāna. And what is that Dhamma? It is this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma that accords with reality... the Dhamma that is the meaning of Nibbāna. [The Buddha continued: “Bhikkhus, I say that the Tathāgata is liberated from birth, liberated from aging, liberated from death, liberated from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is liberated from suffering, I say. And why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata has fully understood, as they really are, the origin of birth, the origin of aging, the origin of death, the origin of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he has fully understood suffering, I say. And what is that? It is this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view... right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma that accords with reality... the Dhamma that is the meaning of Nibbāna. [The Buddha continued: “Bhikkhus, I say that the Tathāgata has fully understood, as they really are, the cessation of birth, the cessation of aging, the cessation of death, the cessation of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he has fully understood suffering, I say. And what is that? It is this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view... right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma that accords with reality... the Dhamma that is the meaning of Nibbāna. [The Buddha concluded: “Bhikkhus, I say that the Tathāgata has fully understood, as they really are, the way leading to the cessation of birth, the way leading to the cessation of aging, the way leading to the cessation of death, the way leading to the cessation of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he has fully understood suffering, I say. And what is that? It is this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view... right concentration.

This, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma that accords with reality, the Dhamma that conforms to the truth, the Dhamma that is in accordance with the Dhamma, the Dhamma that is the true Dhamma, the Dhamma that is the ultimate Dhamma, the Dhamma that is the final goal, the Dhamma that is the supreme good, the Dhamma that is the ultimate good, the Dhamma that is the highest meaning, the Dhamma that is the ultimate meaning, the Dhamma that is the supreme meaning, the Dhamma that is the final meaning, the Dhamma that is the ultimate meaning, the Dhamma that is the unsurpassed meaning, the Dhamma that is the meaning of peace, the Dhamma that is the meaning of bliss, the Dhamma that is the meaning of security, the Dhamma that is the meaning of the deathless, the Dhamma that is the meaning of Nibbāna. And what is that Dhamma? It is this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

This, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma that accords with reality, the Dhamma that conforms to the truth, the Dhamma that is in accordance with the Dhamma, the Dhamma that is the true Dhamma, the Dhamma that is the ultimate Dhamma, the Dhamma that is the final goal, the Dhamma that is the supreme good, the Dhamma that is the ultimate good, the Dhamma that is the highest meaning, the Dhamma that is the ultimate meaning, the Dhamma that is the supreme meaning, the Dhamma that is the final meaning, the Dhamma that is the ultimate meaning, the Dhamma that is the unsurpassed meaning, the Dhamma that is the meaning of peace, the Dhamma that is the meaning of bliss, the Dhamma that is the meaning of security, the Dhamma that is the meaning of the deathless, the Dhamma that is the meaning of Nibbāna. [The Buddha concluded: “Bhikkhus, I say that the Tathāgata has fully understood, as they really are, the way leading to the cessation of birth, the way leading to the cessation of aging, the way leading to the cessation of death, the way leading to the cessation of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he has fully understood suffering, I say. And what is that? It is this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma that accords with reality, the Dhamma that conforms to the truth, the Dhamma that is in accordance with the Dhamma, the Dhamma that is the true Dhamma, the Dhamma that is the ultimate Dhamma, the Dhamma that is the final goal, the Dhamma that is the supreme good, the Dhamma that is the ultimate good, the Dhamma that is the highest meaning, the Dhamma that is the ultimate meaning, the Dhamma that is the supreme meaning, the Dhamma that is the final meaning, the Dhamma that is the ultimate meaning, the Dhamma that is the unsurpassed meaning, the Dhamma that is the meaning of peace, the Dhamma that is the meaning of bliss, the Dhamma that is the meaning of security, the Dhamma that is the meaning of the deathless, the Dhamma that is the meaning of Nibbāna. And what is that Dhamma? It is this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma that accords with reality, the Dhamma that conforms to the truth, the Dhamma that is in accordance with the Dhamma, the Dhamma that is the true Dhamma, the Dhamma that is the ultimate Dhamma, the Dhamma that is the final goal, the Dhamma that is the supreme good, the Dhamma that is the ultimate good, the Dhamma that is the highest meaning, the Dhamma that is the ultimate meaning, the Dhamma that is the supreme meaning, the Dhamma that is the final meaning, the Dhamma that is the ultimate meaning, the Dhamma that is the unsurpassed meaning, the Dhamma that is the meaning of peace, the Dhamma that is the meaning of bliss, the Dhamma that
And for the purpose of shattering the false doctrines of those who hold various views, and for the purpose of demonstrating that the great Nibbāna of the Deathless exists in the ultimate sense,
as well as for the purpose of demonstrating its power— such as its nature as the ultimate escape—
he uttered this discourse by way of an inspired utterance (*udāna*) through the force of rapture. For indeed, this discourse is included even among the *Udānas*.
In this context, "exists" (*atthi*) means it is found and is apprehended from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*).

"Unborn," "unbecome," "unmade," and "unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*)—all these terms are synonyms for one another. Alternatively, it is "unborn" because, unlike feeling and the other aggregates, it is not born or produced by a causal complex consisting of the conjunction of causes and conditions.
It is "unbecome" because it has not come into being of its own accord without a cause.
It is "unbecome" (*abhūta*) because it has not appeared and has not arisen. Thus, because it is unborn and unbecome, it is "unmade" (*akata*) by any cause whatsoever.

Furthermore, the characteristics of being born, become, and made belong to conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*) such as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), but not to the unconditioned nature of Nibbāna;
it is for the purpose of showing this that it is called "unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*). [In reverse order:]...

That which is produced by conditions having come together and combined is "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*); that which is not thus conditioned, being devoid of the characteristics of the conditioned, is "unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*).

When, through these various reasons, the state of being produced has been negated, the term "unmade" (*akata*) is stated to show—by way of the doubt, "Could it perhaps have been made by a single cause alone?"—that it was not made by anything whatsoever. Thus...
Even though it is without conditions (*appaccaya*), the term "unborn" (*abhūta*) is stated to dispel the suspicion that "this has appeared as something that has come into being by itself.
Furthermore, this state of its being unborn—its unconditioned nature—is stated as "unborn" in order to show that it is entirely and in every way a phenomenon devoid of birth (*ajāti-dhamma*).
In this way, the meaningfulness of these four terms should be understood.

Thus the Blessed One, having stated from the perspective of ultimate reality that “there is, monks, an unborn, unbecome, unmade, and unconditioned,” spoke the passage beginning with “If this, monks,” etc., in order to show the reason for that. This is the summary of it:
monks, if the unconditioned element, whose intrinsic nature is unborn and so forth, were not to exist—that is, were not to be—then here...
The escape from the conditioned world— consisting of the five aggregates of form and so forth, which by their very nature are subject to birth and the like in this world—
the complete pacification of the round of existence, would not be discerned, would not be found, and would not be possible.
For it is by taking Nibbāna as its object that the factors of the Noble Path, such as right view and the rest, proceeding [in that way], utterly eradicate the defilements.
In this context, the non-occurrence and departure of the entire suffering of the round (*vaṭṭadukkha*) is recognized as the escape (*nissaraṇa*).

Having thus shown the existence of Nibbāna by way of negative concomitance (*byatireka*), the passage beginning with "But because" (*yasmā ca kho*) is now stated to show it also by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*);
its meaning is exactly as previously explained. And here, since "unconditioned phenomena (*apaccayā dhammā*), unconstructed... [is said].
“...phenomena (dhammā). There is, monks, that sphere where there is neither earth...
This state too is difficult to see, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
And I shall teach you, monks, the unconditioned (asaṅkhata) phenomenon and the way leading to the unconditioned,” and by many such passages from the Suttas, [it is established that] “there is...”

By this Sutta as well—“...O bhikkhus, it has not been born”—the existence of the element of Nibbāna in the ultimate sense was taught by the Fully Enlightened One who has compassion for the entire world; therefore, it must not be rejected.

In this regard, there is no doubt or perplexity whatsoever even for the wise who have not witnessed it directly. However, for the sake of dispelling the uncertainty of those individuals lacking such understanding:
This is the investigation by way of reasoning through the determination of the underlying intention here:

just as the escape (nissaraṇa)— which is the opposite of and possesses a nature contrary to sensual pleasures and material forms that are surpassable because they are to be fully understood— is made known,
so too is there an escape by means of a nature contrary to and opposed to all conditioned phenomena that possess that same nature.
It must be so. And that which is this escape is the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*).
Furthermore, even insight-knowledge having conditioned phenomena as its object—even conformity-knowledge—is not able to abandon defilements by way of their total eradication;
likewise, knowledge in the first jhāna and so forth, having conventional truth as its object, abandons defilements only by way of suppression.

Not by way of eradication. Thus, because knowledge whose object is conditioned phenomena and whose object is conventional truth is incapable of eradicating the defilements through their eradication, the Noble Path-knowledge—which effects that eradication—must have as its object something whose intrinsic nature is the opposite of both of those;
that is the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*). Likewise: "It exists..."

“Monks, it is unarisen, unbecome, unmade, and unconditioned”—this statement indicates that Nibbāna exists in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), because it was spoken by the Blessed One as having an unerring meaning.
For whatever has been spoken by the Blessed One is of unerring meaning and is the ultimate truth, just as in the case of:
“All conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) are impermanent; all conditioned phenomena are suffering; all phenomena (*dhammā*)...”

“...non-self. Likewise, in certain contexts, the term *nibbāna* has as its object the ultimate reality as it truly is (*yathābhūta-paramattha*), because of the presence of figurative usage (*upacāra-vutti*), just like the word “lion.

Alternatively, the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*) does indeed exist in the ultimate sense, because its intrinsic nature is free from all other opposing characteristics, just like the earth-element or feeling.
By such methods, [the existence] of the unconditioned element is established through reasoning (*yutti*).
In the ultimate sense, their existence should be understood.
In the verses, "born" (*jāta*) means born in the sense of being produced; the meaning is that it has reached the characteristic of birth.

"Become" (*bhūta*) means become in the sense of having come to be; the meaning is that it has arisen after not having existed. "Fully arisen" (*samuppanna*) means arisen by way of association; [arisen] by means of associated [factors].
The meaning is: "arisen from phenomena. "Made" (*kata*) means produced by conditions acting as causes.
"Conditioned" (*saṅkhata*) means made by those very same [conditions] coming together and combining; this is a designation for everything produced by conditions.
It is "unstable" because it is devoid of any permanent core or essence. It is "entirely conjoined" (*saṃsaṭṭha*) with aging and death.
The aggregate of aging and death. Some also read it as "the clash of aging and death" (*jarāmaraṇasaṅghaṭṭa*), meaning afflicted and oppressed by aging and death.
It is a "nest of diseases" (*roga-nīḷa*), a dwelling place for the many diseases such as eye-diseases and so forth.
It is "fragile" (*pabhaṅgura*) because its nature is to break up and perish both through natural processes and through external intervention.
It has its origin and source in nutriment and the guide known as craving; thus it is "originated from the guide of nutriment" (*āhāra-netti-pabhava*).
Alternatively, every condition whatsoever is "nutriment. However, since craving is already included here by the mention of the "guide," it should be understood as excluding craving.

Therefore, it is "originated from the guide of nutriment" in the sense that its origin consists of both nutriment and the guide. Or else, nutriment itself, in the sense of leading [to rebirth], is the "guide."
"Guidance (nettī) in the sense of causing to proceed"—thus it is also "born from the guidance of nutriment. "It is not fit to be delighted in":

that pentad of the aggregates of clinging, which exists in such a way dependent on conditions, and is therefore impermanent and suffering, is not fit to be delighted in—that is, to be relished—by means of craving and views.
Its escape (*nissaraṇa*) refers to the escape from that personality-view (*sakkāya*) described by the words "born," "become," and so forth;

it is peaceful (*santa*) because of the absence of all conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*) and the defilements such as lust, which are by nature unpeaceful, and because of its state of being praised through the subsiding of those [defilements];
it is beyond the sphere of reasoning (*atakkāvacara*) because it is not within the range of speculative knowledge; and in the sense of permanence...
It is certainly permanent (*dhruva*) because it is unborn and unarisen from that very state; it is sorrowless (*asoaka*) because of the absence of causes for sorrow;

it is stainless (*viraja*) because of being free from the dust of passion and so forth; it is the "footprint" (*pada*) because it is to be attained by those who are weary of the suffering of *saṃsāra*;

it is cessation (*nirodha*) because it is the cause for the cessation of the phenomena of suffering such as birth; it is the subsiding of formations (*saṅkhārūpasama*) because it is the cause for the pacification of all conditioned things; and for that very reason—
By the phrase "blissful because of ultimate bliss," he praises nothing other than the great Nibbāna, the Deathless, with every term.
Thus, through the method of contrast in the first verse and the method of agreement in the second verse, the Blessed One elucidated Nibbāna.
The commentary on the sixth sutta is concluded.
7. Commentary on the *Nibbānadhātu-sutta* 44.

Regarding the seventh [verse], "these two": these are the two. *Vāna* is said to be craving (*taṇhā*). It is called *nibbāna* because it has departed from craving (*vāna*), or because there is no craving here, or because when this is attained, there is an absence of craving.
That very thing, in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being and devoid of a soul (*nissattanijjīvaṭṭhena*)...
And because it maintains its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), it is called a "constituent" (*dhātu*), namely, the constituent of Nibbāna (*nibbānadhātu*).

Although there is no differentiation of it in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), nevertheless, it is manifested through a figurative method (*pariyāyena*); thus, with reference to that figurative differentiation, it was said: "Monks, these two are the constituents of Nibbāna.
Having stated this, in order to show the specific divisions as intended, it was said: "With residue remaining," and so forth. In that context, by means of craving and the rest...
It is called *upādi* because it is grasped as a state of fruition; this refers to the five aggregates (*khandha*).
That which remains as the residue of what is grasped is *upādisesa*. Together with that residue of the grasped is *sa-upādisesa*; due to the absence of that, it is *an-upādisesa*.
They are "Worthy Ones" (*arahant*) because their defilements (*kilesa*) are far removed; the meaning is that their defilements are distant. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu an arahant, one from whom evil, unwholesome states—
those that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, vexatious, resulting in suffering, and conducive to future birth,
aging, and death— are far removed? It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is an arahant.”
"One whose taints are destroyed" (*khīṇāsava*): the four taints, beginning with the taint of sensual desire, have been exhausted, cut off, abandoned, and stilled by the Arahant;
they are incapable of arising again and have been burnt away by the fire of knowledge—thus he is "one whose taints are destroyed. "One who has lived [the holy life]" (*vusitavā*):

he has dwelt, fully dwelt, and completed his dwelling in the company of teachers, in the Noble Path, and in the ten noble dwellings; he has fulfilled his course and practiced the conduct—thus he is "one who has lived [the holy life]."
"Katakaraniyo" refers to the seven trainees (*sekha*), starting from the virtuous worldling (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*), who are said to be performing what is to be done by means of the four paths.

For one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), all that was to be done has been done and brought to completion; there is nothing further to be done for the attainment of the destruction of suffering—thus he is "one who has done what was to be done. And this has also been said:
“For that bhikkhu who is rightly liberated, whose mind is at peace, there is no accumulation of what has been done, nor does anything further to be done exist.

“Laid down the burden” refers to the three burdens: the burden of the aggregates (*khandha-bhāra*), the burden of the defilements (*kilesa-bhāra*), and the burden of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra-bhāra*). Of these...
Those burdens too have been laid down, removed, cast off, and dropped; thus he is "one who has laid down the burden" (*ohitabhāra*).
"One who has attained his own goal" (*anuppattasadattha*) means he has reached his own goal; it is said that "his own goal" (*sakattha*) is intended, with the letter *k* changed to *d*.

He is "one who has attained his own goal" because his own goal has been reached by him. And "own goal" (*sadattha*) should be understood as *arahatta* (Arahatship), for that is so called in the sense of being bound up with oneself.
Because he possesses his own welfare through the sense of not abandoning himself and through the ultimate sense of self, he is "one who has his own welfare" (*sakattha*).

"One whose fetters of existence are completely destroyed": the fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of aversion, and the fetters of conceit, views, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, lust for existence, envy, stinginess, and ignorance—these are the "fetters of existence" (*bhavasaṃyojana*) that bind beings to the various states of existence, or rather, they yoke and tie them fast to existence by means of existence.
[These are] names. For the Arahant, these have been completely exhausted, abandoned, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge; thus he is "one whose fetters of existence are completely exhausted.
Regarding the phrase "liberated through perfect knowledge" (*sammadaññā vimutto*): here, "through perfect knowledge" (*sammadaññā*) means "having rightly known. This is what is meant:
having rightly known the nature of the aggregates as aggregates, the nature of the sense-bases as sense-bases, the emptiness of the elements, and the oppressive nature of suffering.

Having rightly known, understood, discerned, weighed, and made manifest the meaning of the origin as arising, the meaning of cessation as peace, and the meaning of the path as seeing—according to the classification beginning with "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent"—and having thus realized them as they truly are;
he is "liberated. There are two kinds of liberation: the liberation of the mind and Nibbāna. For the Arahant...
Because he is liberated from all defilements, he is liberated by the liberation of mind (*cittavimutti*), and he is also liberated in *nibbāna*. Therefore it is said:
"Liberated through perfect knowledge.
For him, the five faculties remain; that is, for that Arahant, the karma that serves as the cause for his final existence [remains] until—
They do not perish; rather, the five faculties beginning with the eye simply persist. "Because they are unimpeded" means because they have not ceased by way of non-arising and cessation.
"Pleasant and unpleasant" refers to the desirable and undesirable range of objects such as visible forms.
"Experiences" means finds or obtains. "Experiences pleasure and pain" means he experiences pleasure and pain that have become fruition (*vipāka*).
He attains it through those doors.
Having thus far shown the "residue of clinging" (*upādisesa*), the passage beginning with "Of him who... is now stated in order to show the element of Nibbāna with residue (*saupādisesa*).
Therein, "of him" refers to that Arahant who still possesses a residue of clinging. "The destruction of lust" refers to the lust...
Exhaustion (*khaya*) is the state of being exhausted, non-existence, and absolute non-arising. This same method applies to the remaining [defilements] as well.
Up to this point, it has been shown that the exhaustion of lust and the other [defilements] is the *nibbāna*-element with residue remaining (*saupādisesa*).

"In this very life" (*idheva*) means in this very personal existence (*attabhāva*). "All feelings" (*sabbavedayitāni*) refers to all indeterminate feelings (*abyākatavedanā*), such as pleasure and so forth.
Furthermore, wholesome and unwholesome feelings have already been abandoned previously. "Not rejoiced in" means they are not delighted in by craving and the like.
"They will become cool" means they will become cooled through the complete subsiding of the fever of formations (*saṅkhāra-daratha*) by means of absolute pacification;
the meaning is that they will cease through cessation without rebirth-linking. Not only the felt objects themselves, but all [formations] as well—
However, since the five aggregates will cease within the continuum of one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), the teaching is given under the heading of "feeling" (*vedayita*).

In the verses, "by the Visionary One" (*cakkhumatā*) refers to one who possesses vision by means of the five eyes: the Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, the divine eye, the wisdom-eye, and the universal eye. "Independent" (*anissitena*) means [independent] of any phenomenon by way of dependence on craving or views.
"Independent" means being unbound by the fetters of passion and so forth.

"Such-like" (tādi) means such-like by virtue of the characteristic of such-likeness—which is defined as having a single nature toward all things, whether desirable or otherwise—by way of the sixfold equanimity.

"Belonging to this present life" means existing within this current personal existence. "With the destruction of the guide to becoming" means through the total exhaustion of craving, which is the guide to becoming.

“Pertaining to the future life” (*samparāyika*) means those states that exist in the future, subsequent to the breaking up of the aggregates (*khandha*). “In which” (*yamhi*) refers to that *nibbāna* without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*).
“Existences” (*bhavāni*) is stated with a change of gender; all existences of rebirth (*upapatti-bhava*) cease entirely without remainder and no longer proceed.
“Those” (*te*) refers to those whose minds are thus liberated. “Attainment of the essence of the Dhamma” (*dhammasārādhigama*) is due to this Dhamma and Vinaya having liberation as its essence.
Because it is the attainment of arahantship, which is the essence among all phenomena (*dhamma*).

"In destruction" means they delight in and are devoted to Nibbāna, which consists in the destruction of lust and the other defilements. Alternatively, Nibbāna is the "essence of phenomena" (*dhammasāra*) because it is the permanent state and the supreme state among all phenomena.
For this has been said: "Dispassion is the best of phenomena; dispassion is declared to be their foremost."

Because of their attainment of that essence of the Dhamma, they delight in the destruction of all formations—that is, in the extinction without remainder (nibbāna) where everything has been exhausted.
"Pahaṃsu" means they abandoned. "Te" is a mere particle. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the seventh sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Paṭisallāna Sutta 45.
In the eighth [sutta], "delighting in seclusion" (*paṭisallānarāmā*): *paṭisallāna* is the withdrawing from various conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*);
it means dwelling alone, frequenting solitude, or physical seclusion. They delight in—that is, they find pleasure in—that seclusion.
“Delighting in seclusion” (*paṭisallānarāmā*). There is also a reading: “delighting in seclusion” (*paṭisallānārāmā*).

As it has been stated, they are “delighting in seclusion” because seclusion is their delight (*ārāma*)—that which is to be delighted in. “Dwell” means: having become such as this, dwell. “Delighting in seclusion” (*paṭisallānaratā*) means:
those who are devoted to, intent upon, and fully rejoiced in seclusion. By this much, the application to wakefulness (*jāgariyānuyoga*) is indicated, as well as its causal sign.
And seclusion of the body is also shown. It should be understood that the practice of wakefulness, restraint by virtue, guarding of the sense doors,
moderation in eating, and mindfulness and clear comprehension— these factors cannot function without those [preceding qualities],
and thus they too are effectively stated here by implication.
"Devoted to internal mental tranquility" means devoted to the tranquility of one's own mind. "Internally" and "of oneself" have the same meaning;
there is only a difference in expression. And here, in the sense of a locative case, the word *samatha* takes the accusative case due to its connection with the prefix *anu*.
"Not having discarded jhāna" means not having cast out jhāna externally, or not having lost jhāna. "Casting out" (*nīharaṇa*)...
“Destruction blows away”: this is called *nirākata* (rejected), as in such passages as “having rejected arrogance, living in tranquility.
“Endowed with insight” means being engaged in the sevenfold contemplation (*anupassanā*). The sevenfold contemplation consists of:

contemplation of impermanence, contemplation of suffering, contemplation of non-self, contemplation of disenchantment, contemplation of dispassion, contemplation of cessation, and [contemplation of relinquishment].
And the contemplation of relinquishment has already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Those who increase [their practice] in empty huts" means those who augment their stay in empty huts.
Here, "empty huts" refers to any secluded place suitable for devotion to meditation. The meditation subject is practiced by way of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
Monks who, having taken up [this practice], enter an empty hut day and night and sit down devoted to meditation should be known as "increasers of empty huts.
Furthermore, even those meditators who dwell in palaces with one story or more should likewise be known as increasers of empty huts.

And here, that state of physical seclusion which was prescribed in the passage, “Monks, dwell delighting in seclusion, rejoicing in seclusion,” belongs to one whose virtue is purified, not to one who is unvirtuous or whose virtue is unpurified;
for there would be no turning away of the mind from visible objects and so forth for such a person.
Thus, it is said that by this meaning, purification of virtue is shown. This is the sense already stated.
By the two phrases, “devoted to internal mental tranquility” and “not neglecting jhāna,” the cultivation of concentration (samādhi-bhāvanā) is shown;
by the phrase “endowed with insight” (vipassanā), the cultivation of wisdom (paññā-bhāvanā) is established. Thus, the three mundane trainings (sikkhā) have been demonstrated.
Now, in order to show the fruit that necessarily arises for one established in those [trainings], it is said: “delighting in seclusion,” and so forth.
In this context, "of those who increase" (*brūhetānaṃ*) means of those who cause [the fruit] to grow. "Of the two fruits" (*dvinnaṃ phalānaṃ*) refers to the third and fourth fruits.
"To be expected" (*pāṭikaṅkhaṃ*) means desirable and certain to occur. "Higher knowledge" (*aññā*) refers to *arahatta* (Arahatship).

For that is called "higher knowledge" because it knows by not overstepping the boundary of what has already been known through the knowledges of the lower paths, because its knowing is complete, and because there is no further function of knowing remaining above it.
"Or when there is a residue of clinging" (*sati vā upādisese*) means: when there is a residue of defilements (*kilesūpādisesa*), that is, when they cannot yet be abandoned.

For when knowledge (*ñāṇa*) is not fully matured, those defilements which are to be abandoned by its full maturation are not abandoned. With reference to this, he said: "or when there is a residue of clinging.
And while the defilements exist, the formations of the aggregates (*khandhābhisaṅkhārā*) certainly persist. Thus, in this sutta, the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) [is intended].
"Arahantship" indicates two qualities. As it is here, so it is in the two subsequent suttas.

In the verses, "those whose minds are tranquil" refers to those practitioners who, by means of that factor (*tadaṅga*) and by means of suppression (*vikkhambhana*), have tranquil minds due to the pacification of the defilements.
"Circumspection" (*nepakka*) is said to be wisdom; they are "circumspect" because they are endowed with it. By this, their knowledge of maintaining the meditation subject is indicated.
He shows this. "Mindful and meditative" means: they are mindful by means of that mindfulness which is the cause for not abandoning the meditation subject while standing, sitting, and so forth;
they are meditative by means of jhāna characterized by the close contemplation of the object. "They see the Dhamma rightly, having no regard for sensual pleasures" means:
even previously, through such passages as "Sensual pleasures are like a skeleton," [they have seen] both objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāmā*) and defilement-sensual pleasures (*kilesakāmā*).
Being indifferent and having no desire for them through the contemplation of their dangers, they abandon them;
then, taking as a basis either access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) or absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) that has been attained, they discern name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and its conditions.

Following the sequence beginning with the comprehension of aggregates (kalāpa-sammasana), they correctly and without error practice insight (vipassanā) into the five aggregates as impermanent and so forth.
“Delighting in heedfulness” means they take pleasure and find delight in the non-neglect of the cultivation of serenity and insight as previously described;
they spend their days and nights solely through such heedfulness. “Peaceful” means being composed. There is also a reading “beings” (*sattā*), which means persons.
“Seeing danger in negligence” means seeing the danger in negligence, such as rebirth in hell and so forth. They are incapable [of falling away].
"Unfailing" means that they are incapable of falling away from such qualities as serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), or from the paths and fruits (*magga-phala*).
For they do not fall away from the attainment of serenity and insight, and they reach those other states they have not yet attained.
"In the very presence of Nibbāna" means in the presence of both Nibbāna and the final extinction through non-clinging (*anupādā-parinibbāna*); that is, before long.
"They will not attain it.
The commentary on the eighth sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Sikkhānisaṃsa Sutta.
46. Regarding "the benefits of training" (*sikkhānisaṃsa*) in the ninth [section]: here, that which is to be trained in is "training" (*sikkhā*). That is threefold:

training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*), training in higher mind (*adhicitta-sikkhā*), and training in higher wisdom (*adhipaññā-sikkhā*). These three kinds of training are the benefits for these [monks], not gain, honor, or fame;
thus, they are "the benefits of training. "Dwell" means: dwell having the benefits of training as your [goal], seeing the benefit in the three trainings.
The meaning is: "Dwell perceiving only the benefits to be obtained through those trainings. "Wisdom supreme" (*paññuttarā*):
among those trainings, that wisdom which is reckoned as the training in higher wisdom (*adhipaññā-sikkhā*) is "supreme," "foremost," and "distinguished" for them;
thus they are "wisdom-supreme. For those who dwell perceiving the benefits of the trainings become "wisdom-supreme. "Emancipation-essence" (*vimuttisārā*):
"Those for whom liberation, known as the fruit of arahantship, is the essence are 'those whose essence is liberation' (*vimuttisārā*);

the meaning is that they stand having grasped precisely the aforementioned liberation as the essence. For those who possess the benefits of training and have wisdom as their preeminent quality do not long for a particular state of existence;
rather, desiring non-existence (*vibhava*), they regard only liberation as the essence. 'Those who have mindfulness as their dominant influence' (*satādhipateyyā*)..."

"Having mindfulness as their dominant influence" (*satādhipateyyā*) means that mindfulness is the dominant factor (*adhipati*) for them in the sense of being the primary instrument (*jeṭṭhakakaraṇaṭṭhena*). Taking "dominant influence" (*adhipati*) itself as "that which has a dominant influence" (*adhipateyya*), the meaning is:

those whose minds are well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and who are devoted to the cultivation of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) by way of the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*) and so forth.

Alternatively, [the phrase] "the benefit of the training" (*sikkhānisaṃsa*) means, O monks, that when such a rare opportunity has been obtained, one should indeed train in the threefold training (*sikkhā*).

Dwell having made this your benefit; and dwelling thus, dwell being pre-eminent in wisdom—surpassing others through wisdom, endowed with supramundane wisdom—and being such, dwell having liberation as your essence, Nibbāna as your essence, and nothing else as your essence.
And this is the means for becoming so: dwell with mindfulness as your dominant influence, being devotedly engaged in the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness.
"Be mindful, or dwell with a mind protected by mindfulness"— thus should the meaning here be understood.
Thus the Blessed One, while enjoining the bhikkhus to the three trainings, having briefly shown how they are to be trained and by what means they reach fulfillment,
now [proceeds] by showing the distinction of the fruit for those practicing according to the instruction.
Demonstrating the fruitfulness of that practice, he said, "The benefits of the training," and so forth. That has the same meaning as already stated.

In the verses, "one whose training is perfected" means one whose training is purified by the attainment of the highest fruit; the sense is "one beyond training" (*asekha*). Regarding the term "of a nature to abandon":
here, "states subject to abandoning" refers to unstable liberations. For "a state subject to abandoning" (*pahānadhamma*) means a state subject to falling away (*hānadhamma*).
“Subject to shaking” (*kuppadhamma*). “Not subject to abandoning” means not having the nature of being abandoned; thus, it is unshakable (*akuppa-dhamma*).
There is also a textual reading “not subject to non-abandoning” (*appahāna-dhamma*), which has the same meaning. “Destruction itself is the end” is *khayanta*;

the end of birth is the “end of birth” (*jātikhayanta*), which is Nibbāna. Alternatively, destruction is death; the end of birth is Nibbāna itself, and because one has seen that, one is a “seer of the end of birth” (*jātikhayantadassī*).
Therefore, because this benefit—culminating in the crossing to the further shore of old age—is the result of the fulfillment of the training, [it is said]:

"Always" means at all times. "Delighting in jhāna" means delighting in both kinds of jhāna: that which contemplates characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*) and that which contemplates objects (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*);
for that very reason, they are "concentrated. "Having overcome Māra together with his army" means having overcome both the army of defilements (*kilesasena*) and the army of death (*anaṭṭhasena*).
Having overcome the fourfold Māra together with his army, leaving none remaining.

For even in the case of the Devaputta-Māra, the defilements (*kilesa*) are called the "army" because they act as his allies in the slaying of those possessed of virtue. Likewise, diseases and so forth are the "non-advantages" (*anaṭṭha*) of the Māra of Death. As it is said:
"Sensual desires are your first army; the second is said to be discontent."
The third is hunger and thirst for you; the fourth is called craving.
The fifth is sloth and torpor for you; the sixth is called fear.
The seventh is doubt for you; the eighth is hypocrisy and obstinacy.
“Gain, fame, and honor, and whatever reputation is wrongly acquired;
whoever exalts himself and despises others—
this, O Namuci, is your army, the assault of Kaṇha.”
"The non-hero does not conquer it, but having conquered it, one obtains happiness.
And as it is said:
"One should exert oneself this very day; who knows if death will come tomorrow?"
"For we have made no compact with that Death who possesses a great army.
"Become those who have gone beyond birth and death" means: become those who go beyond both birth and death, those who go to Nibbāna.
The commentary on the ninth sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Jāgariya-sutta* 47.

In the tenth [verse], "one who is wakeful" (*jāgaro*) means one who is awake, free from sleep, and devoted to wakefulness; the meaning is that he is diligently engaged in attending to the meditation subject day and night. For this has been said:
"And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night?"
Here, a bhikkhu purifies his mind of obstructive states by means of walking and sitting during the day;
he purifies his mind of obstructive states by means of walking and sitting during the first watch of the night;
and during the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, with one foot overlapping the other.
Mindful and clearly comprehending, having directed his attention to the perception of rising,
he rises during the last watch of the night and purifies his mind from obstructive states by means of walking and sitting. In this way,
a bhikkhu is devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night.
The word *ca* has the sense of conjunction; by it, he conjoins the states of mindfulness and so forth that will be mentioned hereafter.
*Assa* means "might be" (*siyā*), "should exist"—this is the meaning. Some read: "And a bhikkhu should dwell wakeful.

In all cases and at all times, by way of not abandoning the meditation subject and through non-separation from mindfulness, one is "mindful and clearly comprehending" (*sato sampajāno*) with respect to the fourfold clear comprehension belonging to the seven stations.

"Clearly comprehending" means being fully aware by way of that [practice]. "Concentrated" means being concentrated with a one-pointed mind through both access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) and absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*).
"Glad" means being joyful and full of rapture by seeing the benefits of the practice, by attaining ever-higher distinctions, and by seeing that the exertion of energy is not in vain.
"Serene" means, for that very reason, regarding those things which constitute the practice...
He is well-pleased through an abundance of faith in the Teacher who teaches the practice of the three trainings.
The connection is "he would possess [this] in all respects," or "he would dwell [thus].

In that context, "one who has insight at the proper time regarding wholesome states" means one who possesses insight (*vipassaka*) at that time, or one who possesses it there in the application of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"Insightful at the right time" means one who practices insight in accordance with the proper occasion. What is meant by this?

Having established insight and contemplating by way of the "comprehension by groups" (kalāpasammasana) and so forth, one avoids the seven unsuitable conditions such as the [wrong] dwelling and cultivates those that are suitable;

without falling into despondency in the interim, being resolute and observing the state of mental concentration, one diligently and continuously practices the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and the rest.
While practicing, at whatever time the insight-consciousness becomes sluggish, one should apply oneself to those wholesome, blameless factors of enlightenment known as investigation-of-phenomena,
energy, and rapture; but at whatever time the consciousness becomes agitated, one should apply oneself to those wholesome, blameless factors of enlightenment known as tranquility,
concentration, and equanimity— thus, in each respective case, at that particular time, or during that specific application of the meditation subject.
"One who possesses insight should be timely. Furthermore, the mindfulness enlightenment factor (satisambojjhaṅga) is desirable in all circumstances; for it has been said:
"And mindfulness, monks, I declare to be beneficial in all respects.
Having thus shown wakefulness through a teaching focused on the individual, he now explains those factors by which the practice of wakefulness succeeds.

Thus, having shown in brief the course of comprehension along with the factors that assist it for a bhikkhu who has initiated insight, the Blessed One now spoke the passage beginning with “For a bhikkhu, monks,
who is wakeful,” demonstrating the unfailing nature of the practice for one who proceeds in such a manner.
Therein, the application to wakefulness consists of the undertaking of mindfulness and clear comprehension.
These [qualities] are all-pervasive and bring about joy and confidence. In this context, "timely insight" (*kālavipassanā*) refers to insight that has reached maturity and is ready to conceive.

For when the knowledge of insight (*vipassanāñāṇa*) is free from defilements, has entered the right path, and is sharp, courageous, and flowing, the practitioner experiences sublime joy and confidence; and through these, the attainment of distinction is indeed close at hand. For it has been said:
“From whatever point one contemplates the arising and passing away of the aggregates, one gains rapture and gladness; that is the deathless for those who understand it.
A bhikkhu full of gladness, having confidence in the Buddha’s teaching...”
"One shall attain the peaceful state, the bliss that is the subsiding of all conditioned formations.
Regarding the phrase "Listen to this, you who are awake," listen to these words of mine with absolute earnestness;

being awake for the sake of awakening from the sleep of negligence and the sleep of ignorance, you should listen while devoted to wakefulness through the application of such qualities as mindfulness and clear comprehension.

"Ye suttā te pabujjhatha": those who are "asleep," having fallen into sleep by means of the aforementioned slumber—those of you, by way of devotion to wakefulness (*jāgariyānuyoga*), should gather together the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment (*indriya-bala-bojjhaṅga*), and while exerting yourselves in insight (*vipassanā*), awaken from that [sleep] through the practice of heedfulness (*appamāda*).
Alternatively, "those who are awake" refers to the signs of wakefulness. In the phrase "suṇāthetaṃ," the word "etaṃ" (this) has been stated.

"What is that speech? he asks, and replies: "Those who are asleep, wake up," and so forth. Therein, "those who are asleep" refers to those who are asleep with the slumber of the defilements (*kilesa*);
you, therefore, should wake up by means of the awakening of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). "Sleeping is worse than waking"—this is a statement of the reason for awakening.
For one who desires their own welfare, the kind of waking or vigilance described above is superior to the aforementioned sleep.
It is better for a clansman, more praiseworthy, and brings welfare and happiness; therefore, wake up.

"There is no fear for one who is awake"—this is the vision of the benefit therein. For he who is awake, being endowed with the qualities of wakefulness such as faith and the rest, does not succumb to the sleep of negligence;
for him there is no fear of self-reproach or fear of reproach by others.
There is no fear of punishment, no fear of an evil rebirth, and no fear of the round of existence (vaṭṭabhaya) characterized by birth and so forth.
"At the proper time" means at the time when one has obtained what is suitable for the dwelling and other such necessities. "He" is a mere particle.

"Investigating the Dhamma correctly" means investigating, by way of the right method, the phenomena belonging to the three planes that have become the object of insight, in such a way that disenchantment, dispassion, and so forth [arise].
"They arise"—thus, "examining all around" means "insight-penetrating in every aspect.

"Becoming one-pointed" (*ekodibhūta*): it is called *ekodi* because, being alone (*eka*), it arises as the best (*seṭṭha*); that is, concentration (*samādhi*). One who has become, been born, or arisen with that *ekodi* is "one who has become one-pointed" (*ekodibhūta*).
Here, the word *bhūta* should be understood as a secondary member of the compound, as in words such as *aggi-āhita*. Or alternatively, he has become (*bhūta*) one-pointed (*ekodi*).

“Having become one” means being solitary. Here, “one-pointedness” (ekodi) refers to the concentration of the path; however, in the phrase “being concentrated,” it refers to both the foundational jhāna-concentration and the insight-concentration.
Alternatively, “at the proper time” means at the time of penetrating the path.
“Thoroughly investigating the Dhamma” means correctly investigating the Dhamma of the Four Truths by way of full understanding, clear realization, and so forth.
Investigating, he realizes through a single penetration. "Becoming unified" (*ekodibhūta*): he is called "unified" (*ekodi*) because he arises alone, supreme, and without companion;
he is the one who accomplishes the four tasks through right exertion. That he has become unified and arisen—all this is exactly as explained before.
"He dispels the darkness": such a noble disciple, by means of the path of arahantship, dispels the darkness of ignorance without remainder.
"One should dispel it; one should utterly eradicate it.
Thus, having shown the fruitfulness of practice, the Blessed One now spoke this concluding verse, "Therefore indeed," in order to firmly enjoin [the practitioner] therein.
In that context, "therefore" means because for one who is awake, through the non-lapse of mindfulness and so forth, there is the cultivation of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
It reaches fulfillment; gradually the Noble Path becomes manifest, and thereafter he has no fear of the entire cycle of existence (vaṭṭa).
Therefore: *hava* means "certainly" or "firmly. *Bhajetha* means "one should cultivate.

And a bhikkhu who thus cultivates wakefulness, endowed with qualities such as ardor (*ātāpa*), having broken the fetters, [attains] the unsurpassed [state] known as the knowledge of the highest fruit.
One would touch and attain enlightenment free from further rebirth. The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the tenth sutta is finished.
11. Commentary on the Āpāyika Sutta.
48. "Destined for states of misery" (*āpāyika*) means those who will be reborn in a state of misery (*apāya*); "destined for hell" (*nerayika*) means those who will be reborn there in hell.

"Without abandoning this" means without having relinquished the two kinds of evil conduct that will be explained hereafter, and likewise without having renounced the speech, the mind, and the view that proceed by way of such practice and such exertion.

The meaning is as follows: "One who does not lead the holy life" (*abrahmacārī*): one who practices what is most excellent and supreme (*brahma*) is a "practitioner of the holy life" (*brahmacārī*); or, one who possesses the most excellent conduct (*ācāra*) that is supreme (*brahma*) is a "practitioner of the holy life.

One who is not such a practitioner is "one who does not lead the holy life"; the meaning is that he is an immoral person who merely resembles a practitioner of the holy life. "Claiming to be a practitioner of the holy life" (*brahmacāripaṭiñño*):
one who makes the claim, "I am a practitioner of the holy life. "Complete" (*paripuṇṇaṃ*): by way of being unbroken and so forth.
“Complete” means without deficiency. “Pure” means pure by virtue of the absence of defilements (*upakkilesa*).

“Without foundation” means devoid of the foundations for an accusation—namely, what was seen, heard, or suspected—and thus free from these bases of reproach. “By unchaste conduct” means by conduct that is not noble.
“Accuses” means that even while knowing, “This person is pure,” one ruins or destroys them with a matter involving defeat (*pārājika*), or accuses or reviles them.
"In verses, one who speaks what is untrue" refers to one who, without seeing the fault of another, slanders them by making a false, empty, and lying statement.
"Having done [it]" refers to one who, having committed an evil deed, says, "I did not do this.
"Both of them become equal after death" means that both these persons, having gone from here to the world beyond, are equal because they have entered hell.
They are equal in their destiny (*gati*). In this regard, it is only their destiny that is determined for them, not their lifespan.
For having committed much evil, one is cooked in hell for a long time; whereas having committed little, one remains for only a short duration.
Since the karma of both these types of people is equally base, it is said: "Human beings of base karma in the next world. Regarding the word "paratthā": it means "in the next world" (*parattha*).
However, the word "pecca" is connected with the preceding word— meaning that after departing from here and going elsewhere, those of inferior karma become equal [to that state].
Thus, having shown the ripening of false speech— which occurs both through the making of unfounded accusations and the concealing of actual faults—
the Blessed One now [describes] the ripening of the evil deeds of the many wicked monks seated in that place.
He spoke two verses for the purpose of inspiring spiritual urgency by showing the results of karmic maturation (*vipāka*).

Therein, "with yellow robes around their necks" (*kāsāvakaṇṭhā*) means those whose necks are wrapped in yellow cloth because it has been dyed with a yellow decoction. "Of evil nature" (*pāpadhammā*) means those of base character. "Unrestrained" (*asaññatā*) means lacking restraint in body and so forth.
"Evil ones" (*pāpā*) refers to such wicked persons who, having been reborn through evil deeds, [experience] even their bodies...
"Blazing, aflame, and glowing—his very outer robe is ablaze," and so forth; according to the method stated in the *Lakkhaṇa-saṃyutta*, they indeed experience great suffering.
This is the summary meaning of the third verse: even if an immoral person, an individual devoid of virtue, were to consume [the world] with his body and so forth...

It would be better, more excellent, for one who falsely claims “I am an ascetic” to take and eat a country alms-meal given out of faith by the inhabitants of the realm—unrestrained by discipline—than for him to eat a red-hot iron ball glowing like fire. Why is that?
Because on account of that [iron ball], only a single lifetime would be consumed; whereas, having become immoral and yet eating what is given out of faith, [the consequences are far worse].
"May I arise in hell for even many hundreds of births.
The commentary on the eleventh sutta is finished.
12. Commentary on the *Diṭṭhigata-sutta*.

49. Regarding the phrase "by two types of views" (*diṭṭhigatehi*) in the twelfth [verse]: here, *diṭṭhiyo* (views) themselves are *diṭṭhigatāni* (types of views), as in expressions such as "excrement-type" (*gūthagata*) or "urine-type" (*muttagata*).

Alternatively, they are called *diṭṭhigatāni* because they are merely the destinations (*gata*) of views, being empty of the grasped aspect. By those types of views, they are "obsessed" (*pariyuṭṭhitā*), meaning overcome or obstructed. For the word *pariyuṭṭhāna* also has the sense of an obstruction, as in "robbers... [the text continues].
In passages such as "they were overwhelmed on the path," the term *devā* refers to deities by rebirth (*upapatti-devā*).

For they "shine" (*dibbanti*) with the most sublime strands of sensual pleasure and with meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), etc., or they go to and attain whatever object they desire through the power of their psychic potency (*iddhi-anubhāva*);

thus they are called "deities. They are called "human beings" (*manussā*) because of the abundance of mind (*manasa ussannattā*); this is stated according to the method of designating the pre-eminent (*ukkaṭṭha-niddesa*).

As in the passage: “The Teacher of gods and humans. “Some shrink back” means that some gods and humans shrink back, cling, and fall into contraction due to the state of eternalism—which consists of a clinging attachment to existence, thinking “the self and the world are eternal”—and they do not escape from it.
“They run too far” refers to those who [cling] even to things whose intrinsic natures are ultimately distinct.
Failing to grasp that connection between phenomena which exists by way of cause and effect, they run hither and thither even while grasping at the method of diversity;

therefore, they either overreach or transcend the state of being a phenomenon that negates annihilationism—namely, "The self and the world are annihilated; there is nothing after death"—or they overreach the practice that leads to the cessation of existence.
Regarding the phrase "and those with vision see": the word *ca* (and) is used here in the sense of contrast.

However, gods and humans who possess the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*) through the perfection of their prior spiritual practice and the maturation of their knowledge, do not fall into the two extremes of eternalism and annihilationism; rather, by seeing the Middle Way through that very eye of wisdom, they realize it for themselves.
For they [see] that "this is merely name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) arisen through dependent origination; therefore, it is not eternal."
Nor is it annihilated; thus they see it without error.
In this way, to point out [the faults] such as indolence by way of reference to the person, the passage beginning with "And how, bhikkhus... was spoken.

Therein, "existence" (bhava) refers to sense-sphere existence, fine-material existence, and immaterial existence. Furthermore, there are three other types of existence: percipient existence, non-percipient existence, and...
The state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. There are also three other states of existence: the state of one constituent, the state of four constituents, and the state of five constituents.
They delight in and rejoice in these states of existence; thus they are "delighting in existence" (*bhavārāmā*). They take pleasure in and are fond of existences;

thus they are "attached to existence" (*bhavaratā*). They are thoroughly gladdened by existences; thus they are "rejoicing in existence" (*bhavasammuditā*). "For the cessation of existence" means for the absolute cessation of those states of existence.
"For the sake of non-arising. "When the Dhamma is being taught" means when the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata that leads to liberation is being spoken.
"Does not leap forward" means that because of his adherence to eternalism and because the Dhamma is concise, he does not enter into it or plunge into it.
"Does not become confident" means he does not attain confidence; he does not have faith in it. "Does not settle down" means in that teaching...
They do not stand firm, nor do they resolve. Thus, by adhering to eternalism, they cling to states of existence (*bhava*).
"Being distressed" means being agitated upon seeing aging, sickness, death, and so forth, as well as killing, binding, mutilation, and the like;
being oppressed and tormented by existence through association with those things. "Being ashamed" means feeling shame or loathing.

"Perceiving [the body] as repulsive": they burn away [defilements]. "They exist through annihilation": they delight in annihilation. "They delight" means they take pleasure by way of clinging through craving and views.
"From which, O lady," and so forth, is a demonstration of the manner of their delighting. Therein, "from which" (*yato*) means when. "O lady" (*bho*) is a form of address.
"This self" (*ayam attā*) refers to that which is conceptually imagined as a self by way of being an agent and so forth. "It is annihilated" (*ucchijjati*).
"It is cut off" means it ceases. "It perishes" means it is no longer seen; it goes to destruction, which is non-existence. "There is nothing after death" means that beyond death, nothing exists.
"This is peaceful" means that this—namely, one's own annihilation and so forth—is peaceful because of the subsiding of all becoming and the subsiding of all feverish distress.
Precisely because it is peaceful, it is sublime; because its state is true and not inverted, it is suchness.
In this context, they say that the pair "peaceful" and "sublime" refers to the delight of craving, while "as it really is" refers to the delight of views.
"Thus" means by way of the aforementioned adherence to annihilationism.
"Becoming" refers to the five aggregates; for they are called "becoming" because they have arisen from conditions and exist in the ultimate sense.
It is said thus. Therefore he said: “Bhikkhus, behold this as it has come to be.
One sees it as it has come to be—that is, from its unerring individual nature, its specific characteristic, and its general characteristic. For this pentad of aggregates is merely name-and-form.
Therein, “these phenomena beginning with earth are form; these phenomena beginning with contact are name; and these are their characteristics and so forth.”

The meaning is that he sees them by way of the contemplation of impermanence and so forth, thinking: "These are their conditions, beginning with ignorance," thus by way of seeing name-and-form together with its conditions;

and also: "All these phenomena, having not been, come to be; having been, they vanish; therefore they are impermanent; because they are impermanent, they are suffering; because they are suffering, they are non-self.
Up to this point, [the section on] the conclusion of nascent insight is complete.

The stage of insight (vipassanā) has been shown. "For the sake of disenchantment" (nibbidāya) means for the purpose of becoming disenchanted with the mass of phenomena belonging to the three planes, which are reckoned as "real";

by this, he shows powerful insight. "For the sake of dispassion" (virāgāya) means for the purpose of dispassion, for the purpose of fading away; by this, he shows the Path (magga). "For the sake of cessation" (nirodhāya) means for the purpose of ceasing;
by this also, he shows the Path itself. Or alternatively, "for the sake of cessation" refers to cessation by way of subsiding (paṭippassaddhi-nirodha).
...together, he demonstrates the Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*). "In this way, monks, those with eyes see":
thus, those possessing the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*)—by means of the eye of path-wisdom (*maggapaññā-cakkhu*) together with its prior stage—see the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.

Regarding the verses, "those who have seen what is real as it really is" refers to those noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*) who have seen the five aggregates (*khandha-pañcaka*), which are real, as they truly are, that is, according to their non-perverted nature.
"Having seen with the wisdom of the path accompanied by insight-wisdom. By this, he shows the realization through full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*).

"And they transcend what has come to be" refers to the realization through development (*bhāvanābhisamaya*). For the Noble Path transcends what has come to be; thus it is called "the transcending of what has come to be.
"As it truly is" means in Nibbāna, which is the unerring nature of reality. "They are liberated" means they are resolutely intent upon it.

By this, he shows the realization through direct knowledge (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*). "Through the complete exhaustion of craving for existence" means by the utter wearing away and cutting off of craving for existence;
by this, he shows the abandoning of the origin (*samudayappahāna*).

In the phrase "he is one who has full understanding of what has come to be," the word *save* is merely a particle. He is one who has full understanding of what has come to be by means of the method for transcending what has come to be.
Through the path, with the total destruction of craving for existence, he has fully understood the aggregates; for that very reason, he is intent upon Nibbāna as it truly is.

"In various states of being" (*bhavābhava*) means in both small and great [existences], or rather, one who is free from craving regarding views such as annihilationism and whose defilements are shattered.

A "bhikkhu" is so called because of the dissolution (*vibhava*) of this existing personal identity (*attabhāva*), which is comprised of the aggregates of clinging, due to its non-arising in the future.
"He does not come to renewed existence; he goes to a state of non-designation"—thus he concluded the teaching on the element of Nibbāna without residue.

Thus, in this chapter, the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is explained in the eleventh sutta; in the third, fourth, and fifth, as well as in the concluding sutta, both the cycle of existence and its reversal (*vivaṭṭa*) are explained; it should be understood that in the remaining suttas, only the reversal is explained.
The commentary on the twelfth sutta is finished.
The commentary on the *Itivuttaka*, the *Paramatthadīpanī* sub-commentary on the *Khuddakanikāya-ṭīkā*, is completed. 3.
The Third Chapter (Tikanipāta).
1. First Chapter. 1.
Commentary on the Root Sutta. 50.
In the first [chapter] of the Triads (*Tikanipāta*), "three" is the numerical limit. "These" is the act of bringing them to mind. "Roots of unwholesomeness" (*akusalamūla*)...
This is an indication of the defined phenomena (*paricchinnadhammanidassana*). In this context, they are "unwholesome roots" (*akusalamūlāni*) because they are both unwholesome and roots.
Alternatively, they are "unwholesome roots" because they are roots in the sense of being the cause, condition, source, producer, originator, and generator of the unwholesome;
that is to say, they are the causes of unwholesome states. For a cause is so called because the fruit proceeds (*hinoti*) from it.

It is called a *hetu* (cause) because it causes [a state] to proceed; a *paccaya* (condition) because by depending on it, [something] comes about; a *pabhava* (source) because from it [something] originates;
a *janaka* (producer) because it generates its own fruit; a *samuṭṭhāpaka* (originator) because it brings [it] forth; and it is called a *nibbattaka* (actualizer) because it produces [it].
Thus, in the sense of being a foundation, it is a "root" (*mūla*); therefore, the "unwholesome roots" (*akusalamūlāni*) are those things that effect the well-established state of unwholesome states.
It is meant that they are the causes.

However, some say: "Just as the seeds of rice and so forth are for rice and so forth, and as the colors of gems and so forth are for the radiance of gems, the root-status of greed and so forth is that which establishes the unwholesome nature of the unwholesome [states]. This being the case, regarding the material phenomena originating from unwholesome consciousness...
Their status as root-conditions would not exist. For those [unwholesome roots] do not establish the unwholesome nature of those [associated states], yet they are not non-conditions.
For this has been said:
"Roots are a condition, by way of root-condition, for the states associated with them and for the material phenomena originated by them."
Furthermore, rootless delusion (ahetuka-moha) would not possess the quality of unwholesomeness, because there is no other root to establish its unwholesome nature.

If it were argued that while greed and the others have their unwholesome nature established by their own intrinsic essence (sabhāva), the unwholesome nature of those associated with them is dependent upon greed and the rest—then, just as it is for greed and the others, the wholesome nature of non-greed and the others would also be established by their own intrinsic essence;
thus, non-greed and the others [would likewise be intrinsically wholesome].

[The roots] would have to be exclusively wholesome (*kusala*), not indeterminate (*abyākata*), yet they are not so. Therefore, just as with the associated states (*sampayutta*), the status of being wholesome and so forth must be sought in the roots as well.

For it should be understood that just as appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and the like are the cause for the state of wholesomeness, inappropriate attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*) and the like are the cause for the state of unwholesomeness.
Thus, the root-status (*mūlaṭṭha*) of greed and the others is established by way of their accomplishing the state of unwholesomeness.
There is no fault in taking them as "roots" in the sense of establishing a state of being well-established once they have been grasped.

For phenomena that have obtained causes and conditions become firm and well-established like trees with deep-set roots; however, those devoid of a cause do not stand well, like moss from sesame seeds and the like.
Thus, because they assist the unwholesome states in the sense of being their causes and so forth, they are called "unwholesome roots" (*akusalamūla*).

However, since there is no unwholesome state of consciousness that is not released from a root, it should be understood that the entire mass of the unwholesome has been shown by way of exhausting [the analysis] through the three roots.
To show those unwholesome roots according to their specific nature, it was said: "Greed is an unwholesome root," and so forth. In this regard, concerning greed and the others:
What ought to be said has already been stated above. However, there, greed and the rest were mentioned as being abandonable by the third path;
here, however, they are "without remainder"—this alone is the distinction.

In this verse, "evil-minded" (*pāpacetasa*) refers to a base mind due to its association with unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*). "They harm" (*hiṃsanti*) means at the moment of their own occurrence...
And they cause affliction at the time of future ripening. "Born from oneself" means produced within oneself.
"Bamboo with a pith of bark" means knotted; the meaning is "bamboo. "Its own fruit" means its own result. This is what is meant:
