Furthermore, this wisdom has the characteristic of penetrating things according to their true nature, or the characteristic of unerring penetration, like the penetration of an arrow shot by a skilled archer; its function is the illumination of the object.
It is like a lamp; it is like a guide who has gone into the forest, manifesting as non-delusion.

Specifically, however, in this context, wisdom—consisting of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints—is intended by the term "eye of wisdom" in the sense of seeing the Four Truths. It is with reference to this that it was said:
"The eye arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true insight arose, light arose."
Among these, the fleshly eye is limited (*paritta*), the divine eye is exalted (*mahaggata*), and the other is immeasurable (*appamāṇa*).
The fleshly eye is material (*rūpa*); the others are immaterial (*arūpa*). Both the fleshly eye and the divine eye are mundane (*lokiya*), subject to taints (*sāsavā*), and have form as their object;

the other is supramundane (*lokuttara*), free from taints (*anāsava*), and has the Four Truths as its object. The fleshly eye is indeterminate (*abyākata*); the divine eye may be [either determinate or indeterminate].

The wholesome may be indeterminate, and likewise the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*). The fleshly eye belongs to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), the divine eye to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), and the other to the supramundane (*lokuttara*);
such distinctions are to be understood.

In the verses, the term "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) is said with reference to the eye of wisdom; for that is unsurpassed because it consists in the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*).

"He has proclaimed" means that the Supreme among Men, the Foremost of men, the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), taught. "Arising" refers to the functioning of the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*).
"Path" means the means; it is the cause for the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).

For it is only one who possesses the natural eye that the divine eye arises, because the production of the knowledge of the divine eye occurs by expanding the light of the *kasiṇa*, and that [expansion] takes place within the *kasiṇa*-mandala.

"There is nothing without the learning-sign (uggahanimitta). "When" means at which time. "Knowledge" refers to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa). For this reason it is said:

"the unsurpassed eye of wisdom. "With the acquisition of which eye" means through the arising and cultivation of which noble eye of wisdom one is liberated and completely released from all the suffering of the round of existence (vaṭṭadukkha).
The commentary on the second sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Indriya Sutta: 62.
In the third [sutta], "faculties" (*indriyāni*) means faculties in the sense of being predominant (*adhipateyyatthena*). For those which are sovereign over their co-nascent states...

They must be followed by those [faculties] as if they were a lord; thus they are called "faculties" (*indriya*). Furthermore, the Blessed One is the Lord (*inda*), the Master of Dhamma, endowed with supreme sovereignty of mind.

Because these [qualities] were first seen, attained, and seen by others by that Lord, and because they were taught, established, and seen through the cultivation and practice of their respective spheres, they are called "faculties."

Or, the "faculties" (*indriyāni*) are so called because they are either the meritorious deeds that serve as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the attainment of the Path, or the signs (*liṅga*) thereof.

Regarding the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*): it is the faculty that arises in one who has entered the practice with the thought, "In this beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), I shall come to know that which was previously unknown and unattained—the state of the Deathless, or the Dhamma of the Four Truths"—by means of this preliminary stage.

This is a designation for the wisdom of the stream-entry path (*sotāpatti-magga-paññā*). "Faculty of final knowledge" (*aññindriya*) means the faculty of full understanding. Herein, this is the etymological analysis:
it is called "final knowledge" (*aññā*) because it understands—meaning it knows—without overstepping the boundary already seen by the knowledge of the first path.
For just as the wisdom of the first path proceeds by way of the clear comprehension (*pariññā*) and realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding suffering and the other truths, so too does this.
It is called the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*) because it is both "final knowledge" (*aññā*) and, in the sense already stated, a "faculty" (*indriya*).

Alternatively, it is the faculty of one who possesses final knowledge—that is, of a noble person (*ariyapuggala*)—in the sense of "understanding" (*ājānana*); this is a designation for the knowledge existing in six stages beginning from the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*).
The faculty of one who has already known (*aññātāvindriya*) refers to one for whom the task of knowledge regarding the four truths has been completed.
The faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya) arises because of the exhaustion of the taints (āsava) and because of the occurrence of the meaning of the faculties.

Herein, it should be understood that the first and the last [faculties] share a single basis by way of the first path and the fourth fruit, respectively, while the other [faculty] has six bases by way of the remaining paths and fruits.
In the verses, "of one training" (sikkhamānassa) means of one who is developing the trainings in higher virtue and so forth; "following the straight path" (ujumaggānusārino).

The "straight path" (ujumagga) refers to the Noble Path; because one recollects it as being free from the two extremes, one is a "follower of the straight path," meaning one who generates the path in successive order.
Regarding the phrase "in the destruction" (khaye): because it exhausts all defilements without remainder, knowledge first arises prior to that very moment in the supreme path known as destruction.
Immediately after that is "subsequent knowledge" (aññā); that is, immediately after that knowledge of the path.

Immediately thereafter, Arahantship arises. Alternatively, "one who follows the straight path" refers to one who, having abandoned the bases for sluggishness, agitation, exertion, and so forth, recollects, pursues, and practices the preliminary path that proceeds by way of meditation through the coupling of serenity and insight;
for such a person, immediately after the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*), [the path] that eliminates what is to be abandoned by vision...

Because it exhausts the defilements, the first knowledge regarding the path of stream-entry that leads to destruction arises as the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*).

Then, "subsequent to that, there is the final knowledge": from immediately after that first knowledge, starting from that very moment until the highest path, the final knowledge arises as the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*).
"Then, for one liberated through final knowledge": "then" means after the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*);

"for one liberated" means for one liberated by the faculty of one who has already known (*aññātāvindriya*), which is the liberation of wisdom through the fruit of arahantship immediately following the knowledge of the path of arahantship. "Truly there is knowledge for such a one":

this refers to the reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*) of the one whose taints are destroyed, who has attained the characteristic of equanimity (*tādilakkhaṇa*) regarding the desirable and undesirable and so forth at a time subsequent to the arising of the fruit of arahantship.
It arises. How does it arise? He says: "My liberation is unshakable. He shows the cause for that state of being unshakable by saying:
"Through the destruction of the fetters of existence.
Now, praising such a one whose taints are exhausted, he recites the third verse: "He indeed is endowed with the faculties. Therein:
“Endowed with the faculties” means being possessed of the three aforementioned supramundane faculties;
or else, being complete and endowed with the pure faculties such as faith and so forth, which have been attained through subsiding;

and for that very reason, being endowed with faculties such as the eye and so forth that are perfectly stilled and free from worldly activity. Therefore he says “peaceful,” by virtue of the subsiding of the fever of all defilements.
The meaning is "one who is tranquil. "Delighting in the state of peace" means being devoted to and finding joy in Nibbāna.

Here, by the phrase "endowed with the faculties," his state of having developed the Path and his full comprehension of the aggregates are shown. By the word "tranquil," the abandoning of the defilements is shown;
by the phrase "delighting in the state of peace," the realization of cessation is shown. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the Third Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Addhā Sutta: 63.
In the fourth [sutta], "addhā" means periods of time. Regarding such expressions as "the past addhā," there are two modes of exposition: the mode of the Suttanta and the mode of the Abhidhamma.
In this regard, according to the method of the Suttas, the period prior to rebirth-linking is called the past time;
the period after death is called the future time; and the period immediately following death and rebirth-linking, together with them, is called the present time.
According to the method of the Abhidhamma, those phenomena that have ceased after reaching these three moments—arising, presence, and dissolution—are called the past time. All three...
The future time is that which has not yet reached the present moment; the present time is that which possesses the three moments [of arising, presence, and dissolution].
Another method: this division into past and so forth should be understood in four ways—by way of extent (*addhā*), continuity (*santati*), period (*samaya*), and moment (*khaṇa*).
Among these, the division by way of extent has been stated. By way of continuity, [states] are similar when they arise from the same season, or arise from the same nutriment.

And even when occurring in a sequence of prior and posterior moments, they are "present. Prior to that, those produced by dissimilar temperature or nutriment are "past," and subsequent to it, they are "future.
Those born of consciousness are called "present" when produced by a single cognitive series (*vīthi*), a single impulsion (*javana*), or a single meditative attainment (*samāpatti*);
prior to that, they are "past," and subsequent to that, they are "future. As for those produced by kamma, [the distinction is made] by way of their individual continuity (*santati*).

There is no distinction such as "past" and so forth inherent in them; rather, their state as past and so on should be understood by way of the support provided by temperature, nutriment, mind, or kamma-originated matter.

By way of time—occurring as a continuity during specific times such as one muhutta, forenoon, afternoon, night, or day—they are called "present" at that particular time; prior to that, they are "past."

...and afterwards they are future. This, first of all, is the method regarding material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*). Regarding immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*), however, those included within the three moments of arising and so forth by way of the momentary process are present;
prior to that, they are past; and afterwards, they are future. Furthermore, those whose functions of cause and condition have already passed are past;
those whose function of cause has been completed but whose function of condition is not yet completed are present; and those that have not yet reached either function are future.
Or, [phenomena] are present at the moment of their own function; prior to that, they are past; and subsequent to that, they are future.

And herein, only the discourse on moments and so forth is non-figurative (nippariyāya); the rest are figurative (pariyāya). For this distinction of past and so forth belongs to phenomena, not to time.
However, by resorting to phenomena distinguished as past and so forth, "time"—though non-existent in the ultimate sense—is here treated by that very conventional designation.
It should be understood that this is stated by the passage beginning with "the past," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "those who perceive what is expressible" (*akkheyyasaññino*) in the verses: here, "what is expressible" (*akkheyya*) means that which is spoken of, described, or designated; it is the subject matter of discourse. In terms of its actual meaning, it refers to the five aggregates, such as form (*rūpa*), and so on.
For this has been said: "One might speak about the past time, or about the future... or one might speak about the present time."
Likewise:
"Bhikkhus, whatever form is past, ceased, and changed, it has the designation 'it was,' it has the convention 'it was,' it has the description 'it was';
it does not have the designation 'it exists,' nor will it have the designation 'it will be.'"
The meaning here should also be illustrated by the *Niruttipatha-sutta* spoken in this way.

Thus, regarding the five aggregates—which are reckoned as "the expressible" (*akkheyya*) by virtue of being the basis for discourse—one is "possessed of the notion of the expressible" through the occurrence of notions such as "I," "mine," "god," "human," "woman," and "man.
[This occurs] with respect to the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*).

The meaning is: "perceiving [them as] seven persons, etc. They are established in the expressible (akkheyya) by way of grasping through craving and views, or else they are established in eight ways by way of lust and so forth.
For one who is lustful is established by way of lust; one who is corrupted by way of hatred; one who is deluded by way of delusion;
one who is misapprehending by way of views; one who is entrenched by way of underlying tendencies (anusaya); one who is bound by way of conceit (māna).
One becomes established through doubt by way of wavering, and through restlessness by way of distraction.

"Without fully understanding the 'to-be-expressed'" means that, having not understood those phenomena of the three planes through the three kinds of full understanding (*pariññā*), one fails to understand them;
for that reason of non-understanding, "they enter into the bond of death" means they come upon the bond, the fetter, of death.
The meaning is "they do not enter into disjunction.

Alternatively, *yoga* means "means" (*upāya*); thus, it is said that they approach the net of harm and the net of defilements—which stand in the place of Māra’s army—joined with and extended by that [means]. For it has been said:
"We have no pact with him, with Death and his great army."

Having thus far shown the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), the passage beginning with “and having fully understood what is expressible” (*akkheyyañca pariññāya*) is now stated in order to show the turning away from it (*vivaṭṭa*).

Herein, the word “and” (*ca*) signifies contrast; by means of it, he illuminates the specific distinction that is to be attained through the full understanding of what is expressible, which will indeed be explained below.
“Having fully understood” (*pariññāya*) means having discerned and known [the aggregates] as suffering by means of the wisdom of the path accompanied by insight (*vipassanā*).
Or, by abandoning the defilements bound to that [contact], having transcended it and brought the task of all three types of full understanding (pariññā) to its ultimate conclusion.
"He does not conceive of one who explains": because all forms of conceiving (maññanā) have been abandoned, the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) does not conceive of one who explains;
the meaning is that he does not recognize any self whatsoever as having the nature of an agent and so forth. Touched...
"Deliverance by means of the mind, the unsurpassed state of peace": because it is liberated from all conditioned things, it is called "deliverance" (*vimokkho*);
and because it is the locus for the subsiding of the heat of all defilements, it is called the "state of peace" (*santipada*).

Since this Dhamma of Nibbāna—so named—has been touched, felt, and attained, one does not conceive of a speaker. Alternatively, by the term "having fully understood" (*pariññāya*), [it refers to] the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).

Having explained the clear realization through full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*) and the clear realization through abandonment (*pahānābhisamaya*) regarding the truth of the origin, he now speaks of the clear realization through cultivation and actualization (*bhāvanā-sacchikiriyābhisamaya*) of the path and cessation with the words: “Liberation has been touched by the mind; the unsurpassed state of peace. Its meaning is as follows:
it is called liberation (*vimokkho*) because by means of its total eradication, one is liberated from all defilements; it is the Noble Path.

Thus, by means of that path-consciousness, it has been touched, contacted, and cultivated; and by that very [consciousness], the unsurpassed state of peace, Nibbāna, has been touched, contacted, and realized.

"Endowed with what is to be told" (*akkheyyasampanno*) means that, because he has abandoned the perversions (*vipallāsa*), even though the world is afflicted by various misfortunes which are the signs of what is to be told (*akkheyyanimitta*).
Thus he is well-liberated, endowed and possessed of the attainments produced by the full understanding of the expressible.
"One who uses after deliberation" means one whose habit is to use the requisites such as robes only after having deliberated and weighed them through the attainment of the abundance of wisdom;

and because he has discerned all phenomena, his habit is to use every object that comes into his range after deliberating upon it by way of the sixfold equanimity. "One who stands firm in the Dhamma."

He stands either in the qualities of one beyond training (*asekkha-dhamma*) or in the quality of Nibbāna itself. He is called a "Vedagū" because he has gone to the further shore (*pāraṅgata*) of what is to be known, namely the Four Noble Truths.
An Arahant endowed with such qualities does not fall into the reckoning of "human" or "divine" in any future existence due to the absence of renewed becoming;
he simply passes into a state of non-designation (*apaññatti*). Thus, he brought the teaching to its conclusion through Parinibbāna without clinging (*anupādā-parinibbāna*).
The commentary on the fourth sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Duccarita-sutta* (Sutta 64):
"Badly conducted" (*duccarita*) means either conduct that is bad, or bad conduct. Bad conduct by way of the body...
Misconduct that occurs through the body is bodily misconduct (*kāyaduccarita*). The same method applies to the others as well.
These forms of misconduct may be explained either by way of their formal designation (*paññatti*) or by way of the courses of action (*kamma-patha*). In this regard, first, by way of designation:

the transgression of a training rule (*sikkhāpada*) prescribed for the door of the body is bodily misconduct; the transgression of a training rule prescribed for the door of speech is verbal misconduct.
The transgression of that which is prescribed for both [body and speech] is mental misconduct (*manoduccarita*); this is the discourse on what is prescribed (*paññatti-kathā*).
Furthermore, the three volitions (*cetanā*) beginning with the destruction of life, whether they arise at the door of the body or the door of speech, constitute bodily misconduct;
likewise, the four volitions beginning with false speech constitute verbal misconduct; and the three factors associated with volition—covetousness, ill will, and wrong view—are [mental misconduct].
“Mental misconduct” (manoduccaritaṃ) refers to this discussion of the courses of kamma.
In the verse, it is the unwholesome state that has reached the status of a course of kamma which is described by way of bodily misconduct and so forth;
therefore, in order to include other unwholesome states, it is said: “and whatever else is associated with hatred” (yañcaññaṃ dosasañhitaṃ). Therein, “associated with hatred” (dosasañhitaṃ) means:
"Endowed with the defilements of lust and so forth. The remainder is easy to understand.
The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Sucarita-sutta* (The Discourse on Good Conduct).
65. In the sixth [section], "well-conducted" (*sucarita*) means either well-practiced or beautiful conduct.
Good conduct by way of the body is bodily good conduct (*kāyasucarita*). The same method applies to the remaining [two] as well. Here too, however, there is a twofold exposition:
by way of formal designation (*paññatti*) and by way of courses of action (*kammappatha*). Among these, non-transgression of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) designated at the door of the body—

Good bodily conduct is [the observance of precepts]; non-transgression of the training rules prescribed for the door of speech is good verbal conduct; and non-transgression of what is prescribed for both is good mental conduct—this is the discourse on the prescribed.

Furthermore, the three volitions and the three abstinences that arise in one who refrains from killing living beings and so forth are good bodily conduct; likewise, the four [volitions and abstinences] in one who refrains from false speech and so forth...
Volition and the abstentions constitute verbal good conduct; while non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view—these three factors associated with volition—constitute mental good conduct.
This is the discourse on the courses of kamma. The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the sixth sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Soceyyasutta (Discourse on Purities) 66.

Regarding the seventh [verse], *soceyyāni* means states of purity (*sucibhāva*). *Kāyasoceyya* is bodily good conduct; likewise, *vacīmano-soceyyāni* are simply verbal and mental good conduct. For it has been said: "In this context, what is bodily purity? It is abstention from taking life," and so forth.
In the verse, one is called "pure in body" (*kāyasuci*) because of being pure by body through having abandoned all bodily misconduct by way of its total eradication. *Soceyyasampannaṃ* means...
It is endowed with the perfection of purity (*soceyya*) which is utterly cleansed due to the subsiding of the defilements (*kilesa*). The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the seventh sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Moneyya Sutta.

67. Regarding the eighth [section], "the states of a sage" (*moneyyāni*): here, one is called a "sage" (*muni*) because he is silent regarding this world and the next world, as well as his own welfare and the welfare of others;
these include the seven types of trainees (*sekkhā*) together with the noble ordinary person (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*). However, in this context, only the arahant is intended.
The "states of a sage" (*moneyyāni*) are the modes of conduct of body, speech, and mind belonging to the arahant.
Alternatively, the states that produce the state of a sage (*munibhāva*)—namely, the qualities of the practice of sagehood (*moneyyapaṭipadā*)—are the "sage-qualities" (*moneyyāni*).
This is their detailed exposition: "In this context, what is bodily sagehood (*kāyamoneyya*)? The abandoning of the three kinds of bodily misconduct is bodily sagehood;
the three kinds of bodily good conduct is bodily sagehood; knowledge regarding the body as an object is bodily sagehood; full understanding of the body is bodily sagehood."
The path accompanied by full understanding is bodily integrity; the abandoning of desire and lust for the body is bodily integrity;
the attainment of the fourth jhāna through the cessation of bodily formations is bodily integrity.
"In this context, what is verbal integrity? The abandoning of the fourfold verbal misconduct is verbal integrity. The fourfold..."

Virtuous verbal conduct, knowledge regarding the object of speech, full understanding of speech, the path accompanied by full understanding, the abandoning of desire and lust for speech, and the attainment of the second jhāna through the cessation of verbal formations—this is verbal integrity (*vācī-moneyya*).
In this context, what is mental integrity (*mano-moneyya*)? The abandoning of the threefold misconduct of mind is mental integrity. The threefold...
"Good conduct of mind, knowledge regarding the object of mind, full understanding of mind, the path accompanied by full understanding, the abandoning of desire and lust for the mind,
and the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling through the cessation of mental formations— this is the purity of mind.
"One whose evil has been washed away" means one whose stain of evil has been thoroughly cleansed by the water of the supreme path.
The commentary on the eighth sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the First Rāga Sutta: 68.
In the ninth [sutta], the phrase "of whomever" (*yassa kassaci*) is an indefinite expression; therefore, it refers to any person whatsoever, whether a householder...
Or for one who has gone forth. "Lust is not abandoned" means that in the sense of coloring, lust has not been abandoned by way of total eradication;

it has not been brought to a state of non-arising through the Path. The same method applies to hatred and delusion as well. In this context, the lust, hatred, and delusion that lead to the states of misery are [abandoned] by the first Path;
the coarse sensual lust and hatred are [abandoned] by the second Path; and those very same [defilements], without remainder, [are abandoned by the third].
By the third path, attachment to existence (*bhavarāga*) and the remaining delusion (*moha*) are abandoned by the fourth path.
When these are thus abandoned, all defilements (*kilesa*) are likewise abandoned because they are associated with them.
Thus, for whichever monk, nun, layman, or laywoman these [defilements] such as lust have not been abandoned by the path, they are "bound by Māra," that is, by the Defilement-Māra (*kilesamāra*).

He is said to be "bound. And to the extent that he is bound by the Māra of the defilements (kilesamāra), to that same extent he is also bound by the Māras of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāramāra) and the others.

"The snare of Māra is set for him" means that for this person whose defilements have not been abandoned, by virtue of those very unabandoned defilements, the defilement known as the snare of Māra is set—that is, it has been cast and introduced—into the continuum of his own mind.
The meaning is that by him [the snare] was caused to be bound. Alternatively, Māra’s snare might be fastened upon him.
In the case of the bright side (*sukkapakkha*), "omukka" means it has been unfastened, released, and removed. The rest should be understood by reversing what was stated above.
Here, the verses have been presented according to the bright side alone. In this regard, the summarized meaning is as follows: for whichever noble person (*ariyapuggala*)...
Lust, hatred, and ignorance have been stripped away and ceased through the supreme path;

he is one among those Arahants who have developed their body, virtue, mind, and wisdom—indeed, one who has become Brahmā within, a single being who has attained the state of Brahmā, the most excellent fruit of Arahantship.
Just as other ones whose taints are destroyed have arrived, having been endowed with the excellence of past supporting conditions. Just as...
And they have gone to, that is, attained Nibbāna by means of the Middle Way— which is free from the two extremes and accompanied by the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom. Or rather,
just as they have penetrated the true characteristic of the aggregates and so forth as it really is,
and just as they have directly known the truths such as suffering regarding those phenomena exactly as they are, and regarding objects such as form...
They saw [him] merely by way of what was seen and so forth; or rather,

just as they had abandoned the eight ignoble modes of speech and proceeded with speech according to the noble mode of speech, with body proceeding in accordance with that speech, and with speech proceeding in accordance with that body—
so too is this person a "Tathāgata" because he is thus, a "Buddha" because of his awakening to the Four Noble Truths, and one who has overcome personal enmity.
Because it has transcended both the enmity of the defilements (*kilesavera*) and the fear of self-reproach and so forth, it is called "beyond the fear of enmity" (*verabhayātīta*).
Because all defilements, volitional formations, and the like have been abandoned, the Noble Ones—the Buddhas and others—have said, speak, and proclaim it as "the abandoner of all.
The commentary on the ninth sutta is concluded.
10. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Lust (Dutiyarāgasutta) 69.

In the tenth [verse], "atarī" means "crossed over"; "not crossed over" is *atiṇṇo*. "The ocean" (*samudda*) refers either to the ocean of saṃsāra or to the ocean of the sense bases beginning with the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*).
Both of these are called "the ocean" because they are like an ocean in the sense of being difficult to fill. Alternatively, it is so called in the sense of "overflowing" (*samuddana*).
"Samuddaṃ" means the ocean; the meaning is that it is the dwelling place of defilements for the continuum of beings due to the rain of defilements.
"Savīciṃ" means with waves (vīci) of the taints of anger and resentment. For this has been said: "The fear of waves, bhikkhu, is a designation for anger and resentment.
"Sāvaṭṭaṃ" means together with the whirlpools (āvaṭṭa) of the five strands of sensual pleasure. And this too has been said: "The fear of whirlpools..."
“Monk, this is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure. It is “with crocodiles and with demons” because it produces harm for those who have entered its range;
that is, it is accompanied by dissimilar persons who resemble fierce makaras, fish, turtles, and demons.
Thus it is said: “‘With crocodiles and with demons,’ monk, this is a designation for womankind. He crossed over.
Having crossed the aforementioned ocean by means of the ship of path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*), he is "one who has crossed over" (*tiṇṇo*), meaning he has completely crossed over.
"One who has gone to the further shore" (*pāraṅgato*) means he has reached the further shore, the other bank, which is cessation (*nirodha*). "He stands on dry land" (*thale tiṭṭhati*):

having thus transcended both the great flood of saṃsāra and the great flood of sensual desire and so forth, that brahmin who has warded off evil stands on dry land—that is, on the further shore, in Nibbāna. Thus it is said.

Here too, the verse is presented according to the bright side (sukkapaṭipadā). In this context, "fear of waves" refers to the aforementioned fear of waves; because one must fear it, it is called "wave-fear. "Hard to cross" means difficult to transcend. "He has crossed over" means he has transcended.
"One who has gone beyond attachments" means one who has gone beyond and abandoned the five attachments, beginning with lust (rāga).

"He has set and is no longer measurable" means that such an Arahant, having brought to utter cessation those phenomena such as lust that serve as the basis for measurement, is no longer subject to being measured.

Because he has gone (gatatta), he has "gone to rest" (atthaṅgata); for that very reason, due to the fulfillment of the aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue and the rest, he cannot be measured by anyone as being "such in virtue, concentration, or wisdom," and thus he does not come within the scope of measurement.

Alternatively, that Arahant who has gone to the goal (attha) known as Nibbāna without residue cannot be measured by saying, "He stands in this particular state of existence, and he is such-and-such by name and clan."
"Because it is impossible [to measure], it does not come within the scope of measurement; for that very reason, he did not delude the King of Death, meaning I say he was impossible for him to pursue.
Thus he concluded his teaching with the element of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*).
Therefore, in this chapter, the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is discussed in the first, fifth, and sixth [sections], while in the second, seventh, and eighth...
It should be understood that in the remaining [suttas], both the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) are explained.
The commentary on the tenth sutta is finished.
The commentary on the second chapter is finished.
3. Third Chapter. 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Those of Wrong View (Micchādiṭṭhikasutta). 70.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the third chapter: "I have seen" (*diṭṭhā mayā*) means they were seen by me with my universal eye, that is, my divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
"Seen by both eyes" means directly perceived. By this, he rejects hearsay and the like;
and this meaning will be presented in the Pāḷi text immediately hereafter. "Endowed with bodily misconduct" means possessed of bodily misconduct.
"Revilers of the noble ones" means those who disparage the virtues of the noble ones, such as the Buddhas and others, down to even householders who have attained the stream-entry fruit (sotāpanna).
"Accusers" means those who revile, abuse, and criticize by making false accusations. "Holding wrong views" means having a perverted perspective.

"Adopting actions based on wrong views" refers to those who, for the sake of such a perverted perspective, have undertaken various kinds of kamma, as well as those who encourage others in bodily actions and so forth rooted in wrong view.
And here, by the very mention of verbal and mental misconduct, the reviling of the Noble Ones and wrong views are included.

The repetition regarding those already mentioned is for the purpose of showing their extreme blameworthiness. For slandering the Noble Ones is extremely blameworthy, being similar to an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense. As it is said:
"Just as, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom, in this very life..."
"One might attain final knowledge regarding the Dhamma. It is in this way, Sāriputta, that I declare:
without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that mind, and without relinquishing that view, one is placed in hell just as if carried there.
And indeed, there is nothing more blameworthy than wrong view. As it has been said:
“Monks, I do not see even a single other thing that is so greatly blameworthy as wrong view. Monks, wrong views are the supreme defilements.
The passage beginning with “That, moreover,” is undertaken to demonstrate more firmly the personal realization of the meaning already stated. That too is easy to understand.
In the verses, “having directed the mind wrongly” means having placed the mind in an improper manner by way of covetousness and so forth. Wrong...
"And having spoken words" means having uttered speech by way of wrong speech, such as false speech (*musāvāda*) and so forth.

"Having performed wrong actions" means having performed bodily actions by way of killing living beings (*pāṇātipāta*) and so forth. Alternatively, "having directed the mind wrongly" means having established the consciousness in a perverted state by way of wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*).
The same method applies to the remaining two phrases as well. Now, regarding his practice of such misconduct:
He shows the cause for being "of little learning" (*appassuta*); the meaning is that he is devoid of the learning that brings benefit to himself and others.
He is a "doer of demerit" (*apuññakāra*) because, for that very reason, he is unskilled in the noble Dhamma and is thus a person of evil character (*pāpadhamma*).
"In this short life here" means in this human world, life being extremely limited. And so it has been said: "He who lives long..."
“Whether for a hundred years or even more,” and “The lifespan of humans is short.
Therefore, one who is learned and wise, having quickly performed meritorious deeds, either goes to heaven or becomes established in Nibbāna.
But he who is of little learning and does not perform merit, being devoid of wisdom at the breaking up of the body, is reborn in hell.
The commentary on the first sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Sammādiṭṭhika-sutta*: 71.
In the second [sutta], the meaning should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated in the first sutta.
The commentary on the second sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Nissaraṇiya Sutta: 72.
In the third [sutta], "nissaraṇiyā" means connected with escape. "Dhātuyo" means the elements whose intrinsic nature is empty of a self. "Kāmānaṃ" means...
It refers to both defilement-desires (*kilesakāma*) and object-desires (*vatthukāma*). Alternatively, "desires" (*kāmānaṃ*) refers to defilement-desires.
For by escaping from defilement-desire, one necessarily escapes from object-desire as well; it is not otherwise. Thus it has been said:
"Those variegated things in the world are not desires..."
"Intentional lust is the desire of a person;
the various beautiful things remain just as they are in the world,
yet herein the wise subdue their longing."
"Departure" (*nissaraṇa*) means going away. "Renunciation" (*nekkhamma*) refers to the first *jhāna*; specifically, it should be understood as having the foul (*asubha*) as its object.

However, for one who takes that *jhāna* as a basis, comprehends conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), attains the third path, and realizes *nibbāna* by means of the non-returner (*anāgāmin*) path, his mind has departed from sense pleasures forever; this is the highest [form of renunciation].
The escape from sense-desires (kāmānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ) should be understood. "Of forms" (rūpānaṃ) means of form-phenomena;

specifically, this refers to all fine-material-sphere phenomena, distinguished by way of the wholesome, resultant, and functional [states], together with their objects. "Formless" (ārūppaṃ) means the formless-sphere jhāna.
Some, however, explain the word "of sense-desires" (kāmānaṃ) as meaning "of all sense-sphere phenomena. "Renunciation" (nekkhammaṃ): [is the escape].
And [the phrase] “the five fine-material-sphere jhānas”: this is not found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) and is not logical.
“Bhūta” means arisen. “Saṅkhata” means made by conditions having come together and combined. “Paṭiccasamuppanna” means produced from a cause.
By all three terms, conditioned phenomena (*tebhūmaka-dhamma*) are encompassed without remainder. “Nirodha” means Nibbāna.

And here, the full understanding of sense-desires is stated with respect to the first element; the full understanding of form, with respect to the second; and the full understanding of all conditioned things, as well as the transcendence of all states of existence, is stated with respect to the third.
In the verses, "having known the escape from sense-desires" means: "This is the escape from sense-desires, and this is how one escapes from sense-desires."

"Having known": it is called "transcending" (*atikkama*) because one transcends by means of it; that is, the method of transcending. Having known that formless attainment (*āruppa*) as that transcendence.
"The stilling of all formations" (*sabbasaṅkhārasamatha*): it is so called because all formations are stilled and pacified therein; this is Nibbāna. "Touching" it means touching it.
The rest is exactly according to the method explained below.
The commentary on the Third Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Santatara Sutta 73.

In the fourth [sutta], "by means of forms" (*rūpehi*) refers to phenomena belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). "More peaceful" (*santatarā*) means exceedingly peaceful. [This refers to] the phenomena of the fine-material sphere.

Indeed, they are called "peaceful" because of the suppression of the defilements, the abandonment of gross factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*), and the state of being the plane of concentration (*samādhi*).
However, the formless attainments (*āruppa*) possess an even more distinguished peacefulness, both by way of the peace of their own factors and the peace of their objects;

therefore, they are said to be "more peaceful. Cessation (*nirodha*) is Nibbāna. Furthermore, it is so called because it has reached a state of extreme subtlety, with only the residual formations (*saṅkhāra*) remaining.

For indeed, even the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) is more peaceful than the fourth formless attainment (*catutthāruppa*), owing to the subsiding of the distress of the defilements (*kilesa-daratha*) and its having Nibbāna as its object;

how much more so, then, is Nibbāna, which is the stilling of all conditioned phenomena (*sabbasaṅkhāra-samatha*)? Therefore it is said: "Cessation (*nirodha*) is more peaceful than the formless realms.
In the verses, *rūpūpaga* means those who have gone to the form existence (*rūpabhava*). For here, "form" (*rūpa*) refers to form existence; thus, for the sake of rebirth in form...
"...cultivates the path," and so forth. "Abiding in the formless" (*arūpaṭṭhāyino*) means those belonging to the formless realm (*arūpāvacara*).

By the phrase "not understanding cessation, they return to renewed existence," he demonstrates that cessation possesses the very nature of peace (*santa*) among the phenomena of the form and formless realms.

"Not settled in the formless" (*arūpesu asaṇṭhitā*) means not establishing themselves in formless existences due to craving for the formless; the meaning is that they fully understand even those [formless states]. Regarding cessation...
Regarding the phrase "those who are liberated" (*ye vimuccanti*): here, *ye* is merely a particle. The remainder is exactly as explained in the method stated below.
The commentary on the fourth sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Putta-sutta.
74. "Sons" (*putta*) means those born from one's own womb (*orasa*), or those such as *dinnaka* (given) and so forth.

"Existent" (*santa*) means being present (*bhavanta*), existing (*saṃvijjamāna*) in this world; that is, they are found (*upalabbhamāna*) in this world. They are "existent" by virtue of their presence (*atthibhāva*), and "found" by virtue of their manifestation (*pākaṭabhāva*).

"Born superior" (*atijāta*) means born surpassing one's mother and father in one's own qualities; the meaning is that one possesses qualities exceeding theirs. "Born equal" (*anujāta*)... [text continues]
“Born in accordance with the qualities of his parents” means he is born possessing qualities equal to theirs; “born inferior” means he is born possessing qualities lower than theirs.
To show by way of analysis those qualities endowed with which a son is intended to be superior to, equal to, or inferior to his parents, [the Blessed One said]: “And how, monks, is a son...?”
Having posed a question out of a desire to explain, "He is one who has surpassed others," the exposition beginning with "In this case, monks, regarding a son... was commenced.

In that context, regarding the phrases "they have not gone for refuge to the Buddha" and so forth: "Buddha" refers to the continuum of aggregates (*khandhasantāna*) which is cultivated by the attainment of the unsurpassed liberation characterized by unimpeded knowledge regarding all phenomena;
or it is a designation based on the Perfect Enlightenment of the Truths, which is the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) for omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
The Buddha is one whose being is preeminent. As it is said:

"‘Buddha’ refers to that Blessed One who is self-become and teacherless; he himself fully awakened to the truths among doctrines unheard of before, and therein attained omniscience and mastery over the powers.
This, first of all, is the analysis of the Buddha according to its meaning.

As for the etymological derivation (*byañjana*): he is called "Buddha" because he has awakened (*buddhavā*) by means of the absolute departure of the sleep of defilements together with their latent tendencies;

or he is called "Buddha" because he has fully awakened (*vibuddhavā*) through the blossoming of his intelligence (*buddhi*); or he is called "Buddha" because he has awakened (*bujjhitā*), or because he causes others to awaken (*bodhetā*).
It should be understood in such a manner as this. As it has been said:
“One who has awakened to the truths is a Buddha; one who awakens the generation is a Buddha; through omniscience he is a Buddha; through all-seeingness he is a Buddha;

through being unknowable by others he is a Buddha; through flowing wisdom he is a Buddha; through being reckoned as one whose taints are exhausted he is a Buddha; through being reckoned as one free from defilements he is a Buddha;
through being entirely free from lust he is a Buddha; through being entirely free from hatred he is a Buddha; through being entirely free from delusion he is a Buddha.”
He is called *Buddha* because he is utterly free from defilement; he is called *Buddha* because he has traveled the path that goes alone;
he is called *Buddha* because he alone has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; he is called *Buddha* because, through the destruction of non-enlightenment, he has attained wisdom.
Furthermore, this name "Buddha" was not given by his mother, nor by his father, nor by his brother, nor by his sister...
"This was not done by friends or companions, nor by kinsmen or blood relations, nor by recluses or brahmins,
nor by deities; rather, this is a designation realized at the root of the Bodhi tree by the Blessed Buddhas upon the simultaneous acquisition of omniscient knowledge— namely, 'Buddha'."

It destroys (*hiṃsati*), thus it is a refuge (*saraṇa*). The meaning is that it destroys, dispels, and utterly shatters all harm, the suffering of the states of woe, and all the suffering of *saṃsāra*.

"They have gone for refuge" means that they [have gone] to the Buddha, the Blessed One, with this intention: "The Buddha, the Blessed One, is our refuge, our destination, our ultimate resort, our place of return;
he is the destroyer of misfortune and the provider of welfare. Thus, [they have gone] to the Buddha, the Blessed One.
"Let us go, let us resort to, let us serve, let us attend upon; or let us thus know and awaken"—having gone and approached in this way, they have gone for refuge to the Buddha.
By contrast, those who have not done so have not gone for refuge to the Buddha.
"They have gone for refuge to the Dhamma" means [to those] who have attained the path, realized cessation, and are practicing according to the instructions.
It is called *dhamma* because it holds one back from falling into the four states of misery. In its essential meaning, this consists of both the Noble Eightfold Path and Nibbāna.
For it has been said in detail: "Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are conditioned phenomena, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared to be the foremost among them.
Furthermore, it is not only the Noble Path and Nibbāna, but also the Noble Fruits together with the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*). For it has been said in the *Chattamāṇavaka-vimāna*:
“The Dhamma free from passion, dispassionate, unshakable, sorrowless, unconditioned, and not repulsive—
sweet, well-mastered, and well-analyzed.”
"Come to this Dhamma for refuge.

In that passage, "fading away of lust" (rāgavirāga) refers to the Path; "unshaken and sorrowless" (anejam asokaṃ) refers to the Fruit; "the well-constituted Dhamma" (dhammasaṅkhataṃ) refers to Nibbāna;
and "this non-repulsive, sweet, skillful, and well-analyzed" (appaṭikūlaṃ madhuraṃ imaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhattaṃ) refers to all the aggregates of Dhamma analyzed according to the Three Piṭakas.

It has been explained. Having gone to that Dhamma as a refuge in the manner already stated, they have "gone for refuge to the Dhamma. By contrast, those who have not done so have not gone for refuge to the Dhamma.

That which is unified by way of view and virtue is the Saṅgha. In its actual meaning, it is the collection of the eight noble persons (ariya-puggala). For this has been said regarding that very celestial mansion:
“And where they say a gift yields great fruit,
among the four pure pairs of persons;
those eight individuals are seers of the Dhamma.”

“Go for refuge to this Saṅgha. Having gone to that Saṅgha as a refuge in the manner described, they have “gone for refuge to the Saṅgha. By contrast, those who have not done so have “not gone for refuge to the Saṅgha.

In this context, for the sake of skill regarding the going for refuge, one should understand the following method: the refuge, the act of going for refuge, the person who goes for refuge, the classification of the going for refuge, the fruit, the defilement, the breach, and the purification.

In this context, first of all, regarding the meaning of the words: it is called *saraṇa* because it "destroys" (*hiṃsati*). The meaning is that for those who have gone for refuge, by that very act of going for refuge, it destroys, dispels, and eliminates fear, terror, suffering, miserable rebirth, and affliction;

this is a designation for the Triple Gem. Alternatively, it is called *saraṇa* because it "destroys" (*hiṃsati*) the fear of sentient beings by promoting their welfare and turning them away from what is harmful.

The Buddha is a refuge by virtue of delivering one from the wilderness of existence and by bestowing consolation; the Dhamma [is a refuge] by virtue of granting the attainment of abundant fruit even for small deeds;
and the Saṅgha [is a refuge] by virtue of causing the acquisition of vast results even from minor acts. Therefore, it is also by this method that the Triple Gem is a refuge.
Going for refuge is an arising of consciousness that proceeds in the mode of having that [Triple Gem] as its supreme resort, with defilements dispelled through confidence and reverence for it.

The being endowed with that [state] goes for refuge; the meaning is that he approaches [the Triple Gem] with the aforementioned arising of consciousness, thinking, "These Three Jewels are my refuge, these are my ultimate resort.
Thus, first of all, the refuge and the act of going for refuge, as well as the one who goes for refuge—these three should be understood.
As for its classification, going for refuge is twofold: mundane and supramundane. Therein, the supramundane occurs at the moment of the path for those who have seen the Truths;

by way of cutting off the defilements of going for refuge, it takes Nibbāna as its object, and by way of its function, it extends to the entire Triple Gem. The mundane [going for refuge] occurs for worldlings by way of suppressing the defilements of going for refuge.

In terms of its object, it succeeds by having the qualities of the Buddha and so forth as its object. In terms of its meaning, it is the acquisition of faith (*saddhā*) toward the bases such as the Buddha, and right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) rooted in that faith;
among the ten bases for meritorious action, this is called "rectification of view" (*diṭṭhi-ujukamma*).
This occurs in four ways: by surrendering oneself, by making them one’s supreme refuge, by entering into the status of a pupil, and...

Regarding "by prostration": therein, "surrendering oneself" (*attasanniyyātana*) means the relinquishing of oneself to the Buddha and the others, thinking, "Starting from today, I surrender myself to the Buddha, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha.
"Having them as one's refuge" (*tapparāyaṇa*) means, "Starting from today, I have the Buddha as my refuge, the Dhamma as my refuge, and the Saṅgha as my refuge; thus [I declare] me..."

"Remember me as such"—this is the state of having him as one's refuge and the state of having him as one's ultimate resort. "Entering into the status of a pupil" means entering into the status of a pupil by thinking:
"From today onwards, may [the Teacher] remember me as a resident pupil of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.
"Prostration" means: "From today onwards, I shall perform acts of salutation, rising from my seat, joining the palms in reverence, and respectful service..."
"May it be held of me that I perform [this service] for these three objects, beginning with the Buddha"—thus is the supreme act of self-surrender toward the Buddha and the others.
For by performing any one of these four modes, the going for refuge is indeed accomplished.
Furthermore: "I surrender myself to the Blessed One; I surrender myself to the Dhamma; I surrender myself to the Saṅgha; [I surrender] my life..."
“I relinquish [myself]; my very self and life have been relinquished by me. For as long as life lasts, I go for refuge to the Buddha;
the Buddha is my refuge, my protection, my shelter”—thus too should the surrendering of oneself be understood.
“May I indeed see the Teacher! May I indeed see the Blessed One! May I indeed see the Well-Gone One! May I indeed see the Blessed One!”
“May I see him! May I indeed see the Perfectly Enlightened One!
May I see only the Blessed One!”—thus should his entering into discipleship be understood, just like the Elder Mahākassapa’s going for refuge.
“Thus shall I wander from village to village, from town to town...”
“Paying homage to the Fully Awakened One and to the excellent nature of the Dhamma”—
thus, as in the case of Āḷavaka and others, one’s taking refuge should be understood as having that as one’s ultimate resort.
Then, Brahmāyu the brahmin rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and prostrated himself with his head at the Blessed One’s feet.
He kisses the Blessed One’s feet with his mouth, strokes them with his hands, and announces his name, saying:
“I am Brahmāyu, O Gotama; I am Brahmāyu, O Gotama, a brahmin. In this way, prostration is to be understood.
Furthermore, it is fourfold according to relatives, fear, teachers, and those worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇīya*). Among these, by means of prostration to those worthy of offerings—
The going for refuge occurs [only] through these [three], not through the others. For refuge is taken on the basis of excellence alone, and it is broken on the basis of excellence alone.
Therefore, when one pays homage thinking, "This one alone is the supreme among all beings in the world, the most worthy of offerings," by that very act the refuge has been taken;
it is not so for one who pays homage out of a sense of kinship, fear, or respect for a teacher. For a lay follower who has thus taken refuge...
Nor does the refuge break for one who salutes even a person gone forth among other sects, thinking, "This is my relative," let alone one who has not gone forth.
Likewise, it does not break for one who salutes a king out of fear; for since he is honored by the whole kingdom, if he were not saluted, he might even cause harm.
Similarly, [it does not break] for one who salutes even a teacher of some craft or sectarian teacher.
Even for one who pays homage thinking, “This is my teacher,” it does not break. In this way, the classification of going for refuge should be understood.

And herein, regarding supramundane going for refuge, the four fruits of recluseship are the fruit of ripening (*vipākaphala*), and the destruction of all suffering is the fruit of benefit (*ānisaṃsaphala*). For this has been said:
“Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha...”
One sees the four noble truths with right wisdom:
suffering, the origin of suffering, the overcoming of suffering,
and the noble eightfold path leading to the cessation of suffering.
“This indeed is the secure refuge, this is the supreme refuge;
by coming to this refuge, one is liberated from all suffering.
Furthermore, its benefits and fruits should be understood as including the non-approach [of the world] as permanent and so forth. For this has been said:

“Bhikkhus, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view could regard any conditioned phenomenon as permanent, or regard anything as pleasant, or regard anything as a self;
or that such a person could take the life of his mother, take the life of his father, or take the life of an arahant; or that, with a mind of hatred, he could shed the blood of a Tathāgata.”
“It is impossible that he would shed blood [from the Tathāgata’s body], split the Saṅgha, or point to another teacher; such a thing cannot exist.
However, for the mundane going for refuge, the attainment of existence and the attainment of wealth are indeed the fruits. For it is said:
“Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha...”
They shall not go to a plane of misery;
having abandoned the human body,
they will fill the host of devas.”
Furthermore, it is said:
"Then Sakka, lord of the devas, together with eighty thousand deities, approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna...
[as before]... To Sakka, lord of the devas, who was standing to one side, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna..."
He said this: “It is indeed good, Lord of the Devas, to go for refuge to the Buddha.
It is, Lord of the Devas, because of going for refuge to the Buddha that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
They surpass other devas in ten respects: in divine life-span, in divine beauty, [and so forth].”

“With divine happiness, divine glory, divine sovereignty, with divine forms, divine sounds, divine odors, divine tastes, and divine tangibles… [and so on] …with regard to the Dhamma, the Saṅgha… [and so on] …with tangibles.
The specific excellence of the fruit of going for refuge should also be understood by way of the Velāma Sutta and others. Thus should the fruit of going for refuge be understood.
In this context, mundane going for refuge is defiled by ignorance, doubt, wrong knowledge, and so forth regarding the three objects;
it is neither of great radiance nor of great extension. However, there is no such defilement in the supramundane [going for refuge].
Furthermore, mundane going for refuge has a twofold division: blameworthy and blameless. Therein, the blameworthy occurs with respect to other teachers and so forth.
It occurs through such acts as surrendering oneself, and its fruit is undesirable. Death while remaining blameless is without fruit because it lacks karmic ripening.
However, for one who has transcended the world (lokuttara), there is no schism at all; for even in another existence, a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) does not designate another teacher.
Thus should the defilement and the schism of going for refuge be understood.
Furthermore, purification belongs only to the mundane; for whatever is subject to defilement, it must also be purified from that very state. The supramundane, however, is eternally pure.

Regarding the term *pāṇātipāta*: here, *atipāto* is the causing of one who is already of a nature to fall by his own essence to fall prematurely—that is to say, the causing of a rapid fall by not allowing him to fall slowly.
Or else, it is falling after having been overcome by a weapon or similar means.

"Causing to fall" means "overstepping," which is to say, the killing of a living being (*pāṇaghāta*). Here, "living being" (*pāṇa*) refers to the continuum of the aggregates (*khandhasantāna*), which is conventionally designated as a "sentient being";
in the ultimate sense, however, it is the material and immaterial life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

For when the material life-faculty is destroyed, the other [the mental life-faculty] also perishes due to its connection with it. Regarding that living being, for one who perceives it as a living being, [it is the volition] originating from the application that cuts off the life-faculty.
Killing is the volition of killing that proceeds through either the door of body or the door of speech.

For that volition, when it is occurring, causes the great primary elements—which arise by way of the condition of the great primaries acting as the cause for the performance of violence—to arise as something dissimilar rather than similar to those previously existing; it is this volition that originates such an application.
Volition (*cetanā*) is the act of taking life. For beings that have already acquired their own [present] formations are not as distinct as previous beings;

thus, they do not serve as causes for [beings] of the same class. The phrase "occurring through either the door of body or the door of speech" demonstrates that volition to kill, even when occurring in the mind-door (*manodvāra*), constitutes the taking of life.
For in the *Kulumpasutta* it is said: "In this case, a certain ascetic..."

Or, whether he be a brahmin possessing psychic power who has attained mastery over the mind, he gazes with an evil mind upon the embryo in another's womb"—here, "psychic power consisting of knowledge" (*vijjāmaya-iddhi*) is intended.
And since that cannot be produced without releasing the door of speech, it is accomplished by means of the door of speech alone.
As for those who say, "In this context, psychic power consisting of meditation (*bhāvanāmaya-iddhi*) is intended," [they are mistaken].
Their doctrine contradicts the [Abhidhamma] matrices (mātikā) of the triads of the wholesome, the triads of feeling, the triads of applied thought, and the matrices of the planes.

Furthermore, this killing of living beings is less blameworthy when directed toward small creatures such as animals that lack special qualities, and more blameworthy when directed toward large-bodied beings. Why?
Because of the greatness of the effort involved. Even when the effort is equal, it is more blameworthy due to the greatness of the object (vatthu) and other such factors.
Among humans and others who possess qualities, killing a being with few qualities is less blameworthy, while killing one with great qualities is more blameworthy.
However, when there is equality in the bodily qualities of the victim, it is less blameworthy if the defilements and the effort are mild, and more blameworthy if they are intense.
And in this context, the greater blameworthiness resulting from the magnitude of the application and the object is due to the volition arising through those conditions.
It should be understood by way of the magnitude of the action (*payoga*).

The magnitude of the action consists in the fact that the concluding volition (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā*)—which accomplishes its own function by suddenly bringing about the intended application and which has acquired proficiency through javanas occurring many times—performs a great task.
Even when the action is equal toward both small and large living beings, for one who kills a large being...
A more intense volition arises; thus, the greatness of the physical basis (*vatthu*) is also a cause for the strength of the volition.
Therefore, both of these serve as causes for its great culpability precisely through the strength of the volition.

Likewise, when the object to be killed possesses great virtue, the volition of harm directed toward it becomes strong due to the production of a specific field (*khetta*), just like a volition of benefit directed toward that same object.
The fact that it arises more frequently should be understood as its great blameworthiness.

Therefore, even when the conditions such as the preliminary effort (*payoga*) and the object (*vatthu*) are not great, the great blameworthiness of the action is to be understood solely by way of the strength of the volition (*cetanā*) due to conditions such as the greatness of its qualities.
Its five constituent factors (*sambhāra*) are: a living being, the perception of it as a living being, the intention to kill, the means employed, and death by that means.

"Killing living beings is endowed with five factors"—this should be understood as being inseparable from those five factors. Among them, the perception of a living being and the murderous mind are present even in the preliminary stages;
the means (upakkama) is that which is originated by the volition to kill. There are six modes of application for this:
by one's own hand, by command, by relinquishment, by persistence, by means of spells, and by means of psychic power. Among these, that which is accomplished by one's own hand is "by one's own hand."
That which proceeds by way of commanding others is "by command" (*āṇattika*). That which proceeds by way of relinquishing things such as a spear or a sword is "by relinquishment" (*nissaggiya*).

That which proceeds by way of digging pits and so forth is "stable" (*thāvara*). That which consists in the application of incantations, like that of sorcerers and the like, is "consisting of science" (*vijjāmaya*).
That which consists in the supernormal power born of the ripening of karma, like the gnashing of fangs and so forth, is "consisting of the result of action" (*kammavipākaja-iddhimaya*).
Here it is asked: since conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) have the nature of ceasing moment by moment, who is the killer, or what is killed?

If it is the continuum of mind and mental factors, then because it is formless (arūpa), it is incapable of being disturbed by means of cutting, breaking, and so forth, nor is it capable of being disturbed.
If, on the other hand, it is the continuum of matter (rūpa), then because it is insentient (acetana), like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, there is no cutting or the like to be applied to it.

Taking life occurs, as in the case of a dead body. Furthermore, the application for taking life—consisting of the aforementioned striking with a weapon and so forth—might occur in past formations, or in future or present ones.
In that regard, it cannot occur in the past or the future because their intrinsic nature no longer exists;
nor can it occur in present formations because of their momentariness.
Since they possess a nature of ceasing as if by an arrow, their application [toward an object] would be purposeless when they are already facing destruction;

and since destruction is devoid of a cause, death is not caused by such applications as striking with a weapon. Furthermore, because conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) are inactive, to whom would that application belong?
Due to their momentary nature, that which breaks up at the very same time as the intention to kill does not persist until the conclusion of the action.
To whom does the taking of life belong as a karmic bond?
It is said: it belongs to the "slayer," which is a designation for an aggregate of formations (saṅkhāra) possessing the aforementioned volition of a killer.
On account of the murderous application set in motion by him, one whose vital force and life-faculty have departed is the basis for the conventional expression "dead."
When the aforementioned application of killing is not carried out, the aggregate of material and immaterial phenomena—which, as before, is liable to proceed upward—is killed;
or rather, it is the continuum of consciousness and mental factors that is killed.

Even though that [continuum] is not the direct object of the application of killing, because in the five-aggregate existence its functioning is dependent upon the material continuum, by means of the application directed toward the primary material elements, there occurs the severance of the life-faculty for that [continuum] as well.
"It is cut off" does not mean that there is no occurrence of killing, nor is it causeless, nor is the preliminary effort (payoga) purposeless.
This is because, due to the preliminary effort performed upon present formations, the aggregate of formations that ought to arise immediately thereafter does not so arise;
and because here, "death" in the sense of momentary death (khaṇika-maraṇa) of momentary formations is not what is intended.
And because death within a continuity possesses a cause according to the method already stated, there is no such thing as causeless death.

Even though the formations (*saṅkhāras*) are devoid of volition, they are called "agents" in the sense that, having arisen according to their respective conditions, they are determined to produce their own corresponding fruits by the mere fact of their existence—just as one says, for example, "the lamp illuminates.
It is in this very way that the conventional expression "killer" is used. Not...
And it is intended that taking life (*pāṇātipāta*) belongs to the aggregate of mind and mental factors (*cittacetasikakalāpa*) that arises simultaneously with the intention to kill;
however, it is intended [only] for that which proceeds by way of a continuum (*santāna*). Thus, there is indeed the binding of karma through taking life.

Furthermore, since the accomplishment of purposeful activity (*atthakiriyā*) is seen in the case of lamps and so forth proceeding by way of a continuum, this same analysis applies to stealing and the other [unwholesome courses of action] as far as possible.
[These things] are to be abandoned. Therefore, "not abstaining from the taking of life" means one who does not abstain.
Taking what is not given is *adinnādāna*; it is said to be the seizing of another's property, theft, or robbery.

In that context, "what is not given" (*adinna*) refers to that which is possessed by another, such that if one were to exercise authority over it as one pleases, one would be subject to punishment and reproach.

And it is so. When there is another’s property, and one perceives it as another’s property, the volition of theft—which originates from the act of taking that [property]—is the taking of what is not given (*adinnādāna*).
That [offense] is less blameworthy when the other’s property is inferior, and more blameworthy when it is superior. Why?
Because of the superiority of the object (*vatthu*). Likewise, it is less blameworthy when the other’s property is small, and more blameworthy when it is large.

Why? Because of the greatness of the object (*vatthu*) and the greatness of the effort (*payoga*). However, when the object is equal, there is greater culpability (*mahāsāvajja*) in the case of an object belonging to one who possesses superior qualities;
conversely, relative to each successive higher quality, there is less culpability (*appasāvajja*) in the case of an object belonging to one whose qualities are inferior.
But when both the object and the qualities are equal, it depends on the defilements (*kilesa*) and the effort.
In a mild state [of intention], it is a minor offense; in an intense state, it is a major offense.

It has five constituent factors: that which is possessed by another, the perception that it is possessed by another, the intent to steal, the preparatory effort, and the taking away by means of that effort.
There are six modes of application, beginning with "by one's own hand" (sāhatthika) and so forth; these, moreover, constitute the act of stealing according to their respective natures.
[These are] those occurring by way of the following types of theft: open theft, theft by artifice, concealed theft, and theft by fraud.
And herein, the taking of another's property through the recitation of mantras is a practice consisting of supernatural power (*vijjāmaya*).

The drawing away of another's property by means of a physical or verbal effort accomplished through such psychic power, even without such mantras, [is likewise a practice consisting of supernatural power].
This should be understood as an application consisting of supernormal power (*iddhi*).
"In sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu*) means in sexual practices. "Wrong conduct" (*micchācāra*) is a reprehensible and base practice, universally censured.

By way of its characteristic, however, wrong conduct in sensual pleasures is the volition that transgresses against places not to be approached, proceeding through the door of the body with the intention of unrighteousness (*asaddhamma*).

In this context, "unapproachable places" refers, first, for men, to twenty women: the ten such as those protected by their mother and so forth, and the ten such as those purchased with wealth and so forth.
Among women, however, it refers to other men in the case of twelve women: the two who are protected and subject to punishment, and the ten beginning with those purchased with wealth.
This sexual misconduct occurs in an unapproachable place that is devoid of virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*).

It is of slight offense when directed toward one endowed with virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*), but of great offense toward one who possesses such virtues. Furthermore, it is of great offense for one who acts wrongly by overcoming even a person devoid of virtues;
however, it is of slight offense when both parties share the same intention (*samānacchandatā*).

Even when there is equality of intention, it is of slight offense due to the mildness of the defilements (*kilesa*) and the effort (*upakkama*), but of great offense due to their intensity. Of that [offense], there are four...

The requisites are: the object that should not be approached, the intention to engage with it, the actual application of engagement, and the acceptance of the practice of what is the path as being what is not the path.
In this context, there are three [factors] for that which occurs through one's own desire, and three for that which occurs by force;

thus, by including all cases without exception, four [offenses] are to be understood, though the accomplishment of the matter occurs through only three. One application is indeed that which is performed by one's own hand.
*Musā* refers to a physical or verbal application that destroys one's welfare for one who has the intention to deceive;
however, *musāvāda* (false speech) is the volition that, with the purpose of deceiving, originates such a physical or verbal application intended to deceive another. According to another method:
*musā* is an unreal matter, and *vāda* is the making known of that [matter] as real and true. Therefore, it is the making known of an untrue matter as if it were true.
False speech is the volition that initiates the process of making such a representation by one who wishes to mislead another.
It is less blameworthy when the matter it destroys is minor, and more blameworthy when the matter is great.
Furthermore, for householders, it is less blameworthy when it proceeds in the manner of saying "I have nothing" out of a lack of desire to give away their own possessions; [likewise] for a witness...
Having offered [the oil], it is called a grave offense by way of destroying one's welfare.

For those who have gone forth, having obtained even a small amount of oil or ghee and speaking with a sense of humor according to the manner of "filling up" talk—saying, for example, "Today in the village the oil flows like a river"—is a minor offense.
However, for those who speak of what has not been seen as "seen," and so forth, it is a grave offense.
Likewise, for one who destroys another’s welfare, the offense is slight if that person has few virtues, and grave if they have great virtues.
Furthermore, the degree of lightness or gravity of the offense is obtained according to the mildness or intensity of the underlying defilements (*kilesa*).
Its four constituent factors (*sambhāra*) are: an untrue matter, the intention to deceive, the corresponding effort, and [the communication] to another.

"Another constituent is the other person's comprehension of that meaning. For even if an action is performed with the intention to deceive, if the other person does not comprehend that meaning, the deception is not accomplished;
therefore, the other person's comprehension of that meaning should be understood as one constituent.
However, some say: "The three constituents are the false statement, the intention to deceive, and the other person's comprehension of that meaning."

They say this. However, if another person understands that matter after deliberating slowly due to dullness, one is bound by the kamma of false speech at the very moment the volition that initiates the action occurs, because it proceeds from a volition of determination (*sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā*).
"Liquor" (*surā*) refers to five types: flour liquor, cake liquor, rice liquor, that mixed with fermenting agents, and that prepared from various ingredients.
*Surā*. There are five kinds of fermented liquors (*āsava*): flower-liquor, fruit-liquor, honey-liquor, molasses-liquor, and that which is composed of various ingredients.
Both of these are intoxicants (*majja*) in the sense of being intoxicating. The volition by which one drinks them is a "basis for negligence" (*pamādaṭṭhāna*) because it is a cause of negligence.
As for its characteristic, however, it is derived from the seed of the intoxicant known as *surā* and *meraya* as previously described.
The basis for negligence through fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants is the negligent volition that proceeds via the door of the body by means of intoxication.
Its four constituent factors are: its state as an intoxicant (*majja*), the intention to drink it, the corresponding effort, and the act of swallowing.
Because it must be drunk with an unwholesome mind alone, it is exclusively blameworthy (*sāvajja*). However, for noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*), the physical substance...
It does not even enter the mouth of those who do not know [of its nature], let alone those who do. Drinking a quantity of half a *pasata* is slightly blameworthy;
drinking a quantity of half an *āḷhaka* is greater than that and very blameworthy.
For one who drinks a large amount sufficient to move the body and then commits acts such as plundering a village, it is indeed very blameworthy. For the taking of life is an evil deed.
Taking what is not given is a great offense when directed toward one whose taints are destroyed;
sexual misconduct is a great offense when it involves the transgression against a bhikkhunī whose taints are destroyed; false speech is a great offense when it results in a schism in the Saṅgha;
and drinking liquor is a great offense when one drinks enough to move the body and commits acts such as plundering a village.
Among all these, the schism of the Saṅgha through false speech is the most blameworthy; for having committed it, one is cooked in hell for an eon.
Now, the analysis of these [offenses] should be understood by way of six aspects: by nature, object, feeling, root, action, and fruit.
Therein, by way of nature, all these beginning with the destruction of life are of the very nature of volition (*cetanā*). By way of object...
Killing has the life-faculty as its object, and thus has formations (*saṅkhāra*) as its object; taking what is not given has either beings or formations as its object;
sexual misconduct has formations as its object by way of the tangible, though some say it has beings as its object; false speech has either beings or formations as its object;
drinking fermented liquor has formations as its object. In terms of feeling, killing is painful feeling.
Taking what is not given has three feelings; sexual misconduct has two feelings—by way of pleasure and indifference—and so too does the drinking of intoxicants.
