However, by means of the determining consciousness (*sanniṭṭhāpakacitta*), neither of these two results in a feeling of indifference. False speech has three feelings. As for the roots:
killing is rooted in two—hatred and delusion; taking what is not given and false speech are rooted in hatred and delusion.
Or, through greed and delusion, wrong conduct and the drinking of fermented liquor have two roots—greed and delusion. In terms of action (*kamma*), only false speech here is verbal action;

the remaining fourfold [set] is exclusively bodily action. In terms of fruit, all of them result in rebirth in the states of misery (*apāya*), and even in the happy destinies (*sugati*), they yield various undesirable fruits such as short life expectancy.
Thus, the analysis of these [unwholesome courses of action] should be understood according to their intrinsic nature and other factors.
"Appaṭiviratā" means they are not abstinent because they lack both abstention through formal undertaking (*samādāna-virati*) and abstention through natural attainment (*sampatti-virati*).
"Dussīlā" means, for that very reason, devoid of virtue (*nissīlā*) due to the absence of even the mere five precepts. "Pāpadhammā" means those of base character, following inferior conduct.

"Paṭivirato pāṇātipātā" means one who is abstinent from taking life through the undertaking of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*), remaining far removed from it. This same method applies to the rest as well.

Here too, the exposition should be understood by way of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), object (*ārammaṇa*), feeling (*vedanā*), root (*mūla*), action (*kamma*), undertaking (*samādāna*), breach (*bheda*), and fruit (*phala*). Among these, as for their intrinsic nature, all five are both volitions (*cetanā*) and abstinences (*virati*);
however, the teaching has come down by way of the abstinences. When one abstains from the destruction of life, that which... [is the volition].
At that time, "abstinence from taking life" refers to the abstinence associated with wholesome consciousness as described.
It is threefold by way of classification: abstinence through possession, abstinence through undertaking, and abstinence through eradication.
Among these, for those who have not formally undertaken the training rules, it is the reflection upon one's own birth, age, learning, and so forth, thinking: "This is improper..."
Abstention that arises in those who do not transgress the objects of attainment with the thought, "We shall do this," is called abstention by attainment (*sampattavirati*).

Abstention that arises in those who have undertaken the training rules, who—both at the time of undertaking the training rules and thereafter—even renounce their own lives rather than transgress the object, is called abstention by undertaking (*samādānavirati*). [That which is] associated with the Noble Path...

Furthermore, there is the abstinence called "abstinence through eradication" (*samuccheda-virati*), from the arising of which even the thought "we shall kill a living being" does not occur to noble persons (*ariya-puggala*).
Among these, it is "abstinence through undertaking" (*samādāna-virati*) that is intended here.

As for their objects: the very objects of killing living beings and so forth are the objects of these [types of abstinence]. For it is precisely because they are to be transgressed [that they serve as objects].

It is called abstinence (*virati*). Just as the Noble Path, having Nibbāna as its object, abandons the defilements, so too these wholesome states, having precisely the life-faculty and other such factors as their objects, abandon the unwholesome conduct of killing and so forth.
From the perspective of feeling, they are all exclusively pleasant feeling.

From the perspective of roots, for one who abstains with a consciousness associated with knowledge, they possess three roots by way of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion; [for one who abstains] with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge...
For one abstaining, they have two roots by way of non-greed and non-hatred. In terms of action, the abstention from false speech is verbal action; the rest are bodily action.

In terms of undertaking, they are undertaken either by receiving them together or individually from another person worthy of respect when one does not find such a person, or by undertaking them oneself. In terms of division, they belong to householders.
Whatever precept is transgressed, only that one is broken; the others are not broken. Why is this? For householders have unbound morality;
they observe only whatever they are able to maintain. But for those who have gone forth, when even one precept is transgressed, all are broken.
Regarding the fruit: from abstaining from taking life here, there arise perfection of limbs and members,
excellence of height and girth, excellence of speed, well-planted feet, beauty, softness, purity, gentleness, great strength, distinctness of speech,
being dear and agreeable to beings, having a retinue that does not envy, fearlessness, and invincibility.

The fruits [of abstaining from taking what is not given] are: immortality through the efforts of others, having a large retinue, a beautiful complexion, a well-proportioned form, freedom from illness, freedom from sorrow, non-separation from those who are dear and pleasing, and long life—and so forth.
From abstaining from taking what is not given, there arise great wealth and grain, infinite enjoyments, stable enjoyments, and [the attainment of] all that is desired.
The rapid acquisition of enjoyments; the possession of enjoyments not shared with kings and others; the possession of magnificent enjoyments;
preeminence in various places; the state of never knowing want; dwelling in happiness—these and other such qualities [result from this].
Through abstaining from unchastity, there is freedom from adversaries, being dear and pleasing to all beings, and [the abundance of] food, drink, clothing, shelter, and so forth.
The attainment of gains; sleeping in comfort; waking in comfort; liberation from the fear of the states of misery; the incapacity for the female state or the neuter state;
freedom from anger; truthfulness in conduct; absence of dejection; ease in pleasing others; perfection of the sense faculties; perfection of the physical marks;
freedom from anxiety; lack of preoccupation; dwelling in happiness; fearlessness from any quarter; and the absence of separation from what is dear.
And so forth. Since the fruits of abstaining from sexual misconduct are also included herein, therefore [one speaks of] abstaining from unchastity.

From abstaining from false speech come: clarity of the sense faculties, distinct and sweet speech, teeth that are even and pure, being neither too thick nor too thin, neither too short nor too tall, a pleasant touch, and a mouth with the fragrance of a blue lotus.
An assembly that desires to listen, speech that is worthy of being accepted, a tongue that is soft, red, thin, and like a lotus petal, absence of timidity, lack of arrogance, and so forth.
Through the abstention from fermented liquor, spirits, intoxicants, and the basis for negligence, there is heedfulness regarding duties and obligations in the past, future, and present.
Possession of wisdom, constant mindfulness, presence of ready wit regarding duties and tasks as they arise,
lack of indolence, lack of dullness, lack of insanity, fearlessness, lack of aggression, lack of envy,
lack of stinginess, truthfulness in speech, avoidance of malicious, harsh, and frivolous speech, gratitude, thankfulness, and generosity.

The fruits [of these virtues] are such as: being virtuous, uprightness, freedom from anger, being endowed with moral shame and dread of blame, straightness of view, greatness, wisdom, and skill in discerning what is beneficial and what is harmful.
In this way, the definition of the abstention from taking life and the other [precepts] should be understood according to their essential nature and so forth.
"Virtuous" means being virtuous by way of the five precepts as previously described. "Of beautiful character" means one of noble character;

the meaning is that he is endowed with wisdom through the perfection of view, which is illustrated by his taking of the refuges. Furthermore, it should be understood that a son who, while his parents are faithless and immoral, is himself likewise [faithless and immoral], is indeed of low birth.
For here, lack of faith and the other such qualities constitute the state of being low-born.

The characteristics have been stated, and these are indeed found in him. However, it is said that a son’s status as "born superior" (*atijāta*) and so forth is defined in relation to his mother and father.

One who is called a "stain upon the family" (*kulagandhana*) is a destroyer of the family, a ruin of the lineage. For here the word *gandha* has the sense of "destruction," as in such expressions as "enemies of the lotus-fragrance" (*uppalagandhapaccatthikā*). Some, however, read "destroyer of the family" (*kuladhaṃsana*), which has the same meaning.
"These indeed are sons in the world"—these three types of sons, beginning with the "born superior," are alone what are called "sons" in this world of beings.

There are none who are exempt from this. Among these, those who become lay followers (*upāsaka*) by virtue of attaining the going for refuge, and who are skilled in action through the knowledge that one is the owner of one's own deeds—they are wise and possessed of wisdom, endowed with and perfected in the five precepts and the ten precepts.
They understand the speech of supplicants, fulfilling their intentions merely by observing the expression on their faces.

"Generous" (*vadaññū*): either because they give to those [who ask], or because upon hearing their words "Give this," they think, "These people became like this because they did not give gifts in the past;
however, I must not be like that," and thus, by relinquishing [their own wealth] for their sake, they understand that purpose—therefore they are "generous.

Alternatively, they are "generous" because they understand the words of the wise which illuminate such things as the doctrine of being the owner of one's own actions (*kammassakatā*). Some also read "padaññū," meaning "one who knows the tracks" (*padāniyā*).
The meaning is "those whose nature is relinquishment. For that very reason, because they are free from the stain of stinginess, they are "free from avarice" (*vītamaccharā*).

Like the moon released from clouds—whether from clouds designated as "clouds" (*abbha*) or from thick layers of dense clouds—they shine forth, they radiate, they are resplendent among assemblies of lay followers and so on, and among assemblies of kshatriyas and so on; this is the meaning.
The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Avuṭṭhika Sutta: 75.
In the sixth [sutta], "equal to a rainless cloud" means equal to a cloud that does not rain. For a certain cloud may consist of a hundred layers or a thousand layers.
Having offered the sacrifice, rising up, thundering, roaring, and flashing with lightning, it vanishes without letting fall even a single drop of water;
showing that such is the likeness of a certain person, he said, "like one who does not rain. "One who rains in a limited area" means like a cloud that rains in only one part.
For "one who rains in a limited area" (padesavassī) is so called because he is like a cloud raining in a limited area. A certain person, among people situated in only one place...
Some are soaked, some are not; thus it rains gently. In this way, he shows a certain person who is like that as "one who rains locally.
"One who rains everywhere" is like a cloud that rains over every part of the world, including the earth, mountains, oceans, and so forth.
For a certain [cloud] indeed spreads out over the entire interior of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) and rains everywhere.
It rains; having used that great cloud which rains over the four continents as a simile for a certain person, it is said:
"He rains everywhere. *Sabbesānaṃ* means "of all"; or rather, *sabbesaṃ* is the reading. "He does not give" means he has a nature of non-giving;
the meaning is that due to his stubborn stinginess, he gives nothing to anyone. Now, in order to show by way of distinction the field of giving and the object to be given:

He said, “ascetics and brahmins,” and so forth. In this context, those who have stilled their evil deeds—both ascetics by virtue of their renunciation and brahmins by virtue of having banished evil—are intended here as “ascetics and brahmins. The “miserable” are unfortunate people who are destitute.
The “travelers” are wayfarers who lack provisions for the journey. The “beggars” are those who [say], “I desire...”

They wander about, encouraging others in giving and extolling the praise of generosity by such means as: "Give what is lovely, pleasing, timely, and blameless, with an uplifted mind and a serene mind; by giving thus, you shall go to a happy destination; go to the Brahma-world!
As for those called beggars, they are simply those who say, "Give even a mere handful, give even a mere *pasata*, give even a mere bowlful..."
“Give this!”—thus they wander about, asking for even a little. Therein, by the mention of “ascetics and brahmins,” he shows the field of virtue and the field of benefactors;
by the mention of “the poor and so forth,” he shows the field of compassion. “Food” refers to anything edible or chewable.
“Drink” refers to beverages such as mango juice and the like. “Clothing” refers to coverings such as undergarments and upper robes. “Conveyance” refers to...
"Carriages and so forth" refers to any means of locomotion, down to sandals. "Garlands" refers to all flowers, whether strung together or not.
"Fragrances" refers to any kind of fragrant substance, whether ground or unground, as well as the materials used for perfuming.
"Unguents" refers to that which colors the skin. "Beds" refers both to the physical objects such as couches and stools, as well as the coverings such as curtains and rugs upon which one lies.
And here, by the term "taking up a bed," it should be understood that a seat is also included. "A dwelling" (*āvasatha*) refers to a shelter that wards off dangers such as wind and heat.
"Lighting materials" (*padīpeyya*) refers to the equipment for lighting, such as lamp-stands, bowls, and so forth.
"In this way, monks" means that even when there are goods worthy of being given, this is the manner in which the gift should be bestowed upon the recipients.
A person who gives nothing at all is like a cloud that does not rain. This is what is meant:

"Monks, just as that cloud, having arisen with a hundred layers and a thousand layers, vanishes without raining anything at all, even so, monks, whoever, having accumulated abundant and vast wealth, dwells at home and gives not even a mere ladleful to anyone..."
If one departs without giving even a morsel of almsfood or a ladleful of rice-gruel, and passes away alone, falling into the power of death, such a person is said to be "like one who has not rained.
In this manner, the conclusion should be understood for the remaining cases as well.
Among these three types of persons, the first is to be censured without exception; the second is praiseworthy; and the third is even more praiseworthy.
It should be understood that the first is exclusively the most inferior, the second is middling, and the third is the best.
In the verses, the plural form "samaṇe" is used in the sense of the accusative case, and likewise for the remaining terms. "Laddhāna" means having obtained;
having been invited by recluses worthy of offerings and questioned, he does not share [the food]. "Annaṃ pānañca bhojanaṃ" means either solid food (anna) or drink (pāna).
Or any other food fit to be eaten, he does not share it. This is the summary of the meaning here:
having obtained recipients who have approached him out of need, if he does not make even a mere distribution of food and so forth, what other gift will he give?
Such a person, characterized by stubborn stinginess, is the lowest of men.
"The wise say that a base person is like a cloudless sky when they speak.

"He does not give to some" means that even though there is a great amount of property to be given, he does not give it to certain beings either out of anger toward them or out of greed for the object to be given. "He bestows upon others" means that he gives only to certain [beings].
He gives. "Medhāvino" means wise and learned people.
"Subhikkhavāco" means one who, when approached by beggars, causes them to receive various gifts by saying, "Give food! Give drink! and so forth;
because alms are easily obtained from him, he is one whose speech is "subhikkha" (abounding in food), thus "subhikkhavāco. He is also called "subhikkhavassī" (one who rains down abundance).

They recite [the following]: Just as the world is said to have "good harvests" when there is abundant rain from a great cloud, so too this [Buddha], by means of his great gifts, is one who rains everywhere and brings about good harvests.
"Rejoicing, he scatters" means that with a mind thrilled and joyful, while giving a gift with his own hand, he scatters the object of generosity upon the field of the recipients.
It is as if [the earth] were speaking; even with his voice he says, "Give! Give!
Now, in order to show the state of having abundant rain and food, the passage beginning with "Just as a cloud" was spoken. Herein, this is the summary of the meaning:
just as a great cloud first thunders with a gentle sound, and then again makes all the rivers and caves resound with a single roar—
Roaring as it goes, it rains down, overflowing and filling both the dry land and the low-lying places with water everywhere,
making them all into one flood; even so, in this world of beings,
a certain noble person is like that great cloud because he must rain down with universal impartiality— just as wealth acquired through enterprise is produced by one's own initiative and energy.
Thus, being diligent, having acquired that wealth through righteous means and according to the law,
he satisfies and serves the beggars who arrive at his door with the food, drink, and other gifts produced thereby, doing so properly and correctly,
in accordance with the time and place, and according to their desires.
The commentary on the sixth sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Sukhapatthanā Sutta: 76.
In the seventh [sutta], "pleasures" means signs of pleasure. "Aspiring" means wishing or longing for. "Virtue" (sīla) means...

The virtue of the householder and the virtue of the one gone forth. The intended meaning is that if one is a householder, it is the virtue of a householder; if one is gone forth, it is the virtue of the fourfold purification.
"One should guard" means that having undertaken them, one should protect them properly by not transgressing them.
"May praise come to me"—desiring that "my good reputation may spread"—the wise person possessed of discernment should guard their virtue.

For a virtuous householder, indeed, a fine reputation spreads through the assembly, such as: "So-and-so, the son of such-and-such a family, is virtuous, of lovely character, faithful, confident, a donor, and a doer of good deeds. And for one who has gone forth, [a reputation spreads] such as:
"The bhikkhu named so-and-so is virtuous, perfect in conduct, gentle, pleasant to dwell with, respectful, and reverential," and so forth...pe...
"It rises up" means: for this has been said—"Furthermore, householders, a good report of one who is virtuous and endowed with virtue rises up.
Likewise—
“Monks, if a monk should wish: ‘May I be dear and agreeable to my fellow celibates, and respected and esteemed,’ he should be one who fulfills the precepts,” and so forth.

Regarding the thought, “May wealth accrue to me”: first, for a layperson who is virtuous and of good character, whatever means of livelihood they employ—whether by agriculture, trade, or service to the king—that [wealth shall arise].
If one practices that [generosity] at the proper time and according to the proper method with extreme heedfulness, then both unarisen wealth will arise for him,
and wealth already arisen will increase. Furthermore, for one who has gone forth,

who is endowed with virtue and conduct, who dwells in heedfulness, and who is perfected in virtue— the deities, being inspired by his perfection of virtue and his qualities such as fewness of desires, [will provide assistance].
People bring him very excellent requisites; thus his unarisen wealth arises, and his arisen wealth becomes stable. For it has been said:
"Furthermore, householders, one who is virtuous and perfected in virtue acquires, through the basis of heedfulness, a great mass of wealth."
Likewise:

“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu should wish: ‘May I be one who obtains robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,’ he should fulfill the precepts alone”—the rest is exactly as stated in the method already explained.

In the verses, *patthayāno* means "desiring. *Tayo sukhē* means "three kinds of happiness. *Vittalābhaṃ* means "the acquisition of wealth"; the sense is the arising of enjoyments. Furthermore, here specifically, through praise there is mental happiness, through enjoyments there is physical happiness, and by the other [the third] there is the happiness of rebirth.
Likewise, by the first [verse] there is happiness in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammasukha*), and by the third there is happiness in the future life (*samparāyasukha*).
By the second [term], it should be understood that both types of happiness are included.

Now, demonstrating—along with their disadvantages and benefits—the avoidance of evil friends and the cultivation of virtuous friends as the specific cause for praise and so forth, just as virtue is the specific cause for praise and so forth, he says, "One who does not... and so on. Therein:
"Is suspected" means he is to be suspected of evil: "Surely this person has done or will do evil, for he associates with wicked people.
"Upon him"—that is, upon this person who frequents wicked folk—even an unfounded disrepute takes root, grows, and reaches full maturity because of his association with wicked people.
It spreads. Or, *assa* is the genitive case used in the sense of the locative; the meaning is "in that person.

"He indeed becomes just like that" means that whichever kind of person one associates with or serves—whether a bad friend or a virtuous friend—that person becomes just like them, as water does according to the nature of the ground; he becomes either of evil character or of virtuous character. Why?

For association is indeed of such a nature: because association is a contact that, like a dye on crystal gems, causes one to grasp the form of the person who serves as the supporting condition, therefore the intention is that one should not dwell together with a person of evil character.
"Associating with one who associates"—this refers to another person who is pure by nature, associating with oneself from time to time.
A person of evil character who serves and associates with [such a one], or one who is served by him;
or a person of evil character who is touched—that is, touched by living together and association with that naturally pure person—himself becomes likewise affected as he touches them.
Just as an arrow smeared with poison, when it enters a quiver—that is, a collection of arrows known as a heap of arrows—[becomes tainted].

Just as a lotus stalk, though untouched by the mud it has emerged from, becomes smeared by it, so too a wise person—being "wise" (*dhīra*) because of his possession of fortitude (*dhiti*)—should not become a companion to evil out of fear of being defiled by it.
As for the phrase "rotten fish on the tip of a blade of *kusa* grass": just as one might [hold] a fish that has become rotten through its foul state upon the tip of a *kusa* blade...
A man wraps [grass] and binds it together; although those blades of grass are not rotten, they emit only a foul and putrid odor due to their connection with the rotten fish.
"In this way, by associating with fools" means that association with foolish people should be understood as having such a consequence.
"In this way, by associating with the wise" means that just as even unscented leaves emit a fragrance through their connection with *tagara* (nard), so too is it with the wise.
Thus, associating with the wise is the cause for one who is by nature unvirtuous to acquire the fragrance of virtue through the undertaking of moral discipline and so forth.
Therefore, because such is the disadvantage and the benefit respectively of associating with bad friends and associating with good friends, one should [avoid the former and cultivate the latter],

just as a leaf-basket or a flower-basket acquires a foul or sweet odor through contact with foul-smelling or fragrant substances, depending on whether it rests upon a wicked person or a virtuous person.

"Having understood the ripening of one's own [deeds]" means: having known and understood the production of results—both the nature of suffering and the nature of happiness for oneself—one should not associate with wicked friends who do not exist [in truth], but should associate with those who are good, peaceful, whose faults have been vomited out, and who are praised by the wise. For it is said:
"The wicked lead one to hell; the good cause one to go to a happy destination. Thus spoke the Blessed One in the first verse.
Having shown the three signs of happiness as previously described, and having then, by means of the five following verses,

shown the arrival of the happiness of praise along with the avoidance of its opposites, he shows the final happiness by means of the concluding verse together with the cause for the arrival of all three types of happiness.
The commentary on the Seventh Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Bhidura Sutta: 77.
In the eighth [sutta], "bhidurāyaṃ" means "this body is fragile. "Body" refers to the material body (*rūpakāya*). For it consists of the limbs and members, as well as the hair and so forth.
In the sense of a collection, it is also called "body" (*kāya*) because it is the source (*āya*), that is, the place of arising, for things that are vile and loathsome.

Herein, this is the etymological analysis: they arise (*āyanti*) in this, thus it is a source (*āya*). What arises? Vile things such as hair and so forth. Thus, it is a body (*kāya*) because it is the source of what is vile.
As for its meaning, however, it is a heap of the phenomena consisting of the primary elements and their derivatives, occurring by way of the four continuums. This is what was stated.
“Monks, this material body composed of the four great elements is fragile, subject to breaking, of a nature to break, and its very essence is to disintegrate moment by moment.
There is also a reading, “bhindarāyaṃ,” which has the same meaning. As for “consciousness” (viññāṇa):
it refers to the wholesome and other types of consciousness belonging to the three planes. Regarding the etymological derivation: it is called “consciousness” because it cognizes various objects.
For that which is the cognition of an object devoid of perceiving and understanding is consciousness (*viññāṇa*).
"Subject to fading away" (*virāgadhamma*) means having the nature of fading away; the meaning is that its intrinsic nature is to disintegrate. "All acquisitions" (*upadhī*):

the acquisition of the aggregates, the acquisition of defilements, the acquisition of volitional formations, and the acquisition of the five strands of sensual pleasure—these are designated as "acquisitions" (*upadhī*) because "suffering is acquired here."

All phenomena—namely, the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), the defilements (*kilesa*), volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), and the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*)—are impermanent in the sense of non-existence;

they are suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away; and they are subject to change in the sense of abandoning their natural state due to their nature of being transformed in two ways, namely through aging and death.
Thus, herein, for the sake of the ease of seeing impermanence, [one should contemplate] material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*).

Having taken consciousness separately and then again having taken all phenomena of the three planes together under the classification of the acquisitions (upadhi), the course of comprehension was described according to the inclination of those persons who awaken to reality by way of contemplating impermanence and suffering.
Although only two characteristics are mentioned here in the Pāli, [the third is implied] by the statement: "That which is suffering is non-self."
It should be understood that by the characteristic of suffering (*dukkha-lakkhaṇa*) alone, the characteristic of non-self (*anatta-lakkhaṇa*) is also shown.

In the verse, "having seen fear in acquisitions" (*upadhīsu bhayaṃ disvā*) means having seen fear by way of the knowledge of the appearance as terror (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa*) regarding acquisitions; that is, having perceived that they are to be feared.
By this, he shows powerful insight (*balava-vipassanā*). It is precisely the knowledge of the appearance as terror.

Indeed, when analyzed according to its specific characteristics, the contemplation of danger is called both the contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassanā*) and the contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā*).

"He has transcended birth and death"—thus reflecting and joining the knowledge of insight (*vipassanāñāṇa*) with the Path, one attains Arahatship through the succession of the Paths and becomes one who has "transcended birth and death.
How so? "Having reached the supreme peace"—the supreme, the highest, the unsurpassed.
Having attained Nibbāna, the peace that is the stilling of all conditioned phenomena, one who is thus become "one whose self is developed" (bhāvitatta) awaits his time.
By means of the four Noble Paths, through the accomplishment of development and clear realization, he is one whose body, virtue, mind, and wisdom are developed;
such a person, neither rejoicing in death nor clinging to life, simply awaits the time for the final Parinibbāna of his own aggregates.
He awaits and looks forward [to it], yet he has no longing for anything else. Therefore he said:
“I do not rejoice in death, nor do I rejoice in life;
I await my time as a servant awaits his wages.”
The commentary on the eighth sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Dhātusosaṃsandana-sutta*: 78.

In the ninth [sutta], "from the elements" (*dhātuso*) means from the perspective of the elements. And by "elements," the intention-element (*ajjhāsayadhātu*)—that is, the nature of one's inclination—is intended.

That which is called "resolute intention" (*adhimutti*) is also mentioned. "They come together" means that by virtue of that commonality of elements (*dhātusabhāgatā*), they adhere to and become one with each other according to their respective elements and inclinations (*ajjhāsaya*).
"They agree" means that by virtue of that very same commonality of inclination, having become of one mind, they meet, associate with one another, and approach;
or rather, they [align] their own preferences, dispositions, tolerances, and views in various instances.
They proceed acting in the same way. "Those of inferior inclination" (*hīnādhimuttikā*) means those whose inclination (*adhimutti*) is toward inferior things such as the strands of sensual pleasure;
they are those with inferior aspirations (*hīnajjhāsaya*). "Those of noble inclination" (*kalyāṇādhimuttikā*) means those whose inclination is toward noble things such as renunciation;
they are those with refined aspirations (*paṇītajjhāsaya*). For if the teachers and preceptors are not virtuous, [then] the resident pupils and co-residents...
Those who possess virtue do not even approach their own teachers and preceptors; they approach only those bhikkhus who are similar to themselves and of suitable character.

However, if the teachers and preceptors are virtuous while the others are not, they still do not approach them as teachers and preceptors, but rather approach only those of inferior inclination who are similar to themselves. Such is this manner of approaching.
However, showing that this was not only the case now, but also in the past and the future, he said: "In the past too, monks," and so forth.

In brief, those who are attached to things of defilement (saṅkilesadhamma) are of inferior disposition (hīnādhimuttika); those who are attached to things of purification (vodānadhamma) are of noble disposition (kalyāṇādhimuttika).
This, moreover, is simply the association of the immoral with the immoral, and the association of the virtuous with the virtuous; [likewise] of the unwise...
What determines that one associates only with the unwise or only with the wise? It is determined by the element of one’s inclination (*ajjhāsayadhātu*).
It is said that a number of bhikkhus were wandering for alms in a certain village.
Those people brought a great deal of food, filled their bowls, and having said, "Enjoy this according to your respective shares," they sent them on their way.
The bhikkhus said, "Friend, people employ it for work connected with the elements.
Thus, the element of inclination determines [the result]. This meaning should be illustrated by a connection with the elements:

for when the Blessed One was lying on his deathbed on Vulture Peak Mountain, while Sāriputta, Moggallāna, and others were staying around him for protection, he addressed each one of them individually...
Having observed Sāriputta walking back and forth together with his own retinue of monks, he addressed the monks:
"Do you see, monks, how Sāriputta is walking back and forth together with many monks? "Yes, venerable sir.
"All these monks, monks, are of great wisdom. [The rest] should be recited in full.
In the verses, "associations" (*saṃsagga*) refers to conjunction through defilement by way of living together and so forth; or alternatively, it refers to the fivefold associations:
association by sight, association by hearing, association by conversation, association by enjoyment, and physical association—from any such association.
"A thicket has arisen" means that a defilement has arisen which has not been eradicated by the Path.
"It is severed by non-association" means that after having been severed in the preliminary stage through physical seclusion and so forth— which involve the rejection of association—
it is further severed and abandoned through absolute non-association, which is the seclusion of complete eradication. To this extent,
the origination and the passing away of those of inferior inclination have been shown in brief.
However, since those associations and those defilements arise and increase through laziness rather than through the exertion of energy,
one should avoid persons of inferior inclination who are indolent and associate with those of noble inclination who have aroused energy; thus, by avoiding such [unwholesome] association,
the thicket born of association must be cut down— this is the meaning as previously stated.
Showing this in detail, he spoke the words beginning with "A small piece of wood" in order to reveal the danger of associating with the lazy.
Therein, "a small piece of wood" refers to a tiny raft made of wood.
"It would sink in the great ocean" means that one who, having boarded a tiny raft and wishing to cross the great ocean, would sink in the very middle of the ocean before reaching the shore.
He would sink, and having fallen, he would become food for fish and turtles. "In this way, by relying on one who is indolent, even one who lives rightly sinks"— in just this way,
by depending on a person who is indolent, lacking the exertion of energy, and enslaved by the defilements, even one who lives rightly,
whose livelihood is pure and whose virtue is pure, [sinks] due to association with the inferior, through the [defilements] arising from that association.
Devoured by sensual thoughts and the like, one who is unable to reach the further shore sinks right into the ocean of saṃsāra.
Therefore—because association with the indolent brings such harm—one "sinks" (sīdati) in a base way through the pursuit of laziness by relying on them; thus, they are called *kusīta*.
For that very reason, one should avoid those of inferior energy, those lacking vigor, and bad friends. This must be done with absolute certainty.
But by those who are secluded through physical seclusion and so forth, as well as through seclusion by way of its factors;
by those who are noble because they are far removed from defilements, and who have set out for Nibbāna because their very being has been directed toward it;
by meditators who meditate by means of contemplation on the characteristics of objects; and by the wise who have initiated energy through the constant exertion of vigor.
"One should dwell and live together only with those who possess wisdom.
The commentary on the ninth sutta is finished. 10.
Commentary on the Parihāna Sutta (The Discourse on Decline).
79. In the tenth [section], "they lead to decline" means they result in non-increase;
they become obstacles to the attainment of the Path. However, there is no such thing as the decline of a Path already attained.

Expounding, by way of teaching focused on persons, the phenomena that were previously listed under a teaching focused on phenomena—namely, "three phenomena"—the Blessed One said: "Here, monks, a bhikkhu who is a trainee... and so forth.

In this context, "one who delights in work" (*kammārāma*) means one for whom work is a pleasure (*ārāma*) because it is to be resorted to. "One who rejoices in work" (*kammarata*) means one who finds delight in work.
"Devoted to and intent upon the state of delighting in work" (*kammārāmatamanuyutta*) means being engaged and occupied with that delight in work.
Herein, "work" (*kamma*) refers to the duties to be performed, such as: the distribution of robes, the making of robes, providing support, and the alms-bag.
The making of such requisites as shoulder-straps, waist-bands, water-strainers, foot-wipers, foot-scrubbers, and brooms;
and the repairing of what is broken or dilapidated in the monastery.
For some, while performing these tasks, do nothing else all day long. It is with reference to such a person that this was said. But as for one who... [of these]...

He performs these very tasks at the time for performing them: he takes up the recitation at the time for recitation, he recites at the time for recitation, he performs the duties such as the monastery courtyard service at the time for performing those duties, and he applies his attention at the time for applying attention—whether to a universal meditation subject or a task-related meditation subject.
He is not called "one who delights in work. For him, that [work]—

“Furthermore, regarding those various duties for one’s fellow celibates, he is skillful and diligent therein, endowed with the investigation of appropriate means, capable of acting and capable of arranging”—it is precisely the performance of what has been thus authorized by the Teacher.
One who delights in talk (*bhassārāmo*) is one who spends his days and nights in such things as the discourse on kings, which have been prohibited by the Blessed One. This [is the meaning].

"One who does not set a limit on speech is called 'one who delights in talk' (*bhassārāma*). However, one who speaks on the Dhamma and answers questions both by night and by day is indeed 'one who has little talk' and 'one who sets a limit on speech. Why? Because he has followed the very method prescribed [by the Buddha]:
'When you have gathered together, monks, two things are to be done: either talk on the Dhamma or noble silence.'"

"One who delights in sleep" refers to one who, having eaten as much as he likes until his belly is full, devotes himself to the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of drowsiness;
or one who, whether walking, sitting, or standing, falls asleep overcome by sloth and torpor—this is called "one who delights in sleep.
However, when the mind sinks into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) due to the physical exhaustion of the karmic body, this is not "delighting in sleep"; for this very reason it was said:

“Moreover, Aggivessana, I recall that in the last month of summer, having returned from my alms round after the meal, I would spread out my outer robe folded fourfold and lie down on my right side, mindful and clearly comprehending, to take a nap.
And here, even a virtuous worldling (puthujjanakalyāṇaka) should be understood as one still in training (sekha). Therefore, regarding all his specific attainments...
It should be understood that for others, these [defilements] function for the sake of falling away from further distinguished attainment.
The exposition of the meaning for the bright side (sukkapakkha) should be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated.
Regarding the verses: "agitated" (uddhata) means agitated and unpacified by restlessness (uddhacca), which causes the distraction of the mind. "Of little business" (appakicca) means...
He would have few duties because he would perform even those permitted tasks of the aforementioned kind only at the proper time for application and exertion.
He would be free from drowsiness by means of the practice of wakefulness described as "by walking and sitting during the day," and so forth.
He would be undisturbed, being one who does not delight in talk, thus avoiding the mental distraction that arises from a delight in chatter.

"Having sacrificed [the defilements] through avoidance, he is not arrogant, his mind being calmed"—this is the meaning of "concentrated. The remainder is easily understood because it follows the method already explained above.
Thus, in this chapter, the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is discussed in the first, second, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth suttas;
in the others, both the round and its unraveling (*vaṭṭa-vivaṭṭa*) are discussed.
The commentary on the tenth sutta is finished.
The commentary on the third chapter is finished.
4. The fourth chapter.
1. Commentary on the *Vitakkasutta* 80.
In the first [sutta] of the fourth chapter, "unwholesome thoughts" (*akusalavitakkā*) means thoughts produced by lack of skill; the meaning is "wrong thoughts" (*micchāvitakkā*).
Regarding the phrase "connected with non-disparagement" (*anavaññattipaṭisaṃyutto*): here, "non-disparagement" (*anavaññatti*) means not being held in contempt by others.
Non-contempt is the conduct of desire proceeding thus: "Oh, that others would not despise me!
It is associated with non-contempt, being either the social interaction connected with it, or the thought proceeding with reference to it and connected with non-contempt.
Therefore, out of a desire for esteem, thinking: "How indeed might householders and renunciants not regard me as inferior? [one acts].
This is a designation for a thought that has arisen while remaining in self-willed conduct.
"Connected with gain, honor, and praise" means being connected by way of taking as an object both the acquisition of robes and so forth, as well as honor and reputation.
"Connected with compassion for others" means being connected with a worldly affection that merely resembles compassion for others.
It was with reference to this that it was said:
"He dwells in association with kings, royal ministers, brahmins, householders, members of other sects, and followers of other sects;
he shares their joys and sorrows; he is happy when they are happy and sorrowful when they are sorrowful; and when duties and tasks arise..."
“He himself incurs the consequence.
In the verses, a person associated with non-contempt is one “associated with non-contempt. One who has reverence for gain and honor, but not for the Dhamma, is “one who reveres gain and honor.
Those who are together with one in pleasure and pain, sharing in them, are “companions,” being like friends.
"Attendants. One who has the habit of rejoicing together with them by way of worldly affection is "one who rejoices with [them]," namely, with ministers;

by this, he shows a thought associated with compassion for others. "Far from the destruction of the fetters"—a person overcome by these three types of thoughts is far from the destruction of the fetters, that is, from Arahantship;
the meaning is that it is difficult for him to attain.

"Children and livestock" refers to children and cattle. Here, by the word "children," wives and so forth are included; by the word "livestock," horses, buffaloes, fields, lands, and so forth are included.
"He marries" means he causes a marriage to be performed. By this, the taking of a wife (*āvāha*) is also included. "She gathers" means she takes possession of;
the meaning is that she gathers the requisites for household life. Some also read "santhavāni," which means "friendships."

The connection is with the word "having abandoned" (*hitvā*) in all instances. "Such a bhikkhu is capable" means that such a person—having completely relinquished all the aforementioned conceptual proliferation (*papañca*) and because he must view things according to the right practice as taught by the Teacher—is called a "bhikkhu" because he beholds the terror of *saṃsāra*;
thus, he is worthy of attaining supreme enlightenment, which is *arahatta*.
The commentary on the first sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Sakkāra-sutta: 81.
In the second [verse], "by honor" means by honor acting as a cause; or alternatively, "by honor" means for the sake of honor.

Or by means of honor as a cause. For here, relying on honor, some individuals who are of evil intent and dominated by desire, standing in a state of wanton conduct, engage in various kinds of improper and unrighteous seeking with the thought, "We shall produce honor for ourselves.

Having done so, when they pass away from this world, they are reborn in the states of misery. Others, having received honor according to their merit, [act] on account of that through pride, intoxication, envy, and so forth.
Having fallen into negligence, when they pass away from here, they are reborn in the states of misery.
It is with reference to this that it was said: "Overcome by honor, their minds consumed. In this context, "overcome" means overwhelmed.

"Consumed in mind" means their minds have been exhausted; their wholesome minds have been brought to ruin through lustful conduct, pride, intoxication, and so forth. Alternatively, "consumed in mind" means...

"Whose minds are seized on all sides" means that their mental continuum is grasped from every direction by the aforementioned categories of unwholesome states, such that there is no opportunity for the arising of wholesome consciousness;
the sense is that the stream of mind has been taken hold of all around.

"By disrepute" means by way of contempt and humiliation—by reason of the disrepute directed toward oneself by others, or by pride and so forth caused by such disrepute. "By repute... [is explained similarly].
"Both by honor and by dishonor" means both by the honor performed by some and the dishonor performed by others.
This is said with reference to those who, having first been honored by certain people, later become dishonored by those very same people once they have recognized their worthlessness;
it is in regard to such persons that it is said, "both by honor and by dishonor."
In this context, Devadatta and others who were overcome by honor should be cited as examples. For it has been said:
"The fruit indeed destroys the plantain tree; the fruit destroys the bamboo, the fruit destroys the reed;
honor destroys the base man, just as the fetus destroys the mule."
The kings Daṇḍaki, Kaliṅga, Majjhāra, and others, who were overcome by their failure to show respect toward the virtuous, should be cited as examples. And this has been said:
“Having showered the emaciated Vaccha with dust, Daṇḍaki, together with his kinsmen and his kingdom, was cut off at the root.”
He is cooked in the hell named Kukkuḷa;
sparks fall upon his body.
"He who deceived those who were self-restrained and had gone forth..."
“When the harmless ascetics are preaching the Dhamma,
those dogs gather together and devour that coconut palm, writhing in agony, in the next world.”
“Having struck down Mana, the illustrious Mātaṅga,
together with his retinue was destroyed, and then the Middle Forest became [desolate].
By this, the followers of other sects, such as Nāṭaputta and others, who were overcome by both honor and dishonor, should be illustrated.
In the verses, "by both" means by both honor and dishonor. "Concentration does not waver" means it does not shake;
it remains in a state of one-pointedness. To the question "Of whom does it not waver?", he says: "of one who dwells in heedfulness.
This refers to the Arahant who dwells in heedfulness because of having thoroughly abandoned the defilements such as lust that cause negligence. He...

For he is not shaken by the worldly conditions (lokadhamma). "One who possesses subtle insight into vipassanā" means that because his vipassanā frequently proceeds by means of subtle vision—that is, wisdom—he is one who possesses subtle insight into vipassanā for the sake of attaining the fruition-attainment (phalasamāpatti).

"One who delights in the destruction of clinging" means that the fruit of arahantship, which consists in the destruction and final end of the four kinds of clinging, is what he must delight in; thus, he is one who delights in the destruction of clinging.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the second sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Devasadda Sutta.
82. "Among the third-order devas" means among those reborn as devas other than the non-percipient devas and the devas of the formless realm.
"The sounds of the devas" refers to the sounds produced by the joy of the devas. "They issue forth" means they proceed by way of mutual conversation and discourse.
"From time to time" means depending on one occasion after another. This is what is meant:
"At whatever time those deities are stationed, having come at that time, they will see him; thus, 'having come at the arrival of that occasion' [is meant].
Some read "samayaṃ samayaṃ upādāya," for which the meaning is "depending on this or that occasion.
"At whatever occasion" means when [it is said], "Sensual pleasures are like a skeleton," and so forth, or "Household life is a confinement," and so forth.
And at that time, the dangers in sensual pleasures and in the household life, as well as the benefits in renunciation, are clearly seen by him from their opposite nature.
For then his mind inclines exclusively toward the going forth.
"A noble disciple" (ariyasāvaka) means a disciple of the Noble One, the Blessed Buddha; one who desires to attain the state of a disciple, or one who is destined to become a noble disciple.
This undertaking refers to a disciple-bodhisattva in his final existence. "Having shaved off hair and beard" means having shaved off and removed both the hair of the head and the facial hair.
"Having clothed himself in saffron-colored robes" means having put on and wrapped himself in robes dyed with a decoction (kasāya), which are appropriate for those leading the holy life.

"He intends for the going-forth from home into homelessness" means: having gone out from the home, the house, he intends for, plans for, the going-forth into homelessness; the meaning is that he goes forth.

And here, since the work beneficial to the home—such as agriculture, trade, and so on—is called "home-life" (*agāriya*), and that does not exist for one who has gone forth, [the term is used in this sense].
Therefore, it should be known that going forth into homelessness is [the path].
"By Māra" means by the defilement-Māra (*kilesamāra*). "He intends for battle" means he arouses the mind for the purpose of fighting; he equips himself to utterly conquer Māra.
Furthermore, even for a person practicing in such a manner, the Devaputta-Māra cannot create an obstacle.
He exerts himself; therefore, by way of that [exertion] as well, the meaning of "by Māra" here should be understood as "by the Devaputta-Māra.

For even he will surely cause the frustration of his desire. However, from the day of going forth or from the time of shaving the head onwards, one who undertakes and purifies the precepts and performs the work of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) as appropriate—
By means of abandoning through the factors [of the path] and abandoning by suppression, one is said to "overthrow" the Māra of the defilements;
yet it is not "engaged in combat," because there is an absence of actual physical conflict. Therefore, it is said: "He intends to wage war against Māra.
Regarding the phrase "of the seven": this refers to seven in terms of groups, but in terms of their subdivisions, they become thirty-seven. How so? Four...

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path—thus, although they are thirty-sevenfold when divided, they are said to be "of seven" because they consist of seven groups beginning with the foundations of mindfulness.
Regarding the term *bodhipakkhiyānaṃ*: it refers to that which has received the name "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) in the sense of awakening.

“Factors conducive to enlightenment” (*bodhipakkhiya*) means those states belonging to the side of the noble person’s knowledge of the path; the meaning is: those that are constituent parts of enlightenment.
There is also a reading “*bodhipakkhikānaṃ*,” which means “possessing the wings of enlightenment” or “engaged in the side of enlightenment.
“Devoted to the practice of development” (*bhāvanānuyogamanuyutto*) means being devoted to the practice of developing the Noble Path by intensifying insight (*vipassanā*).
For at the moment of insight (vipassanā), the foundations of mindfulness and so forth are called factors conducive to enlightenment only in a figurative sense;
however, only at the moment of the Path (magga) do they truly become factors conducive to enlightenment in an absolute sense.
"With the destruction of the taints" means with the destruction of all taints, such as the taint of sensual desire and the rest. For when the taints have been destroyed, all [fetters]...
The defilements (*kilesa*) have indeed been exhausted; by this, the path of Arahatship is indicated. "Untainted" (*anāsava*) means free from the taints (*āsava*).
Regarding the phrase "liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*) and "liberation by wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*):

here, by the word "mind" (*ceto*), the concentration of the fruit of Arahatship is meant, and by the word "wisdom" (*paññā*), the wisdom associated with that [concentration] is meant. Therein, concentration is "liberation of mind" because it is liberated from lust (*rāga*); wisdom is...
Because of being liberated from ignorance, it should be understood as "liberation by wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*).

For this was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, whatever concentration there is, that is his faculty of concentration. Whatever wisdom there is, that is his faculty of wisdom. Thus, bhikkhus, through the fading away of lust comes liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*); through the fading away of ignorance comes liberation by wisdom.

Furthermore, in this context, it should be understood that liberation of mind is the fruit of serenity (*samatha*), while liberation by wisdom is the fruit of insight (*vipassanā*). In this very life...

"In this very life" (*dhamme*) means in this very selfhood (*attabhāve*). "Having realized it for oneself through direct knowledge" (*sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā*) means having made it manifest by one's own superior wisdom, having known it independently of others.
"Having attained and dwelling [in it]" (*upasampajja viharati*) means dwelling having reached and accomplished it.
"Having conquered that very head of the battle and dwelling [therein]" (*tameva saṅgāmasīsaṃ abhivijiya ajjhāvasati*) means having completely conquered Māra.

Because he has conquered victory, he dwells— meaning he masters and enters— the state of sovereignty consisting of the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship, which is the head of the Noble Path known as "battle.
It should be understood that these words "devas" (deities) refer to those who have seen the Truths, specifically to the Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) devas.
In the verses, "great" (*mahanta*) means great by virtue of the greatness of qualities such as moral discipline (*sīla*).

"Free from timidity" (*vītasārada*) means one who is devoid of timidity (*vigatasārajja*), having abandoned all diffidence (*maṅkubhāva*) due to the absence of defilements (*kilesa*) that cause timidity.

"Noble men" (*purisājañña*) refers to supreme persons who, among men, are like thoroughbred horses (*assājānīya*) and so forth among horses. "Difficult for the common folk to conquer" (*dujjayamajjhabhū*) means one whom ordinary people are unable to overcome.
He overcame and overwhelmed that which carries the defilements. They also read it as “ajjayī,” meaning he conquered.
Having conquered the army of Māra, [he attained] the unobstructed liberation (*vimokkha*);

for it is "unobstructed" (*anāvaraṃ*) because it pervades the three worlds, because of its vastness—being divided into one thousand five hundred parts and so forth—and because it is impossible for others to obstruct or prevent it. [This refers to] Māra, the Death-dealer.

The connection is as follows: "Homage to you, O noble steed among men (purisājañña), who have conquered that which is difficult to conquer, having defeated the army by means of the noble path of liberation.
"Iti" refers to the manner already described. "Hi" is merely a particle. He shows, by way of conclusion, the very meaning already stated:
"The deities pay homage to this one whose mind has attained [its goal], who has realized Arahantship, and whose taints are exhausted. Alternatively, "iti" may mean "for this reason."
But what is the reason for this? It is because he has attained his heart's desire through his victory over the army of Namuci.
For this reason, those deities pay homage to him; such is the meaning. Now, in order to show that reason by way of its fruit, it is said:
"For they do not see that by which he might fall under the power of Death. The meaning of this is: because, having made a resolution toward that noble steed of a man...
Even though the gods search for it, they do not see even the slightest cause by which he might fall under the power of death, of Māra.
Therefore, the pure gods pay homage to him.
The commentary on the third sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discourse on the Five Portents 83.
In the fourth [discourse], "yadā" means at whatever time. "Devā" refers to deities by birth (*upapattideva*). For there are three kinds of deities:

deities by convention (*sammutideva*), deities by birth (*upapattideva*), and deities by purification (*visuddhideva*). Among these, those called "deities by convention" are kings and members of the warrior-noble class (*khattiya*). Deities by birth...
"Devas" refers to those deities starting from the realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika) and above. "Pure deities" (*visuddhideva*) refers to those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).

However, in this context, a deity of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) is intended. Therefore it is said: "A 'deva' is a deva by birth. "Deva-kāyā" means from a multitude of deities, or from a place of deities;
that is to say, from the world of the deities (*devaloka*). For this word *kāya* denotes both a multitude and an abode. "Subject to falling away" (*cavanadhamma*)...
"Subject to death" means that death has become imminent, whether through the exhaustion of the life-span or the exhaustion of merit.

"Five portents appear for him" means that five portents of death arise or become manifest for that son of the gods whose death has become imminent. "The garland withers" refers to the garland worn by him.
At midday, they become withered and stripped of their splendor, like flowers cast into the heat;

the garments become soiled. This means that those various robes of manifold colors, which at the time of autumn resemble the radiance of the young sun rising into a cloudless sky, are at that very moment as if thrown into mud and trampled.
As if their radiance were shattered, they become soiled.
"Sweat breaks forth from the armpits" means that just as with a perfectly pure natural gem or a gold statue fashioned by a well-trained master artisan,
which previously had a body free from sweat, dirt, and grime, at that moment streams of sweat [break forth] from both armpits.
They flow and drip. Not only from the armpits, but even from the entire body, drops of perspiration are released, by which his body becomes as if covered with a net of strung pearls.
"Ugliness descends upon the body" means that from the moment of rebirth-linking onwards, according to its power, for a distance of one league—
His body becomes radiant, illuminating an area extending from two yojanas up to twelve yojanas with its light;
it is free from wrinkles, grey hair, and other such signs of aging, and is neither cold nor heat-injurious.
The female deity appears like a girl of sixteen years, and the male deity like a youth of twenty years; yet at that very moment, their bodies become lusterless and devoid of splendor.
He enters into and settles into a state of deformity.
"The god does not delight in his own divine throne" means he does not find pleasure in his celestial seat for sporting and enjoying himself with his own host of apsarases;
he finds no satisfaction of mind. It is said that his death will occur after seven days by human reckoning.
"These are the preliminary signs that it will come to pass. With the arising of these signs, he becomes overwhelmed by intense sorrow, thinking, "I shall be separated from such prosperity as this.
Consequently, a great fever arises in his body, and because of it, sweat breaks out from all his limbs. Having for a long time been unaccustomed to suffering, he—
Unable to endure it, some wander here and there wailing and lamenting, "I am burning! I am burning!", finding no comfort anywhere, merely whimpering and moaning.
Another, though maintaining mindfulness and making no outward display through body or speech, wanders about distressed, unable to bear the suffering of separation from what is dear.

However, just as in the world signs such as the falling of meteors, earthquakes, lunar eclipses, and so forth, appear only to those of great merit—such as kings, royal ministers, and the like—and not to everyone;

even so, these signs appear only to gods of great power. And when they have arisen, some gods recognize them, thinking, "These are indeed the premonitory signs of death," but not all do. In this regard:
One who has been reborn through weak wholesome karma fears, thinking, "Now who knows where I shall be reborn?
But one who possesses great merit does not fear and does not waver, thinking, "I have given much in alms, I have guarded my virtue, and I have accumulated merit;
when I pass away from here, a happy destination is surely to be expected for me. Thus is the prior sign manifested.
But having taken them, the deities lead them into the Nandana Grove; for the Nandana Grove exists in all the worlds of the devas.
"They express their appreciation with three words" means they express their appreciation with the three utterances now being spoken;
they produce joy and rapture, they offer consolation, or they manifest delight appropriate to that moment by way of addressing them. However, some [say]:
Regarding the word "anumodentī" (rejoicing), they say it means "ovadantī" (exhorting). "Ito" means from the world of the devas. "Bho" is a form of address.
"Sugatiṃ" means a beautiful destination; they say this with reference to the human world. "Gaccha" means go, in the sense of taking rebirth.
"Evaṃ vutte" means when such words as "Go from here, sir, to a good destination," and so forth, were spoken by those devas at that time.

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, a certain bhikkhu sitting in that assembly—one whose name and clan were unknown, who was skilled in logical connections—thought, "These states such as 'good destination' and so forth have been stated by the Blessed One without distinction and without being made clear; well then, let me cause them to be made clearer.
Thus he spoke these words beginning with, "But what, venerable sir? This was because [the Blessed One] provided the causes for the acquisition of the specific qualities of faith and the rest.

Because human existence is highly esteemed by the devas due to its being the cause for rebirth among them, it was said: "Human existence, bhikkhu, is reckoned as going to a good destination (sugati) for the devas.
"Reckoned as going to a good destination" means it is rightly called "going to a good destination"; the sense is that it is praised, extolled, and lauded.
Regarding the phrase "one who has become human" (*yaṃ manussabhūto*): here, *yaṃ* is a demonstrative pronoun referring to an action;

by it, the action of obtaining (*paṭilabhati*) in the phrase "obtains" is touched upon. The meaning is: "that which is the acquisition of faith. "Become human" (*manussabhūto*) means one born among humans, or one who has attained the human state.
This is because for those born in the world of the gods, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma is generally difficult to encounter.
It is for the sake of hearing [the Dhamma], not so for human beings; therefore it is said, "having become a human being.
"In the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata" means in the teaching consisting of the three trainings as taught by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata.

For that is called "Dhamma" because it does not deviate from the truth (dhamma), and it is called "Vinaya" because it disciplines those to be trained according to their dispositions; thus it is "Dhamma and Vinaya."

Alternatively, it is "Dhamma-Vinaya" because, through the excellence of the supporting conditions (*upanissaya-sampatti*), it guides those of a nature with little dust (*apparajakkha-jātika*) by means of the Dhamma, as they do not deviate from the Dhamma.
Or, it is "Dhamma-Vinaya" because the discipline (*vinaya*) is by means of the Dhamma alone, and not by means of physical force or weapons.

Or, it is "Dhamma-Vinaya" because the discipline is connected with the Dhamma. Or, it is "Dhamma-Vinaya" because the discipline is together with the Dhamma—namely, with the Path, the Fruition, and Nibbāna.
Alternatively, the Vinaya is called *dhammavinaya* because it proceeds from such phenomena (*dhamma*) as great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).

Or, the Blessed One is the Dhamma, he has become the Dhamma, he is the Dhamma-body, and he is the Lord of the Dhamma; the Vinaya belongs to that Dhamma and is not to be reached through mere reasoning—thus it is *dhammavinaya*.
Or, the Vinaya is called *dhammavinaya* because it proceeds with respect to the Dhamma, namely the Path and the Fruit, which constitute the sphere of what is to be accomplished.
It is said: "In that Dhamma and Vinaya, one acquires faith" means that one generates faith by thinking, "The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One," and so forth.
For one who possesses faith and practices in this Dhamma and Vinaya according to the instructions, [attains] the ultimate goals pertaining to the present life and the future life.
He will succeed. Regarding the phrase "reckoned as a gain well-obtained":

here, just as the acquisition of gold, silver, fields, lands, and so forth brings about the pleasure of enjoyment for beings, wards off the suffering of hunger, thirst, and the like, pacifies the poverty of lacking wealth, serves as the cause for obtaining treasures such as pearls, and maintains the continuity of the world; even so, [the attainment of] mundane and supramundane [states...]

Faith, according to its occurrence, brings about both mundane and supramundane resultant happiness; for those who have practiced with faith as their primary quality, it wards off the suffering of birth, aging, and so forth;
it pacifies the poverty of virtuous qualities; it serves as the cause for the acquisition of the jewels such as the mindfulness factor of enlightenment;
and it brings about the continuity of the world. For this has been said:
“Endowed with faith and perfected in virtue, possessed of fame and wealth, whatever region one frequents, there indeed one is honored.
Thus should the great gain of obtaining faith be understood. For this obtaining of faith—
It is ever-present, not shared by others, and the cause of all success; it is also the reason for obtaining worldly wealth such as gold, bullion, and so forth.

For it is only through faith that one performs meritorious deeds such as giving and thereby acquires magnificent and abundant riches and requisites, and through these, one accomplishes the welfare of both oneself and others. However, for one who lacks faith, those same things bring about misfortune.
“...both in this world and in the life to come. In this way, too, the great gain of faith should be understood.
For it is said: “Faith gathers one’s provisions for the journey,” and “Faith is a person’s second self.”
“Faith is the supreme wealth of a person in this world,” and “The great elephant has faith as his trunk,” and “Faith is the seed, austerity is the rain.”
“Monks, the noble disciple has faith as his guide,” and “By means of faith one crosses the flood.
In these and many other places, faith is praised for numerous reasons.

Now, in order to show that faith by which one is said to be "well-established" in the wholesome qualities within the Teaching and has entered the path of certainty (*niyāma*), the passage beginning with “Sā kho panassā” was spoken. Therein, “assā” means “of this [person]” or “for him.
“Niviṭṭhā” means firmly established, having entered into the continuum of consciousness. “Mūlajātā” means having taken root. What?
But what is called the root of faith? It is the application of means consisting of mental attention (*manasikāra*) which serves as the cause for conviction regarding an object worthy of faith.

Furthermore, the four factors of stream-entry—association with superior persons (*sappurisasevanā*), hearing the true Dhamma (*saddhammassavana*), wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), and practice in accordance with the Dhamma (*dhammānudhammappaṭipatti*)—should be understood as its roots. "Established" means by means of the attainment of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). By no one...
They are established in an unshakable state. For this very reason, it is said: "Firm and unshakeable. "Firm" means stable.
"Unshakeable" means incapable of being gathered, diminished, or removed by anyone. Thus those gods speak in this way, wishing for his attainment of the path of stream-entry.
For an Ariya person is indeed worthy of enjoying the sensual pleasures of their own divine world.
They desire this; therefore he says, "Come, O King, again and again.
In the verses, since even death through the exhaustion of merit occurs only through the cutting off of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), he says, "one passes away at the end of one's lifespan.
"Rejoicing" refers to those who are rejoicing. "Companionship with humans" means being together with humans. "He goes together with them" (*saha byeti*).
"Companion" means one who proceeds together; the state of that is "companionship. "Of one who is settled" means she would be settled [therein].
"As long as life lasts" means for as long as the process of living continues; the meaning is "until final Nibbāna.
"Immeasurable" means, by way of performing it with care, extensively, loftily, and many times, it is without measure. "Without substrate" (nirupadhi).

"Free from the substrate of defilements" means it is perfectly purified and stainless. However, since those gods do not desire sublime wholesome states because they have transcended the sense-sphere world, but desire only sense-sphere merit, the meaning here should be understood as follows:
"Having passed away from this divine world and been reborn among humans, having attained full consciousness, [he engages in] bodily misconduct and so forth..."
“Having abandoned all misconduct and having accumulated all noble and vast good conduct, such as bodily good conduct and so forth,

may you become one who has arrived at the Noble Path through faith. However, since they desire either the first or the second supramundane path because they do not transcend rebirth in their own world of the gods,
therefore, according to their view as well, [the text says] “immeasurable...”
The meaning of “without substrate” (*nirūpadhi*) should be understood as follows:
it is "immeasurable" because of the cutting off of those gross defilements such as sensual lust, which are associated with views and act as limiting factors;

and it is "without substrate" because of the abandoning of the aggregates as a substrate that would otherwise arise from the seventh existence, of the formative activities as a substrate that produce them, and of the defilements as a substrate to be abandoned by the respective paths, thereby ensuring their non-arising, and because it is dependent upon Nibbāna, which is designated as "without substrate."

Having thus shown the karma that completely closes the doors to the states of misery (apāya), the text now says, "Then, that which is connected with the substrata" (*tato opadhikaṃ*), etc., in order to show the karma that produces the attainment of heaven.

Therein, "connected with the substrata" (*opadhika*) means that which ripens as a substratum (*upadhivepakka*), i.e., that which produces both the excellence of personal existence (*attabhāva*) and the excellence of wealth (*bhoga*). For "substratum" (*upadhi*) is said to be personal existence. As it has been said:
“Some undertakings of evil kamma do not ripen because they are warded off by the attainment of acquisitions (*upadhi*).
This refers also to the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). As it is said: “Through acquisitions there is sorrow for a man. Herein, this is the meaning of the word:

it is called an *upadhi* because pleasure and pain are acquired (*upadhīyati*) therein; thus, it is the personal existence (*attabhāva*) and the strands of sensual pleasure. Virtue has these as its basis; [it is] the *upadhi*...
Or, it is called *opadhika* because one is worthy of it; that is, having performed much and sublime merit. How? By means of giving (*dāna*).

For it is said that giving is indeed easier than the others. Alternatively, by the word "giving," the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*) is also included, and not merely the gift of material things (*āmisa*);

thus, it should be understood that virtue (*sīla*) is also comprised therein. Furthermore, since those gods [bring about] the certain decline of the asura hosts and the complete fulfillment of the divine hosts...
They desire this; therefore, showing him the means to achieve it, they urge him toward the gift of the Dhamma, saying: "Establish other mortals as well in the true Dhamma and in the holy life.

When the wise know—meaning at whatever time the gods might recognize a god passing away—at that time, out of this aforementioned compassion and the desire to remove suffering, [they say]: "O God, these [beings] in the divine host again and again..."
And she offered thanks by saying, “Come, come hither,” in the sense of arising [in her mind].
The commentary on the fourth sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Bahujanahita Sutta.
84. Regarding the phrase "in the fifth world": here there are three worlds—the world of beings (*sattaloka*), the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*), and the world of space (*okāsaloka*).
Among these, the world of beings is the collection of material phenomena bound to the faculties, immaterial phenomena, and both material and immaterial phenomena, existing as a continuity.
The world of space consists of the divisions such as earth and mountains. Both types of aggregates together constitute the world of formations. Of these, the world of beings...

This is what is intended here. Therefore, "in the world" means in the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*). Even there, it is not in the world of the gods, nor in the world of Brahmā, but in the human world (*manussaloka*).
Even in the human world, it is not in another world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), but in this very world-system. Even there, it is not in all places; [it is said]:
"In the eastern direction there is a market town named Gajaṅgala; beyond that is Mahāsālā; further beyond that is the border region."

To the east and south, there is the river named Sallavatī; beyond that are the bordering districts, and on this side of it is the middle country. To the south, there is the market town named Setakaṇṇika;
beyond that are the bordering districts, and on this side of it is the middle country. To the west, there is the brahmin village named Thūṇa.
Beyond that are the bordering districts, and within that is the Middle Country. To the north is the mountain named Usiraddhaja;
beyond that are the bordering districts, and within that is the Middle Country.
Thus, within this delimited area—three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty yojanas in width, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference—the Buddha arises in the Middle Country.

It is the Tathāgata. Not only the Tathāgata, but also Paccekabuddhas, chief disciples, the eighty great elders, the mother of the Buddha, the father of the Buddha, a Wheel-turning Monarch, and other Brahmins and householders who have attained the essence, arise in this very place.
However, this principle applies in its entirety only in the case of the Tathāgata’s appearance; in the cases of others, it applies only partially.
Regarding the phrase "arising, they arise," both of these are indeed incomplete expressions;
the meaning here should be understood as follows: "Arising, they arise for the benefit and welfare of many people, and not for any other reason.
For such a grammatical characteristic (*saddalakkhaṇa*) cannot be refuted by any other grammatical characteristic.
Furthermore, this distinction should be understood: that which is "arising," that which is "in the process of arising," and that which is "arisen.

For the Tathāgata, while making the Great Resolve, seeking the qualities that constitute a Buddha, fulfilling the perfections, relinquishing the five great sacrifices, practicing the conduct for the benefit of relatives, the conduct for the benefit of the world, and the conduct for the sake of Buddhahood—
Reaching the pinnacle, fulfilling the perfections, and dwelling in the Tusita heaven;
then descending from there and taking rebirth in his final existence; living in the midst of the household life, renouncing the world, and exerting himself in the Great Struggle;
having matured his knowledge, ascending the seat of enlightenment and crushing the host of Māra; and during the first watch of the night, recollecting his former births.
