During the middle watch, while purifying the divine eye, and during the last watch, having applied knowledge to dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) and having comprehended all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) in their many aspects, even when one penetrates the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) up to realizing the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), it is said that [the path] is arising;
at the moment of the path of arhatship (arahatta-magga), it is said to arise; and at the moment of the fruit of arhatship (arahattaphala)—
However, it is said to have "arisen. For Buddhas, unlike the disciples, there is no requirement to produce the various supernormal powers (iddhividha-ñāṇa) and so forth in a sequential order;
rather, together with the path of Arahantship, the entire mass of Buddha-qualities is as if already arrived.

Therefore, because they have accomplished all their functions, these [powers] are said to have "arisen" at the moment of the fruit of Arahantship. Here, the moment of the fruit of Arahantship is intended.
Having intended this, it is said that [the path] "arises. Here, the meaning is that it "has arisen.

Even a disciple whose taints are exhausted, while accumulating the equipment of merit that serves as the cause for the enlightenment of a disciple, fulfilling his former application and former conduct—the practice of going and returning—and being reborn in his final existence, gradually attains full maturity within saṃsāra...
Having seen the peril [of household life] and intending to go forth, one brings the going-forth to its ultimate conclusion; fulfilling the precepts and so forth,
undertaking and practicing the ascetic qualities (dhutaṅga), applying oneself to wakefulness, generating the various knowledges, and establishing insight—
even while attaining the lower paths— it is indeed said that [the fruit] arises at the moment of the path of Arahatship.
It is said to "arise" [in the future], but at the moment of the fruit of Arahatship, it is said to have "arisen.

However, for one in training (sekha), from the beginning of the decisive support (pubbūpanissaya) up until the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa), it is said to be "arising"; at the moment of the first path, it is said to "arise";
and from the moment of the first fruit onwards, it is said to have "arisen. To this extent, [the passage] "Bhikkhus, these three persons arise in the world as they are arising... is explained.
The meaning of the words has been stated.
Now, regarding the phrases beginning with "for the welfare of many" (*bahujanahitāya*): "for the welfare of many" means for the sake of the benefit of the great multitude.

"For the happiness of many" means for the sake of the happiness of the great multitude. "Out of compassion for the world" means out of compassion for the world of sentient beings. For which world of sentient beings?
For whoever, having heard the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, penetrates the Dhamma and drinks the drink of the Deathless— it was for such a person that,
through the Blessed One’s delivery of the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta*,
eighteen koṭis of Brahmās headed by Aññāta-Koṇḍañña penetrated the Dhamma. In this way, [the penetration of the Dhamma continued] as far as the conversion of the wanderer Subhadda.

There is no counting those beings who have attained penetration; there is no limit to the number of beings who have reached realization in these four instances: during the preaching of the Mahāsamaya Suttanta, the Maṅgala Sutta, the Cūḷarāhulovāda, and the teaching on the even mind.
Thus it is out of compassion for this immeasurable world of beings. But as for the disciple—whether an Arahant or one still in training—

And [this occurs] through the arising [of the teaching] out of compassion for the world, by way of the beings who have attained penetration through the teachings preached by the Dhamma-General (Sāriputta) and others, as well as the Dhamma-Treasurer (Ānanda) and others;
and later, by way of those who have penetrated the Truths through the teachings preached by the Elder Mahinda and others;
and from now on until the end of time, and in the future as well, [by way of those] relying upon the Dispensation regarding the paths to heaven and liberation.
This meaning should also be clarified by way of those who establish themselves [in the teaching].

Furthermore, "for the welfare of many" (*bahujanahitāya*) means for the sake of the benefit of many people; it refers to one who teaches the welfare pertaining to both the present life and future lives through their perfection of wisdom (*paññā*).

"For the happiness of many" (*bahujanasukhāya*) means for the sake of the happiness of many people; it refers to one who bestows the attainment of the happiness of requisites through their perfection of generosity (*cāga*).

"Out of compassion for the world" means for the sake of commiserating with the world; through the perfection of loving-kindness and compassion, they are the protectors and guardians of the world like parents.
"For the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans": here, by the mention of "gods and humans," only those capable persons who are beings susceptible to instruction are included;
[this refers to] the Tathāgata’s [teaching] for their attainment of *nibbāna*, the path, and the fruits.
The arising [of the fruit] was shown in the first section; however, in the second and third sections, it should be applied by way of the arahant and the trainee (sekha) respectively.
Therein, by the phrase "for the sake of" (*atthāya*), it is meant "for the ultimate goal," that is, for Nibbāna.

By the phrase "for the welfare" (*hitāya*), it is meant "for the sake of the path that leads to its attainment. For indeed, there is no benefit superior to the path that leads to the attainment of Nibbāna.

There is none. "For the sake of happiness" means for the sake of the happiness of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*); this is because there is no happiness beyond that. For it has been said:
"This concentration is pleasant in the present and results in happiness in the future.
The meaning of the words beginning with "Tathāgata" has been explained above. Regarding the phrases beginning with "perfect in knowledge and conduct," all three [knowledges]...

He is "endowed with true knowledge and conduct" (vijjācaraṇasampanna) because he is possessed of, and has attained, true knowledges— whether they be the three knowledges according to the method of the arrival [of the Buddha], the six knowledges by way of the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā),
or the eight knowledges as they appear in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta— as well as of the restraints of virtue (sīlasaṃvara) and so forth,
and of the fifteen factors of conduct (caraṇadhamma), all of which are not shared by others. He is so called because his gait is beautiful and because he has gone to a beautiful state.
He is the Sugata because he has gone rightly and because he has spoken rightly. He is the Knower of the World (*lokavidū*) because he has thoroughly understood the world in every respect.

He is the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara*) because there is no one superior to him. He is the Charioteer of Men to be Tamed (*purisadammasārathi*) because he impels and disciplines those among men who are capable of being tamed.
He is the Teacher (*satthā*) because he instructs, as appropriate, in the ultimate truths concerning both the present life and the future life. [He is the one who knows] all that is to be known...
"He is called a Buddha because he has awakened through self-born knowledge in every respect"—this is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be taken from the *Visuddhimagga*.
"He teaches the Dhamma... which is beautiful in the beginning, beautiful in the middle, and beautiful in the end"—that Blessed One, out of compassion for beings... [and so on].

Even having abandoned the unsurpassed bliss of seclusion, he teaches the Dhamma. And whether teaching little or much, he teaches it in such a manner that it is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end. How so?

For even a single stanza, because of the all-pervading excellence of the Dhamma, is good in the beginning with its first line, good in the middle with its second and third lines, and good in the end with its final line.

A discourse with a single sequence of meaning is "good in the beginning" by way of its introduction (nidāna), "good in the end" by way of its conclusion (nigamana), and "good in the middle" by way of what remains.

A discourse with multiple sequences of meaning is "good in the beginning" by way of the first sequence, "good in the end" by way of the last sequence, and "good in the middle" by way of those in between.
Alternatively, the entire Dhamma of the Dispensation is "good in the beginning" by virtue of its own purposeful goal.
It is beautiful in the beginning through virtue; beautiful in the middle through serenity, insight, the paths, and the fruits; and beautiful in the end through Nibbāna.
Alternatively, it is beautiful in the beginning through virtue and concentration; beautiful in the middle through insight and the paths; and beautiful in the end through the fruits and Nibbāna.

Or, it is beautiful in the beginning through the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment; beautiful in the middle through the Dhamma’s perfect nature as Dhamma; and [beautiful in the end] through the Saṅgha’s perfect practice.
It is beautiful in the conclusion. For one who has heard it and is practicing accordingly, it is beautiful in the beginning because of the full enlightenment (abhisambodhi) that is to be attained;
it is beautiful in the middle because of the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha; and it is beautiful in the conclusion because of the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvakabodhi).

Furthermore, while being heard, it brings about what is beautiful even through the mere hearing, because it suppresses the hindrances (nīvaraṇa); thus it is beautiful in the beginning. When practiced...
Because it brings about the bliss of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), the practice itself brings about bliss; thus, it is "good in the middle.

Furthermore, for one who practices in such a way, once the fruit of the practice is accomplished, it brings about the state of being "suchness" (*tādibhāva*); thus, it is "good in the end" by virtue of the fruit of the practice.
And because it originates from a Protector (*nātha*), it is "good in the beginning" through the purity of its source; [it is good in the middle] through the purity of its purpose (*attha*).
It is beautiful in the middle and beautiful in the conclusion through the purification of what must be done. Therefore it is said: "He teaches the Dhamma that is beautiful in the beginning...
beautiful in the conclusion.
Furthermore, when the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, he reveals both the holy life of the Dispensation (*sāsanabrahmacariya*) and the holy life of the Path (*maggabrahmacariya*).

He illuminates it through various methods; it is "possessed of meaning" (sāttha) because of its perfection of meaning according to what is appropriate, and "possessed of phrasing" (sabyañjana) because of its perfection of phrasing.

It is possessed of meaning through the conjunction of the words that express the meaning—namely, through indicating, manifesting, disclosing, analyzing, clarifying, and defining—and it is possessed of phrasing through the perfection of syllables, words, phrases, modes of expression, etymologies, and explanations. It is [also profound] through the profundity of its meaning and the profundity of its penetration.
Or, it is "with meaning" (*sāttha*) by virtue of the profundity of the Dhamma and the profundity of the teaching;

it is "with phrasing" (*sabyañjana*) by virtue of being the domain of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) and the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*). Or, it is "with meaning" because it is to be understood by the wise and inspires confidence in those who investigate;
it is "with phrasing" because it is credible and inspires confidence in worldly people. It is "with meaning" because its intention is profound.
It is "with phrasing" because its words are clear. It is "entirely complete" by virtue of being whole and perfect, as there is nothing to be added;
it is "pure" by virtue of being faultless, as there is nothing to be removed.

Furthermore, it is "meaningful" because the practice results in realization, and it is "with phrasing" because the study results in the mastery of the scriptures. This is due to the fulfillment of the five aggregates of dhamma, beginning with virtue.
It is "complete" (paripuṇṇaṃ); it is "pure" (parisuddhaṃ) because it proceeds for the sake of crossing over from the absence of defilements and because it is indifferent to worldly gain;

it is "the holy life" (brahmacariyaṃ) because it is embraced by the three trainings, because it is to be practiced by those who have become sublime (brahmabhūtehi), and because it is the state of conduct of those [sublime ones].
Therefore, it is said: "He reveals that which has meaning and possesses the letter... [and so on]... he elucidates. "The first" (paṭhamo) is according to the sequence of enumeration.
And because he possesses the state that is supreme over the entire world, he is the first person.

He is a disciple of that very Teacher; that is, a disciple similar to the General of the Dhamma, born at the conclusion of hearing the Dhamma-teaching of that very Teacher, the Perfectly Enlightened One who possesses the aforementioned qualities, and not merely by way of a formal declaration like Pūraṇa and others.

A disciple (*sāvaka*). One who has been born into the noble birth by means of the Noble Path, which is designated as the "way of practice" (*paṭipadā*), is called one who has "gone forth on the way" (*pāṭipada*);

the meaning is that he is one who is practicing while the duties of his practice are not yet completed. One who has heard much of the Dhamma of the scriptures, such as the *Sutta* and *Geyya*, is called "learned" (*bahussuta*). By means of the virtue of restraint according to the *Pātimokkha* and so forth, as well as by the vows of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) such as the forest-dweller’s practice (*āraññikaṅga*),...
And "endowed, perfected, and possessed" means endowed with virtue and conduct (*sīlavatūpapanno*).
Thus the Blessed One shows that "compassion for the world" consists in teaching the Dhamma with the intention of welfare, and that this is dependent upon these very three types of persons.
The rest is easily understood.
In the verses, *tassanvayo* means "following after him," that is, following the practice and the teaching of the Dhamma of that very Teacher; thus he is "born after" (*anujāta*).
They are called "light-makers" (*pabhaṅkarā*) because, having dispelled the darkness of ignorance, they produce light—termed the "light of the Dhamma"—within their own and others' mental continuums.
*Dhammam udīrayantā* means "proclaiming the Dhamma," that is, speaking on the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. *Apāpuranti* means "they open up."
They open the door to the deathless Nibbāna, the Noble Path. "Yokes" refers to the yoke of sensual desire and so forth.
"By the Caravan Leader": because he leads the caravan of those to be trained and carries them across the wilderness of existence, the Blessed One is the Caravan Leader; by that Caravan Leader.
"Following the well-taught path" means following the Noble Path correctly taught by him, in accordance with his teaching.
They follow and practice. "Right here" means in this very personal existence (*attabhāva*). The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Asubhānupassī-sutta* (The Discourse on Contemplating the Foul).
85. In the sixth [precept], "contemplating foulness" (*asubhānupassī*) means:

dwell contemplating foulness by way of the thirty-two aspects (*dvattiṃsākāra*), and by way of applying the sign grasped from the bloated corpse (*uddhumātaka*) and so forth; thus, dwell as those who contemplate the body as foul and in its foul aspect.

"Mindfulness of breathing" (*ānāpānassati*) means mindfulness regarding inhalation and exhalation; it is the mindfulness that occurs with reference to that, which comprises the grasping of inhalation and exhalation.
The meaning is "being present. For this has been said: "Āna is inhalation, not exhalation; pāna is exhalation, not inhalation," and so forth. *Vo* means "for you.
*Ajjhattam* here refers to the internal range of the object of meditation (*gocarajjhatta*). *Parimukham* means "facing toward" or "in front of.
*Sūpaṭṭhitā* means "well-established. This is what is meant: mindfulness of breathing is well-established for you, facing toward the meditation subject.

"May it be well-established. Alternatively, "at the mouth" (*parimukham*) means "having the outlet encompassed. For this is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*: "‘Encompassing’ (*pari*) has the sense of encompassing;
‘mouth’ (*mukha*) has the sense of an outlet; ‘mindfulness’ (*sati*) has the sense of establishing; therefore it is called ‘mindfulness at the mouth’ (*parimukhaṃ sati*).
By this, the development of the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing, which has sixteen divisions based on the four foundations of mindfulness, [is explained].
It is to be seen as "shown.

Thus, having briefly pointed out the meditation subject for serenity (samatha-kammaṭṭhāna) and the meditation subject for insight (vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna) suitable for those of a lustful temperament (rāga-carita) and a discursive temperament (vitakka-carita) by way of attention to repulsiveness and the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā), [the author] now [explains] the pure insight meditation subject alone.
Showing this, he said: "Dwell contemplating impermanence in all conditioned phenomena.
In this context, one should understand this tetrad: the impermanent, the characteristic of impermanence, the contemplation of impermanence, and the one who contemplates impermanence.

The pentad of aggregates is called "impermanent" because it does not exist after having come to be, because it is subject to arising and passing away, because it is temporary, and because it is the negation of permanence. That mode of its non-existence after having come to be—
That is called the characteristic of impermanence (*anicca-lakkhaṇa*). Insight that proceeds with reference to that is the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*).
One who contemplates it as "impermanent" is a practitioner of the contemplation of impermanence. And herein, the elevenfold discourse on the foul (*asubha-kathā*) leads to the first jhāna;
the discourse on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-kathā*) based on the sixteen bases leads to the fourth jhāna; and the discourse on insight (*vipassanā-kathā*) [leads] in detail...
It should be stated that this has been explained in every detail in the *Visuddhimagga*, and thus it should be understood according to the method set forth there.
Now, in order to show the specific fruits to be accomplished through the contemplation of foulness (*asubhānupassanā*) and so forth, he says: "For those who contemplate foulness," and so on.

Therein, "of the beautiful element" (*subhāya dhātuyā*) means in the state of beauty; the meaning is: in the sign of beauty (*subhanimitta*). "Underlying tendency to lust" (*rāgānusaya*) refers to [the tendency] toward a beautiful object (*subhārammaṇe*).
The underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) is liable to arise.

For those who, contemplating the foulness of the hair and so forth, or of the bloated corpse (*uddhumātaka*) and so forth, have grasped the sign of foulness (*asubhanimitta*) and, having produced the first jhāna therein, established insight by making that [jhāna] the basis, it is abandoned by the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*) which they have attained;
the meaning is that it is completely severed. For this has been said:
“The foul should be developed for the abandoning of sensual lust.

“External” means external because they have an external basis and because they bring about harm; they are situated outside. “Latent tendencies of thought” refers to wrong thoughts such as sensual intentions and the like. For these, when unabandoned, follow along with the latent tendencies (*āsaya*) since they arise when conditions converge;
thus they are called “latent tendencies of thought. And here, the thought of sensual pleasure is included by the mention of “sensual lust.”
"Only those [are taken]" means it should be understood that only the remaining types of thought (vitakka) are what have been mentioned.
"Belonging to the side of vexation" means they partake of suffering, or they produce the frustration of one's desires. "They do not exist" means they are abandoned.

[These are: thoughts of ill-will, thoughts of cruelty, thoughts concerning relatives, thoughts concerning one's country, thoughts concerning immortality, thoughts associated with not being held in low esteem, and thoughts associated with gain, honor, and fame.
There are eight types of applied thought (*vitakka*), including the thought associated with compassion for others;

together with sensual thought, these nine kinds of "great thoughts" are suppressed in the preliminary stage by concentration on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati-samādhi*) and the insight (*vipassanā*) based upon it.
Having made that the foundation, they are abandoned without remainder according to their respective degrees by means of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) attained therefrom. As it has been said:
This is what was said: “Mindfulness of breathing should be developed for the cutting off of discursive thoughts.

As for ignorance—that ignorance which conceals the true nature of reality, which brings about all that is harmful, and which is the root of the entire suffering of saṃsāra—it is utterly severed for those who dwell contemplating impermanence. This, it is said, was taught by the Blessed One.

This is stated with reference to a dry-insight practitioner (sukkha-vipassaka) whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), who has emerged from the contemplation of the aspect of impermanence. Its summary meaning is as follows:

for those who, having established the comprehension of all conditioned phenomena belonging to the three planes as impermanent and so forth, are practicing insight, when the insight leading to emergence—which occurs as "it is impermanent"—is joined with the Path, the path of Arahantship arises in due course.
As they dwell contemplating impermanence, ignorance is abandoned without remainder, and the knowledge of the path of Arahantship arises.
The phrase "dwell contemplating impermanence" is stated because the characteristic of impermanence is evident to them, or because it serves as the means for grasping the other two characteristics;
it is not, however, [a statement] regarding only one characteristic.
Because it is to be contemplated thus. For this has been said: "What is impermanent, that is suffering; what is suffering, that is non-self. Furthermore, it has been said:
"For one who perceives impermanence, Meghiya, the perception of non-self becomes established; perceiving non-self, one attains the eradication of the conceit 'I am'.
In the verses, "mindful of in-and-out breathing" means being mindful (*sato*) of each [breath] with respect to the sign of in-and-out breathing; the meaning is "one whose mindfulness is established."
Seeing with the eye of knowledge that destroys the taints (*āsava*), he sees Nibbāna, which is the subsiding of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
Being ardent (*ātāpī*) at all times, without falling into intermediate despondency, he is constantly ardent and devotedly applied to the contemplation of the foul (*asubha*) and other practices;

and thus, striving with effort, or being fixed by the certainty of rightness (*sammatta-niyāma*) therein—in that Nibbāna, the pacification of all formations—he [attains] the liberation of the fruit of Arhatship.
He is liberated. The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the sixth sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Dhammānudhammapaṭipanna Sutta.
86. Regarding the phrase "in the seventh [case], for one practicing in accordance with the Dhamma": here, "Dhamma" refers to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma;
the "anudhamma" (conformity to that Dhamma) is the practice of the preliminary stage, such as purification of virtue and so forth.
For one who has practiced that *dhammānudhamma*—that is, for one who is proceeding toward its attainment—this [following] becomes the *anudhamma*. This means it is a corresponding or suitable nature.
He possesses a suitable nature. "For the sake of explanation" means for the purpose of speaking.
Regarding the phrase "one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma," the nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. This is what is meant:
when one explains that "he is practicing in accordance with that Dhamma" by way of the *anudhamma*, he may be said to be explaining correctly; on that account, he is not to be censured by the wise.
“Siyā” means: or it is a grasping of the activity [of speaking]. By this he shows:

“Insofar as there is the speaking of the Dhamma alone and the thinking of a thought of the Dhamma alone—in the absence of both of these, through knowledge and equanimity—this is the corresponding cause and the suitable reason for describing a bhikkhu who has entered upon the practice in accordance with the Dhamma as ‘one who goes thus. Speaking, he speaks only the Dhamma.”
"Should speak": if he speaks, he should speak only on the Dhamma of the ten bases of discourse, and not on the un-Dhamma of its opposite, such as great desire and so forth. For this has been said:

"That discourse which is conducive to effacement, favorable to the opening of the heart, and leads to utter disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna—namely, the discourse on fewness of desires..."

“He is one who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, such talk as discourse on contentment, discourse on seclusion, discourse on non-association, discourse on the arousal of energy, discourse on virtue, discourse on concentration, discourse on wisdom, discourse on liberation, and discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation.”
Indeed, only one who has attained [the goal] through discourse that is self-effacing would speak thus. By this, the possession of virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitta) is shown.

Regarding "thoughts on the Dhamma" (dhammavitakka): for one who thinks thoughts not departing from the Dhamma—such as thoughts of renunciation (nekkhammavitakka)—the effort to fulfill the practice of virtue and so forth will increase further and further. However, that thought [is ineffective] toward those qualities that do not assist virtue and the rest.

Having abandoned the unwholesome states (*adhamma-dhamma*) that are contrary to benefit, and having removed the state conducive to decline (*hānabhāgiya*) by way of cultivating the beneficial states, one should understand that there are many varieties of mental activity occurring through the process of reaching the state conducive to stability (*ṭhitibhāgiya*), as well as the states conducive to distinction (*visesabhāgiya*) and penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).
"No unwholesome thought" (*no adhammavitakka*) means one should not think thoughts of sensual desire (*kāmavitakka*); or, it refers to both of those [unwholesome thoughts].
"But" (*pana*) refers to that which was stated as preaching the Dhamma for the sake of assisting others and reflecting on the Dhamma for one's own benefit.
Or else, "but" means having avoided both of those, not engaging in them, and not performing them.

"Equanimous" (*upekkhako*) means that one should dwell indifferent toward such practice, cultivating only the development of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), specifically within the practice of serenity.
Being equanimous, he should dwell performing the work of insight alone. Having brought even that insight to excellence,
being equanimous there too by way of the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa*),
he should dwell mindful and clearly comprehending so that, until the knowledge of insight is joined with the path, it proceeds in a manner that is sharp, keen, and clear.
In the verses, one who has a "pleasure grove" (*ārāma*)—in the sense of being delighted by—the Dhamma of serenity and insight is called a *dhammārāma*.
One who delights in that very same Dhamma is a *dhammarata*. Because of repeatedly reflecting upon that very Dhamma, he is "contemplating the Dhamma" (*dhammaṃ anuvicintayan*);
the meaning is that he adverts to and attends to that Dhamma. They "recollect" (*anussaranti*) that very same Dhamma by way of successive cultivation.

Recalling. Alternatively, he is a *dhammārāma* (one who delights in the Dhamma) because the Dhamma—consisting of virtue and the other factors—is his "pleasure grove" (*ārāma*) in the sense that it is to be resorted to while standing at the head of the bases of liberation (*vimuttāyatana*), by way of teaching others.
Likewise, he is a *dhammarata* (one who rejoices in the Dhamma) because he takes delight and finds pleasure in that very same Dhamma.

Furthermore, while investigating the courses of those very factors such as virtue, he does not allow any opportunity for sensual thoughts (*kāmavitakka*) and the like, but [cultivates] only the Dhamma of renunciation (*nekkhammasaṅkappa*) and so forth.

Reflecting upon the Dhamma, one reflects on it; or else, perceiving both of those as coarse, one looks on with equanimity and, by way of successive development, recollects and intensifies only the states of serenity and insight.
"True Dhammas" refers to the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment and the ninefold supramundane Dhamma.
"He falls away, yet before long he attains it"—this is the meaning.
Now, showing the method for recollecting that, he says "whether walking," and so forth.
Therein, "whether walking" means either walking in the course of going for alms or walking while pacing up and down. Or whether standing, or sitting, or even lying down...
They lie down while lying; thus it is in all four postures. "He calms his own mind internally":

he calms (*sameti*) his own mind—which is within the internal sphere (*ajjhatta-gocara*) consisting of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*)—by means of the subsiding and abandoning of defilements such as lust.
"He attains peace itself" means that he reaches ultimate peace, which is Nibbāna itself.
The commentary on the seventh sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Andhakaraṇa Sutta 87.

In the eighth [sutta], "unwholesome thoughts" (*akusalavitakkā*) refers to thoughts arisen from lack of skillfulness (*akosalla*). Regarding the terms "causing darkness" (*andhakaraṇā*) and so forth: for one who... [text continues]
They arise and, by obstructing the vision of things as they truly are, they make one blind; thus they are "blind-making" (*andhakaraṇā*). They do not produce the eye of wisdom;
thus they are "eyeless-making" (*acakkhukaraṇā*). They produce ignorance; thus they are "ignorance-making" (*aññāṇakaraṇā*).

They are "cessators of wisdom" (*paññānirodhikā*): because they bring to cessation—by way of non-arising—the three kinds of wisdom, namely the wisdom of the ownership of kamma, the wisdom of meditative absorption (*jhāna*), and the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā*), they are called cessators of wisdom.
They are "on the side of vexation" (*vighātapakkhika*) because they belong to the faction of the vexation known as suffering, owing to their yielding undesirable fruits.
They are "not conducive to Nibbāna" (*anibbānasaṃvattanika*) because they do not lead to the extinction of defilements.
"Sensual thought" (*kāmavitakka*) is a thought associated with sensual desire; for that, being accompanied by defiled sensual desire, [operates] upon sense-objects (*vatthukāma*).
It occurs. A thought associated with ill will is a thought of ill will (*byāpādavitakka*). A thought associated with cruelty is a thought of cruelty (*vihiṃsāvitakka*).
These two arise both with respect to sentient beings and with respect to formations (*saṅkhāra*).
For a thought of sensual desire arises when one thinks of a beloved and pleasing sentient being or formation; a thought of ill will [arises] toward a disliked and displeasing sentient being...
Whether toward beings or toward formations, from the moment one looks with anger until the anger subsides, it arises;
however, the thought of cruelty does not arise toward formations, for there are no formations that can be made to suffer.
Rather, it arises toward beings at the time of thinking, "May these beings be killed, or bound, or cut off, or destroyed, or may they cease to exist."

These, moreover, are precisely the sensual intentions (*kāmasaṅkappa*) and so forth. For in terms of their actual meaning, there is no difference between sensual thoughts (*kāmavitakka*) and the like on one hand, and sensual intentions and the like on the other; however, the perception and other mental factors associated with them are "sensual perceptions" (*kāmasaññā*) and so forth.

As for the sensual element (*kāmadhātu*) and the others, since it is stated in the Canon: "Thought, applied thought... up to ... wrong intention associated with sensuality—this is called the sensual element.
All unwholesome states are the sensual element. Thought, applied thought... up to ... wrong intention associated with ill will—this..."
It is called the element of ill will (*byāpādadhātu*). The resentment, hostility, and mental dissatisfaction toward the ten bases for resentment—this is called the element of ill will.
Thought, applied thought, and wrong intention associated with cruelty—this is called the element of cruelty (*vihiṃsādhātu*).
Here, someone [acts] with the hand, or with a clod of earth, or with a staff, or with a sword...
"Or when one harms beings with a rope or by some other means, this is the element of cruelty"—since this has been stated, a distinction is obtained.
Therein, there are two explanations: the all-inclusive and the undifferentiated. Therein, when the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*) has been grasped, the others [are included].

Both are indeed included [within the sense-sphere element]. However, having extracted them from there, he shows: "This is the element of ill-will (byāpādadhātu); this is the element of cruelty (vihiṃsādhātu). Thus, this is called the "all-inclusive" [definition].

But when the Blessed One speaks of the sense-sphere element (kāmadhātu), he does so after placing the element of ill-will in the place of the element of ill-will and the element of cruelty in the place of the element of cruelty, [thereby leaving] the remainder as the sense-sphere element.
"He spoke by name" refers to what is called "unmixed discourse.
The meaning should be understood by reversing the sequence stated for the bright side (the wholesome). A thought associated with renunciation is a "thought of renunciation.

That is, in its preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*), it belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) when directed toward the foul (*asubha*); in the foul-jhāna itself, it belongs to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). That jhāna serves as the foundation (*pādaka*).
When it has arisen at the time of the attainment of the supramundane paths and fruits, it is supramundane. Thought associated with non-ill will is "thought of non-ill will.

This is of the sense-sphere level during the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (*mettā*); it is of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) within the loving-kindness jhāna; and when that jhāna is made the basis for the arising of the paths and fruits, it is supramundane.
Thought associated with non-cruelty is "thought of non-cruelty. This...
In its preliminary stage, compassion belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*); in the actual absorption (*jhāna*) of compassion, it belongs to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*);

and at the time when the path and fruit arise by making that absorption the basis, it is supramundane (*lokuttara*). Furthermore, when non-greed (*alobha*) is the primary factor, the other two [factors] follow along with it;
when loving-kindness (*mettā*) is the primary factor, the other two follow along with it; and when compassion (*karuṇā*) is the primary factor, the other two...
Two [factors] follow upon that.

These, moreover, are precisely the intentions of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saṅkappa*) and so forth. For in terms of their actual meaning, there is no difference between the thoughts of renunciation (*nekkhamma-vitakka*) and the intentions of renunciation;

however, the perception and other mental factors associated with them are the perceptions of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saññā*) and so forth. [This applies likewise to] the elements of renunciation (*nekkhamma-dhātu*) and the rest.
However, because it is said in the Pāḷi:
"Thought, applied thought, and intention associated with renunciation—this is called the element of renunciation;
all wholesome states are also the element of renunciation. Thought, applied thought, and intention associated with non-ill will—this is called..."

The element of non-ill will (*abyāpādadhātu*). That which is loving-kindness toward beings, the state of loving-kindness, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness—this is called the element of non-ill will.
Thought, applied thought, and intention associated with non-harming—this is called the element of non-harming.
That which is compassion toward beings, the state of compassion, the liberation of mind through compassion—this is called the element of non-harming.
Because it has been brought forth, a distinction is obtained. Here too, two discourses—the all-inclusive and the undifferentiated—should be understood according to the method already stated.
The rest is easily understood. Regarding the verses: *vitakkaye* means "one should apply thought. *Nirākare* means one should remove from one's own mental continuum, dispel, or abandon;
such is the meaning. *Savē vitakkāni vicāritāni, sameti vuṭṭhīva rajaṃ samūhatam*: just as rain settles dust and sweeps it away...
Just as the dust raised from the earth, stirred up and rising on all sides in the last month of summer,
is immediately settled by the rain falling from a great unseasonable cloud, even so that practitioner of yoga settles,
pacifies, and utterly cuts off his thoughts— both wrong thoughts and the discursive thoughts associated with them.
And being thus, with a mind through which thought has been stilled— because all wrong thoughts have been stilled by means of the noble path-mind characterized by the stilling of thought—
he has attained, right here and in this very life, the state of peace, Nibbāna.
The commentary on the eighth sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Antarāmalasutta 88.
Regarding the ninth [verse], "internal stains" (*antarāmala*):
here, the word *antara*—“On riverbanks, in dwellings, in assembly halls, and on carriage roads;”
In such passages as, “People gather and deliberate: what is the difference between me and them?,” it occurs in the sense of a cause.

In such passages as, “Venerable sir, a certain woman saw me while she was washing a vessel by the light of a flash of lightning,” it occurs in the sense of a moment. In such passages as, “Moreover, this Tapodā flows through the interval between two great hells,” it occurs in the sense of a gap or opening.
“In yellow robes, with yellow banners, adorned with yellow ornaments...”
In such passages as, “You shine indeed, adorned with lovely yellow garments,” it refers to the upper garment (*uttarisaṭaka*).
In such passages as, “He in whom there are no internal corruptions,” it refers to the mind (*citta*). Here too, it should be understood as referring precisely to the mind.
Therefore, *antarā* means that which exists within the mind (*citte*). Because it causes the defilement of the continuum (*santāna*) in which it has arisen, [it is called *antarāya*].
Impurities. In this context, impurity is twofold: bodily impurity and mental impurity.
Of these, bodily impurity consists of sweat, filth, and so forth produced on the body, as well as adventitious dust clinging to it;
this is to be removed by water and is not inherently defiling. Mental impurity, however, consists of the defilements such as lust and the like; this is to be removed only by the Noble Paths.
For this was said by the ancients:
“By form defiled, young men are defiled;
by form purified, they are cleansed— this was not declared by the Great Seer.”
“By a defiled mind, young men are defiled;
by a pure mind they are purified—so it was said by the Great Seer.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, through the defilement of the mind, beings are defiled; through the purification of the mind, they are purified.”
Therefore, showing that one must likewise practice here for the purification of the stains of the mind, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, there are these three internal stains.

Just as these [defilements] such as greed, having arisen in the minds of beings, cause them to become soiled and produce various kinds of corruption—thus being "internal stains"—so too, by eating together and sleeping together, they are like a hostile enemy seeking a vulnerability within the mind.
Having thus arisen, they bring about various kinds of harm to sentient beings and produce manifold forms of suffering;

showing this, he said, "enemies in between," and so forth. In that context: they are "enemies" (*amitta*) because they are the opposite of friends; "rivals" (*sapatta*) because they perform the functions of an adversary;
"killers" (*vadhaka*) because they cause injury; and "opponents" (*paccatthika*) because they act as direct adversaries.
In this regard, the enmity of greed and the other [unwholesome roots] should be understood in two ways.
For when an enemy person finds an opportunity, he either strikes off his enemy’s head with a sword or brings about a great misfortune through some stratagem.
Yet these [defilements], such as greed and the rest, bring about a misfortune even greater than that—comparable to striking off the head—with the thorough destruction of wisdom.
They produce [results]. How so? For when desirable and other such objects have come into the range of the eye-door, greed and the rest arise with respect to them as appropriate;
at this point, it is said that his "wisdom-head" has been struck off. The same method applies to the ear-door and the others.
Thus, first of all, his resemblance to an enemy and so forth should be understood from the striking off of the wisdom-head. As for greed and the rest, however—
Having karma as their cause, they lead one toward the four modes of birth, such as the egg-born and so forth.

Rooted in that approach to the modes of birth, the twenty-five great fears and the thirty-two types of karmic actions come into being. Thus, their resemblance to enemies and the like should be understood even from the perspective of their leading one to these modes of birth.
Therefore, greed and the rest are [likened to enemies] because of their resemblance to enemies and the like, and because they are produced within the mind.
And they are described by such passages as “enemies in between,” and so forth. Furthermore, greed and the other [defilements] perform what enemies cannot do;
moreover, the state of being an enemy and so forth arises from greed and the others—thus their status as enemies and so forth should be understood. For this has been said:
“Whether one goes from place to place, an enemy might do harm to an enemy;”
“A mind wrongly directed makes one worse than that.
In these verses, it is called *anatthajanano* because it produces harm for oneself and others. For this has been said:
“Whatever a greedy person performs by way of body, speech, or mind—that too is unwholesome; whatever a greedy person...”

“Overcome by greed, with a mind possessed by it, one causes suffering to another through falsehood—by means of killing, or binding, or confiscation, or censure, or banishment—thinking, ‘I am powerful; I desire power. That too is unwholesome.
Thus, from greed, with greed as their source, with greed as their origin, with greed as their condition, numerous evil and unwholesome states arise.”
Furthermore, it has been said:

"Brahmin, one who is lustful, overcome by lust, and whose mind is consumed by it, intends for his own affliction, intends for the affliction of others, and intends for the affliction of both; he experiences mental pain and dejection."
"Experiences," and so forth.

"Agitation of the mind" means that which disturbs the mind. For greed, when arising with respect to an object of greed, arises by disturbing, agitating, transforming, and bringing about a distortion of the mind, so that it does not proceed by way of clarity and so on.

He does not give. "The fear born from within—that people do not understand": this great multitude of fools does not perceive, nor does he know, that very fear—characterized by greed—which arises from within, from inside one's own mind, and which is the cause of fear consisting in the production of harm and the agitation of the mind.

"A greedy person does not know the goal" means that a greedy individual does not know, as it truly is, the goal or welfare consisting of the divisions such as one's own benefit and the benefit of others.

"He does not see the Dhamma" means that a greedy person, overcome by greed and with a mind consumed by it, does not see—even the Dhamma of the ten paths of wholesome action—and does not know it through direct experience, much less the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma). And this has also been said:

“O Brahmin, one who is lustful, overcome by passion, and whose mind is consumed by it, does not understand his own welfare as it truly is; he does not understand the welfare of others as it truly is; he does not understand the welfare of both as it truly is,” and so forth.
“Blinding darkness” (*andhatama*) means the darkness that causes blindness. “Where” (*yatra*)—this is the nominative case used in the sense of the locative.
When greed overcomes and masters a person, at that time there is blinding darkness. Alternatively, *ya* is a word expressing the cause.
The construction is: "Because greed, when arising, overcomes and masters a person, therefore at that time it becomes blinding darkness.
This is because the words *ya* and *ta* possess an absolute state of connection. Alternatively, *ya* is a reference to the action;
that which was stated here as "greed overcomes"—namely, this overcoming or mastering by greed—is [the cause] of the darkness that produces blindness.
"Going" means arising. Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as follows: when greed overcomes or masters a person, then for him there is blinding darkness;
consequently, the greedy one does not know the goal (*attha*), and the greedy one does not see the Dhamma.

And "he who, having abandoned greed... refers to one who, in the prior stage, [abandons it] according to the circumstances by way of its specific factor (*tadaṅga*) and by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*).

Having abandoned greed through serenity and insight, one does not become greedy even when divine forms and other such objects that provoke greed appear, because greed is abandoned by the power of strong insight.
Therefore, for noble persons, greed is abandoned and relinquished by the noble path; it is utterly renounced. How so? Like a drop of water.
"Like a drop of water from a lotus leaf"—thus the meaning of the remaining verses should be understood according to this method.
Likewise regarding hatred (*dosa*):
"Whatever one who is hating performs by way of body, speech, or mind, that too is unwholesome; whatever one who is hating..."

"Overcome by hatred, with a mind possessed by it, one inflicts suffering upon another through falsehood—whether by killing, imprisonment, confiscation, censure, or banishment—thinking, 'I am powerful; I seek power. That too is unwholesome.
Thus, from hatred as their source, hatred as their origin, hatred as their arising, and hatred as their condition, many evil and unwholesome states come into being."
Likewise:

"A person who is corrupt, O brahmin, overcome by hatred and with mind consumed by it, intends for his own harm, intends for the harm of others, and intends for the harm of both; he experiences mental pain and dejection."

Likewise, according to the words of such suttas as: “A hater, O Brahmin, overcome by hatred and with mind obsessed by it, does not understand his own welfare as it really is; he does not understand the welfare of others as it really is;
he does not understand the welfare of both as it really is,” one should understand that [hatred] is the producer of harm and the cause for the loss of benefit.
Likewise, regarding delusion (*moha*), it should be understood by following the words of the suttas as they have come down: such as “Whatever one who is deluded performs by way of body,
speech, or mind,” and “Deluded, O Brahmin, overcome by delusion and with his mind possessed by it,
he intends even for his own harm,” and “He does not understand his own welfare as it really is.”

"Like the fruit of the palmyra tree from its stalk": just as the fruit of the palmyra tree is severed from its stalk by the production of heat, so too is defilement abandoned—that is, it is relinquished—from that mind by the arising of the knowledge of the third path.
"He destroys all delusion": that noble person destroys, disperses, and utterly eradicates all delusion without exception by means of the fourth path.
"Like the rising sun, he dispels the darkness. Like the sun rising, he dispels the darkness, the gloom.
The commentary on the ninth sutta is concluded.
10. Commentary on the Devadatta Sutta.
89. Regarding the tenth [case], "overcome by three things contrary to the true Dhamma" (asaddhamma), what is its origin?

When Devadatta had entered the great Avīci hell, those on Devadatta’s side and other sectarians slandered him, saying, "Devadatta has been swallowed up by the earth because he was cursed by the ascetic Gotama.
Hearing this, people who lacked faith in the Teaching thought, "It might be..."
"Is this really as these people say? they thought, giving rise to doubt. The monks reported that matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One said, "Monks, the Tathāgatas do not utter curses against anyone;
therefore, Devadatta was not cursed by me, but entered hell solely through his own karma," and thus he cleared away their misconception.
Prohibiting [such conduct], he spoke this discourse on account of this occasion.
Therein, "by unrighteous states" (*asaddhammehi*) means by the states of the wicked, or by non-existent states.
"Incurable" (*atekiccho*) means incurable because it cannot be turned back even by Buddhas due to the production of rebirth in Avīci; the meaning is "one who is beyond healing."
"Pāpiccho" means one who has evil desires (*pāpiccha*) characterized by the intention to falsely esteem qualities that do not exist;
the state of being such is "pāpicchatā," and it is by means of this. The desire arose in him: "I shall become a Buddha; I shall lead the Saṅgha.
"Pāpamitto" means one who has evil, base friends (*pāpamitta*); the state of being such is "pāpamittatā," and it is by means of this.

"Regarding 'there is still more to be done' (uttarīkaraṇīya)': this means that as long as the path and fruit—those things to be attained which are further to be accomplished through meditation and direct knowledge (jhāna-abhiññā)—have not yet been reached;
that is, without having attained them. 'By a mere trifle' (oramattakena) means by a small amount, such as mere meditation and direct knowledge.

'By the attainment of distinction' (visesādhigamena) means by the attainment of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma). 'In the middle' (antara) means in the interim. 'He falls into complacency' (vosānaṃ āpādi):"
While his task was yet unaccomplished, he imagined, "I have accomplished my task," and thus fell away from the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
Thus, by means of this sutta, the Blessed One specifically revealed the danger in the state of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*);

heavy indeed is the state of an ordinary person, for even after having produced the various attainments culminating in the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), one may still bring about manifold kinds of harm.

One who does not abandon the cause of suffering—namely, the false attribution of qualities one lacks, association with unworthy persons, and devotion to laziness—will produce an evil deed that is incurable and remains for an eon in the Avīci hell.
In the verses, *mā* is a particle used in the sense of prohibition. *Jātu* means "certainly" or "ever. *Koci* is a term that includes all [persons]. *Lokasmiṃ* means "in the world."
"In the world of beings. This is what is meant: "Let there be no person whatsoever in this world of beings who is possessed of evil desires.

By this also, you should know the destiny of those with evil desires—what kind of destination, what kind of outcome, and what kind of future state awaits persons of evil desires; you should know that by this very reason, [regarding] Devadatta.
Showing this, he spoke thus: "Known as wise" means he was known as wise through his great learning in the scriptures (*pariyatti*). "Of developed self" means he was esteemed;
his mind was developed through the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), and thus he was held in high regard.
For indeed, even by the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), he had previously been praised as: "The son of Godhī is of great psychic power, the son of Godhī is of great majesty. Like a flame...
"Renowned by fame": he became well-known and famous as "Devadatta," standing as if blazing and radiating with his own reputation and retinue.
There is also the reading "me suttaṃ," meaning "heard by me"—it was merely heard; because it did not remain so for even a few days, that wisdom and so forth were merely a matter of hearing.
Thus, having practiced in common with him, thinking, "The Tathāgata has been offended by me," Devadatta, being in such a state, [thought]:
"The Buddha is a Sakyan son, and I too am a Sakyan son; the Buddha is an ascetic, and I too am an ascetic; the Buddha possesses supernormal power, and I too possess supernormal power;
the Buddha possesses the divine eye, and I too possess the divine eye; the Buddha possesses the divine ear, and I too possess the divine ear."
“The Buddha has attained the knowledge of others’ minds, and I too have attained the knowledge of others’ minds; the Buddha knows phenomena of the past, future, and present, and I too know them.
Thus, failing to recognize his own measure, he equated himself with the Perfectly Enlightened One by placing himself on an equal footing, saying:
“Now I shall become a Buddha; [I shall lead] the Saṅgha of bhikkhus...”
Thinking, "I shall avoid [this]," he assailed, attacked, and harassed the Tathāgata with the intent to kill.

Some also read "pamādamanujīno," the meaning of which is: "Falling into negligence in the manner described, and by relying on that negligence, he was 'anujīno'—that is, fallen away and deprived—of the jhānas and direct knowledges (abhiññās) simultaneously with the arising of a mind of rivalry toward the Blessed One. He fell into the Avīci hell.

"Having four gates and terrifying": because of the density of the flames arising there for the beings born within it, that great hell—which has received the name "Avīci" (the Uninterrupted)—is "four-gated" due to its connection with four great gates on its four sides;
it is exceedingly terrifying, and [the being] has reached it by way of taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). For thus it is said:
“Four-cornered and four-doored, divided and measured out in sections;
surrounded by an iron wall and closed over with iron.
Its ground is made of iron, blazing and filled with heat.”
"Pervading a hundred yojanas all around, it remains forever.
"Of one who is not ill-disposed" (*aduṭṭhassa*) means of one whose mind is not corrupted. "Corrupts" (*dubbheyya*) means he would defile. "That very evil touches him" (*tameva pāpaṃ phusati*):
that evil person, being corrupt and ill-disposed, is touched by, reaches, and is overcome by evil—that is, by the lowly fruit of evil. "Terrible" (*bhesma*) is said because of its vastness.
"By his profound nature," meaning as if causing terror, [he is] "vast and deep. "By debate" means by fault. "He harms" means he afflicts or assails.
"Debate does not take root in him" means that when a fault is imputed by another against that Tathāgata, it does not take root;
it does not remain, just as a jar of poison [does not affect] the ocean; the meaning is that it does not produce any change in him.

Having thus, by means of these six verses, demonstrated that one possessed of evil desires and so forth is not liberated from suffering by showing their destiny for hell, he now speaks the concluding verse, "Such a friend," demonstrating the destruction of suffering for one who possesses qualities contrary to those.
Its meaning is as follows: for him who has practiced rightly, the follower of the path [sees] the path of practice...
One who has followed [the path] and practiced rightly, being endowed with qualities such as fewness of desires, may reach the destruction and end of all the suffering of saṃsāra.
A wise and discerning person should make such a Buddha or a disciple of the Buddha their friend,
treat them with loving-kindness, associate with them, and attend upon them alone.
Thus, in this chapter, turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) is explained in the sixth and seventh suttas, while in the others, both the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and turning away are explained.
The commentary on the tenth sutta is finished.
The commentary on the fourth chapter is finished.
5. The Fifth Chapter. 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Supreme Confidence (Aggappasādasutta). 90.
Regarding the phrase "supreme confidence" (*aggappasāda*) in the first [discourse] of the fifth chapter: here, this word *agga* refers to the beginning, the peak, a portion, and the best.
It is seen [in these senses]. For instance, it is seen at the beginning in such passages as: “From this day forward, friend gatekeeper, I close the door to the Nigaṇṭhas and Nigaṇṭhīs;
from this day forward, I have gone for refuge for as long as life lasts,” and so on. It is seen at the end in such passages as: “With that very fingertip, one might touch that fingertip;
the tip of a sugar-cane, the tip of a bamboo,” and so on. Or, as in: “The sour tip... [and so forth].

In such passages as, "Whether it be a portion of sweet [food] or a portion of bitter [food], I allow you, monks, to divide it according to the dwelling (vihāra) or according to the courtyard (pariveṇa)," it refers to a *koṭṭhāsa* (portion).
In such passages as, "This one is the foremost, the best, the highest, and the most excellent among these four persons;
I am the foremost in the world," it refers to the *seṭṭha* (best). And here too, it is used precisely in the sense of the *seṭṭha*.

It should be understood thus. Therefore, "confidence in the foremost" (*aggappasāda*) means confidence that is directed toward the foremost or best, or confidence that has become foremost or excellent.
In the first sense, the word "foremost" (*agga*) refers to the Three Jewels, beginning with the Buddha.

Among these, the Blessed One is foremost in the sense of being peerless, in the sense of having distinguished qualities, and in the sense of being unequaled. For he, through his Great Resolve and the ten perfections...

Beginning with analytical investigation (*pavicaya*), he is "foremost" in the sense of being peerless because, through those qualities that are the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra-guṇa*) and the qualities of a Buddha, he is unlike any other person.

Furthermore, his qualities—such as great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and so forth—are superior to the qualities of other beings; thus, he is also foremost by virtue of the excellence of his qualities (*guṇavisiṭṭha-ṭṭhena*), owing to his supremacy among all sentient beings.
Moreover, the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones (*sammāsambuddha*) [were likewise] by all sentient beings...

He is unequal; because he alone is equal to them in both the qualities of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the qualities of the Dhamma-body (*dhammakāya*), he is supreme in the sense of being "unequalled among equals" (*asamasama*).

Likewise, the Blessed One is called the foremost in the world because his manifestation is rare, because he possesses a marvelous human nature, because he brings benefit and happiness to many people, and because he is peerless and without equal. As it has been said:
“Bhikkhus, the appearance of one person is rare in the world. Of which one person? Of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Bhikkhus, when one person appears in the world, he appears as a wonderful man.
Bhikkhus, when one person appears in the world, he appears for the benefit of many people... [as before] ...he appears as a Perfectly Enlightened One.”

“Monks, one person, when arising in the world, arises without a second, without a companion, peerless, matchless, incomparable, without rival, unequaled, the equal of the unequaled, the foremost of bipeds. What is that one person?
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
The Dhamma and the Saṅgha are also pre-eminent in the sense of being incomparable with other Dhammas and Saṅghas, owing to their distinguished qualities and the rarity of their manifestation.

For indeed, by virtue of their specific qualities—such as the well-expounded nature of the former and the state of being well-practiced by the latter—there are no other Dhammas or Saṅghas that are equal to them, let alone inferior; how much less could there be any superior? Moreover, they are pre-eminent precisely because of those distinguished qualities inherent within them.

They are the best (*seṭṭha*). Likewise, they are those whose appearance is rare, who possess a nature of wonder, who bring benefit and happiness to many people, and whose very essence is peerless, without equal, and so forth.
For in the same measure that the Blessed One’s manifestation is rare, in that same measure are the Dhamma and the Saṅgha [rare].

This same principle applies to their state of being wonderful and so forth. Thus, "confidence in the foremost" (*aggappasāda*) refers to confidence in those who are foremost, best, supreme, excellent, and distinguished by their qualities.

In the second sense, however, "supreme confidence" (*aggappasāda*) refers to the confidences that have become supreme by arising toward the "supremes" (*agga*) already mentioned—the Buddha and so forth.
Furthermore, those "confidences based on penetration" (*aveccappasāda*) which are attained through the Noble Path are exclusively supreme confidences;
thus they are called "supreme confidences. As it is said: "Here, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with unshakable confidence in the Buddha," and so forth.
And these are called "supreme confidences" because they have a supreme ripening. For it is said: "For those who have confidence in what is supreme, the ripening is supreme.
*Yāvatā* means "as many as. *Sattā* means "living beings. *Apadā* means "those without feet. *Dvipadā* means "those with two feet. The same method applies to the remaining two phrases.
The word *vā* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), not the sense of option (*vikappa*). Just as in the phrase: "the unarisen taint of sensual desire..."
In the phrase, “the unarisen taint of sensual desire arises, or the arisen taint of sensual desire increases,” the meaning is “both the unarisen and the arisen.

And just as in the phrase, “for the stability of beings who have come to be, or for the assistance of those seeking rebirth,” the meaning is “both of those who have come to be and those seeking rebirth.
And just as in the phrase, “from fire, or from water, or from dissension,” [the meaning is “from either one or the other”].
The meaning is: "from fire, from water, and from the breaking of friendships. Likewise, in the passage "whether footless...
[or] it is declared supreme," the meaning should be understood through the method of compounding as "footless and two-footed. Therefore it was said:
"The word *vā* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), not the sense of option (*vikappa*)."

"Material" (*rūpin*) means possessing form. "Non-material" (*arūpin*) means without form. "Perceiving" (*saññin*) means possessing perception. "Non-perceiving" (*asaññin*) means without perception. Those called "neither-perceiving-nor-non-perceiving" (*nevasaññīnāsaññin*) are included within the peak of existence (*bhavagga*).
And by this much, there are: sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*), immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*);

existence with one base (*ekavokārabhava*), existence with four bases (*catuvokārabhava*), existence with five bases (*pañcavokārabhava*); perceiving existence (*saññībhava*), non-perceiving existence (*asaññībhava*), and neither-perceiving-nor-non-perceiving existence (*nevasaññīnāsaññībhava*).
The Dhamma King has shown, exhausting them without remainder, that beings exist within ninefold existence (*bhava*).

For here, by the mention of "those with form" (*rūpī*), sensual existence (*kāmabhava*), fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*), five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*), and one-aggregate existence (*ekavokārabhava*) are shown; by the mention of "those without form" (*arūpī*), immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*) and four-aggregate existence (*catuvokārabhava*) are shown.
Furthermore, the states of "possessing perception" (*saññībhava*) and so forth are shown according to their own specific nature. By the mention of "the footless" (*apada*) and so forth...
A portion of the sense-sphere existence, the five-aggregate existence, the existence of perception, and the existence of non-perception has been shown here.
But why, in this context, is there a mention of those "without feet" and so forth, rather than simply mentioning "two-footed beings" as in the *Adutiyasutta* ("the foremost of two-footed beings")?
It is said: in the *Adutiyasutta*, the mention of "two-footed beings" was made specifically because they are superior.
It has been said. For when one who is called "the Best" arises in this world, he does not arise among those without feet, four-footed beings, or many-footed creatures;
he arises only among two-footed beings. Among which two-footed beings? Among humans and among devas.
When arising among humans, he arises as a Buddha, capable of bringing the entire world under his influence. (As stated) in the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā*.
However, it is said that he is "capable of exercising authority over a great trichiliocosm.
When arising among the devas, he arises as a Mahābrahmā capable of exercising authority over ten thousand world-systems;
he becomes either his attendant (kappiyakāraka) or his monastery attendant (ārāmika). Thus, by way of being even more excellent than that, he is called "the foremost of bipeds" therein.
[This] was stated [previously]; however, here it is stated in the sense of an exhaustive inclusion.

For as many beings as there are who are comprised within individual existence—whether footless, or [the rest], up to those with neither-perception-nor-non-perception—the Tathāgata is declared to be the foremost among them.

This genitive case is used for selection (*niddhāraṇa*), and the letter *m* serves to facilitate the euphonic junction (*sandhi*) of the words. The analysis of the phrase is: "He is declared to be the foremost" (*aggo akkhāyati*).
"The fruit is supreme" means that for those who have faith in the Supreme Buddha, that faith is supreme, best, highest, or the very pinnacle;
therefore, its fruit as well is supreme, best, highest, the very pinnacle, most exalted, and most refined.
That faith, moreover, is twofold, distinguished as mundane and supramundane. Of these, first, regarding the mundane:
“Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha will not go to a plane of misery;
having cast off the human body, they will fill the host of devas.
In the body of one who extols ‘the Buddha,’ there arises a joy.”
Indeed, that joy alone is better than even the whole of Jambudīpa.
A hundred elephants, a hundred horses, a hundred chariots with mares,
and a hundred thousand maidens adorned with jeweled earrings—
“They are not worth even a sixteenth part of a single step forward.
“It is indeed good, Lord of the Devas, to go for refuge to the Buddha;
it is because of going for refuge to the Buddha, Lord of the Devas, that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, [are reborn] in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.”
They are reborn there. They surpass other devas in ten respects:
in divine lifespan, in divine beauty, in divine happiness, in divine fame, in divine sovereignty, and in divine forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects.”
By means of such sūtra passages as these, the connection of confidence (*pasāda*) with specific fruits should be understood.
Therefore, it should be seen that this [confidence] bestows the ripening of happiness within states of prosperity, together with the turning away from the suffering of the miserable realms (*apāya*).

The supramundane [confidence], however, bestows the ripening of the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) and turns one away from the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). And all this confidence, by way of succession, indeed turns away the suffering of the round of existence. For this has been said:
“Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion a noble disciple recollects his own faith, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor obsessed by hatred, nor obsessed by delusion;
on that occasion his mind is simply straight. In one whose mind is straight, gladness is born.”
“In one who is gladdened, rapture arises... [and so on] ...he understands: ‘there is nothing further beyond this state of being.

Here, “phenomena” (*dhammā*) refers to phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). “Conditioned” (*saṅkhata*) means made by causes coming together and combining; thus, they are conditioned phenomena that possess conditions.

“Unconditioned” (*asaṅkhata*) means not made by any causes or conditions; it is nibbāna, which is devoid of conditions. By virtue of being the opposite of the conditioned, [the unconditioned is established].
“Unconditioned” (*asaṅkhata*) is a plural term. “Dispassion is declared the foremost among them” means that among those conditioned and unconditioned phenomena,

that unconditioned phenomenon termed dispassion is called the foremost, the best, the supreme, and the most excellent precisely because of its inherent state of being subtle and refined, its state of being more peaceful and more sublime, its state of being profound and so forth, and its state of sobering the intoxicated and so on.
The word *yadidam* is a particle; its meaning is "that which. Terms such as *madanimmadano* (the crushing of intoxication) and so forth are all indeed synonyms for Nibbāna.
For, by resorting to it, every form of intoxication—such as the intoxication of pride (*māna*) and the intoxication of manhood (*purisa-mada*)—is crushed and destroyed;

every thirst, such as the thirst for sensual pleasures (*kāma-pipāsā*), is removed; all attachments, such as attachment to sense-pleasures (*kāma-ālaya*), are uprooted; and all the cycles of kamma, defilements, and karmic results (*kamma-vaṭṭa*, *kilesa-vaṭṭa*, *vipāka-vaṭṭa*) are brought to an end.
They are cut off; all craving, in its eight hundred divisions, is exhausted;
all defilements fade away; all suffering ceases. Therefore, it is called "the crushing of intoxication" … [as above] … "cessation.

Furthermore, because this craving binds (*vinati*) one existence to another existence, and because it weaves together (*saṃsibbati*) action with its fruit, it is called "bondage" (*vāna*). That bondage is here—
It does not exist [in the sense of being produced], or rather, it does not arise for a noble person once this has been attained; thus it is *nibbāna*.
Regarding the statement "it is the supreme fruition," here too:
"Whoever has gone for refuge to the Dhamma... and so forth.
“The rapture that arises in the body for one who praises the Dhamma...
and so forth. “It is good, Lord of Devas, to go for refuge to the Dhamma. It is because of going for refuge to the Dhamma, Lord of Devas, that some here... [experience] divine tactile sensations.
Through such passages from the Suttas, the connection between confidence in the Dhamma and the attainment of specific fruits should be understood. Thus it is here.

The state of being supreme is established by way of the unconditioned dhamma alone; however, this same meaning can also be understood by way of the Noble Eightfold Path for the purpose of showing the escape from all conditioned things. For it has been said:
"Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are conditioned phenomena, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared to be their foremost."
“The Eightfold Path is the best of paths,” and so forth.
“Assemblies or groups” refers to all assemblies or groups in the world that are comprised of multitudes of people.

“The Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples” refers to the assembly of the Tathāgata’s disciples, which consists of a multitude of eight noble persons (ariyapuggala) united by their commonality of view and virtue.

"He is declared the foremost among them" means that by virtue of his own distinguished qualities—such as morality (*sīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*paññā*), and liberation (*vimutti*)—he is called the foremost, the best, the highest, and the most excellent among those Saṅghas. "Yadidaṃ" (namely) refers to these. "Four pairs of persons":

by way of being a pair, one who stands at the first path and one who stands at the first fruit constitute one pair; and so on, up to one who stands at the fourth path... [and one who stands at the fourth fruit]. This constitutes the four pairs.
"The one at the stage of the fourth fruit"—this constitutes one pair; thus there are four pairs of persons (*purisayuga*). "Eight individuals" (*puggala*):
by way of individual persons, according to this method, there are eight individuals—one at the stage of the first path and one at the stage of the first fruit, and so on.
And here, the terms "person" (*purisa*) and "individual" (*puggala*) are synonymous; they are used according to the needs of those to be trained (*veneyya*).
Thus it has been said: "This is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples. This refers to those four pairs of persons, or eight individual beings, according to their pairs;
this is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples. Regarding the terms beginning with "worthy of offerings" (*āhuneyya*):
that which is to be brought and offered is an *āhuna*; it is that which should be given to those possessed of virtue even after coming from afar.
*Attha*: This is a designation for the four conditions. Because he makes [offerings] bear great fruit, he is worthy of receiving offerings (*āhuneyya*).
Alternatively, even from afar, one’s entire property may be offered (*hunitabba*) here;
or, because he is worthy of the offering (*āhavana*) even by Sakka and others, he is *āhavanīya*. And this is the one whom the brahmins call the *āhavanīya* fire.
The Aggikas hold the view that "the fire is that in which an offering brings great fruit.

If it is the fire that is the recipient of the offering because of its capacity to yield great fruit, then the Saṅgha alone is the recipient of the offering, for an offering made to the Saṅgha yields great fruit. As it has been said:
"And though a person might tend the fire in the forest for a hundred years..."
“One should honor for even a moment one whose self is developed;
that very act of honoring is better than a hundred years of sacrifice.

In another Nikāya, the word *āhavanīyo* has here the same meaning as the word *āhuneyyo*, though there is a slight difference in their phonetic form (*byañjana*); therefore, the explanation of the meaning was made in this way.

Regarding the term *pāhuneyyo*: here, "guest" (*pāhuṇa*) refers to the hospitality prepared with honor for the sake of dear and agreeable kinsmen and friends who have arrived from all directions and intermediate points;
setting aside even such guests, it is more fitting to give [the gift] to the Saṅgha itself.
For this [Saṅgha] is seen even during the interval between two Buddhas, and it exists without interruption. This is...

Herein, the meaning of the words is as follows: one who is "endowed with qualities that produce what is dear and pleasing" is worthy of being given hospitality (*pāhuṇa*) and worthy of receiving hospitality; thus, he is *pāhuṇeyya*.

However, for those in whose text the reading is *pāhavanīya*, since the Saṅgha deserves priority (*pubbakāra*), the Saṅgha is to be brought here first and offered (*hunitabba*). Thus, it is *pāhavanīya*.
"Pāhavanīyo" means one who is worthy of being offered oblations in every way; thus, in this very sense, he is called "pāhuneyyo.
"Dakkhiṇā" refers to the gift that ought to be given with faith in the next world; he is worthy of that gift (dakkhiṇā), hence [he is called] "dakkiṇeyyo."
He is "one worthy of offerings" (*dakṣiṇeyya*) because he purifies [them] by bringing about the state of great fruitfulness for those who have offered.

He is "one to whom one should pay homage with joined palms" (*añjalikaraṇīya*) because he is worthy of the act of joining palms performed by the entire world, placing both hands upon the head. He is "the unsurpassed field of merit for the world" (*anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassa*), meaning a place incomparable to any other for the growth of merit for the whole world. For just as [it is for] red rice or barley...
Just as a place where rice grows is called a "red-rice field" or a "barley field," so too is the Saṅgha the place for the growth of merit for the world together with its devas.
For it is by depending on the Saṅgha that the various kinds of merit which produce welfare and happiness for the world grow;
therefore, the Saṅgha is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Here too—
“Those who have gone for refuge to the Saṅgha... [as above] ...
‘The Saṅgha,’ as one proclaims it, there arises in the body a rapture... [as above] ...
‘It is good, Lord of Devas, to go for refuge to the Saṅgha; for by reason of going for refuge to the Saṅgha, Lord of Devas... [as above] ... one experiences divine tactile sensations.’”
The excellence of the fruit of confidence in the Saṅgha should be understood by way of the specific fruits of the initial words of the Sutta;

thus its preeminence and its preeminent ripening are to be known. Likewise, its preeminent ripening should be understood by way of the production of such sublime fruits as the attainment of the unsurpassed, the cutting off of the suffering of the round from the seventh existence onwards, and the achievement of unsurpassed happiness.
