"Foremost among those who recite verses" means: among those who have faith in the Three Jewels as supreme, or because they possess a state of supremacy.

"The supreme Dhamma" refers to those who understand the supreme nature—the perfectly enlightened state of the Buddha, the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma, and the excellent practice of the Saṅgha—which is the unsurpassed, unique essence of the Three Jewels not shared by others;
or it refers to those who understand the essential qualities such as the ten powers of the Buddha, his well-expounded teaching, and the excellent practice of the Saṅgha.

"For those who understand. Having thus shown the objects of confidence in the supreme [Dhamma] in a general sense, he now says "In the supreme Buddha," and so forth, in order to show them specifically and by way of classification.
Therein, "of those who have confidence" means of those who are confident through verified confidence (*aveccappasāda*) and other forms of confidence, and who are resolutely intent (*adhimutta*).
"In fading away and peace" means in fading away (*virāga*) and in peace (*upasama*), of everything...
The meaning is: "in that which is the cause of absolute detachment from passion and all defilements, and the cause of absolute peace.
"In bliss" means in that which is bliss by virtue of being the destruction of the suffering of saṃsāra and by virtue of being the bliss of the subsiding of conditioned formations (*saṅkhārūpasama*).
"Giving gifts to the foremost" means among those giving gifts—that is, relinquishing the objects of charity—to the foremost, the Three Jewels.
In this context, those who serve, honor, and revere the Blessed One while he is still living with the four requisites, and those who, after the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna, serve, honor,
and revere the relic-shrines and so forth dedicated to the Blessed One, are said to give a gift to the Buddha. Likewise, those who,
thinking "We shall honor the Dhamma," serve persons who uphold the Dhamma with the four requisites...
Those who worship, honor, and ensure the long endurance of the Dhamma give a gift to the Dhamma.

Likewise, those who serve and worship the Noble Saṅgha with the four requisites, and who act in the same manner toward others for its sake, give a gift to the Saṅgha. Thus, supreme merit increases through these three Jewels.
For those who, with a serene mind, practice sublime relinquishment and perform sublime offerings and honors, the highest and most sublime merit is accumulated day by day.
Now, in order to show the preeminence of that merit through its supreme ripening, it is said:
"The highest life," and so forth. Therein, "the highest life" means either divine or human life that is supreme and most exalted.
Longevity (*āyu*): it increases, meaning it grows further and further. Beauty (*vaṇṇa*): perfection of form. Fame (*yasa*): perfection of retinue.
Renown (*kittī*): the sound of praise. Happiness (*sukha*): bodily and mental happiness. Strength (*bala*): physical strength and the strength of wisdom.
"A giver of the foremost" (*aggassa dātā*): a giver of the foremost Triple Gem; or alternatively, a giver of the foremost gift (*deyyadhamma*).
Having performed great merit there and set it in motion, he is "composed in the supreme Dhamma" (*aggadhammasamāhita*);
that is, he is composed and endowed with the supreme quality of serene confidence (*pasāda*) and the qualities of giving and so forth, possessed of unshakable faith;

or rather, he is endowed with those qualities such as being dear and pleasing to many people, which are the results of that [merit]. He "rejoices having reached the summit" (*aggappatto pamodati*) in whichever realm among the classes of beings...
Having arisen, having attained the state of being foremost and the state of excellence in various instances, or having attained the state of being foremost— the supramundane path and fruit—
one rejoices, delights, and is thoroughly satisfied.
The commentary on the first sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Jīvikasutta 91.
The second [sutta] was taught by way of an introductory occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
For at one time, while the Blessed One was dwelling at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park, the monks were assigning lodgings to visiting monks and [distributing] their bowls and robes.
The novices receiving [the requisites] and those distributing the gains at the place of distribution became loud and noisy as they took their shares.
Hearing this, the Blessed One dismissed the monks. It is said that they were all newly ordained and had only recently entered this Dhamma and Vinaya.
Knowing this, Mahābrahmā approached and said, "May you rejoice, O Bhante!"
The Blessed One requested the favor of readmitting those monks who had been sent away, saying, "Bhikkhu-saṅgha.
The Blessed One granted him leave. Then Mahābrahmā, thinking, "I have received permission from the Blessed One," paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
Then the Blessed One said to the Elder Ānanda, "Let the Bhikkhu-saṅgha come."

He showed his form. Then those bhikkhus, summoned by the Elder Ānanda, approached the Blessed One and sat down to one side with an appearance of timidity. The Blessed One, seeking a suitable teaching for them, reflected:
"These men have been sent away because of material gain; a discourse on the Dhamma using the simile of the alms-gathering is appropriate for them. Having thought this, he said: "This is the end..."
“Monks,” he said, and gave this teaching.

In this context, the word *anta* (end) occurs in the sense of a "portion" in such passages as: “There are, monks, some recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the past and hold views concerning the past.
It occurs in the sense of a "limit" or "delimitation" in such passages as: “He has made an end of suffering; finite is this world, encompassed by death.”
In such passages as “the edge of the green,” “the edge of the road,” or “the edge of the rock,” it refers to a boundary. In “the end and the inner gut,” it refers to a part of the body.
In “they move about in the world, concealed by their retinue, impure within but shining without,” it refers to the mind.
[And in: “Some lotuses, or lilies, or white lotuses, born in the water, grown in the water...”
In such passages as “not emerged from the water, submerged within, nourishing [the roots],” it means “inside.
Regarding the verse: “The leopard is the chief among beasts, but the crow among birds;
the castor-oil plant is the chief among trees—the three chiefs have come together.”—it means “in the midst.”
In these [contexts], "low" means base. Here too, it should be understood as base.
Therefore, "this, monks, is the end of livelihoods" means: monks, this is the end, the last, the base, the most inferior of all livelihoods;
that is to say, the life of one who maintains his existence by seeking alms through the practice of wandering for food.
The meaning of the words here is as follows: one who goes about for alms (*piṇḍa*) is a *piṇḍola*; his occupation is *piṇḍolya*, which means a livelihood by the seeking of alms.

*Abhisāpa* is an insult. For when people are angry, they insult their adversary, saying, "May you go about seeking alms, wearing a piece of rags and with a bowl in hand. Or else: "What is there that you have not done?"
"Is it true that you, though endowed with such strength and energy, having abandoned shame and fear of blame, wander about as a miserable beggar with bowl in hand?"—thus they revile him.
And yet, even while being thus cursed, he remains a beggar. "Noble sons approach for the sake of the goal":
in my teaching, both those noble sons by birth and those noble sons by conduct [approach].
And being motivated by purpose and motivated by reason, they approach and go forth depending on the influence of that reason.

Regarding the terms "led away by the king" and so forth: those who, having consumed what belonged to the king, were imprisoned by the king in a prison and then escape and go forth, are called "led away by the king" because they were led away by the king's imprisonment. However, those who [are captured] by thieves in the wilderness...
Having been seized, while some were being executed, others—being released by them with the words, "Master, we have been dismissed by you;

without returning home, we shall go forth into homelessness. Whatever merit we perform there, such as worship of the Buddha and so forth, from that we shall give you a share"—go forth, having been thus released.
These are called "those led away by thieves," meaning they are subject to execution by the thieves.
Because they have been led away. However, those who, having taken a loan and being unable to repay it, go into hiding and then go forth, are called "those driven by debt.
Now, this state of mendicancy in my teaching is not something that sons of good family enter because they are led away by kings...
[or] because they have made a living... but rather, the connection of the words is: "We have descended into birth... [and so on]... may we be known," thus they enter.

In that context, "we have descended" means we have entered [into existence]. Regarding "birth" and so forth: birth (*jāti*) is the initial manifestation of the aggregates within this or that class of beings;
aging (*jarā*) is their maturation; death (*maraṇa*) is their dissolution.

Sorrow (*soka*) is the internal burning and brooding of one who is afflicted by calamities concerning relatives, illness, wealth, virtue, or views. Lamentation (*parideva*) is the verbal outburst of one who is afflicted by those same things. [The phrase] "of one whose body is struck by an undesirable touch... refers to the body being impinged upon by an unpleasant tangible object.
Physical affliction is suffering (*dukkha*); mental affliction is grief (*domanassa*), which occurs when the mind is impaired by grounds for resentment.
Despair (*upāyāsa*) is an intense exhaustion arising from mental anguish in one who, having been struck by the loss of relatives and so forth, is unable even to endure it through lamentation.
Those who have descended into these [states] beginning with birth are "descended into suffering" (*dukkhotiṇṇā*); they have entered within those sufferings beginning with birth.

"Afflicted by suffering" means overcome by those bases of the suffering of suffering. For birth and the rest are "suffering" because they serve as the basis for suffering, while sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are "suffering" because they are themselves states of suffering. "Perhaps...
may it become manifest": this refers to the delimitation and the bringing to an end of this entire mass of the suffering of the round of existence; may that indeed become manifest.

"And he is covetous" is said to show that noble son who, having previously generated the thought, "I shall bring an end to suffering," went forth into homelessness, but later was unable to make his renunciation conform to that ideal.
In this context, "covetous" (*abhijjhālu*) means one who covets the goods of others; "one of intense passion" (*tibbasārāga*) means one whose lust is powerful.
"Malicious-minded" (*byāpannacitta*) means one whose mind has become corrupted (*vipannacitta*) due to being putrid with ill-will (*byāpāda*).
"With corrupt mental intention" (*paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappa*) means one whose mind is defiled through the intent to harm others, like a fierce bull with sharp horns.

"Muddle-minded" (*muṭṭhassati*) means one who has lost mindfulness, like a crow that has dropped its food or a dog that has dropped its meat; he does not remember what was done here or there. "Unaware" (*asampajāno*)...
"Devoid of wisdom" means lacking the discernment of the aggregates and so forth. "Unconcentrated" means being unsettled, like a boat tied in a violent current.
"With a wandering mind" means having a distracted mind, like a deer that has strayed onto a path.
"With unguarded senses" means that, just as householders—due to a lack of restraint—look upon their possessions and family members with unrestrained senses, so too does he have unrestrained senses.
*Chavālātaṃ*: a firebrand at the place where corpses have been burned. *Ubhatopadittaṃ majjhe gūthagataṃ*:
eight finger-breadths in length, burning at both ends—that is, at both tips—and smeared with excrement in the middle. *Neva gāme*:
for if it were possible to bring it into a village for the purpose of making a yoke, a plough, a roof-rafter, a crossbeam, or similar items, it would serve as firewood in the village.
One might spread it out. If it were possible to bring [the fire] to a field hut for the sake of a wooden bed, a mat, and so forth, one might spread it out in the forest for the sake of wood.
But since it is not possible for either purpose, therefore this was said. "Tathūpamāhaṃ" means:
I say that this person mentioned above is similar to that, like a brand from a charnel ground. "Gihibhogā" (householder-enjoyments).
"And he has fallen away" means that when the inheritance was being divided among householders living at home, he fell away from whatever wealth might have been obtainable from that source.

"And the goal of recluseship" means that by remaining in the instruction of his teachers and preceptors, he does not fulfill the goal of recluseship to be attained through mastery of the scriptures and penetration [of their meaning].
However, the Teacher did not give this simile with reference to one who is immoral.
It should be understood that this was stated with reference to a person who, though pure in virtue, is indolent and whose mind is defiled by faults such as covetousness.

In the verses, "householder's enjoyments" refers to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures. "Fallen away" means defeated. "The goal of recluseship" refers both to the analytical knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-bāhusacca*) and...
And there is erudition in the scriptures (*pariyatti-bāhusacca*). For one such as that, being lazy, is unable to hear what has not been heard or to purify what has been heard.
"Dubbhago" means unfortunate; it refers to an unlucky person with ill-omened characteristics (*kāḷakaṇṇi-purisa*).
"Paridhaṃsamāno" means perishing. "Pakireti" means to scatter, to destroy. All of this results in the non-arising of the goal of recluseship (*sāmañña-attha*) for one who possesses [such qualities].

This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya vuttaṃ*). "Like a brand from a funeral pyre, he perishes" means that such a person, like the aforementioned brand from a funeral pyre, perishes because he is of no use to anyone, having fallen away from both [virtue and wisdom].
Thus, even one who does not transgress through body or speech perishes if he does not purify his mind, let alone one who is immoral and has transgressed. Regarding him:

Having shown the danger in those of immoral conduct by demonstrating how they share in the suffering of the states of misery (apāya), and desiring to separate living beings from that state, he spoke these two verses beginning with "Those with saffron robes around their necks. Their meaning has already been explained above.
The commentary on the second sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Saṅghāṭikaṇṇa Sutta 92.
Regarding the third [sutta], "at the corner of the outer robe" (*saṅghāṭikaṇṇe*) means at the edge of the robe. "Having taken hold of" (*gahetvā*) means having grasped.
"He would follow along" (*anubandho assa*) means he would go after him. This is what is meant: "Bhikkhus, here a certain bhikkhu, with his own hand..."
"May he follow me as if touching the hem of the great robe of the Sugata that I am wearing;

thus may he dwell even closer to me. "Placing foot upon foot" means: as I walk, placing his own foot immediately after lifting his foot at the very spot where my foot has been placed. By both [expressions],...
This shows: "Even if he were to dwell always right near me, never leaving my side while standing, walking, and so forth, [he would still be far from me].
"He is far from me, and I am far from him"—this means that because that bhikkhu does not fulfill the practice prescribed by me, he remains far from me, and I remain far from him.
By this, it is shown that seeing the Tathāgata with the fleshly eye and the presence of the form-body (rūpakāya) [are insufficient].

This shows that there is no other cause, but rather that seeing with the eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*) and the actual convergence with the Dhamma-body (*dhammakāya*) alone are the criteria. Therefore he said:
"Monks, that monk does not see the Dhamma; not seeing the Dhamma, he does not see me.
In this context, "Dhamma" refers to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (*lokuttara-dhamma*). And that [Dhamma] cannot be seen by one whose mind is defiled by covetousness and the like.
It is possible to see [the Buddha]; therefore, because of not seeing the Dhamma, one does not see the Dhamma-body. For it has been said:
“What is the use to you, Vakkali, of seeing this putrid body? He who sees the Dhamma, Vakkali, sees me;
he who sees me sees the Dhamma. And also: “Become the Dhamma, become the Brahma.”
“Known as the ‘Dhamma-body,’ and also known as the ‘Brahma-body,’” and so forth.

“A hundred leagues” means in a location measuring a hundred leagues; the meaning is “to the height of a hundred leagues. The remainder should be understood by reversing what has been stated. Furthermore, his state of being free from covetousness and so on should be seen as resulting from the attainment of the Noble Path.
In the verses, “one of great desire” (*mahiccha*) refers to one who has intense lust for sense pleasures. “One who is distressed” (*vighātavat*) refers to one whose mental intentions are corrupted.
He is one who suffers frustration toward beings through resentment, through great desire, and through not obtaining what is desired.
He is "one who follows after agitation" (ejānuga), meaning he follows after craving, as if being its slave. He is "unquenched" due to being overwhelmed by the fever of defilements such as lust.
He is "greedy" through his longing for sense objects such as forms. Behold how far [he is] from the unagitated and the quenched!

The meaning is this: although he is near to the Perfectly Enlightened One who is free from greed—being in his very presence—yet the foolish worldling, full of great desire, afflicted, following the stream of craving, unquenched, and greedy, is as far removed from the true nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva) as it is possible for anyone to be;
see how difficult it is even to describe that distance between them. For this has been said:
“The sky is far, and the earth is far;
likewise, they say the further shore of the ocean is far.
But they say that even further than those is—”
"And the Dhamma of the virtuous, and the king of the wicked.

Regarding "having directly known the Dhamma": having directly known—that is, understood—the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths by means of the full understandings of knowing, scrutinizing, and fully comprehending, as appropriate, through knowledge in the prior stage.
Regarding "having understood the Dhamma": having understood that very same Dhamma in the subsequent stage by means of path-knowledge through the process of full comprehension and so forth.
"Having known according to the proper measure. "Wise" means wise through the abundance of penetration (*paṭivedha*).
"Like a lake in a windless place": just as a lake in a windless location is unagitated and free from the movement of defilements (*kilesa*), he becomes tranquil;
just as that lake, being unassailed by wind in a windless place, remains perfectly still, so too this person has all defilements completely subsided.
Being devoid of the agitation caused by defilements, it is pacified through the concentration of the fruit of arahantship;

its very nature is one of perpetual peace. "Unshakable" (anejo): such an arahant, whose nature is thus unshakable and so forth, although far removed from the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—who possesses that same unshakable nature—in terms of physical location, is nevertheless near and close to him in terms of the nature of the Dhamma.
The commentary on the Third Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Fire Sutta (Agni-sutta) 93.
In the fourth [sutta], fire is so called in the sense of burning; passion itself is the fire, thus "passion-fire" (rāgaggi). For when passion arises, it burns sentient beings.
It burns and consumes; therefore it is called "fire. The same principle applies to the other two as well.

In this regard, just as fire, depending upon whatever fuel it arises from, consumes that very fuel and becomes a great conflagration, so too these [fires] of lust and the rest, having arisen within whichever continuum (santāna), consume that very continuum and become great conflagrations difficult to extinguish.
Among those beings whose hearts are scorched by the fever of lust and who have met death through the suffering of not obtaining what they desire, there is no measure.
This, first of all, is the non-consumption [destruction] of lust. As for the non-consumption of hatred, the Manopadosika devas are specifically the illustration;
as for the non-consumption of delusion, the Khiddāpadosika devas are the illustration. By way of delusion—
For they indeed experience forgetfulness of mindfulness; therefore, by indulging in play, they pass away having transgressed the time for food.

This, first of all, is the state of burning in this very life caused by lust and the other defilements. But in the future life, it is even more terrible and difficult to endure, as it causes rebirth in the hells and other realms of misery.
And this meaning should be clarified by means of the "Discourse on the Burning."

In the verses, "infatuated with sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu mucchite*) means having fallen into infatuation, folly, negligence, and misconduct (*micchācāra*) by way of craving for sense-objects (*vatthukāma*).
"Malicious" (*byāpanne*) is connected with the phrase "he burns," referring to one whose mind is corrupted. "A man who takes life" (*nare pāṇātipātino*) refers to one who possesses hatred.
"Unskilled in the noble Dhamma" (*ariyadhamme akovide*) refers to those who are entirely devoid of learning, inquiry, and mental attention regarding the aggregates, sense-bases, and so forth.
Those who are unskilled in the noble Dhamma, being overcome by delusion, are said to be "especially deluded.

"Not knowing these fires" means not understanding that "these fires of lust and so forth burn here and in the life to come," and thus failing to penetrate them through the realization of full comprehension (*pariññā-abhisamaya*) and the realization of abandonment (*pahāna-abhisamaya*).
"Delighting in self-identity" (*sakkāyābhiratā*) refers to delighting in self-identity, which is the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*).
Delighting in craving, views, conceit, and joy; "increasing" means they increase and accumulate through repeated arising.
"Hell" refers to all hell, including the eightfold great hells and the sixteenfold neighboring hells (*ussada-niraya*).

"And the wombs of animals" refers to the animal realm (*tiracchānayoni*). "Asuras" refers to the host of asuras and the sphere of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*); the connection is that they increase these.

Having thus far shown the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) by way of demonstrating how the fires of passion and the rest burn both in this world and in the life to come, the passage beginning with "And those who, day and night...
is now spoken in order to show the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭa*) through the extinguishing of those very fires.

Therein, "engaged" means engaged by way of devotion to the practice of meditation (*bhāvanānuyoga*). Where? In the teaching of the Fully Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*). By that [statement], it is excluded from other teachings.
This demonstrates the absence of extinguishing the fires of lust and the other defilements.
For, showing in brief the meditation subject on the foul (*asubha-kammaṭṭhāna*), which is the unique method for extinguishing them, [the Buddha said]:
“They extinguish the fire of lust, always perceiving the foul;”
"But the supreme among men extinguish the fire of lust with loving-kindness,
and the fire of delusion with wisdom— that wisdom which leads to penetration," he said.
In this context, "perceiving the foul" refers to the practice of the meditation on foulness by way of the thirty-two aspects and by way of the bloated corpse and so forth.
“Perceiving the foul”: this refers to the development of loving-kindness (*mettā*) as described in the passage, “He dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness.

In this context, it should be understood that by taking the jhāna on the foul as a basis, the fires of the defilements of lust and hatred are extinguished through the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*) that has been produced.
“By wisdom” (*paññā*): this refers to the wisdom of the path accompanied by the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā*).
For this very reason it says: “That which leads to penetration. For it is called “leading to penetration” because it proceeds and functions by piercing through the aggregate of defilements.

“They attain final Nibbāna without remainder” means that, having extinguished the fire of lust and the other fires without remainder by means of the path of Arahantship, they abide in the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining;
being prudent through the attainment of the fullness of wisdom, they [act] even before...
Because of the complete abandonment of laziness through right effort, because of the state of being untiring due to the attainment of the fruition-attainments,
and because of the cessation of the final consciousness through being unwearied day and night, they attain final Nirvana in the element of Nirvana without residue.
And from that, they have completely and utterly transcended and passed beyond the suffering of the round of existence.
Having thus shown the extinction (*nibbuti*) through the *nibbāna* without remainder for those who extinguish the fire of passion and the other fires,
he now spoke the concluding verse in praise of them by way of the qualities they have realized. In that context, "those who see the Noble" (*ariyaddasa*) refers to those who have seen the Noble—
either *nibbāna*, which is called "Noble" because it is to be seen by the Noble Ones such as the Buddhas, or because it is far removed from defilements— or indeed the Noble Truths themselves.

"Ariyaddasā" means those who see with noble vision. Or, they are "vedaguṇo" because they have gone to the end of *veda*—that is, the knowledge of the Path—or because through that *veda* they have reached the end of *saṃsāra*.

"Sammadaññāya" means having thoroughly and correctly understood everything that is to be known, such as the wholesome factors and so forth, as well as the aggregates and so forth. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the fourth sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Upaparikkha Sutta 94.
In the fifth [sutta], "in such and such a way" (*tathā tathā*) means by this or that manner. "One should examine" (*upaparikkheyya*) means one should investigate, weigh, or thoroughly consider.
"In whatever way he examines it" (*yathā yathāssa upaparikkhato*) means in whatever way that bhikkhu, while examining it, [examines].

"And his consciousness is undistracted and not scattered externally": because there is an absence of distraction arising toward external objects such as forms, it is "undistracted" (*avikkhitta*), that is, concentrated; for that very reason, it may be "not scattered" (*avisaṭa*). This is what is meant:
"Monks, in whatever manner this monk who has begun insight, while examining and comprehending formations..."

For one who has grasped the sign of serenity by means of observing the mode of previous concentration and who applies the knowledge of comprehension (sammasanañāṇa) carefully and continuously, their own insight-consciousness (vipassanācitta) should not arise upon external objects such as forms and so forth apart from the meditation subject;
nor, due to excessive energy, should it fall into the side of restlessness (uddhacca). In those various ways...

"A bhikkhu should examine and weigh it": "not stuck internally" means that when energy is sluggish, because of the strength of concentration, one becomes "stuck"—so called because of being constricted within the internal object of meditation (the *kammatthāna*), which is reckoned as the internal range—due to being overcome by indolence; however, through the balancing of energy...

When it is applied, consciousness becomes non-fixed and enters its proper course. Therefore, one should examine it in such a way that, as one examines it, consciousness does not become fixed internally but remains on its course.
"Without clinging, one should not tremble" means that as one examines it, one should not, by way of grasping through craving and views, think: "This is mine; this is my self."

The connection is as follows: without grasping at any formation among form and the rest, one should not be anxious on account of that very thing through the seizing of craving and views, but should instead investigate it in such and such a manner.

But how does this threefold [balance] come about for one who investigates? By avoiding states conducive to agitation and states conducive to indolence, and by applying evenness of energy, [one should do so] as previously [stated].
Having purified the mind of the defilements of insight, he comprehends in such a way that the knowledge of insight properly enters the path of insight.
Thus, for the bhikkhu whose meditation subject is the four noble truths, the Blessed One [taught] the purification by knowledge and vision of the way in due succession.
Having shown the means for purifying the mind from the defilements of insight— namely, over-exerted energy and overly lax energy—
once insight-knowledge has been thus purified, he now says, "Bhikkhus,
when consciousness is directed externally," etc., showing that before long, by joining insight with the path, it leads to the complete transcendence of the suffering of the round of existence.
That is exactly as previously stated. As for what was said—"there is no further arising of the origin of suffering consisting in birth, aging, and death"—its meaning is this:

when, by joining insight with the path, the defilements have been entirely exhausted by the supreme path according to the sequence of the paths, then in the future, that which is reckoned as the origin of the entire round of suffering consisting of birth, aging, and death, will not arise again.

There is no origination (*sambhava*) or arising (*uppāda*); that is, there is neither the origin of suffering consisting in birth (*jāti*), nor the origination of suffering consisting in aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

In the verse, "of one who has abandoned the seven attachments" (*sattasaṅgappahīnassa*) means: because of the abandoning of these seven attachments—attachment to craving (*taṇhāsaṅga*), attachment to views (*diṭṭhisaṅga*), attachment to conceit (*mānasaṅga*), attachment to anger (*kodhasaṅga*), attachment to ignorance (*avijjāsaṅga*), attachment to defilements (*kilesasaṅga*), and attachment to misconduct (*duccaritasaṅga*)—one is "one who has abandoned the seven attachments."
Some, however, say: "The seven fetters are themselves the seven underlying tendencies.
"Of one whose tether of existence is cut" means one for whom the tether of becoming has been severed.

"The wandering in birth is exhausted": because it proceeds by way of repeated rebirth and because it is caused by birth, the wandering itself is "born," thus it is the "wandering in birth" (*jātisaṃsāra*). That [wandering] is exhausted and utterly consumed because the tether of becoming has been cut; for that very reason, there is no further becoming for him.
The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Kāmūpapatti Sutta (Sutta 95):
"Rebirths in sensual pleasures" (*kāmūpapattiyo*) refers either to the acquisition of sensual pleasures or the indulgence in sensual pleasures. "Present sensual pleasures" (*paccupaṭṭhitakāmā*)...
They have fixed desires and fixed objects of attachment, just like human beings. For humans exercise control over a fixed object;
wherever their minds are bound, they will even pay a hundred or a thousand [coins] to bring back that very woman and enjoy her wealth as their own exclusive possession.
And so it is with some of the gods. Indeed, from the realm of the Four Great Kings upward, those who dwell in the four divine worlds [behave in this way].
They remain subject to their power only within a fixed domain; the case of Pañcasikha serves as an illustration here.
Likewise, with the exception of certain beings destined for the states of misery or hell, all other beings in the woeful states likewise remain subject to their power only within a fixed domain.
For fish are subject to their own female fish, and the tortoise to his mate; thus it is for all animals, ghosts, and those fallen into the lower realms.
Therefore, with the exception of those in hell, all beings from the remaining woeful states up to the Tusita realm are called "those for whom sensual pleasures are present.
As for the "Nimmānaratīs," they are so called because they find delight (*rati*) in the creations (*nimmāna*) they themselves have fashioned.
For they create whatever form they desire—whether blue, yellow, or otherwise—and take their pleasure in it, as was the case with the Venerable Anuruddha.

Like deities belonging to the realm of Mind-pleasing Bodies (*manāpakāyika*) before one. Regarding the *Paranimmitavasavattino*: they are called *Paranimmitavasavattino* because they exercise mastery (*vasaṃ vattenti*) over sensual pleasures created by others (*paranimmite kāme*).

For, having known their intention, others create objects of sensual enjoyment according to their desire, and they exercise mastery therein. How do they know the mind of another? By means of habitual association (*pakatisevanā*).
Just as a skilled cook knows whatever pleases a king while he is eating, so too, having known the object naturally desired by them, they create similar forms;
they exercise mastery over those forms and enjoy sensual pleasures through such means as sexual intercourse.
Some, however, [maintain that it occurs] by mere laughter, mere gazing, mere embracing, or mere taking of the hand.
And they say that their sensual purpose is accomplished; however, this is rejected in the Commentary with the words, "But this is not so.
For one who does not touch a tangible object with the body does not accomplish a sensual purpose.
The sensual pleasures of all six classes of sense-sphere deities are indeed ordinary. For this has been said:
“Of these six classes of beings belonging to the sense-sphere,
who have all their desires fulfilled— how much is the lifespan reckoned for them all as one?
In the verses, the phrase “and others” refers to those other than the aforementioned devas, namely human beings who enjoy sensual pleasures and certain inhabitants of the woeful states.
"And all those" refers to them all. "This state and another state" means they do not transcend, that is, do not go beyond, the two-fold cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*):
namely, this very state of being as it has been obtained, and the state of being otherwise, which is designated as a different birth-existence (*upapattibhava*).

"One should renounce all sensual pleasures" means one should abandon all sensual pleasures—whether divine or otherwise—including both objective objects (*vatthukāma*) and defilements (*kilesakāma*). Regarding defilement-sensual-pleasures...
For it is precisely while abandoning [defilements] by means of the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga) that one is said to renounce the sensual objects of the basis (vatthukāma).
"Attached to what is dear and pleasant" (piyarūpasātagadhitaṃ) means being gripped or greedy through the relishing of pleasant feeling toward agreeable forms and so forth.

"Having cut the stream that is hard to cross" (chetvā sotaṃ duraccayaṃ) means having utterly severed with the path of Arahantship the stream of craving (taṇhāsota), which is difficult for others to cross or transcend. The remainder is exactly as explained in the method below.
The commentary on the sixth sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Kāmayoga Sutta: 96.

In the seventh [sutta], "bound by the bond of sensual desire" (*kāmayogayutta*): the bond of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*) is lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure; one who is bound by that is "bound by the bond of sensual desire."
This is a designation for one whose sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) has not been severed. "Bondage to existence" (*bhavayoga*) refers to desire and lust for the realms of form and formlessness;

likewise, it includes attachment to meditative absorption (*jhānanikanti*) and lust accompanied by the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). One who is joined with these is "joined to the bondage of existence" (*bhavayogayutta*); the meaning is that one whose lust for existence has not been abandoned.
"One who returns" (*āgāmī*) means that even while staying in the Brahma-world, one is of a nature to come back to this human world by way of taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
For this very reason, it is said: "One who comes to this state. The meaning is: one whose nature is to come to this state, which is defined as the human existence;
one whose habit is to be reborn among humans. Granted that, in this context, the bond of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*) is the cause for coming to this state;
however, in order to show that whoever is bound by the bond of sensual desire is necessarily also bound by the bond of existence (*bhavayoga*), [it says]: "Bound by the bond of sensual desire..."
"O monks, one who is bound by the yoke of existence"—this is stated having combined both [phrases] together.
Regarding the phrase "dissociated from the yoke of sensual desire": here, even the jhāna on the foul (asubha) is dissociation from the yoke of sensual desire;

the path of non-returning attained by taking that as its basis is called dissociation from the yoke of sensual desire in an absolute sense. Therefore, the noble person established in the fruit of the third path...

"He is called ‘dissociated from the bond of sensual desire’ (kāmayoga-visaṃyutta). However, because the desire and lust for existence in the realms of form and formlessness is not abandoned by the path of the non-returner (anāgāmimagga), he is called ‘bound by the bond of existence’ (bhavayoga-yutta) due to that bond of existence not having been abandoned.

He is a ‘non-returner’ (anāgāmī) because he does not return to the sense-sphere world (kāmaloka) by way of taking rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). Indeed, it is precisely through the dissociation from the bond of sensual desire that—along with—"
Because the absence of internal fetters is established through the total eradication of the lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*), one does not return to this state of existence;

such a person attains final nibbāna there and is subject to non-returning. Furthermore, for one who has abandoned the bond of existence (*bhava-yoga*) without remainder, the remaining defilements—such as the bond of ignorance (*avijjā-yoga*) and so forth—are also necessarily abandoned, because they are associated with that same [bond].
Thus, with the fetters of existence completely destroyed, he is called an "Arahant, one whose taints are exhausted. Therefore it was said:
"Monks, one who is detached from the bond of sensual desire and detached from the bond of existence is an Arahant, one whose taints are exhausted.
And herein, detachment from the bond of sensual desire is like the non-returner’s abandonment of pleasure, pain, joy, and grief through the fourth jhāna, [and] like the third path’s...

It should be understood that this was stated for the purpose of praising the fourth path, just as [the destruction of] the fetters of views, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances [is praised for the third path].
By the first phrase, all worldlings (puthujjana) together with stream-enterers and once-returners are included;
by the second phrase, all non-returners; and by the third phrase, the arahant. Thus he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of arahantship.
In the verses, "both" means bound by both—the bond of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*) and the bond of existence (*bhavayoga*).

"Beings go to *saṃsāra*" means that these three kinds of beings—ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*), stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), and once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*)—go to *saṃsāra* because they have not abandoned the bonds of sensual desire and existence. For that very reason, they are subject to birth and death. Herein, the "single-seeded" (*ekabījī*)...
Regarding the three types of stream-enterers—*kolaṅkolo*, *kolamkolo*, and *sattakkhattuparamo*—the most feeble of all is the one who "has seven births at most" (*sattakkhattuparamo*).
He does not produce an eighth existence; rather, he transmigrates according to his own limited number of births, and the others are likewise.
Among the once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*), there is also one who, having attained the path of the once-returner here, is reborn in the deva-world and then returns again here.

He is reborn and wanders in saṃsāra solely by way of his own delimited birth. However, those once-returners who—by way of the mixed method—are reborn exclusively among gods or exclusively among humans, they indeed continue to wander because they arise again and again until the ripening of their faculties for the attainment of the higher paths.
As for ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*), however, it must simply be said [that they wander].
This is because there is no complete exhaustion of all the fetters of existence. Therefore it was said:
“Bound by the yoke of sensual desire, and by both the yokes of existence, beings go through saṃsāra, subject to birth and death.”
“Having abandoned sensual desires” means having abandoned the defilements known as sensual desire by means of the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*).

“With doubts severed” means with all uncertainty completely eradicated; this occurs specifically by means of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*), though it is stated here in reference to the fourth path for the purpose of praise.
For it is the Arahants who are intended here by the term “with doubts severed. Therefore, he says: “whose conceit and renewed existence are exhausted.”
They are "those for whom conceit and renewed existence are entirely exhausted" because all nine kinds of conceit and future renewed existence have been completely destroyed.
Here, by the mention of "conceit," all defilements to be abandoned by the fourth path are included, either because they are associated with it or by way of their characteristic.

And by the state of having exhausted conceit, the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining is indicated; and by the state of having exhausted renewed existence, [the element of Nibbāna without residue is indicated].
"Without residue remaining. The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the seventh sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Kalyāṇasīla Sutta.
97. In the eighth [verse], "of beautiful virtue" (*kalyāṇasīla*) means one who possesses lovely virtue, praised virtue, and perfected virtue.
In that regard, the perfection of virtue occurs through two causes: by seeing the danger in the failure of virtue exactly as it is, and by seeing the benefit in the attainment of virtue.
Here, however, [it refers to] the virtue of the Path and the virtue of the Fruit, which are entirely free from all impediments and complete in every aspect.
And its excellence should be understood by way of these [qualities]. "One of beautiful nature" (*kalyāṇadhamma*): all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*) are intended here;

therefore, one is "of beautiful nature" because these beautiful factors conducive to enlightenment, such as the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), belong to him. And "one of beautiful wisdom" (*kalyāṇapañña*):
he is of beautiful wisdom precisely by way of the wisdom of the path and fruit. For it is only supramundane qualities, such as virtue and the rest, that are unconditionally beautiful.
It is so called because its intrinsic nature is unshakable. Some, however, say: "He is of beautiful virtue by way of the fourfold purification of virtue;

he is of beautiful qualities by way of the states of the path of insight; and he is of beautiful wisdom by way of the wisdom of the paths and fruits. Some maintain that these virtues, qualities, and wisdoms belong exclusively to those beyond training (*asekha*).
Others, however, state that the virtue of the paths and fruits of stream-enterers and once-returners is what is called "beautiful virtue."

Therefore, by the term "of virtuous conduct" (*kalyāṇasīla*), the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) and the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*) are included; for they are indeed called "those who fulfill their moral conduct.
The states of the non-returning path and fruit (*anāgāmimagga-phala-dhammā*) and the states of the supreme path (*aggamagga-dhammā*) are called "of beautiful qualities" (*kalyāṇadhamma*);

for therein the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*) reach the perfection of cultivation. Therefore, by the term "of beautiful qualities," starting from one established in the third path...

The three noble ones (ariya) are included. Because it has reached the pinnacle of the function of wisdom (paññā), the wisdom in the fruit of supreme attainment (aggaphala) is called "excellent wisdom" (kalyāṇapaññā);
therefore, the Arahant who has attained the fullness of wisdom is called "one of excellent wisdom. In this way, the persons (puggala) are also included.
What is the use of this elaboration? We maintain that here the states of the supreme path and fruit (aggamaggaphaladhammā) are what are referred to as "excellent virtue" and so forth.
Patience. For this classification of persons is by way of the analysis of phenomena (*dhamma*), not by way of the analysis of phenomena alone.

Regarding the term *kevalī*: here, "the whole" (*kevala*) refers to Nibbāna, which is secluded from all conditioned things due to its being unmixed with anything else; because he has attained that, the Arahant is called "the Whole.
Alternatively, it refers to the perfection of abandonment and development, and the perfection of the faultless phenomena at the conclusion [of the path].
And because it is auspicious and possesses the bliss of non-distraction, it is "complete" (kevala), namely, Arahantship; one who has attained that is "one whose taints are exhausted" (khīṇāsava).
One who has dwelt and brought to completion the dwelling in the holy life of the Path is "one who has lived" (vusitavā).
Because he is endowed with the supreme and pre-eminent qualities of the Asekkhas, he is called "the Supreme Person" (uttamapurisa).
Regarding the term "possessing virtue" (*sīlavā*): in what sense is it "virtue" (*sīla*)? It is virtue in the sense of "steadying" (*sīlana*). What is this so-called steadying? It means composure;
that is to say, the state of bodily action and so forth not being scattered due to good conduct. Alternatively, it means "supporting" (*upadhāraṇa*);

that is to say, the state of being a foundation by way of providing a basis for wholesome states such as meditative absorption (*jhāna*). Therefore, it is called *sīla* because it steadies (*sīlati*) or it causes one to steady (*sīleti*). This, first of all, is...

By way of the method of word-derivation (*saddalakkhaṇa*), its meaning is "virtue" (*sīla*). Others, however, explain the meaning according to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*) as follows: "The meaning of 'head' (*sira*) is the meaning of virtue; the meaning of 'cool' (*sītala*) is the meaning of virtue; the meaning of 'auspicious' (*siva*) is the meaning of virtue.

Thus, one who possesses virtue (*sīlavā*) is so called because he has virtue in an abundant or preeminent degree due to its fulfillment. The meaning is that he is "perfected in virtue" (*sīlasampanna*) by way of the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*). In this regard:
The intention of some teachers is that the passage beginning with "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha" was stated in order to show that foremost virtue (*jeṭṭhakasīla*) in detail.
However, others say: the restraint of the Pātimokkha was taught by the Blessed One in both instances. The restraint of the Pātimokkha...
For indeed, virtue (*sīla*) is [the Pātimokkha restraint]; among the others, restraint of the faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) is merely the guarding of the six doors;

purity of livelihood (*ājīvapārisuddhi*) is merely the procuring of requisites in accordance with the Dhamma; and that which pertains to the requisites is merely the use of requisites already obtained after reflecting, "This is for this purpose.
In the ultimate sense, virtue is only the restraint of the Pātimokkha. For one whose [restraint] is broken, [there is no virtue].
Just as a man whose head has been cut off cannot be said to "protect his remaining limbs," so it is not appropriate to say that one who is ill can protect them.
However, for one who is healthy—like a man whose head has not been cut off—it is possible to restore those [limbs] to their natural state and protect them.

Therefore, having indicated by the term "virtuous" (*sīlavā*) specifically the morality of the Pātimokkha, the phrase "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha" (*pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto*) and so forth was spoken in order to explain it in detail.

In this context, *pātimokkha* refers to the virtue of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). For it is called *pātimokkha* because it protects (*pāti*) and liberates (*mokkheti*)—that is, releases—one who observes it from the sufferings of the states of woe and so forth.
*Saṃvara* means restraint; it is the non-transgression of body and speech. The *pātimokkha* itself as restraint is *pātimokkhasaṃvara*.
One who is restrained by that, with body and speech closed off, is said to be "restrained by the restraint of the *pātimokkha*" (*pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuta*).
This is an exposition of his state of being established in that virtue (*sīla*). "Dwells" (*viharati*) is an exposition of his state of possessing a dwelling appropriate to that [virtue].

"Endowed with proper conduct and resort" (*ācāra-gocara-sampanno*) is an exposition of those qualities that are conducive to both the restraint of the Pātimokkha mentioned below and the pursuit of distinction mentioned above.

"Seeing fear in even the slightest faults" (*aṇumatta-vajjesu bhaya-dassāvī*) is an exposition of the quality of being non-falling away from the morality of the Pātimokkha. "Having undertaken" (*samādāya*)...
The phrase "of the training rules" (*sikkhāpadānaṃ*) is an illustration of their undertaking in its entirety. "He trains" (*sikkhati*) is an illustration of being endowed with the training.
"In the training rules" (*sikkhāpadesu*) is an illustration of the things that ought to be trained in.
According to another method: because of the powerful nature of the defilements, because evil actions are easy to perform, and because meritorious actions are [difficult]...
Because he is prone to falling repeatedly into the states of misery due to his state of difficulty, he is a *pātī*, namely, an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*).

Alternatively, because he wanders about without stability—like a potter’s wheel—being cast by the force of karma through the various realms of existence due to impermanence, he is one whose nature is to go (*gamana-sīla*), thus a *pātī*.

Or else, because he is prone to casting down the individual self (*attabhāva*) into this or that class of beings by way of death, he is a *pātī*; [this refers to] the continuum of a being (*satta-santāna*).
Or rather, it is the mind itself. It is called *pātimokkha* because it releases (*mokkheti*) that [mind] which was falling (*pātinaṃ*) from the suffering of *saṃsāra*.
For by the liberation of the mind, a being is liberated. Thus it is said: "By the purification of the mind, they are purified," and "The mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
Alternatively, it is called *pāti* because, through causes such as ignorance, one falls (*patati*), goes, or proceeds within *saṃsāra*. "Of those hindered by ignorance..."

For it is said: "Of beings who wander and transmigrate, bound by craving. It is called *pātimokkha* because by means of this, there is liberation (*mokkha*) for that being from the three defilements beginning with craving (*taṇhā*).
Its formation as a compound should be understood in the same way as in such terms as *kaṇṭhekāla* ("the one with a black throat").

Alternatively, it is called *pāti* because it causes falling (*pāteti*), casts down (*vinipāteti*), or brings suffering; that is, the mind. For it is said: "The world is led by the mind, by the mind..."

"It scrapes away. It is called *pātimokkha* because liberation (*mokkha*) comes about by means of it. Alternatively, it is a *pāti* because by means of it one falls into the suffering of the states of woe and the suffering of *saṃsāra*;
that is, the defilement consisting of craving and so forth. For it is said: "Craving gives birth to a person; craving is a person's companion," and so forth.
Thus, liberation from what has fallen [into those states] is *pātimokkha*. Or else, it is a *pāti* because one falls into it; [namely, the six]—
The internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*). For it is said: "In the six [bases] the world has arisen; in the six it forms intimacy.
Therefore, because it is liberation from what is reckoned as the six internal and external sense bases, it is the *pātimokkha*.
Alternatively, that which has falling away (*pāta*)—that is, ruin—as its characteristic is *pāti*, namely, *saṃsāra*. Liberation from that is the *pātimokkha*. Furthermore...

Alternatively, the Blessed One is called the *pati* (lord) because he is the sovereign of all the world and the master of the Dhamma; it is "liberation" (*mokkha*) because one is liberated by means of it;

and it is the *pātimokkha* because it is prescribed by that Lord as liberation. Or else, it is the *patimokkha* because it is both the *pati*—in the sense of being the root of all virtues—and liberation—in the sense already described. Thus it is the *patimokkha*. The *pātimokkha* is simply the *patimokkha*.
Such is the *pātimokkha*. For it has been said in detail: “*Pātimokkha* means this is the mouth (*mukha*), this is the foremost (*pamukha*).

Alternatively, *pā* is a prefix meaning ‘in various ways’ (*pakāre*), and *ati* is a particle used in the sense of ‘extreme’ (*accantatthe*). Therefore, it is called *pātimokkha* because it liberates (*mokkheti*) completely (*ati*) in various ways (*pakārehi*).
Indeed, this virtue (*sīla*) itself, by way of its own factor (*tadaṅga-vasena*), and when accompanied by concentration and wisdom, by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana-vasena*).

It is called *pātimokkha* because it liberates by means of absolute release through complete eradication (*samuccheda*). Alternatively, it is *patimokkha* because there is release (*mokkha*) for each (*pati-pati*) [transgression];
the meaning is that there is a specific release from each respective fault that ought to be transgressed.
Thus, *pātimokkha* is simply *patimokkha*. Or else, *mokkha* refers to Nibbāna; it is called *patimokkha* because it is the counterpart (*paṭibimba*) of that liberation.
The restraint of the *pātimokkha* precepts is like the rising of the sun; it is the dawn of *nibbāna*, acting as its counterpart by extinguishing the defilements (*kilesa*) as appropriate.
Thus it is called *patimokkha*. *Pātimokkha* is simply *patimokkha*.
Alternatively, it is called *patimokkha* because it functions toward liberation (*mokkha*), being directed toward liberation; thus, *patimokkha* itself is *pātimokkha*.
Thus, first of all, the meaning of the word *pātimokkha* should be understood here.
It is called *saṃvara* because by means of it one restrains (*saṃvarati*) or covers (*pidahati*). The *pātimokkha* itself as restraint is *pātimokkhasaṃvara*.

As for its meaning, however, it consists of either the abstentions (*virati*) or the volitions (*cetanā*) from various things that ought to be transgressed. One who is "endowed" (*upeta*) with that *pātimokkhasaṃvara*...
One who is thus endowed is said to be "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha. For this is stated in the Vibhaṅga:

"By means of this restraint of the Pātimokkha, he is possessed of it, fully possessed of it, approached with it, fully approached with it, perfected in it, and endowed with it; therefore, he is called 'restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha.

He "dwells" (viharatī) in the sense that he dwells by way of the postures (iriyāpatha); he moves about and conducts himself. "Endowed with proper conduct and resort" (ācāra-gocara-sampanna) refers to [the avoidance of] wrong livelihood such as the giving of bamboo shoots and so forth.
By not committing physical immodesty and so forth, and by completely avoiding improper conduct,
he is "accomplished in conduct and resort" because he possesses the excellence of conduct befitting a bhikkhu— as described as "non-transgression physically and non-transgression verbally"—
and because he has avoided unsuitable resorts such as prostitutes and frequents instead the proper resorts for approaching in order to obtain almsfood and other necessities. Furthermore:
That monk who is respectful and deferential toward the Teacher, respectful and deferential toward his fellow celibates,
endowed with moral shame and moral dread, well-clad and well-robed, pleasing in his manner of going forward and returning, looking ahead and looking aside, drawing in and extending his limbs,
with downcast eyes, perfected in deportment, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, and moderate in eating;

One who is devoted to wakefulness, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, possessing few desires, contented, secluded, unattached, and who dwells performing his duties with diligence and with great reverence toward those worthy of honor—such a person is said to be "perfect in conduct" (*ācārasampanna*).

As for the "range" (*gocara*), it is threefold: the range as a supporting condition (*upanissaya-gocara*), the range as protection (*ārakkha-gocara*), and the range as a tethering point (*upanibandha-gocara*). Among these:
A virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitta) who possesses the ten qualities of the subject matter and the aforementioned characteristics, by relying upon whom one hears what has not been heard,
purifies what has been heard, overcomes doubt, straightens one's view, and gladdens the mind;
and by training under whom one increases in faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom— this is [the virtuous friend].

The objective field of the proximate cause (*upanissaya-gocara*). It is when a bhikkhu, having entered among the houses and set out upon the street, walks with downcast eyes, looking only a yoke’s length ahead, restrained; he does not look at elephants, nor horses, nor chariots, nor infantry, nor women, nor men;
he does not look upward, nor downward, nor toward the intermediate directions.

He goes along looking [at them]; this is the range of protection (*ārakkha-gocara*). As for the range of anchoring (*upanibandha-gocara*), it consists of the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), wherein a bhikkhu anchors his own mind. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"And what, bhikkhus, is the bhikkhu’s own range, his ancestral domain? That is to say, the four foundations of mindfulness."

Thus, because he is endowed with the aforementioned perfection of conduct (*ācāra-sampatti*) and this perfection of resort (*gocara-sampatti*), he is "perfected in conduct and resort" (*ācāra-gocara-sampanna*).

Regarding "seeing danger in even the slightest faults": he is one whose nature is to see danger in even minor, atomic transgressions—namely, those consisting of unintentional lapses in the rules of training (*sekhiya-dhamma*), unwholesome states of mind, and so forth.
For a monk who regards even a fault the size of an atom as being like Sineru, the king of mountains, rising sixty-eight hundred thousand *yojanas* high—

Having done so, he sees [the danger]. Even a bhikkhu who, having treated even a very light mere offense of wrong speech as if it were a *pārājika*, sees [the danger], is called "one who sees fear in even the slightest faults. "Having undertaken, he trains in the rules of training" means:
whatever is to be trained in among the rules of training, having undertaken all of that in every way, in every manner, and without exception.
The meaning is that he trains, conducts himself, and fulfills [the precepts]. Thus, being one of "beautiful virtue" (*kalyāṇasīla*) in this manner—

since virtue was previously explained by way of reference to a person, as in the statement, "In this way, monks, a bhikkhu is of beautiful virtue"— it is now concluded by way of reference to that very same person,
and then [the term] "of beautiful qualities" (*kalyāṇadhamma*) is used here with respect to those qualities.
Desiring to demonstrate this, and to show that "this is the virtue (sīla) and the foundation (adhiṭṭhāna) of those qualities," it was further stated: "Thus, one of beautiful virtue.

The passage beginning with "of the seven factors of enlightenment" and so forth has all its meaning already explained above. The section beginning with "Again, one of beautiful virtue" is the conclusion.
In the verses, *dukkaṭa* means "badly done"; the sense is "misconduct" (*duccarita*). *Hirimaṃ* means "possessing a sense of shame" (*hirimanta*), that is, endowed with moral dread (*hiri*).
The meaning is: having the nature of loathing the occurrence of evil in every respect. Alternatively, *hirimā* means a mind accompanied by moral shame (*hiri*).
It should be understood that by the mention of *hiri* alone, moral dread (*ottappa*) is also included here.

By mentioning both moral shame and moral dread, he demonstrates the cause for the total absence of misconduct, thereby clarifying the state of virtuous conduct from the perspective of its cause. *Sambodhi* refers to noble knowledge (*ariya-ñāṇa*).

They go toward and cultivate that, thus they are "those who go toward enlightenment" (*sambodhigāmin*); the meaning is "factors conducive to enlightenment" (*bodhipakkhika*). "Unagitated" (*anussada*) means free from the agitation of passion (*rāga*) and so forth.

They also read it as "tathāvidhaṃ. Regarding the phrase "devoted to the practice of the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment," the meaning is "of such a kind" or "of that sort," just as was stated previously.
"Of suffering" (*dukkhassa*) refers to the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).

"Or of the cause of the suffering of the round. "Right here, the mere exhaustion [of it]" means that through the attainment of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*), he understands the non-arising—the exhaustion—of the mass of defilements belonging to the side of origination, which is the cause of his own suffering in the round, right here in this very individual existence (*attabhāva*).
Or else, he understands the exhaustion—the state of being destroyed—of the suffering of the round itself right here, by the cessation of the final consciousness. By those...

"Endowed with qualities" means possessed of those aforementioned qualities such as virtue (sīla) and so forth. "Unattached" means unattached because of the abandonment of the bases for craving and views;
that is, independent of anything whatsoever. "Of the whole world" means in the entire world of sentient beings. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the eighth sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Dānasutta 98.
Regarding the ninth [verse], "giving" (*dāna*) means that which is to be given; or, giving is the volition (*cetanā*) together with its objective basis (*vatthu*).

This is a designation for the relinquishing of what has been acquired. "Giving of material things" (*āmisa-dāna*) refers to the four requisites by way of their being objects to be given. For these indeed—

They are called "material things" (*āmisa*) because they are to be grasped by craving and the like; or alternatively, the volition of relinquishing them is "the gift of material things. As for "the gift of the Dhamma":
here, someone [teaches] that "these states are wholesome, these states are unwholesome; these states are blameworthy, these states are blameless;
these are censured by the wise, these are praised by the wise; these, when fully undertaken and practiced, lead to harm and suffering..."
"These lead to welfare; these lead to happiness.

Thus, by analyzing the courses of wholesome and unwholesome action, as if making manifest and directly demonstrating karma and its results in this world and the next, he teaches the Dhamma—turning people away from unwholesome states and establishing them in wholesome states. This is the gift of Dhamma.

But when one teaches the Dhamma for the attainment of the Deathless by distinguishing the Truths—saying, "These phenomena are to be directly known; these are to be fully understood; these are to be abandoned; these are to be realized;
these are to be developed"—this is called the gift of Dhamma that has reached its pinnacle. "Etadaggaṃ" means this is the foremost. "Yadidaṃ" means this which is the gift of Dhamma.
It has been said that between these two kinds of giving, this is the foremost, the best, and the supreme.
For by relying on the gift of the Dhamma that leads to the turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭagāmi*), one is liberated from all harm and transcends the entire suffering of saṃsāra.
However, mundane giving of the Dhamma is the source of all gifts and the root of all success. Therefore, he said:
“The gift of the Dhamma surpasses all gifts; the taste of the Dhamma surpasses all tastes;
delight in the Dhamma surpasses all delights; the destruction of craving surpasses all suffering.
Herein, it should be understood that the gift of fearlessness is included within the gift of the Dhamma itself.
The sharing of material goods (*āmisa-saṃvibhāga*) is the distribution among others of the four requisites that one should use oneself, out of the intention to enjoy them in common.

The sharing of the Dhamma (*dhamma-saṃvibhāga*) is the instruction of others regarding the Dhamma known and attained by oneself, without being indifferent to it, out of that same intention to enjoy it in common. By means of these four...
Assisting and showing compassion toward others by means of the four requisites and the four bases of sympathy is assistance with material things (*āmisa-anuggaha*).
Assisting and showing compassion toward others through the Dhamma, in the manner already described, is assistance with the Dhamma (*dhamma-anuggaha*). The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Regarding the verses, that which is called "the supreme gift" is the gift that is supreme due to the excellence of the mind, the field, and the object to be given.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have called it "supreme" (*uttama*) because it fulfills the attainment of wealth and so forth, or because of its fruitfulness;
and they have called it "ultimate" (*parama*) because it crushes and destroys the opposing factors in others, such as greed and stinginess.

It is "unexcelled" (*anuttara*) because, through the excellence of its volition and other factors, it functions with preeminence and possesses the highest ripening, and is thus devoid of anything superior to it.

And they say it is the means for accomplishing the state of unsurpassed [enlightenment]. Regarding the phrase "that which shares in distribution," here too the two words "supreme" and "unsurpassed" should be brought in and connected.
"He praised" means he extolled [it], as in: "Monks, when a donor gives food, he gives five things to the recipients," and so forth;
and: "If, monks, beings were to know the fruit of giving and sharing in this way..."

And he praised [generosity] with the words beginning, "The result of ripening," and so forth. However, in order to show how giving and sharing become supreme and unsurpassed, the passage beginning with "In the foremost" was spoken.

Therein, "in the foremost" refers to the Fully Enlightened One and the Noble Saṅgha, who are the most excellent and unsurpassed fields of merit due to their possession of distinguished qualities such as virtue. "With a mind full of serene confidence" means through faith in the results of kamma.
He calms and settles his mind through faith in the Triple Gem.
For when there is excellence of mind and excellence of field, even a small gift of material things becomes of great power, great radiance, and great expansion. Indeed, it has been said:
"When the mind is serene, there is no such thing as a small offering."
“Whether toward a Tathāgata, a Perfectly Enlightened One, or his disciple”—one who is “wise” (*viññū*) is one possessed of discernment (*sappañña*).
“They understand” means they understand correctly the fruit of giving and the benefit of giving.
“Who would not sacrifice when the time has come?”—who indeed would not give a gift when the proper and opportune moment has arrived? [This refers to] faith, the object to be given, and the recipient.
For a gift occurs only when these three are present together, not otherwise, nor at a time when it is appropriate to give to the recipients.

Having thus shown, in the first verse, the assistance of sharing and giving material gifts (*āmisa-dāna*), he now spoke the second verse, "And those who speak," in order to show the assistance of sharing and giving the Dharma (*dhamma-dāna*).
In that context, "both" refers to "those who speak and those who listen."
Both the speakers and the recipients have been mentioned. Here, however, is the summary of the meaning:

for those speakers and recipients who, with hearts full of confidence in the True Dhamma—the teaching of the Blessed One, the Sugata—stand at the head of the bases of liberation and both teach and receive, there is this benefit consisting of the gift of Dhamma, the sharing of Dhamma, and the assistance through Dhamma.
It is supreme because it accomplishes the ultimate goal. It is purified by cleansing all the stains of defilement, such as the defilement of craving.
Of what kind [of people]? Those who are heedful in the teaching of the Sugata, and those who—“The non-doing of all evil, the undertaking of the wholesome;”
“The purification of one’s own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

When the instruction and guidance in the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One has been thus explained in brief, those who are heedful diligently accomplish the training in higher virtue and the other trainings.
For them, [the mind] becomes purified; it becomes exceedingly cleansed through the purification of the fruit of Arahantship.
The commentary on the Ninth Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Tevijja-sutta*. 99.
In the tenth [sutta], "by the Dhamma" means by way, that is, by the method known as right practice (*sammāpaṭipatti*), which is the cause and reason. For by whatever path...
He is one possessed of the threefold knowledge; that practice should be understood here as "Dhamma. But what is that practice?

It is the perfection of conduct and the perfection of true knowledge. "Possessed of the threefold knowledge" means endowed with the three knowledges, such as the knowledge of recollecting past lives and so forth.
"Brahmin" refers to a Brahmin who has banished evil. "I make known" means I cause him to be recognized as a "Brahmin," I establish him as such.

"Not merely by reciting and making others recite" means that I do not designate one who is a brahmin merely by birth as a brahmin merely by the recitation and mere prattle of the *Aṭṭhaka* and other [Vedic texts].
Alternatively, "merely by reciting and making others recite" means merely by the study and teaching of the mantras.
In either case, it refers to what the brahmins call a "brahmin of the three Vedas" (*tevijja*) on account of their study of the three Vedas, beginning with the *Sāmaveda*.
He rejects that [claim]. For this teaching was undertaken by the Blessed One with the intention of those individuals who would understand it in this way, in order to show:

"In the ultimate sense, these proponents of 'veneration' (bhovādino), being shrouded in ignorance, speak of a brahmin as 'possessing the three knowledges' (tevijjo) even though he does not possess them; however, a brahmin becomes one possessing the three knowledges in this manner."

In this regard, since one who is perfected in true knowledge (*vijjā*) is necessarily perfected in conduct (*caraṇa*), because there is no perfection of true knowledge apart from perfection of conduct, [the Blessed One], wishing to define a brahmin by means of the pinnacle of true knowledge while including perfection of conduct within it, initiated the teaching with the words:
"Bhikkhus, I define a brahmin possessing the threefold knowledge (*tevijja*) according to the Dhamma," and then asked: "And how, bhikkhus..."
“Monks, it is by way of the Dhamma that I define a Brahmin possessed of the threefold knowledge.
Having thus posed a question out of a desire to speak, and analyzing the threefold knowledge through a teaching centered on the individual, he said: “In this case, monks, a monk...
and so forth. Therein, *anekavihitam* means manifold, or that which has proceeded in many ways; *saṃvaṇṇitam* means described.
The meaning: "Past lives" (*pubbenivāsa*) refers to the continuum of aggregates (*khandhasantāna*) that have dwelt here and there, beginning from the immediately preceding past existence.
"Dwelt" (*nivutta*) means inhabited, experienced, or arisen and ceased within one's own continuum;

or, "dwelt" refers to phenomena that have dwelt, or that which has dwelt by way of abiding in its objective range (*gocara*), or that which has been cognized by one's own consciousness as well as by the consciousness of others.

Or [it is used] in such cases as the recollection of the cutting off of the *vaṭumaka* (the navel-string). "He recollects" means that he remembers by following the sequence of births, thinking, "one birth, two births," and so on;
or he remembers immediately after [the mind has been directed]; or he remembers immediately after the preliminary work when the mind has been directed.
*Seyyathidaṃ* is a particle used in the sense of showing the manner in which [the recollection] has been undertaken. For this very reason, this past life which has been undertaken...
To demonstrate the manner in which this occurs, he said, "even one birth," and so forth.

Therein, "even one birth" refers to a single continuum of aggregates (khandhasantāna) included within one existence (bhava), beginning with rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and ending with death (cuti). This same method applies to "two births" and so on.
However, in the expressions "many eons of dissolution" (saṃvaṭṭakappa) and so forth, an eon that is in the process of contracting is a "eon of dissolution."

The eon is increasing as it evolves (*vivaṭṭakappa*). In this context, by the term "contraction" (*saṃvaṭṭa*), the period of the eon’s duration during contraction is included because it is rooted in that;
and by the term "evolution" (*vivaṭṭa*), the period of the eon’s duration during evolution is included. For it is said:
"Monks, there are these four incalculable periods of an eon. Which four? Contraction, the duration of contraction, evolution, and the duration of evolution."
The four incalculable eons have been stated; they are thus encompassed.
Therein, there are three types of dissolution: dissolution by fire, dissolution by water, and dissolution by wind. There are three limits of dissolution:
the Ābhassara, the Subhakiṇha, and the Vehapphala realms. When the eon dissolves by fire, [everything] from the Ābhassara realm...
Below, it is consumed by fire. When the world-system dissolves by water, everything below the Subhakiṇha realm is dissolved away by water.
When it dissolves by wind, everything below the Vehapphala realm is scattered away by wind.
As for its extent, a hundred thousand million world-systems perish together. Thus, one who recollects such former births—
A bhikkhu recollects even many aeons of world-dissolution, many aeons of world-evolution, and many aeons of both world-dissolution and evolution. How?
By way of the method beginning with, "In that place I was.
Therein, "In that place" means in that particular aeon of dissolution, or in that particular state of existence, or mode of birth, or destiny, or station of consciousness.
Or in a dwelling for beings, or within the class of beings, "I was. "Of such a name" means Tissa or Phussa.
"Of such a clan" means Gotama or Kassapa. "Of such a complexion" means fair or dark. "Having such food" means having rice and meat as food, or subsisting on wild fruits.
"Experiencing such pleasure and pain" refers to various kinds of bodily and mental [sensations].
Or he is one who experiences pleasures and pains distinguished as worldly (*sāmisa*) or unworldly (*nirāmisa*).
"Thus having such a limit to his lifespan" means having a limit to his lifespan measured by one hundred years, or having a limit to his lifespan measured by eight million four hundred thousand eons.

"Passing away from there, he was reborn elsewhere" means: from that state of existence, from that womb, from that destination, from that station of consciousness, or from that abode of beings, I passed away.

"Having passed away from a certain group of beings (*sattanikāya*), I was reborn again in such-and-such a birth, womb, destiny, station of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), abode of beings, or group of beings.
There too I existed"—thus, in that birth, womb, destiny, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or group of beings, I existed once more.
"With such a name," and so forth, is exactly as previously explained.

Alternatively, because the phrase "you were there" is a refuge for one ascending step by step according to one's own aspiration and according to one's strength, and because "having passed away from there" is a retrospective reflection for one returning [to this world], therefore, immediately after this birth here—expressed as "reborn here"—it was said, "you arose there. "There too... [and so forth].
Or [I existed] within a class of beings. "Of such a name" means Datta or Mitta; "of such a clan" means Vāseṭṭha or Kassapa;
"of such a complexion" means dark or fair; "having such food" means food of ambrosia or food such as rice-gruel;
"experiencing such pleasure and pain" means experiencing celestial pleasure or human pleasure and pain; "with such a limit to my lifespan" means thus...
"Reaching the limit of that particular maximum lifespan": "I passed away from there" means I passed away from that state of existence.
"Reborn here" means reborn and arisen here in this final existence as a human being.
