"Thus" (iti) means in this way. "With its modes and details" (sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ): "with its details" refers to [recollection] by way of name, clan, and so forth; "with its modes" refers to [recollection] by way of complexion and so forth.
For beings are designated by name and clan as "Tissa Gotama," while they are known for their diversity by way of complexion and so forth, such as "Sāma is fair-skinned.
Therefore, name and clan constitute the enumeration (uddesa), while the others are the modes (ākāra).

"This first true knowledge (vijjā) has been attained by him" means that this first [knowledge] has been attained by this bhikkhu by way of initial attainment; it is called "true knowledge" (vijjā) in the sense of making something known.
It has been realized. But what does this [knowledge] make known? It makes known one's former births (*pubbenivāsa*).

Ignorance (*avijjā*) is called the delusion that conceals that very same former birth in the sense of making it unknown. "Darkness" (*tama*) is that same delusion called "darkness" in the sense of being a concealer.
"Light" (*āloka*) is that same clear knowledge (*vijjā*) in the sense of producing illumination. And here, clear knowledge has been attained.
This is the meaning; the remainder is words of praise. As for the construction here: "Indeed, this true knowledge (vijjā) has been attained by that bhikkhu;
for him who has attained true knowledge, ignorance (avijjā) has been destroyed"—this is the meaning. Why? Because true knowledge has arisen.
The same method applies to the other two phrases as well.
Regarding the phrase *yathā tanti*: here, *yathā* has the sense of "as" (comparison), while *tan* is merely a particle. "Of one who is heedful" means by not being separated from mindfulness.
"Of one who is ardent" means by the exertion of energy (*vīriya*). "Of one whose self is directed" means of one whose mind is sent forth due to having no regard for body or life;
this is the meaning. What is meant is this: as ignorance [is abandoned] for one who dwells heedful, ardent, and with a directed self...

Ignorance would be dispelled and true knowledge would arise; darkness would be dispelled and light would arise. In the same way, for that bhikkhu, ignorance has been dispelled and true knowledge has arisen; darkness has been dispelled and light has arisen.
Having obtained a result exactly corresponding to his application of effort, he dwells [in that state].
Regarding "with the divine eye," what is to be said there has already been stated above.
"Purified" means it is purified because it is the cause for the purification of view through the seeing of passing away and rebirth.
For one who sees only passing away and not rebirth adopts the annihilationist view; one who sees only rebirth and not passing away adopts the view of the manifestation of new beings.
He grasps it. But he who sees both of these, because he transcends that twofold state of views, his vision becomes a cause for the purification of views;

and this son of the Buddha sees both of them. Therefore it is said: "It is 'purified' because, by seeing the passing away and rebirth [of beings], it serves as a cause for the purification of views. Because it is free from the eleven defilements...
or purified. As it is said: “Having understood that doubt is an imperfection of the mind, I abandoned doubt as an imperfection of the mind;
[I abandoned] lack of attention... lethargy and drowsiness, trepidation, sluggishness, over-exertion of energy, slackness of energy, longing, perceptions of diversity, and excessive brooding.”
It is "purified" because it is untainted by the eleven defilements mentioned when it was said, "forms are a defilement of the mind.
It is "surpassing the human" because it sees forms beyond the range of ordinary humans, or because it surpasses the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*).
By means of that divine eye, purified and surpassing the human.
"He sees beings" means that he sees, beholds, and looks upon beings as if with the fleshly eye of a human.

Regarding the phrase "passing away and being reborn": it is not possible even with the divine eye to see them at the precise moment of death (*cutikkhaṇa*) or the moment of rebirth (*upapattikkhaṇa*).
However, those who are near to death and will die shortly are "passing away" (*cavamāna*); and those who have already taken rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) are "being reborn."
Or those who have attained rebirth; these are intended as "those being reborn. He shows that one sees them thus passing away and being reborn.
"Inferior" means despised and disregarded by way of inferior birth, family, wealth, and so forth, because they are associated with the outflow of delusion (*moha*).
"Exalted" means the opposite of that, because they are associated with the outflow of non-delusion. "Beautiful" means because they are associated with the outflow of non-hatred (*adosa*).

"Endowed with a desirable, pleasing, and agreeable appearance" means possessed of a form that is not undesirable, unpleasing, or disagreeable, due to being associated with the outflow (*nissanda*) of non-hatred (*adosa*).

"Handsome" (*abhirūpa*) also carries the sense of being "well-formed. "Well-gone" (*sugata*) means having gone to a good destination; or, because it is associated with the outflow of non-greed (*alobha*), it means wealthy and possessing great riches.

"Ill-gone" (*duggata*) means having gone to a bad destination; or, because it is associated with the outflow of greed (*lobha*), it means destitute, lacking food, drink, and provisions. "According to their respective karma" (*yathākammūpaga*)...

Whatever karma has been accumulated, by that very [karma] one has arrived. Herein, by the previous terms beginning with "when passing away," the function of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) was described;

but by this present phrase, the function of the knowledge of rebirth according to one's deeds (*yathākammūpagañāṇa*) is described. And this is the sequence of its arising: here, a bhikkhu extends light downward toward the hells.
When he sees beings in hell experiencing great suffering, this seeing is precisely the function of the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*).
He then reflects thus: "What deed have these beings done that they experience this suffering?
Then, the thought "Having done such-and-such," there arises in him knowledge having that specific karma as its object. Likewise, [he directs his vision] upward toward the world of the devas.
Having increased his light, he sees beings in the Nandana Grove, Missaka Grove, Phārusaka Grove, and so forth, experiencing divine success.
This seeing is also merely the function of the knowledge of the divine eye. He then attends to this thus:
"What deed have these beings performed to experience this success? Then [he knows], "Having performed such-and-such a deed..."
Knowledge arises having that kamma as its object; this is called "knowledge of past deeds according to their destination" (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*). There is no separate preliminary exercise for this.
Just as with this, so it is with the knowledge of future states (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*);

for these two depend upon the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) and succeed only together with the divine eye. As for what should be said regarding the passage beginning with "by bodily misconduct," that is exactly according to the method already explained below.

Here, "true knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to the true knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*). "Ignorance" (*avijjā*) refers to the ignorance that obscures the passing away and rebirth of beings.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.

In the third instance, "true knowledge" refers to the true knowledge of the path to Arhatship (*arahatta-magga-ñāṇa*). "Ignorance" refers to the ignorance that conceals the Four Noble Truths. The rest is easily understood because it follows the method already explained above. "Thus indeed," and so forth, is the conclusion.
The summary meaning of these verses is as follows: He who "knows" (aveti)—that is, understands—the aforementioned past lives, making them manifest according to the method described;
or, according to another reading, "yovedi," which means he who stands having known [them] and made them known.
With the divine eye, in the same manner described, he sees the heavens—comprising the twenty-six celestial worlds—and the fourfold plane of misery. "Atha" (then) means after that.
He has attained or reached Arahantship, which is defined as the destruction of birth, or Nibbāna itself.

Precisely because of that, having known the Dhamma of the Four Truths—which must be known by means of the super-knowledge (abhiññā) of the distinguished path-wisdom—he is fulfilled and has reached completion through the termination of his task.

He is a sage (muni) by virtue of being endowed with the qualities of a sage (moneyya-dhamma), for he is one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) by means of these three aforementioned true knowledges (vijjā).
Because he is endowed with this third knowledge and because he has entirely banished evil, he is called a "brahmin possessing the threefold knowledge" (*tevijjo*).

Therefore, it is him alone that I call a brahmin possessing the threefold knowledge; I do not call anyone else a brahmin possessing the threefold knowledge who is merely one who recites and causes others to recite the mantra-words of the *Yajus* and so forth—I do not describe such a person as "possessing the threefold knowledge."

Thus, in this chapter, it should be understood that the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is explained in the second sutta; the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*) is explained in the fifth, eighth, and tenth suttas; and both the cycle and the turning away are explained in the remaining suttas.
The commentary on the tenth sutta is finished.
The commentary on the fifth chapter is finished.
The commentary on the *Itivuttaka* within the *Khuddakanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, entitled the *Paramatthadīpanī*, is concluded. 4.
The Fourth Chapter (*Catukkanipāta*).
1. Commentary on the *Brāhmaṇadhammayāgasutta* 100.

In the first [sutta] of the Catukka-nipāta, "I" (*aham*) is the designation for the self (*attā*). For that which is not another is called "I," being designated as one's own internal self (*niyakajjhatta*).
"I am" (*asmīti*) is the claim of identity. That which is the state of a brāhmaṇa in the ultimate sense, when spoken of as "I," is what is meant.
Indeed, when the Teacher affirmed its existence within himself, he said, "I am" (*asmī*).

And this is not spoken in the same manner as when ordinary worldlings—whose underlying tendencies of views and conceit have not been abandoned—assert "I am" (*ahamasmi*) or "I am Brahmā, the Great Brahmā;
I am superior," due to their adherence to the conceiving of views, conceit, and self-estimation. Rather, it is entirely...
The Blessed One, having abandoned the underlying tendencies of views and conceit, does not overstep conventional designations;

rather, conforming to worldly convention and establishing the Dhamma within the mental continuums of those to be trained, he spoke thus, "I am," merely acknowledging the presence of such a quality within himself.
He is called a "brahmin" (brāhmaṇa) because he has banished evil (bāhita-pāpa) and because he owes nothing to Brahmā (brahma-aṇana). This is the meaning here: "O monks..."

"I am a brahmin in the ultimate sense. The Blessed One has reached the further shore of the undertaking of vows such as generosity and self-restraint in every perfect aspect, through ascetic practice without remainder;

he is one who has properly dwelt the life of the holy life (*brahmacariya*), who has mastered the entirety of the Vedas, whose knowledge and conduct are perfectly pure, whose stains of evil have been washed away in every way, and [who is the possessor] of the unsurpassed Noble Path...
He is one who instructs and exhorts the brahmin, and proclaims the perfectly pure holy life of the Dispensation;
therefore, because he has utterly banished evil and because he speaks and proclaims [the truth] like Brahmā, he is called a "brahmin" in the ultimate sense.
Thus, having proclaimed his own unsurpassed state of being a brahmin in the world with its devas, the Blessed One [spoke of] those things such as the giving of a brahmin...

Six duties are prescribed for a brahmin; in order to show that even these, when perfectly purified, are found in him to the highest degree within himself, he said, "one who is devoted to begging," and so forth.

In this context, "devoted to begging" (yācayoga) means one who is engaged in begging. "Those who beg" (yācā) are the beggars; however, in this case, they should be understood as those who are to be converted (veneyya).
For they approach the Blessed One, saying, "Venerable sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma; let the Sugata teach the Dhamma," and thus request a teaching of the Dhamma.
And the Blessed One, not thwarting their wish, bestows the gift of the Dhamma by teaching it according to their inclination;
thus he is "devoted to being requested" (yācayoga), meaning he is at all times and for all seasons never separated from them. Alternatively, "yācayoga" means:
“Worthy of being requested” (*yācanayogga*) means fit to be asked for because it fulfills one’s intention; there is also a reading, “associated with sacrifice” (*yājayoga*).
In that context, “sacrifice” (*yāja*) refers to a great gift (*mahādāna*), meaning that which is offered. Here, however, it should be understood as the gift of the Dhamma (*dhammadāna*);

thus, “one who is intent upon sacrifice” (*yājayoga*) means one devoted to the gift of the Dhamma. “Always” (*sadā*) means at all times; the sense is that it is a great gift of the True Dhamma proceeding without interruption. Alternatively, by means of sacrifice...
“Yojeti” (he joins) is also called *yājayoga*. By means of sacrifice (*yāja*), which is reckoned as the threefold giving, he joins beings according to their suitability;
the meaning is that he enjoins them to that giving. They also read it as “*yājayoga satatan*” (the constant practice of sacrifice). “*Payatapāṇī*” means one whose hands are pure.
For one who is intent on giving, when bestowing material gifts, always gives the object of charity respectfully with his own hand.
One whose hands are washed is called "pure-handed" (*payatapāṇī*).
Since the Blessed One is intent upon the gift of the Dhamma and is always thoroughly devoted to the giving of the Dhamma, it is said of him that he is "pure-handed.
Furthermore, the word "always" (*sadā*) should be construed with this as well: "always pure-handed. For the Teacher does not make a distinction regarding the world of those to be trained.
He dwells engaged in that practice, constantly and at all times promoting the gift of the True Dhamma.
Another interpretation is as follows: *yoga* is said to mean cultivation (*bhāvanā*), as it is said: "From yoga, indeed, the vast [wisdom] is born.
Therefore, *yājayoga* means one who is devoted to the cultivation of sacrifice—that is, the cultivation of relinquishment. For prior to his full enlightenment, the Blessed One...
Even while he was a bodhisatta, incited by compassion and cultivating giving without remainder, he reached the highest perfection therein and attained full enlightenment.
Having become a Buddha, he too cultivated the threefold giving, especially the gift of the Dhamma, and enjoined others to do likewise.
For instance, to those seekers among his disciples who were worthy of being led, he gave some the refuges and to some...
The five precepts, for some the ten precepts, for some the fourfold purification of virtue,
for some the ascetic practices, for some the four jhānas, for some the eight attainments, for some the five direct knowledges,
the four paths, the four fruits of recluseship, the three types of clear knowledge, and the four analytical insights— thus categorized as mundane and supramundane.

By giving away the wealth of his virtues through the gift of the Dhamma according to his intention, and by exhorting others to "give," he cultivated the meditation on relinquishment (*pariccāga-bhāvanā*).
Therefore it is said: "devoted to the cultivation of relinquishment. Alternatively, *payatapāṇī* means *āyatapāṇī*;
it refers to one whose hand is extended like someone who, when something has come into their hands to give, says, "Come, take it! with their hand outstretched.

The meaning is that he is one who is devotedly engaged in the gift of the True Dhamma without keeping anything back as a teacher’s secret. Or, "pure-handed" (*payatapāṇī*) means having uplifted hands;
the meaning is that he has exerted himself in the gift of the Dhamma just as one would have uplifted hands to give a gift of material things.
"Bearing his final body" (*antimadehadharo*) means one who maintains his last existence due to the fulfillment of those qualities that make one a *brāhmaṇa* through the holy life (*brahmacariya*).

For one who has not lived [the holy life], because they have not abandoned those qualities that make one an outcaste, there may be the designation "outcaste" and a future destination consisting of lying in a womb.
Therefore, the Blessed One demonstrates his own state of being a brahmin who has lived it to the ultimate degree.

He is the "unsurpassed physician, the surgeon," because he is the supreme physician for curing the disease of the suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*), which is difficult to cure; [he is unsurpassed] by others...
He is the supreme physician for extracting the thorns of lust and the other defilements, because he extracts them by means of their total eradication.

By this, it is stated that he brings about the state of a brahmin for others as well, by establishing within the mental continuums of others those qualities that constitute the state of a brahmin and which are firmly established within himself.
"Of me, who am such as this, you are sons"—thus, monks, you have become my own-born sons (*orasā*).
"Own-born" means connected to the breast (*urasi sambaddhā*).

For just as the own-born sons of beings are especially entitled to share in the inheritance belonging to their father, so too these noble persons [are entitled] at the conclusion of hearing the Dhamma from the Perfectly Enlightened One.
They are born of noble birth. They are "legitimate" (orasa) because they share in the same portion as that bliss of liberation and the jewel of the Noble Dhamma which belongs to Him.

Alternatively, by the power of the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, the Noble Disciples—both those entering and those who have entered the plane of the Noble Ones—are to be called, in a non-figurative sense, "legitimate sons," because they are born of the effort exerted by the Teacher.
They are "worthy" (arahant). For they were nurtured by the Blessed One through the nourishment of the body of qualities such as virtue;

having taken them into his heart by surveying their underlying tendencies, latent dispositions, conduct, inclinations, and so forth, and by reflecting upon their faults, he restrained them from what is blameworthy and established them in the blameless.
They are "born from the mouth" because they were born from the noble birth that is the teaching of the Dhamma, which is as if born from his own mouth.

"Born from the mouth": either born from the mouth [of the Buddha]; or else, because it is not shared by others, it is "born from the mouth" in the sense of being born from the mouth of all wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*), or from the *pātimokkha*, or from the "gateways to liberation" (*vimokkhamukha*) consisting of insight leading to emergence, for the class of noble paths (*ariya-magga*).
It is "born of the Dhamma" (*dhammaja*) because it is born within the Dhamma of the Dispensation, which comprises the three trainings, or within the Dhamma of the noble path. For that very reason...
"Created and fashioned by the Dhamma" means *dhammanimmitā*. "Heirs to the Dhamma"—that is, mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, and so forth—are heirs to the Dhamma;
they are not heirs to material things such as gain and honor. The meaning is: "Be heirs to the Dhamma, not heirs to material things. In this context, the Dhamma is twofold:
the non-figurative Dhamma (*nippariyāya-dhamma*) and the figurative Dhamma (*pariyāya-dhamma*). Material things (*āmisa*) are also twofold: [material wealth and the five aggregates].

The direct sense of the Dhamma and the indirect sense of the Dhamma. How so? The ninefold supramundane Dhamma, distinguished as the paths, fruits, and Nibbāna, is the Dhamma in the direct sense; it is the Dhamma produced [as the result], and not a Dhamma by way of any indirect method, cause, or mere semblance.
But as for this wholesome state dependent on turning away (vivaṭṭa), such as: here someone...

One who aspires for the turning away from the cycle of existence gives gifts, undertakes moral discipline, performs the observance-day rites, honors the physical shrine with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, listens to the Dhamma, teaches it, and realizes the meditative attainments (*jhānasamāpatti*);
by acting in this way, one gradually attains the deathless Nibbāna in its ultimate sense. This is the Dhamma of the method. Likewise, robes and so forth...
The four conditions are material gifts (*āmisa*) in the primary sense alone; they are not a gift by any other figurative way, reason, or pretext.
As for this skill pertaining to the round of existence—namely, when someone here, aspiring to the round and desiring a state of success, gives a gift...
[and so on] ...produces meditative attainments; acting in this way, he gradually attains the successes of gods and humans.
This is what is called "conventional material wealth.

In this regard, even the ultimate Dhamma belongs only to the Blessed One. For it is because of what was taught by the Blessed One that the bhikkhus attain the paths, fruits, and Nibbāna. Indeed, it has been said:
"For, brahmin, that Blessed One is the arouser of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path... and now his disciples abide following that path, having subsequently attained it."

“Thus, friends, the Blessed One knows what should be known and sees what should be seen; he is become vision, become knowledge, become the Dhamma, become the Brahma; he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the guide to the goal, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, even the methodical teaching (pariyāya-dhamma) belongs to the Blessed One alone. For it is precisely because it was spoken by the Blessed One that they know: “One who gives a gift aspiring for the turning away from the round of existence...
[and so on]... producing meditative attainments, gradually attains the Deathless Nibbāna.”

Even according to the non-figurative sense, this belongs to the Blessed One alone. For it was precisely because it had been permitted by the Blessed One that the monks obtained fine robes, beginning with the case of Jīvaka.
As he said: "Monks, I allow a householder’s robe. Whoever wishes may be a wearer of rag-robes; whoever wishes may accept a householder’s robe. Monks, I praise contentment with whatever one has."
In this way, the other requisites as well were permitted by the Blessed One and thus became available for the monks to use.

Even the food obtained in turn was the property of the Blessed One alone; for because it was spoken of by the Blessed One himself, they understood: "One who desires a state of prosperity, having given a gift, observed virtue...
[and so on]... and having produced meditative attainments, gradually attains the divine prosperity that is the food obtained in turn."
"And he obtains human excellence. Since both the ultimate Dhamma and the conventional Dhamma,
as well as the ultimate material gifts and the conventional material gifts, belong to the Blessed One alone,
he spoke thus, demonstrating his own ownership over them and directing them toward that which is most excellent and brings about absolute welfare and happiness.
“Of me, you are the legitimate sons... [etc. ...not heirs to material things.

Thus the Blessed One—whose undertaking of vows was complete, who had practiced asceticism, who had rightly lived the holy life, who was fully perfected in the most purified knowledge and conduct, who had reached the further shore of the Vedas without exception, who had cast out all evil, who was constantly devoted to self-sacrifice, and who had attained the state of being the unsurpassed recipient of offerings in the world with its devas—[spoke thus].
He proclaimed his own status as a brāhmaṇa in the ultimate sense, and the status of the noble disciples as his own legitimate sons and so forth.

For the Blessed One said: "‘Lion,’ monks, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One"—here he is like a lion—and "‘A man skilled in the path,’ Tissa, is a designation for the Tathāgata."
In this context, [the Tathāgata] is like the man who points out the path; he is like the king in the passage, “I am the King, O Sela”;
he is like the physician in the passage, “‘Physician, surgeon’—this, Sunakkhatta, is a designation for the Tathāgata”;
and he is like the brahmin in the passage, “‘Brahmin,’ monks, this is a designation for the Tathāgata.”
He spoke of himself. Here too, O Brahmin, he spoke by making a comparison.

Now, in order to demonstrate the supreme excellence of his own giving and other virtues—those very virtues through which outsiders consider the duties of a Brahmin to be fulfilled for one endowed with them—he said:
"Bhikkhus, there are these two kinds of giving," and so forth.
It has been undertaken. In this context, "sacrifices" (*yāga*) refers to great sacrifices (*mahāyañña*), meaning great gifts (*mahādāna*), which are also called "offerings" (*yiṭṭha*).

Among these, material sacrifices (*āmisa-yāga*) should be understood as those similar to the Velāma gift, the Vessantara gift, and the great sacrifice of victory; while Dhamma-sacrifices (*dhamma-yāga*) include the teachings found in the Mahāsamaya Sutta, the Maṅgala Sutta, the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta, the Sama-citta Sutta, and so forth.
The rest is exactly as explained below.
In this verse, *ayaji* means he gave. *Amaccharī* means free from stinginess, because all forms of stinginess were completely abandoned right at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
*Sabbabhūtānukampī* means one whose nature it is to favor all beings with great compassion as if they were his own dear son. For it has been said:
"Even toward Devadatta, the murderer, and the thief Aṅgulimāla..."
"Towards Dhanapāla and Rāhula alike, the Great Sage was even-minded.
The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the first sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Sulabha Sutta 101.
In the second [verse], "few" means limited. "Easy to obtain" means they can be acquired with ease, or they can be obtained anywhere.
"Blameless" means free from fault and devoid of blemish, because they are pure in their origin and lack the nature of being a basis for defilements such as bodily adornment.
In this context, by its being easily obtained, the absence of the suffering of seeking is shown; by its being not difficult to obtain, the absence of the suffering of maintaining is shown;
and by its being blameless and beyond reproach, its suitability for a bhikkhu is shown. Alternatively, by its being not difficult to obtain, it shows that there is no basis for fear;
by its being easily obtained, it shows that there is no basis for greed; and by its being blameless, it shows [the absence of danger] through the aspect of disadvantage (*ādīnava*).
The state of being a basis for the wisdom of escape is thus demonstrated. Because they are not difficult to obtain, gain does not produce joy;

because they are easily obtained, loss does not produce grief; and because they are blameless, they do not produce the equanimity of ignorance that is a cause for remorse, since they serve as a basis for non-remorse.
*Paṃsukūla*: It is called *paṃsukūla* in the sense of being "raised up" (*abbhuggata*) because it stands upon dust in places such as carriage-roads, cemeteries, or heaps of refuse;
or it is called *paṃsukūla* because it "goes toward" (*ulati*) a state of loathsomeness like dust.
It refers to a robe made by collecting rags fallen on carriage-roads and other such places.
"Alms-food in lumps" means food obtained by walking for alms from house to house with the strength of one's shanks, taking only as much as can be held in a single mouthful.
"At the root of a tree" means any place near a tree that is suitable for seclusion. "Putrid urine" means any cow's urine.
For just as the body, though it may be gold-colored, is indeed a putrid body, so too even fresh urine is indeed putrid urine. In this regard:
Some say that "rotten urine" (*pūtimutta*) refers to a piece of myrobalan fruit (*haritakī*) treated with cow’s urine;

others maintain that "rotten urine" refers to any medicinal substance whatsoever that has been discarded, cast away, or abandoned from a market or elsewhere due to its state of decay, and is thus unclaimed.
The phrase *yato kho* is an ablative used in the sense of a locative (*paccatte nissakkavacana*); it means "from which," as in the expression "he is satisfied."

He clings to what has been said. "Contented" means fully satisfied. "Thinking, 'This is enough for me'"—this contentment with the fourfold requisites as previously described, being few and easily obtained—I declare this to be one factor of asceticism (*sāmaññaṅga*), a cause for the state of a recluse (*samaṇabhāva*), among the various factors such as the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*) for this bhikkhu.
For in one who is contented, there is the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*).
It becomes perfectly fulfilled, and both serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) reach the fullness of their development. Alternatively, "recluseship" (*sāmañña*) is the Noble Path.
Briefly, it has two factors: the external and the internal. Therein, the external consists of reliance upon a true person (*sappurisa*) and hearing the True Dhamma;
the internal, however, consists of wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) and practice in accordance with the Dhamma (*dhammānudhammapaṭipatti*).

And among those, because these qualities— namely, fewness of wishes, contentment, seclusion, non-association, and the arousal of energy— are both the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhammapaṭipatti) appropriate to that [state] and its very root,
it is therefore said: "I declare this to be one of its factors of asceticism."
In the verses, "concerning lodgings" (*senāsana*) means with reference to monasteries (*vihāra*) and so forth, as well as beds, chairs, and other such furniture.
"Robes, drinks, and food" (*cīvara-pānabhojana*) refers to robes such as the lower garment (*nivāsana*), drinks such as mango juice, and edible items such as solid and soft foods;

this is how the connection is to be understood. "There is no distress" (*vighāta*)—that is, the state of being afflicted or mental suffering—is the construction [of the sentence]. This, in brief, is the meaning here.
For those who are discontented while seeking lodgings and so forth— either by going to places where requisites are easily obtained,
thinking "I shall get it," or by falling into disputes, saying "It falls to me, not to you," or through performing building work and the like—
the distress that arises in their minds due to not obtaining what they desire does not exist for one who is content in that regard.
"It exists. "It is not obstructed by the quarters" means that because of its state of being "four-quarted" through contentment, it is not obstructed by the quarters. For this has been said:
"He is four-quarted and unobstructed, being content with whatever comes his way."
For one in whom the thought arises, "I shall obtain robes and other requisites having gone to such-and-such a place," the directions are said to be obstructed.
But for one in whom such a thought does not arise, the directions are said to be unobstructed.
"Dhammas" refers to the dhammas of practice. "Conducive to the state of a recluse" means conducive to the development of serenity and insight, which constitute the dhamma of a recluse.
Or rather, fewness of wishes and so forth are appropriate to the Noble Path itself.
"Attained" means that all these have been attained by a bhikkhu with a contented mind— one who has overcome opposing states—
and are thus grasped, having entered within, not remaining outside.
The commentary on the second sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Āsavakkhaya-sutta* (102).
Regarding the third [sutta]: "Of one who knows" (*jānato*) means of one who knows; "of one who sees" (*passato*) means of one who sees. Although these two phrases—
The meaning is one, only the phrasing is different. Even so, by taking the characteristic of knowledge (*ñāṇalakkhaṇa*) as "of one who knows," he designates the person.
For knowledge has the characteristic of knowing. By taking the power of knowledge (*ñāṇappabhāva*) as "of one who sees":
for, by taking the power of seeing, a person endowed with knowledge is like a person with eyes [seeing] forms with their eyes; [he sees] what is opened by knowledge.

He sees the Dhamma. Alternatively, "of one who knows" means knowing by means of the knowledge of subsequent realization (*anubodha-ñāṇa*); "of one who sees" means seeing by means of the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*).

Or, conversely, it refers to seeing by means of the path of vision (*dassana-magga*) and knowing by means of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-magga*). Some, however, say: "Of one who knows by means of the full understandings of what is known, investigated, and abandoned, and of one who sees by means of insight that has reached its culmination.
Alternatively, [it refers to] suffering through the clear realization of full understanding (*pariññā-abhisamaya*).

When one knows and sees cessation through the clear comprehension of realization (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*), then, both [cessation and the path] being present, the clear comprehensions of abandoning (*pahāna*) and development (*bhāvanā*) are necessarily established;

thus, the clear comprehension of the Four Noble Truths is stated. Furthermore, when insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) is intended here, the phrases "knowing" and "seeing" should be understood as indicating the sense of cause (*hetu*). However, when path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*) is intended...
When that is intended, it serves to illustrate the function and purpose of the Path.

This is seen in such scriptural passages as the discourse on the restraint of all taints: "Monks, I say that for one who knows and sees, there is the destruction of the taints," as well as in passages such as, "Through the destruction of the taints, there is the taintless liberation of mind."
The abandoning of the taints (*āsava*), their absolute destruction, non-arising, state of being exhausted, and state of non-existence is called “the destruction of the taints” (*āsavakkhaya*).
In such passages as “Through the destruction of the taints, one is a recluse (*samaṇa*),” it refers to the fruit.
[As for the verse: “For one who observes the faults of others, constantly perceiving grounds for reproach;”
His taints increase; he is far from the destruction of the taints.”—In such passages as these, it is *nibbāna*.
“For the trainee who is still in training, following the straight path;”
“First there is knowledge of destruction; immediately after that, higher knowledge (aññā);
then there is the knowledge of one liberated by higher knowledge, such a one (tādin).
Since the path is spoken of as “the destruction of the taints” in this context, just as it is in the Indriya Sutta cited above, [it follows] by the method already stated...
The meaning is: "I speak of the attainment of the Noble Path for one who knows and sees;
not for one who does not know and does not see. By this, he rejects those who claim that purification from *saṃsāra* occurs even for one who neither knows nor sees.
Alternatively, by the first two phrases, the means (*upāya*) [is indicated].

By this, the prohibition of what is not a means is stated. Furthermore, it shows here in brief that knowledge is what brings about the destruction of the taints (āsava), while the rest are its requisites.
Now, in order to show that which, when known and seen, leads to the destruction of the taints, [the Buddha asks]: "And what, bhikkhus, for one who knows...?"
He began the tail [of the treatise]. In this regard, knowledge is of many kinds. For some monk, by his very nature, knows how to make a sunshade;
another knows how to make one of the various requisites such as robes.

When such a person performs these tasks while standing at the head of the observance (vatta), that knowledge cannot be said to "not be a proximate cause for the paths and fruits. However, [that which pertains] to one in the Dispensation...
Having gone forth, one may know how to perform medical treatments and such; for one who knows in this way, the taints (āsava) only increase.
Therefore, showing precisely that which leads to the destruction of the taints for one who knows and sees, [the Buddha] said: "This is suffering," and so forth.
Regarding that, what ought to be said concerning the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths has already been stated in brief below in the *Yonisomanasikāra Sutta*.

In that context, however, because it is stated: "Bhikkhus, by attending wisely (*yoniso manasikaronto*), a bhikkhu abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome," the exposition of the meaning was made by way of the passage beginning, "He attends wisely, 'This is suffering. Here, however, because it is stated:
"Bhikkhus, for one who knows and sees, 'This is suffering,' there is the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*)," [the exposition is made] by way of the passage beginning, "This is suffering..."

It should be applied according to the method beginning with: “For one who knows and sees ‘it is suffering’ by way of penetration through full understanding and by way of the clear realization of full understanding, there is the destruction of the taints (āsava) through path-knowledge.

Furthermore, it should be understood that among the taints, the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava) is destroyed by the first path, the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) by the third path, and the taint of existence (bhavāsava) and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava) by the fourth path.
In the verses, "knowledge of liberation" (*vimuttiñāṇa*) refers to the reviewing knowledge regarding liberation, Nibbāna, and the fruit.

"Supreme" (*uttama*) means supreme because it has the supreme Dhamma as its object. "Knowledge of destruction" (*khaye ñāṇa*) is the knowledge regarding the destruction of the taints (*āsava*) and the fetters (*saṃyojana*), and regarding the Noble Path which effects that destruction.
The phrase "the knowledge that 'the fetters are destroyed'" should also be brought forward and connected here. By that...
This demonstrates the reviewing of defilements already abandoned. Thus, all four kinds of reviewing knowledge are mentioned here.
Indeed, there is no reviewing of remaining defilements here, because the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship is intended.
And just as it was stated here, "of one who knows and sees," by emphasizing the function of right view through the attainment of Nibbāna;
Showing that the function of the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*) must likewise be desired as something superior, he spoke the concluding verse: "But this is not [attained] by one who is indolent.
Herein, *na tvevidaṃ* means "but indeed not this. The word *tu* is a mere particle. The letter *m* in *bālena-m-avijānatā* serves to join the words.
This is the summary of the meaning here: this [state] to be attained by the path of training (*sekkhamagga*) and the path of no-more-training (*asekkhamagga*).
Liberation from all fetters, beginning with the bodily fetter of covetousness, and Nibbāna, which is the sign of such liberation—
just as this cannot be attained by one who is foolish and ignorant because they do not understand the Four Truths, "This is suffering," and so forth, as they truly are,
so too it cannot be attained by one who is indolent and lacking in energy; therefore, for the sake of attaining that, one must apply energy.
"It must be brought about. Therefore the Blessed One said: "This Dhamma is for one who has aroused energy, not for one who is indolent.
'Exert yourselves, strive, apply yourselves to the Buddha’s teaching;
shake off the army of Death as an elephant shakes down a house of reeds.'"
The commentary on the Third Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta. 103.
In the fourth [sutta], "whosoever" (*ye hi keci*) means whoever. "They do not understand as it really is: 'This is suffering'" (*idaṃ dukkhaṃ*... *yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti*) means: "This..."

“Suffering, so much suffering, not more than this”—they do not know and do not penetrate the truth of suffering with the wisdom of the path accompanied by insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*), according to its true nature, essence, and characteristic.
The same method applies to the remaining truths as well.
Regarding the passage beginning “Not those, monks,” the summary meaning is as follows: monks, those who are not devoted to the meditation subject of the Four Truths...

Those who are ascetics merely by their renunciation and brahmins merely by their birth—such as these—I have not recognized or authorized as "ascetics" among those ascetics who have stilled evil, nor as "brahmins" among those brahmins who have banished evil. Why?

Because they lack the qualities that make one an ascetic and the qualities that make one a brahmin. For this very reason, he said, "But those venerable ones... and so forth. In that context, "the goal of asceticism" (sāmaññattha) means...
The meaning of "the goal of recluseship" (*sāmaññattha*) is the four fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*); "the goal of the divine life" (*brahmaññattha*) is a synonym for that same thing.
Others, however, say: "The goal of recluseship refers to the four noble paths (*ariyamagga*), while the goal of the divine life refers to the four noble fruits (*ariyaphala*).
The rest is exactly as previously stated. The white side (*sukkapakkha*) should be understood by reversing what has been said.
There is nothing new in the verses.
The commentary on the fourth sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Sīlasampanna Sutta.

104. Regarding the phrase "endowed with virtue" (*sīlasampannā*) in the fifth [section]: here, "virtue" (*sīla*) refers to the mundane and supramundane virtue of those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).

Those who are endowed with, or possessed of, that are "endowed with virtue. The same method applies to concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*paññā*). Liberation (*vimutti*), however, is specifically the liberation of the fruit (*phalavimutti*);

the "knowledge and vision of liberation" (*vimuttiñāṇadassana*) is the knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*). Thus, in this context, the three beginning with virtue are both mundane and supramundane.
Liberation is exclusively supramundane, whereas the knowledge and vision of liberation is mundane.

They are "instructors" because they exhort and instruct others as appropriate according to the truths pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal. They are "informers" because they inform [others] regarding kamma and the fruits of kamma;
therein they inform [them]: "These states are wholesome; these states are unwholesome. These states are blameworthy..."

"By such statements as 'these phenomena are blameless,' they are the informers and awakeners of phenomena through various methods—by way of the classification into wholesome and so forth, by way of the classification into aggregates and so forth, by way of specific characteristics, and by way of general characteristics. They are the 'showers' (sandassakā) because they show those very same phenomena directly to others as if taking them by the hand.
They are the 'inciters' (samādapakā) because [they encourage] that virtue and so forth which has not yet been undertaken."
They are those who cause him to undertake [the practice], and they are those who establish him therein.

"Encouragers" (*samuttejakā*) means they properly incite the mind by way of directing it toward the further application of higher consciousness (*adhicitta*) for those already established in wholesome states;

they are inspirers by way of reflection so that a specific attainment may occur. "Gladdeners" (*sampahaṃsakā*) means [they gladden him] by means of what has been attained and what is yet to be attained above that.
And they are those who rightly encourage the mind by means of specific qualities (*guṇavisesa*), and who thoroughly satisfy it by way of providing a taste [of the Dhamma].
"Adequate instructors" (*alaṃsamakkhātāro*) means instructors who, without omitting anything as previously described, teach [the Dhamma] precisely with the intention of being helpful.

Alternatively, "showers" (*sandassakā*) refers to those who, while teaching the Dhamma, correctly [point out] the processes of engagement and withdrawal according to their essential nature and intrinsic characteristics.
"Showers" (*dassetāro*). "Exhorters" (*samādapakā*) means those who cause others to grasp that very same meaning by way of establishing it in the mind.

"Inciters" (*samuttejakā*) means those who properly encourage or illuminate by generating enthusiasm for grasping that meaning. "Gladdeners" (*sampahaṃsakā*) means those who properly gladden or satisfy by showing the benefits in the practice of that meaning.
"Adequate exponents" (*alaṃsamakkhātāro*) means being capable [of teaching] in the manner described.
"Proclaimers. "Of the true Dhamma" means of the true Dhamma of realization, or of the threefold true Dhamma;
they are the teachers of it. "I say even seeing": there are two kinds of seeing—seeing with the eye and seeing with knowledge.
Therein, looking upon the Noble Ones with eyes full of faith is called "seeing with the eye. [Regarding] those things that produce the state of a Noble One...
Furthermore, the realization of the noble nature of phenomena through insight, the path, and the fruits is called "knowledge and vision" (*ñāṇadassana*).

However, in this context, "seeing with the eye" (*cakkhudassana*) is intended. For even the mere looking upon beings by the eyes of those who have confidence in the Noble Ones is of great benefit to them.
As for "hearing": [one hears that] "a certain one named so-and-so, whose taints are destroyed, lives in such-and-such a kingdom..."
Hearing with one's own ears those who are saying, "He dwells in a country, or a village, or a town, or a monastery, or a cave"—this too is indeed very helpful.
Approaching means approaching the Noble Ones with such a thought as: "I will give a gift, or I will ask a question, or I will listen to the Dhamma, or I will pay honor."

“Attending upon” (payirupāsana) means attending upon [them] with questions; the meaning is: having heard of the virtues of the Noble Ones, one approaches them, invites them, gives a gift, or performs a service, and then asks questions in the manner of “What, venerable sir, is wholesome? and so forth.
Performing services and the like is also a form of attending upon. “Recollection” (anussaraṇa) refers to [recollection] while staying in night-quarters or day-quarters.

For one who is seated, it is the recollection having as its object the specific qualities of their divine abodes and so forth, thinking: "Now the Noble Ones are spending their time in the caves, rock shelters, pavilions, and other such places, experiencing the bliss of jhāna, insight, the path, and the fruit.
Or, having brought to mind the instruction received from them, [one reflects]: "In this place, virtue was taught; in this, concentration; in this, insight."
Recollection is thus: "In this [path], in this fruit.
Following after [the going forth] means: having inspired confidence in the minds of the Noble Ones, one goes forth from the household life in their presence.
For it is by inspiring confidence in the minds of the Noble Ones, going forth in their very presence, and following their very instruction and exhortation...
Even for one who lives while hoping for [instruction] from others, it is called "following the going-forth";
even for one who lives while hoping for advice and instruction in the presence of others, it is called "following the going-forth";

and even for one who has gone forth elsewhere out of confidence in the Noble Ones and lives while hoping for advice and instruction in the presence of the Noble Ones, it is indeed "following the going-forth."

However, for one who goes forth out of faith in others but receives ordination in the presence of those very others while expecting instruction and guidance from yet others as he wanders about, that is not called "following in the footsteps" (anupabbajjā) of the going-forth.
Among those who went forth according to the method already described, there were approximately one hundred thousand who followed in the footsteps of the Elder Mahākassapa’s own going-forth;
likewise, there were those who followed in the footsteps of the Elder’s own student (saddhivihārika).
[The lineage continued] with the elder Candagutta, his co-resident (saddhivihārika) the elder Sūriyagutta, his co-resident the elder Assagutta, and his co-resident the elder Yonakadhammarakkhita.
Now, the co-resident of that [last-named] was the elder named Tissa, the younger brother of King Asoka. Following him in the going-forth (anupabbajjā)...
Those who went forth numbered two and a half crores; however, there is no limit to the number of those who followed in the footsteps of the Great Elder Mahinda, the illuminator of the Island.
To this very day, those who go forth out of faith in the Teacher on the island of Laṅkā are said to follow in the lineage of the Great Elder Mahinda himself.
Now, in order to show the reason why seeing those Noble Ones and so forth is of great benefit—as was stated—he said, "In such [persons]," and so on.
Therein, "in such" (*tathārūpe*) means in a Noble One endowed with qualities such as virtue (*sīla*).
Since seeing, hearing, and recollecting are occasions for approaching and attending upon, he did not mention those [first three], but rather specifically mentioned approaching and attending upon.
To demonstrate this, it is said: "serving, associating with, and attending upon.
For one who has developed faith in the Noble Ones through seeing, hearing, and recollecting them, approaches them, attends upon them, and asks questions;

having thus obtained the unsurpassed excellence of hearing, they will fulfill those qualities such as virtue that were previously incomplete. Thus it is said: "Having conceived faith, he approaches; approaching, he attends upon," and so forth.
In this context, "serves" (*sevatī*) means approaching from time to time by way of performing the major and minor duties (*vatta-paṭivatta*).
"Frequents" (*bhajati*) means associating with him out of affection and devotion. "Attends upon" (*payirupāsati*) means attending upon him by asking questions and emulating his practice;

thus the analysis of the meaning of these three terms should be illustrated. The fulfillment of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimutti-ñāṇadassana*) occurs through the nineteenth type of knowledge, which is retrospective knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa*).
[This] is to be understood by way of their arising.

And as for the passage beginning, "Such monks as these, bhikkhus," and so forth: those monks who, by virtue of being endowed with the aforementioned qualities, are "such" (evarūpā) and "of this kind" (edisā)—having shattered all defilements—and who instruct by way of directing sentient beings toward welfare pertaining to the present life and so forth, [are meant].
They are called "Teachers" (satthāro). They are also called "Caravan Leaders" (satthavāhā) because they lead [beings] across the wilderness of birth and so forth;

"Abandoners of Strife" (raṇañjahā) because they abandon and cause others to abandon the strifes of passion and the like; "Dispellers of Darkness" (tamonudā) because they dispel and cause others to dispel the darkness of ignorance;
and "Producers of Light and so forth" because they produce and generate the light of wisdom, the radiance of wisdom, and the lamp of wisdom within their own and others' continuums.
Likewise, they are called "torch-bearers" (ukkā-dhārā) because they bear and produce the torches of knowledge and the light of the Dhamma; they are called "light-makers" (pabhaṅkara);

they are called "Noble Ones" (ariya) because they are far removed from defilements, because they do not proceed in what is not the right way, because they proceed in the right way, because they are the cause for others to become such as they are, and because they are to be sought after by the world including the devas;
and [they are so called] through the exceptional acquisition of the eye of wisdom and the eye of Dhamma.
They are also called "possessors of vision.
In the verses, the phrase "a ground for gladness" refers to a ground or cause that produces spiritual joy (*pāmujja*)—that is, joy free from worldly attachment (*nirāmisa*).
The word "this" (*etaṃ*) is said with reference to what is about to be stated. "By those who understand" means by those who [know] defilement and purification as they truly are.
"Of those who know. "Of those whose nature is cultivated" (*bhāvitattānaṃ*) means those whose mental continuum has been cultivated through the cultivation of the body and so forth;

this is the meaning. "Those who live by the Dhamma" means because they have abandoned wrong livelihood and maintain their existence through the Dhamma and the proper method, or because they sustain their personal being through the Dhamma and the proper method, or because they live by means of the Dhamma of the highest fruit due to their abundance of meditative attainments.

"Those who live by the Dhamma. This is the meaning in brief: namely, the sight of Noble Ones (ariya) who have developed themselves and perfected the cultivation of concentration and wisdom, and who for that very reason live by the Dhamma.

For those of wise nature who understand this—because it is the cause for the fulfillment of the factors such as virtue which are the signs of non-remorse—it is exclusively a cause for rapture and gladness.
Now, in order to demonstrate that causal relationship, he spoke the final two stanzas beginning with “They illuminate.
Therein, “they” (te) refers to those Noble Ones (ariya) who have cultivated themselves and live by the Dhamma. “Illuminate” (jotayanti) means they make manifest.

“Proclaim” (bhāsayanti) means they cause the world to shine with the radiance of the True Dhamma; the meaning is that they teach the Dhamma. “Of whom” (yesaṃ) refers to those Noble Ones. “The teaching” (sāsanaṃ) refers to their instruction (ovāda).
"By having fully understood" means having understood correctly by means of the preliminary knowledges (*pubbabhāgañāṇa*). The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Taṇhuppāda Sutta.
105. Regarding the sixth [section], *taṇhuppādā*: here, "arising" (*uppādā*) means that which arises within these things. What arises? Craving (*taṇhā*). The arising of craving is *taṇhuppādā*;
the meaning is the bases for craving, the causes of craving. *Yattha* means in those things that serve as the objective signs (*nimitta*).
*Uppajjamānā* means having the nature of arising. *Cīvarahetu* means for the sake of robes, with the thought: "Where shall I obtain pleasing robes?"—that is, on account of robes.
It arises. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well. Regarding the expression *itibhavābhavahetu*:
here, *iti* is a particle used in the sense of illustration (*nidassana*). The meaning is: "Just as [there is a cause] for robes and so forth, so too there is a cause for existence and non-existence.

Furthermore, by "existence and non-existence" (*bhavābhava*) here, excellent and inferior things such as ghee and fresh butter are intended, because one becomes healthy (*bhavati*) by means of them. [This refers to] "the more or less excellent states among the states of prosperity."
They also say "existence and non-existence. "Existence" means success; "non-existence" means failure. "Existence" means increase; "non-existence" means decrease.
And because craving arises with that as its sign, it is said: "or for the sake of existence and non-existence. The meaning of the verse has already been explained above.
Furthermore, "having craving as his companion" means having craving as his associate. For this being, throughout the beginningless cycle of rebirths...
Wandering through the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), one does not wander alone; rather, having obtained craving as a companion and partner, one wanders.

For just like a hunter who, disregarding the danger of falling into a pit, sees only the honey while seeking to seize it, that [craving] causes one to roam within the net of misfortune, showing only advantages even amidst existences crowded with manifold dangers. "Having understood this danger" means...
Having understood this danger—known as the state of being thus or otherwise—in the aggregates of the past, future, and present;
and having understood craving to be the origin of suffering, thinking, "This craving is the origin, the source, and the cause of the suffering of the round of existence.
By this much, the arising of Arahantship is shown for a certain bhikkhu who has developed insight.
Now, in order to praise that one whose taints are exhausted, he said, "Free from craving," and so forth. Whatever has not been stated here follows the same method as explained below.
The commentary on the sixth sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Sabrahmakasutta.
106. "In the seventh [verse], *sabrahmakāni* means 'together with the best. *Yesaṃ* means 'of those families.
*Puttānaṃ*—this genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental, because of its connection with the word *puttehi pūjita* ('honored by sons'). *Ajjhāgāre* means 'in their own home.
*Pūjitā honti* means 'they are honored,' that is, they are looked after with whatever is available in the house, and attended to with what is pleasing through both bodily and verbal actions."

Thus, having praised families that honor their mother and father as "possessing Brahmā" (*sabrahmakāni*), he spoke the words beginning with "possessing the ancient deities" (*sapubbadevatāni*) in order to show further grounds for their praise.
In this context, the terms "Brahmā" and so forth are stated for the purpose of establishing their status as Brahmā and the rest. Herein, this is the exposition of the meaning:

"Brahmā" is a designation for the supreme. For just as the four meditative developments—loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity—are never abandoned by Brahmā, so too these four meditative developments are never abandoned by parents toward their children.
These should be understood at their respective times: for when the child is still in the womb, [the mother thinks], "When indeed shall my little son be free from illness?"... [and so forth].
"May we see him with all his limbs and members complete"—thus does a mind of loving-kindness arise in the parents.

But when this infant, lying on his back, is bitten by lice or bedbugs, or is oppressed by the pain of illness, and he cries out and wails, then upon hearing his sound, compassion arises in the parents. They run hither and thither.

But at the time of play, or when he has reached an age that is sexually attractive, the parents’ minds—upon looking at their son—become soft, joyful, and delighted, like a layer of cotton-wool split into a hundred pieces and dipped in the cream of ghee;
at that time, joy (muditā) is obtained by them. But when their son, having established his own household, stands apart...
When he dwells in the household, his parents think, "Now our son is able to live according to his own nature," and a state of equanimity arises.

Thus, at that time, equanimity is attained. In this way, because the fourfold divine abode (brahmavihāra) is attained by parents toward their children at the appropriate times, it is said that they lead a life similar to that of the Brahmās.
“Brahmā, monks, is a designation for one’s mother and father.

Regarding the phrase “former deities,” there are three kinds of deities here: conventional deities (*sammutideva*), deities by birth (*upapattideva*), and deities through purification (*visuddhideva*).
Among these, conventional deities are kings and nobles; for they are addressed in the world as “Your Majesty” and “Her Majesty,” and thus are called *devas*.
They are capable of both punishing and favoring the world. "Devas by birth" refers to beings born from the Realm of the Four Great Kings up to the peak of existence (*bhavagga*).
"Devas by purity" refers to those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), due to their purification from all defilements (*kilesa*).
Herein, this is the etymological meaning: they shine, they play, they sport, they illuminate, or they conquer their adversaries; thus they are called *devas*.
The gods. Among them, the most excellent are the *visuddhidevas* (purified gods).

Just as they disregard any offense committed by foolish people and, desiring solely their welfare, the removal of harm, and the arising of benefit, proceed for their sake, welfare, and happiness through the practice of the aforementioned divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), so too do they bring about the great fruitfulness of those deeds due to the worthiness of being recipients of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyyatā*).
And they bring about great benefits; even so, parents— disregarding the faults of their children and desiring solely their loss of harm and the arising of welfare—

by practicing for the sake, benefit, and happiness of those children through the attainment of the fourfold divine abode (brahmavihāra) in the manner described, become supremely worthy of offerings for the [merit] performed toward themselves.
They bring about great fruitfulness and great benefit for their deeds. Because they were the first to be helpful among all the gods, they are "gods" from the very beginning.
It is by means of them that others first recognize other beings as "gods," propitiate them, and attend upon them;
having understood the method of propitiation and practicing accordingly, they attain the fruit of that practice.
Therefore, they are called "the deities who come later. Thus it was said: "‘The deities who come first,’ monks, is a designation for mother and father.
"The former teachers" means the primary teachers. For when parents instruct their children, from the time they are very young, they say:
"Sit thus; walk thus; stand thus; lie down thus; eat this; consume that. This...
They take them in hand and instruct them, saying: "This one should be addressed as 'father,' this one as 'brother,' this one as 'sister';
it is proper to give such-and-such a name, it is not proper to give such-and-such; it is proper to approach such-and-such a person, it is not proper to approach such-and-such.
Later on, other teachers also instruct them in crafts, finger-calculation, arithmetic, and so forth.
Others provide refuges, establish them in the precepts, grant them the going-forth, cause them to learn the Dhamma, confer full ordination, and lead them to the path of stream-entry and so forth;
thus all these are called "later teachers. But parents are the very first.
Therefore it was said: "Bhikkhus, 'former teachers' is a designation for one's mother and father."
“Āhuneyyā” means that which is to be brought and offered, thus it is called *āhuna*.

This is the name for food, drink, clothing, coverings, and so forth, which should be given to those possessing virtuous qualities by one who desires a specific fruit even after bringing them from afar.

Because they are worthy recipients (*upakārakhettatāya*), they are “worthy of offerings” (*āhuneyyā*). Therefore it was said: “‘Worthy of offerings,’ monks, this is a designation for mother and father.”
Now, in order to show the reason for their being designated as "Brahmā" and so forth, it was said:
"For what reason? Because they are of great service," and so on. "For what reason? means: for what cause is that designation of mother and father as "Brahmā" and so forth?
"Of great service" means those who provide much assistance. "Nurturers" (āpādaka) means those who bring about and protect life; for children [are nurtured] by their mother and father.
Life has been brought forth, protected, striven for, maintained through continuous succession, and accomplished.
"Nourishers" means those who nourish them by making their hands and feet grow and by feeding them with the blood of their own hearts.

"Showers of this world" means that for children, the perception of desirable and undesirable objects in this world arises in dependence upon mother and father; therefore, they [are called] "showers" of these things.
They are called "revealers of this world. Thus, their great helpfulness is shown to be the cause for attaining the state of Brahmā and so forth;
by which means a son is simply unable, in any way whatsoever, to make a limited return for the worldly assistance rendered by his parents.
For even if a son were to think, "I shall make a reciprocal return for the assistance given by my parents," [he could not do so].
Even if one were to rise again and again, exerting oneself to carry one’s mother on the right shoulder and one’s father on the other,
and were to live for a full hundred years— providing them with the four requisites and serving them according to their wishes by anointing,
massaging, bathing, rubbing, and so forth, without ever feeling disgust even at their urine and excrement— a son would not have fulfilled his duty merely by that much.
A repayment to one’s mother and father is accomplished only by establishing them in special qualities such as faith; for this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, I declare that there are two for whom it is impossible to repay. Which two? A mother and a father.
Suppose, bhikkhus, one were to carry one’s mother on one shoulder and one’s father on the other shoulder for a hundred years, [and they were long-lived]...”
Even if one were to live for a hundred years, massaging, rubbing, bathing, and anointing them,
and they were to discharge their urine and excrement right there [upon one], still, monks, that would not constitute having done or repaid what was due to one’s mother and father.
And even if one were to exercise sovereign lordship over this great earth, abounding in the seven precious gems, over one’s mother and father...
Even if one were to establish them in sovereignty, monks, that would not constitute having done or repaid what was done for one’s mother and father.
Why is that? Monks, mothers and fathers are of great service to their children; they are their nurturers, their sustainers, and those who show them this world.
But, monks, when one encourages, settles, and establishes one’s mother and father in the perfection of faith where they lacked faith—[that is what truly repays them].
One encourages, settles, and establishes the immoral in the perfection of virtue; the stingy in the perfection of generosity;
and the unwise in the perfection of wisdom. To this extent, monks, parents have been both honored and repaid.
Likewise—
“Attending upon mother and father, supporting wife and children”—
and “Attending upon mother and father, bhikkhus, is prescribed by the wise”—
such suttas as these should be seen as establishing the great helpfulness that parents have for their child.

"In the verses it is said" means they are spoken or recited. "Compassionate toward their offspring" means that even after taking the lives of others or giving away whatever belongs to themselves, they look after and protect their own offspring;
therefore, they are compassionate toward and supportive of their own children.
"One should pay homage" means that, having gone to attend upon them morning and evening, one should offer salutation, thinking: "This is my supreme field of merit.
"One should honor" means one should revere with honor. Now, in order to show what that honoring consists of, he said: "With food," and so forth.
Therein, "with food" refers to rice gruel, boiled rice, and hard foods; "with drink" refers to the eight kinds of beverages.
"By clothing" means by the lower garment and the upper robe. "By bedding" means by a bed, chair, couch, pillow, and so forth.
"By anointing" means by anointing that dispels foul odors and produces fragrance.
"By bathing" means by sprinkling the limbs with warm water during the cold season and with cool water during the hot season, thereby performing the act of bathing. "By washing the feet."
And by means of washing the feet with warm water and cold water, as well as by anointing them with oil.

Regarding the phrase "by that service" (*tāya naṃ pāricariyāya*): here, *naṃ* is merely a particle; it refers to the aforementioned attendance. Alternatively, "by service" (*pāricariyāya*) refers to the fivefold nursing, such as performing the duty of supporting them, establishing the family lineage, and so forth. For this has been said:
"In five ways, householder’s son, should a son attend upon his mother and father as the eastern quarter."
‘I will support those who supported me; I will perform their duties; I will maintain the family lineage; I will provide for their inheritance;
or else, when they have passed away as departed spirits, I will offer them funeral oblations.
It is in these five ways, householder’s son, that parents are attended by a son as the eastern quarter. And in five ways... [the parents] attend him.

“They show compassion for their children: they restrain them from evil, establish them in what is wholesome, train them in a craft, provide them with a suitable wife, and at the proper time, hand over the inheritance.
Furthermore, one who inspires confidence in one’s parents in three respects, or establishes them in the precepts, or [encourages] them in the going forth...
Or having appointed [another], she attends [to them]; this person should be known as the foremost among those who attend to their mother and father.
Furthermore, showing that this service brings benefit and happiness to the son in both worlds, he said: "In this very world they praise him, and after death he rejoices in heaven.
In this context, "here" means in this world. For regarding the person who attends to his mother and father—
Wise people praise, extol, and laud service rendered there;
following his example, they too practice in such a manner toward their own parents and generate great merit.
"Having passed away" means that having gone to the other world and established in heaven, the one who attended upon his parents rejoices, exults, and delights in divine splendors.
The commentary on the seventh sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Bahukāra-sutta* (Sutta 107):
"Brahmin householders" (*brāhmaṇagahapatikā*) means both brahmins and householders. Excluding the brahmins...
"Whoever dwell in a house here should be understood as householders (*gahapatika*). *Ye* is an indefinite demonstrative pronoun used for reference.
*Vā* is the plural accusative case ending. This is the summary of the meaning here:
"O monks, the brahmins and householders are of great benefit to you; those who are both brahmins and other householders [think], 'You alone are our field of merit (*puññakkhetta*')."
"Where we may establish an uplifted offering that leads to heaven, has a pleasant result, and conduces to rebirth in the celestial realms"—
thus they attend upon them with requisites such as robes and so forth.
In this way, "by the gift of material things, by the sharing of material things, and by assistance with material things, householders are benefactors of the bhikkhus."

Having thus shown [the benefit], he now said, "You too, monks," and so forth, in order to show that those monks are also recipients of assistance through the gift of Dhamma, the sharing of Dhamma, and the support of Dhamma; this is exactly as previously explained.
What is expressed by this? It is called "honoring the alms-round. This is the intended meaning here: "Monks,..."
Since these brahmins and householders are neither your relatives, nor your friends, nor do they owe you anything, but rather—thinking, "These ascetics have gone the right way and practiced rightly;
here our offerings will be of great fruit and great benefit"—they attend upon you with robes and other requisitions out of a desire for a specific result. Therefore, that [offering] of theirs...

"Fulfilling the intention, accomplish this through diligence; for the teaching of the Dhamma shines only upon those who act, and it is acceptable to them, not to others"—thus, diligence in right practice is to be undertaken.
Such is the brief meaning of "Thus, monks," and so forth: monks, in this manner, by the way already described...

This holy life of the Dispensation (sāsanabrahmacariya) is for the purpose of crossing over the fourfold flood— consisting of sensual desire and the rest— by means of mutual reliance through the giving of material goods and the giving of the Dhamma by both householders and those gone forth;

and it is for the sake of bringing about the complete and perfect end of all the suffering of saṃsāra by means of the observance of the Uposatha precepts, the rules of conduct, or the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla).
"And the holy life of the path is lived and practiced.
In the verses, "those with a home" (*sāgārā*) refers to householders; "those without a home" (*anagārā*) refers to those who have renounced the home and gone forth.
"Both dependent on one another" means that both are mutually reliant. For householders are reliant on those without a home through the gift of the Dhamma, and those without a home...

And they are dependent on the laypeople’s provision of requisites. "Attaining" means they accomplish and fulfill. "The true Dhamma" refers to both the true Dhamma of practice and the true Dhamma of penetration.
Showing therein that which is supreme, he said: "the unsurpassed security from bondage," which is Arahantship and Nibbāna.
"Among the householders" means by the householders; this is a locative expression used in the sense of the ablative.
"From those with a roof" means from householders. "Requisites" refers to the two remaining types of requisites already mentioned: almsfood and medicine.
"Dispelling of dangers" refers to dwellings such as monasteries that remove dangers like the dangers of climate.
"One who has fared well" (*sugata*) refers to one who has practiced rightly, including both the noble persons of eight types and the virtuous worldlings (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*). For a disciple...
"Here, 'the Sugata' is intended. 'House-seekers' means those seeking a house;
the meaning is that, remaining in the home and living the household life, they are of a nature to seek both the requisites for enjoyment and the virtues of a householder.
'Having faith in the Arahants' means having faith in the words of the noble Arahants, or in their perfect practice. 'Truly, these [are] right..."
The meaning is: "having full confidence" that for those who practice in accordance with what these [sages] declare, that practice leads to the attainment of heaven and liberation.
There is also a reading, "saddahantā" (confident). "By noble wisdom" means by thoroughly purified wisdom.

"Meditators" means those who meditate by means of both types of jhāna: that which consists in the contemplation of the characteristics of the object and that which consists in the contemplation following upon the object.

"Having practiced the Dhamma here" means: having undertaken the practice of the Dhamma—such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth—which constitutes the path to mundane and supramundane happiness, in this very life or within this dispensation;
they go to a happy destination for as long as they have not yet reached final Nibbāna.
"Joyful ones" (*nandino*) means those whose nature is to rejoice through the association with rapture and gladness. Some, however, interpret it as: "having practiced the Dhamma on the path..."
"They say, 'Having attained the path of stream-entry. Regarding "in the world of the gods": this refers to all sixfold realms of the sense-sphere gods (*kāmāvacara-deva*).
"They rejoice, possessing their desires" means that because desired objects are produced according to their wish, they, being possessed of desire and having their desires fulfilled, rejoice.
The commentary on the eighth sutta is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Kuha Sutta (108).
Regarding the ninth verse: "Deceivers" (*kuhā*) refers to those who deceive by means of the grounds for deception such as "hinting" (*sāmantajappana*);

the meaning is that they cause wonder in others by practicing hypocrisy out of a desire to be esteemed for qualities they do not possess. "Stubborn" (*thaddhā*) refers to those whose minds are made rigid by anger and pride.
By anger as described thus: “He is prone to anger, full of distress; even when spoken to slightly, he becomes resentful, agitated, malicious, and stubborn”;
and by being difficult to admonish as described thus: “He is difficult to admonish, possessed of qualities that make him difficult to admonish, impatient, and unwilling to accept instruction.”
"Arrogance of birth, arrogance of clan, arrogance of craft, arrogance of health, arrogance of youth, and arrogance of life"— those who,
due to such types of arrogance as these, fail to show the highest reverence toward those worthy of respect, and instead wander about without bowing down,
like those standing after swallowing an iron rod; "lapā" means flatterers who, by way of wrong livelihood, curry favor with families.
The meaning of *lapaka* is one who speaks by means of speech employed for the sake of gain and by means of insinuation (*nippesikatā*).

They are possessed of "deceit" (*siṅgī*)—that is, they are endowed with manifest defilements similar to deceit, as described in the passage: "In this context, what is deceit? That which is deceit, flirtation, wantonness, cleverness, scheming, and craftiness. They are "haughty" (*unnaḷā*).
“With upraised reeds” means they wander about having raised up an empty conceit that is like a reed.
“Unconcentrated” means they do not possess even a modicum of one-pointedness of mind. “Those bhikkhus, monks, are not mine” means those bhikkhus of mine do not belong to me.
The word “mine” was spoken by the Blessed One because they had gone forth for the sake of himself. However, because—
Because they practice through hypocrisy and the like, they have not practiced rightly; therefore, they are called "not mine.
"Departed" means that although they have gone forth in my dispensation, because they do not practice according to the instructions, they have indeed departed from this Dhamma and Vinaya;
it shows that they stand very far, indeed at a great distance, from here. For this has been said:
“The sky is far and the earth is far,
they say the further shore of the ocean is far;
