but they say that which is even more distant than that— ”
"And the Dhamma of the virtuous and the wicked, O King.
They "attain growth, increase, and abundance" means: they attain *vuddhi* by way of increasing through qualities such as virtue (*sīla*); *virūḷhi* by way of being firm and unshakable therein;
and [abundance] by way of the fulfillment of the aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue, which are spread throughout all things.
"Vepullaṃ" means they do not fall into such states, nor do they reach them; that is the meaning.
"Those monks, bhikkhus, are mine"—here too, he says "mine" because they have gone forth with himself in mind, but he calls them "mine" also because they have practiced rightly.
The bright side (the virtuous alternative) should be understood by reversing what has been stated.
In this context, [the roots] are said to "grow" up to the path of arahantship; however, when the fruit of arahantship is attained, they are said to have reached growth and abundance.
The verses are indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the ninth sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Nadīsotasutta 109.
In the tenth [sutta], *seyyathāpi* is a particle used for the purpose of showing a simile; the meaning is "just as if.
*Nadiyā sotena ovuyheyya* means that one would be carried away downstream by the current of a river—a river with a swift flow that carries things along—being swept away by the force of the water.
"By way of what is lovely and pleasant" means by reason of its lovely nature and pleasant nature.
[Thinking], "There is gold, gems, or some other beloved object or wealth in that river, or on its further bank;
I shall seize it," one falls into the river and is carried away by the current. *Kiñcāpi* is a particle used in the sense of granting a concession or expressing improbability. What?

He allows it; what does he not allow? He allows the existence there of that pleasant object intended by that man, but he does not allow going there because of its being fraught with danger. This is what is meant:
"O man, even if that pleasant object intended by you is found there, yet such is the danger in going."
"Having reached the pool below, you might meet with death or suffering amounting to death.
And here, "there is a pool below" means that in the downstream part of this river, there is a great lake, exceedingly deep and vast.
And it is surrounded on all sides by [waves] arising from the impact of the wind, resembling the peaks of mountains made of jewels.
It is "with whirlpools" (sāvaṭṭo) because it possesses whirlpools together with powerful mouths, like those of a crocodile,
amidst the vast masses of water that swirl here and there due to the great flood of this river as it rushes with great speed over uneven ground and through large waves and billows.
It is inhabited by one who dwells having made the very beings who have entered that lake his own constant prey of raw meat.
With its extremely terrifying appearance and its fierce mind, it is "with crocodiles" (sagaha) because of the water-dwelling rākṣasa;
or it is "with crocodiles" because of the fierce fish, makaras, and so forth, and "with rākṣasas" because of the aforementioned rākṣasa.
"That" refers to that lake which is thus full of danger. "O man! is a form of address. "Or you will meet with death."
Overwhelmed by those waves, or fallen into those whirlpools unable to lift his head, or fallen into the mouths of those fierce fish, crocodiles, and the like;
or having come into the hands of that water-demon, you will meet death;
or else, if there remains some span of life, escaping from there and moving away, you will be [caught] by those waves and so forth.
Through the force of being struck, you undergo suffering amounting to death, reaching the very measure of death. "One should strive against the current":
having previously been carried along with the current, upon hearing that man's words—"Surely a calamity has presented itself for me;
I am indeed turning back into the jaws of Death"—one who has developed intense fear and is agitated redoubles one's effort.
With hands and feet he would strive and cross over, and before long he would reach the shore.
"For the purpose of making the meaning known" means: this simile was made for the sake of awakening to the meaning conducive to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.
"And this is the meaning here" refers to this very meaning now being stated by me, which is the intended object of comparison (*upameyyattha*). Of that—
An analogy has been brought forward for the purpose of making it known.
Regarding the statement “this is a designation for craving,” the similarity of craving to a stream should be understood here in four ways:
by way of increasing in succession, by way of continuous connection, by way of causing one to sink, and by way of being difficult to cross. For just as when a great cloud has rained down above...
Just as water, having filled the mountain clefts, ravines, and creeks, flows down from there to fill the hollows; then,
flowing down from there to fill the small streams, and then entering the great rivers until it becomes a single flood and continues on,
it is called "the river current"— even so, greed [flows] toward objects such as forms, which have many divisions according to the internal, external, and other categories.
Having arisen and gradually increasing, it is called the "stream of craving. And just as the current of a river,
from its source until its arrival at the ocean, proceeds in an uninterrupted succession as long as there is no cause for its interruption,
so too the stream of craving, starting from its origin, proceeds without interruption provided there is no cause for its cessation.
It proceeds in continuous succession, heading toward the ocean of the states of misery (*apāya*). Just as the current of a river causes beings caught within it to sink,
does not allow them to lift their heads, and brings about death or suffering equal to death,
so too the stream of craving causes beings who have entered its current to sink, does not allow them to lift the head of wisdom (*paññā*), and by cutting off the roots of merit (*kusalamūla*)—
And by entering into states subject to defilement, it brings about death or suffering equivalent to death.
Just as when the current of a river flows with a great flood, one who intends to go to the further shore—
relying on a skillful man capable of mooring or pulling a raft or boat— and exerts the appropriate effort, [succeeds].
It must be crossed; it is difficult to overcome, for one cannot cross it by just any means whatsoever.

In the same way, the stream of craving—which consists of the flood of sensual desire and the flood of existence—must be crossed by one who, having aroused the aspiration, "Being skillful, I shall attain arahantship," relies on virtuous friends, boards the ship of serenity and insight, and exerts right effort to fulfill the restraint of virtue and perform the work of serenity and insight.
It must be crossed by one who acts; it is difficult to cross, as one cannot simply go hither or thither.

Thus, craving’s resemblance to the current of a river should be understood through four aspects: by its progressive increase, by its continuous flow, by its causing one to sink, and by its difficulty to cross.
"Pleasant form" (*piyarūpa*) means that which is of a pleasant nature, of a pleasant character, and of a pleasant appearance; it is of a sweet nature, of a sweet character.
"Pleasant form" means having a desirable nature. "Of this concealed" means of this hidden. Regarding "of the internal":
they are called "internal" because they proceed by taking the self as their reference (adhikāra), with the intention: "In this way, we shall be grasped as 'I'.
In that context, there is the internal as object (*gocarajjhatta*), the internal as one's own (*niyakajjhatta*), and the internal as domain (*visayajjhatta*).

"Internal-internal" refers to the fourfold internal. Among these, that which is mentioned in such passages as "delighting in the internal, concentrated" is called the *gocara-ajjhatta* (the internal as object).
That which comes in the passage "internal serenity" is called the *niyaka-ajjhatta* (the internal as one's own).
That which comes in the passage "by not attending to any signs, he enters and dwells in internal emptiness," and so forth, is... [the internal as the state of being].

This is what is called "internal with respect to the object" (*visayajjhatta*). That which is stated in the passage, "Internal phenomena, external phenomena," is called "internal" in the sense of being "internal to the internal" (*ajjhattajjhatta*).
Here too, this very same sense is intended; therefore, those that are internal are themselves "internal-internal" (*ajjhattikāni*).
Alternatively, according to the meaning already stated, they are so called because they are included among them, as in such passages as "internal phenomena, external phenomena."
"Internal" (*ajjhattika*) refers to the states existing within; these are the eye and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of those internal bases" (*ajjhattikānaṃ āyatanānaṃ*):

here, they are called "bases" (*āyatanāni*) because they are a basis (*āyatanato*), because they extend the arrival [of consciousness] (*āyānaṃ tananato*), and because they lead the extended [consciousness] (*āyatassa nayanato*).

For in the case of the eye and so forth, the mental states (*citta-cetasika-dhammā*) that have their respective doors and physical bases experience [their objects] by means of their own specific functions, such as experiencing.
They strive, exert themselves, endeavor, and make an effort through their function; and they stretch out and extend these phenomena that constitute the source of growth (āya).
Furthermore, they lead and set in motion the exceedingly long cycle of suffering in the beginningless saṃsāra.

Thus, in every respect, these phenomena are so called because of their being a source of growth (āyatana), because of their stretching out the growths (āyānaṃ tananato), and because of their leading the long (āyatassa nayanato).

They are called "bases" (*āyatana*). Furthermore, a base should be understood in the sense of a dwelling place, in the sense of a mine, in the sense of a meeting place, in the sense of a birthplace, and in the sense of a cause.

For instance, in common usage, in such expressions as "the abode of Īśvara" or "the abode of the gods," a dwelling place is called a "base. In such expressions as "a gold-mine" or "a silver-mine," [it is used in the sense of a source].
It is a mine. In the Dispensation, however, in such passages as “In a delightful abode, birds frequent it,” it means a place of gathering.
In such passages as “The Southern Land is the abode of cattle,” it means a region of origin.

In such passages as “Right there, in each respective suitable occasion, he attains the state of being capable of realization,” the word *āyatana* is said to mean a cause. And in the case of the eye and so forth, those respective...
Because mental states and mental factors dwell there by virtue of being dependent upon it for their existence, the eye and so forth are their "dwelling place" (*nivāsaṭṭhāna*).

Furthermore, because they are crowded together there due to being supported by it, these [bases] are their "mine" (*ākara*); and they are the "place of convergence" (*samosaraṇaṭṭhāna*) because they converge there by way of being the bases and doors;
they are the "region of birth" (*sañjātidesa*) because they arise right there by way of having that as their support; and they are the "cause" (*kāraṇa*).

"In their absence, those [faculties] are absent. Thus, for these reasons—in the sense of being a place of residence, a source, a meeting place, a region of birth, and a cause—the eye and so forth are called "internal bases" (*ajjhattikāyatanāni*).
Therefore it was said: "Of these six internal bases."
Even though phenomena such as visible form (*rūpa*) are described as "lovely" and "pleasant"— in the sense that "it is in this lovely and pleasant form that this craving arises when it arises"—
because they serve as the objective basis for craving; nevertheless, apart from the eye and so forth,
since there is no designation of a self-identity (*attabhāva*), [the eye, etc.,] are the bases for excessive affection in the form of "my eye," "my ear," and so on.
In order to show that the eye and the other [sense bases] deserve to be designated as "a form that is dear" and "a form that is pleasant," it is said:
"Monks, 'a form that is dear' and 'a form that is pleasant' is a designation for these six internal sense bases.
Regarding the term *orambhāgiyānaṃ*, here *oraṃ* refers to the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*); those included therein are the "lower parts" (*orambhāgā*), by way of being their conditions.

They are "lower" because they conduce to their welfare in the lower realms. They are called "fetters" (*saṃyojana*) because they fetter and bind the person in whom they exist to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). This is a designation for personality-view, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, sensual lust, and ill-will;
for these, acting as conditions for the formations that lead to rebirth in the sense-sphere realm, exist by way of being inferior and lower than the form and formless realms.
They bind sentient beings by means of the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), which constitutes the lower portion.

By this very fact, it should be understood that their resemblance to a deep pool below is illustrated. "The danger of waves" (*ūmibhaya*), monks, is a designation for anger and distress (*kodhupāyāsa*). It is called "danger" (*bhaya*) because one fears it;
since the wave itself is the danger, it is the "danger of waves. Anger (*kodha*) is so called in the sense of being provoked to wrath; that very [anger] is of the mind...
And *upāyāsa* (despair) is so called in the sense of causing intense exhaustion by means of crushing and piercing the body.

In this context, the similarity between anger-despair (*kodhupāyāsa*) and a wave should be understood as follows: having occurred many times, it overwhelms the being with whom it is associated, not allowing the head to be raised, and leads to ruin and calamity.
Likewise, [the similarity of] the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*)...

The similarity to a whirlpool should be understood as follows: having caused beings who are overcome by defilements to wander from here to there and from there to here within the self—which is designated as the objects of sense such as pleasant forms—and having thus turned them back so that even the mind does not arise toward renunciation which lies outside of that [self], one should see it as being like a whirlpool because of its causing ruin.
Furthermore, just as a house-demon [seizes] one who is without protection...

Having overcome and seized a man who has come within his own range of activity, even though that man stands outside his domain, he— by means of a demon-like illusion— leads him back into his sphere; then,
by displaying terrifying forms and other such means, he renders him helpless and incapable of performing any service for himself,
and having possessed him, deprives him even of his beauty, strength, wealth, fame, and happiness, bringing about great ruin and calamity.
In the same way, a woman— devoid of wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and lacking heroic manliness— overcomes and seizes even a man of heroic nature through her own feminine gestures,
charms, and amorous displays. Having possessed him with female guile (*itthimāyā*) by means of her physical beauty and other such allurements,
she renders him incapable of voluntarily accomplishing the qualities conducive to his welfare, such as virtue (*sīla*) and the like, [enticing him] with her excellence, reputation, and so forth.
Having separated them [from their kin], she brings about great misfortune and ruin; in this way, the female sex should be regarded as being like a house-demon (*gaharakkhasa*).
Therefore it was said: "Bhikkhus, 'alluring' is a designation for these five strands of sensual pleasure;
'house-demon,' bhikkhus, is a designation for the female sex."
“‘Against the stream,’ monks, is a designation for renunciation. Herein, renunciation consists of the first jhāna together with its access, the wisdom of insight, and Nibbāna;
indeed, all wholesome states are called renunciation. For this has been said:
“Going forth, the first jhāna, Nibbāna, and insight;
all wholesome states as well are called ‘renunciation.
Now, it should be understood that these states, beginning with going forth, are like a counter-stream to the stream of craving because they flow against it. Without distinction—
For the Dhamma and Vinaya are renunciation, and going forth is its foundation; and the Dhamma and Vinaya are said to be against the stream of craving. For it has been said:
“It goes against the stream, it is subtle, profound, hard to see, and fine.”
“Those who are stained by passion do not see, being shrouded by a mass of darkness.
Regarding “the exertion of energy”: this refers to the energy of the fourfold right striving (*samyakprahāṇa*).

Its similarity to the effort of crossing the current of a four-limbed river with one's hands and feet—crossing the stream of craving which is divided into the flood of sensual desire and so forth—is indeed manifest. Likewise, as for the river’s current...

The similarity between the Blessed One, who possesses the five eyes, and a man with sight standing on the bank who has crossed over the fourfold flood of sensual desire and so forth and stands upon the shore beyond—the state of Nibbāna—is as follows. Therefore it is said:
“A man with sight... [up to] ...of the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
Herein, this is the correlation of the simile: the stream of craving is like the current of a river in its continuous flow;

the being carried away by that stream is like the person being swept along; the being wandering through the cycle of existence whose beginning is unknown is like the being carried away by the stream of craving;
and his fixation upon the objects there that are dear and pleasant is like [the fixation] of this [person] upon the eye and so forth.
Adherence is like a river below a lake, agitated by the five cords of sensual pleasure, anger, despair, and women, and filled with whirlpools, crocodiles, and demons;

it is a mass of the five lower fetters. Having understood that matter as it truly is, one sees all the dangers of saṃsāra and all knowable phenomena as they truly are, like a man with clear vision standing on the further bank of that river’s current.
Having understood this, the Blessed One, the All-Seeing One, stands upon the shore of Nibbāna, which is the further bank of the stream of craving.
Out of compassion for that person being swept away by the current of that river—

just as one might describe the lake and the dangers of the lake— the Blessed One, out of great compassion for the sentient being being swept away by the stream of craving, [describes] the dangers of craving.

And the contemplation of its danger is as follows: just as that man who did not believe his words met with death or with suffering amounting to death in that lake while going downstream, so too for one who does not accept the word of the Blessed One, there is rebirth in the states of misery (apāya) and the arising of suffering even in a happy destination (sugati).
However, for one who believes his words and [acts] with their hands...
Just as one makes an effort with one's feet and, by that effort, reaches the opposite shore and proceeds happily to whatever place one desires, so too,
having received the word of the Blessed One and seen the danger in craving and the like, there is the exertion of energy through the renunciation of setting out against the stream of craving;
and for one who has thus exerted energy, by that very exertion of energy, there is the crossing over the stream of craving to the shore of Nibbāna.
"Having attained it" means that one dwells in happiness according to one's desire by way of the attainment of the fruit of Arahatship.

In the verses, "one should abandon sensual desires even at the cost of suffering" means that while a bhikkhu is engaged in the practice of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) for the sake of attaining the jhānas and the path,
even if their preliminary stages are accomplished with difficulty and hardship, he should not [desist].
One enters the path with ease because of the strength of the defilements through prior-stage cultivation (*pubbabhāga-bhāvanā*), or because of the dullness of the faculties (*indriya*).
If that were so, one would abandon sensual desires even with difficulty;

for while suppressing the defilements of sensual desire by means of the first *jhāna*, one abandons them by means of the third path (*tatiya-magga*) when completely eradicating them. By this, he shows that the *jhāna* and the path belong to the "difficult progress" (*dukkha-paṭipadā*).
"Striving for security from bondage in the future" means desiring and longing for non-returning and arhatship.

This is the intended meaning here: "Even though at present I attain the preliminary stages of jhāna and the first path with difficulty and hardship, yet by relying on these, I shall attain arhatship in the higher stages, fulfill my task, and become one who has abandoned all suffering"—thus he strives together with...
"By means of suffering, one should abandon sensual desire through the jhānas and so forth.

Alternatively, it was said with reference to that person who is full of sensual thoughts (*kāmavitakka*), and who—by relying on a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*)—while practicing the going-forth, the purification of virtue, or the preliminary practice for the jhānas and so forth, suppresses those thoughts only with difficulty and hardship, weeping with tears on his face: "Even together with..."

“One should abandon sensual pleasures through hardship. For even by abandoning sensual pleasures with difficulty, one might generate a jhāna, take that jhāna as a basis, and by practicing insight, gradually establish oneself in Arahantship. Therefore it is said:
“Aspiring for security from bondage in the future.”
"Perfectly wise" (*sammappajāno*) means understanding correctly through the wisdom of the path accompanied by insight (*vipassanā*).
"With mind well-liberated" (*suvimuttacitto*) means having a mind that is thoroughly liberated through the liberation of the fruit immediately following the attainment of that noble path.
"He touches liberation there and then" (*vimuttiṃ phusaye tattha tattha*) means that at each respective time of attaining the fruits of the paths, he touches liberation, which is *nibbāna*.
One would touch, reach, attain, and realize it. For in the sense of the object, this genitive case in “vimuttiyā” [is used].

Or rather, with liberation as its object, at each respective time of entering the attainment of the various fruits, one would touch, reach, and attain one’s own resultant consciousness therein; that is, one would dwell in the attainment of the fruit which plunges into Nibbāna.

The meaning: "He is a master of knowledge" (*vedagu*): he is a master of knowledge because, by means of the knowledge of the path—which is designated as "knowledge" (*veda*)—he has gone to and penetrated the four truths.
"One who has reached the end of the world" (*lokantagu*): he has gone to the limit of the world of the aggregates (*khandha*). The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the tenth sutta is finished.
11. Commentary on the *Carasutta* 110.
In the eleventh [sutta], "while walking" (*carato*) means while going or while pacing up and down (*caṅkamantassa*).

"A sensual thought arises" (*uppajjati kāmavitakko vā*) means that if, due to not being free from lust for sense-objects (*vatthukāmesu*), a thought associated with sensual desire (*kāmapaṭisaṃyutto vitakko*) should arise when such a condition is present.
"If it arises": the connection is that either a thought of ill-will (*byāpādavitakka*) or a thought of cruelty (*vihiṃsāvitakka*) arises;
that is, a thought associated with resentment and ill-will toward an object of provocation, or a thought associated with cruelty by way of harming others with clods of earth, sticks, and so forth.
"He endures" means that he [endures] those aforementioned thoughts of sensual desire and so on according to their respective conditions within himself.

If one tolerates a thought that has arisen in the mind—meaning one allows it to remain by not applying it to the mind—due to the absence of reflection in the manner of: "In this way, this thought is evil; in this way, it is unwholesome; in this way, it is blameworthy; and furthermore, it leads to one's own harm," and so forth;
and while thus tolerating it, one does not abandon it by means of abandonment through its specific factor (*tadaṅga-pahāna*) and the other modes of abandonment.

He does not relinquish them; for that very reason, he does not dispel them—he does not push them away from or extract them from his own mental continuum—and because he does not dispel them in this way, he does not bring them to an end or make them disappear.
While one who is ardent and resolute acts so that not even a trace of them remains, not even as much as a mere fragment, he, however, does not act in such a manner.
The meaning is as follows: "Tathābhūto va" means he does not go to non-existence; "anu anu abhāvaṃ na gameti" means he does not repeatedly go to non-existence.
The meaning should be understood by connecting the word "ce" (if) with phrases such as "na pajahati ce" (if he does not abandon) and "na vinodeti ce" (if he does not dispel).
"Caranti" means while wandering. "Evaṃbhūto" means one who is thus possessed of evil thoughts such as sensual thoughts. "Anātāpī" [means one who is without ardor].
"Anottāpī" means one who does not exert himself (*anātāpī*) due to the absence of the energy that burns away the defilements;
it means one who lacks moral dread (*anottāpī*), which is characterized by the burning and tormenting of fear toward evil. "Satataṃ samitaṃ" means at all times, without interruption.

"Kusīto hīnavīriyo" means one who has fallen away from wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*) and, through association with indolence (*kosajja*), sinks into what is contemptible on the side of the unwholesome.
And "lazy" means one who is deficient in energy and devoid of vigor because of the absence of right effort; he is thus called and described as such.

"Of one standing" means of one who stands having ceased walking. Since the posture of lying down is specifically conducive to indolence, the phrase "of one who is awake" is stated in order to show the kind of thoughts that arise in one who possesses that state.
“Monks, if that [thought] does not take hold in a bhikkhu during the bright fortnight”— this means that even for one who dwells with energy aroused,
if sensual thoughts and the like should arise due to forgetfulness of mindfulness caused by the convergence of such conditions over a long period in beginningless saṃsāra,
if the bhikkhu, having brought them onto his own mind, does not let them dwell there, he does not allow them to remain within.
This is the meaning. What does he do when he does not tolerate [them]? He abandons them; he discards them. Is it like throwing away rubbish into a basket?
No, rather, he dispels them, pushes them away, and removes them. Is it like driving an ox with a goad?
No, rather, he brings them to an end, he makes them reach their limit, so that not even a trace of them remains.
It makes them so even by a mere breaking. But how does it make them so? It causes them to go to non-existence;

it causes them to go to non-existence little by little. What is meant is that it makes them such that they are well-suppressed through abandonment by suppression (*vikkhambhana-pahāna*). Regarding the phrase "one who has become thus" and so forth:
being one whose intention is thoroughly purified by not tolerating sensual thoughts and the like in this way, by that...

And by means of the perfection of his disposition and the perfection of application caused by it, he is one whose virtue is purified, who guards the doors of the sense faculties, who is moderate in eating, and who is endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension;

he is "ardent" because he is possessed of energy characterized by the burning away of the defilements through the method of "tormenting by that factor" (*tadaṅga*) and so forth, and because he is possessed of a total dread of evil.
One who is ardent (*ottāpī*) constantly, day and night, continuously and uninterruptedly through the application to the cultivation of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*),

by means of the accomplishment of the fourfold right exertion (*sammappadhāna*), is called— meaning he is described as— one who has initiated energy (*āraddhavīriya*), is resolute (*pahitatta*), and has directed his mind toward Nibbāna. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

Regarding the phrase "dependent on the household" (*gehanissita*) in the verses: here, because it has not been abandoned by those living in households, because it is the inherent nature of householders, or because it is the characteristic of the household, "the household" (*geha*) refers to sensual desire for objects (*vatthukāma*).

Alternatively, because they are bound to the household, because they are the dwelling place of the defilements of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*), or because they have that as their basis, thoughts of sensual desire and so forth are called "dependent on the household.
Regarding the phrase "has entered upon a wrong path": because of the Noble Path... [text fragment ends]
Because they constitute a state of being on a wrong path, covetousness and the other such factors, along with states associated with them, are the "bad road.
Therefore, a person who is full of sensual thoughts and the like is said to have "entered upon the bad road.

"Infatuated by things that cause delusion" means infatuated with, devoted to, and obsessed by forms and so forth, which lead to delusion. "Full enlightenment" refers to the knowledge of the Noble Path. "To touch" means to touch or to attain.
Such a one, whose range is wrong intention, is incapable; the meaning is that he never attains it.
"Having stilled discursive thought" means having pacified the aforementioned wrong thought by means of the powers of reflection and cultivation.
"Delighting in the stilling of discursive thought" refers to *arahatta* (Arahatship) and *nibbāna*, which consist in the absolute pacification of even the nine great types of discursive thought.

"Delighting in such an inclination" means being fond of and devoted to it. "Such a person is capable" refers to that individual, as previously described, who—practicing rightly—has, in the preliminary stage, stilled all discursive thoughts through the power of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) according to their respective requirements by means of suppression (*tadaṅga*) and other methods;
and having brought insight to its peak, [is capable of attaining] what is termed the knowledge of the path of Arahantship through the successive stages of the path.
He is capable and able to touch and attain the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment known as Nibbāna.
The commentary on the eleventh sutta is finished.
12. Commentary on the *Sampannasīla-sutta*.
111. Regarding the twelfth [quality], "those endowed with perfected virtue" (*sampannasīla*): here, "perfected" (*sampanna*) is threefold, by way of being complete, possessed, and sweet.
Among these—“O Kosiya, crows eat the ripe rice in the field;
O Brahmā, I inform you of this, I am unable to prevent them.”—

In this context, the word *sampanna* has the sense of being complete. In the passage, “By means of this restraint of the Pātimokkha, one is endowed, fully endowed, approached, fully approached, perfected (*sampanna*), and possessed,” the word *sampanna* has the sense of being possessed of [an attribute].
In the passage, “Venerable sir, the lower surface of this great earth is as deep as a small jar of honey...,” it has the sense of depth.
In the phrase “it is not blue, it is thus pleasant,” the word *sampanna* has the sense of “sweetness.

However, here it is appropriate in the sense of “complete” as well as in the sense of “endowment”; therefore, the meaning here should be understood as “those who have accomplished virtue” (*sampannasīlā*) meaning either “having become complete in virtue” or “being endowed with virtue.”
In this context, by the meaning of “possessing fulfilled virtue,” it is called “fulfilled” just as a field is fulfilled through the removal of defects in the field.

Therefore it was said: “Just as the fulfillment of a field occurs through the removal of defects in the field, so the fulfillment of virtue is stated to occur through the removal of defects in virtue.
By the meaning of “endowed with virtue,” however, they have become possessed of virtue and have attained its integration.
"Having become endowed [with these qualities], dwell"—this is what is meant. In this context, perfection of virtue (*sīla*) arises from two causes:
by seeing the danger in the failure of virtue and by seeing the benefit in the perfection of virtue.
Both of these should be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga*. Regarding that, it is said that by the phrase "endowed with virtue" (*sampannasīlā*), the Blessed One—

Having recited the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*), [the Blessed One] shows the "foremost virtue" by means of the phrase "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha," and so forth;
whatever is to be said here has already been stated below. Regarding the question, "What further remains to be done?":
the meaning is, for you who dwell thus with virtue perfected, what further ought to be done or practiced?
Thus, having begun the teaching by enjoining the bhikkhus to the perfection of virtue through the means of accomplishment— starting with the words, "Bhikkhus, dwell possessed of perfected virtue"—
and having done so by way of reference to many individuals, [the Buddha now proceeds] because even though the Blessed One’s teaching proceeds by way of reference to a single individual,
it nonetheless becomes a teaching by way of reference to many individuals due to its universal applicability. Therefore:
Showing that by way of a reference to a single individual, he said: "And if, monks, while a bhikkhu is walking... and so forth.
Therein, it is called *abhijjhā* (covetousness) because one covets (*abhijjhāyati*) by means of it; this is a designation for greed, which has the characteristic of coveting another's property.

It is called *byāpāda* (ill will) because the mind becomes corrupted (*byāpajjati*, i.e., putrid) by means of it; [it refers to] that which proceeds in such a manner as "He has done me harm," and so on.
This is a designation for the hatred (*dosa*) directed toward the nineteen bases of resentment. Regarding both of them, it is said:

"In this context, what is sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*)? It is that which is sensual desire regarding sense-pleasures, sensual affection, sensual thirst, sensual fever, sensual infatuation, and sensual attachment.
Likewise: "Greed, the state of being greedy, the quality of greed, lust, the state of being lustful, the quality of being lustful, covetousness, and greed..."
The detailed exposition should be understood from such passages as "the unwholesome root," and "hatred is hating, the state of having hated, malice, being malicious,
the state of being malicious, opposition, hostility, ferocity, abruptness, and mental displeasure.
"It has vanished" means that this covetousness and this ill will have vanished, have departed, and have been abandoned.
The meaning. Up to this point, the abandoning of the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) and the hindrance of ill will (*byāpāda-nīvaraṇa*) has been shown.
Regarding "sloth and torpor" (*thinamiddha*): it is both sloth (*thina*) and torpor (*middha*). Among these, sloth is the unwieldiness of the mind; it is a designation for laziness.
Torpor is the unwieldiness of the three aggregates beginning with feeling; it is a state of drowsiness.

This is a synonym. For both, the detailed explanation should be understood according to the method beginning: "In this context, what is sloth (*thina*)? It is the unwieldiness, the unworkability, the sinking, and the subsiding of the mind.
In this context, what is drowsiness (*middha*)? It is the unwieldiness, the unworkability, the shrouding, and the enveloping of the body. And so forth.
“Restlessness-and-worry” (*uddhacca-kukkucca*) means both restlessness (*uddhacca*) and worry (*kukkucca*). Therein, restlessness is the state of agitation of the mind;
worry is the remorse (*vippaṭisāra*) regarding what good has not been done and what evil has been done, caused by that [remorse]. For both of them, it is said:
“Therein, what is restlessness? That which is the restlessness of the mind, the lack of tranquility, the distraction of the mind, the unsteadiness of the mind,” and so forth.

The detailed explanation [is as follows]: the mode of its occurrence should be understood through such passages as, "Alas, I have not done what is beautiful; I have not done what is wholesome; I have not provided security for those in fear; I have done evil; I have done cruel deeds; I have done sinful acts.
Doubt (*vicikicchā*) is uncertainty regarding the Buddha and the other [jewels]. Regarding it, [it is said]: "He wavers, doubts, and lacks conviction concerning the Teacher..."
The detailed exposition should be understood according to such methods as: "He does not have full confidence," and so forth; and: "In this context, what is doubt (vicikicchā)?

It is that which is perplexity, the state of being perplexed, the condition of being perplexed, wavering, doubt, a crossroads, a fork in the road, uncertainty, holding to various alternatives, hesitation, sliding back and forth, lack of penetration, trepidation of the mind, and mental distress. And so on.
And here, the suppression of covetousness, ill will, and so forth should be understood both by way of their disappearance and by way of their abandonment. With reference to this it was said:
"Having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.
Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will; he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred."
Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with a mind inwardly calmed;
he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse. Having abandoned doubt, he dwells having crossed beyond doubt.
“Being free from doubt regarding wholesome states, he purifies his mind of uncertainty.
In this regard, it should be understood how the abandoning of the hindrances occurs. And how does their abandoning take place?
First, the abandoning of sensual desire occurs through wise attention to the sign of the unattractive, and through unwise attention to the sign of the attractive.
This is the origin. Therefore the Blessed One said:

“There is, bhikkhus, the sign of the beautiful. Therein, the frequent practice of improper attention is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sensual desire, or for the increase and expansion of sensual desire that has already arisen.
Thus, because it is the opposite of that sensual desire which arises through improper attention toward the sign of the beautiful, [the contemplation of foulness is the means to its abandonment].

Abandonment occurs through appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) toward the sign of the foul (*asubhanimitta*). In this context, the "sign of the foul" refers both to the foul itself and to that which has the foul as its object.
"Appropriate attention" means skillful attention or systematic attention;
it is the attention that contemplates the impermanent as "impermanent," suffering as "suffering," non-self as "non-self," or the foul as "foul."
For one who frequently practices that [meditation] therein, sensual desire is abandoned. Therefore the Blessed One said:

“Bhikkhus, there is the sign of foulness. Frequenting wise attention directed toward it—this is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen sensual desire, and for the abandoning of arisen sensual desire.

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire: the apprehension of the sign of foulness, the cultivation of the meditation on foulness, [the avoidance of persons who provoke sensual desire, the frequenting of persons who do not provoke it, the correct reflection, and the appropriate concentration].
Guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, having virtuous friends, and appropriate conversation.

For sensual desire is abandoned by one who learns the tenfold sign of foulness, by one who develops it, by one who guards the doors of the sense faculties, and also by one who is moderate in eating—having the habit of drinking water and sustaining himself when there is room for only four or five mouthfuls of food. Therefore it was said:
“Having eaten only four or five mouthfuls, one may drink water;
this is sufficient for the comfortable dwelling of a bhikkhu who is resolute.
Even for one who serves virtuous friends such as the Elder Tissa, the practitioner of foulness meditation, sensual desire is abandoned while standing, sitting, and so forth.
It is also abandoned through talk that is connected with the ten unwholesome states and is conducive to the wholesome. Therefore it was said: "Six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire.
Through unwise attention directed toward the sign of repulsion, ill will arises. In this context, both repulsion and the sign of repulsion [are meant].
The object of repulsion is also the sign of repulsion. Unwise attention has the same characteristic throughout all cases.
When one frequently directs the mind toward that sign, ill will arises. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Bhikkhus, there is the sign of repulsion. Therein, frequent unwise attention is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen ill will, or for the increase, expansion, and abundance of arisen ill will.”
But the abandoning of ill will occurs through right attention directed toward the liberation of mind by loving-kindness (*mettā-cetovimutti*).

In this context, when "loving-kindness" is mentioned, both absorption (*appanā*) and access (*upacāra*) are included; however, when "liberation of mind" is mentioned, it refers only to absorption. Right attention has the characteristics already described.
For one who frequently practices that [attention] therein, ill will is abandoned. Therefore the Blessed One said:

“There is, bhikkhus, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (*mettā-cetovimutti*). The frequent practice of wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) directed toward it is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen ill will, or for the abandoning of arisen ill will.

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of ill will: grasping the sign of loving-kindness, the cultivation of loving-kindness, reflection on one’s own karma as one’s own property, frequent analytical reflection, having virtuous friends, and talk that is conducive [to such states].

For even in one who learns loving-kindness (*mettā*) by way of any one of the methods—whether directed toward specific persons (*odhisaka*), non-specific persons (*anodhisaka*), or the pervasion of directions (*disāpharaṇa*)—ill-will (*byāpāda*) is abandoned;
and even in one who develops loving-kindness by way of specific persons, non-specific persons, or the pervasion of directions, ill-will is abandoned [with the thought]:
"What will you do by being angry with this person? Will you be able to destroy his virtue (*sīla*) and so forth? Is it not rather by your own karma?"

Having come here by your own karma alone, you will depart by your own karma alone. Indeed, anger toward another is like desiring to strike someone while holding a glowing charcoal, a red-hot iron rod, or excrement; it is useless. What can this person do to you when he is angry?
Will he be able to destroy your virtue (*sīla*) and other qualities? He has come by his own karma and will depart by his own karma alone, like a gift that was never accepted.
“Just as a handful of dust thrown against the wind falls back upon the thrower’s own head, so too will this anger fall upon his own head.
Thus, for one who reflects on the ownership of action (kammassakata) for both oneself and another; for one who, having reflected, stands firm in discernment;
and for one who serves a virtuous friend like the Elder Assagutta, who delights in the cultivation of loving-kindness (mettā)—[anger does not arise].
Ill will is abandoned; it is also abandoned through talk based on loving-kindness and conducive to its development while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore it is said:
"Six things lead to the abandoning of ill will.
Through unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) toward boredom and the like, sloth and torpor arise. Boredom (*arati*) means a state of discontent.
Drowsiness (*tandi*) means bodily sloth; yawning (*vijambhitā*) means the bending of the body; dizziness from food (*bhattasammada*) means intoxication by food or a burning sensation from food;
mental sluggishness (*cetaso līnattaṃ*) means a state of lethargy in the mind.
When one frequently engages in improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) toward these states such as aversion and so forth, sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) arise. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Monks, there are discontent, lethargy, yawning, drowsiness after meals, and mental sluggishness. Therein,
the frequent application of improper attention is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, or for the increase and expansion of sloth and torpor that have already arisen.”

Furthermore, the abandoning of sloth and torpor occurs through wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) toward the element of initiative (*ārambhadhātu*) and the others. The "element of initiative" is the energy of the initial undertaking;
the "element of exertion" (*nikkamadhātu*) is stronger than that because it has emerged from indolence;
the "element of perseverance" (*parakkamadhātu*) is even stronger than that because it advances to ever-higher stages. In this threefold classification...
For one who frequently applies appropriate attention to energy, sloth and torpor are abandoned. Therefore it was said:
"Bhikkhus, there is the element of instigation, the element of exertion, the element of striving.
Frequent application of appropriate attention to these is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, and for the abandoning of arisen sloth and torpor."
Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sloth and torpor: taking note of overeating; changing one’s posture;

attending to the perception of light; living in the open air; having virtuous friends; and engaging in appropriate conversation. For when one who has eaten food that is like a hand-brought meal, a meal that fills the stomach, a meal that is stuffed, a meal that is rolled up, a meal that is sufficient for clothing, or a meal that is like a crow’s beak, sits in a night-station or a day-station performing the duties of a recluse, sloth and torpor become like a great elephant.

It comes spreading over one as if with a flood; however, for a bhikkhu who drinks water after setting aside space for four or five mouthfuls and whose nature is to maintain himself on that, it does not happen.
Thus, even for one who takes the sign in over-eating, sloth and torpor are abandoned.
Even for one who shifts from the posture in which sloth and torpor descend to another, or who [looks at] the moonlight at night—
Even for one who attends to the light of a lamp, the light of a torch, or the daylight of the sun; even for one living in the open air;

even for one serving spiritual friends like the Elder Mahākassapa who are free from sloth and torpor—sloth and torpor are abandoned. They are also abandoned by talk concerning the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) that are suitable for the various postures such as standing and sitting.
Therefore it was said: "Six things [lead to] the abandoning of sloth and torpor."
“...lead to their abandonment.
Through improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) regarding the lack of tranquility of the mind, restlessness and remorse (*uddhacca-kukkucca*) arise.
“Lack of tranquility” refers to the state of being untranquil; in its actual meaning, it is simply restlessness and remorse. In that context, one frequently applies improper attention...
As he engages in it, restlessness and remorse arise. Therefore he said:

"Bhikkhus, there is lack of mental serenity. Therein, the frequent application of improper attention is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, or for the increase and expansion of restlessness and remorse that have already arisen."
But the abandoning of restlessness and remorse occurs through wise attention directed toward the tranquility of the mind known as concentration. Therefore it was said:

"There is, bhikkhus, tranquility of the mind. Cultivating wise attention therein—this is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, and for the abandoning of arisen restlessness and remorse.
Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse: great learning, being one who asks questions, ...
In the Vinaya, there are: knowledge of what has been laid down, association with the elders, friendship with the virtuous, and appropriate talk.

For even in the case of one who possesses great learning—whether he is mastering one, two, three, four, or five Nikāyas by way of both the text and the meaning—even for him agitation and remorse are abandoned;
as also for one who frequently inquires into what is permissible and what is impermissible regarding the formulation of the Vinaya.

Restlessness and remorse are abandoned by one who has attained mastery, by one who recognizes what has been done, by approaching elder and senior theras, by attending upon virtuous friends such as the thera Upāli who are experts in the Vinaya, and by appropriate talk concerning what is allowable and what is not allowable regarding standing, sitting, and so forth.
Therefore it is said: "Six things [lead to the abandoning] of restlessness and remorse..."
“...lead to their abandoning.
Doubt arises through improper attention toward things that are objects for doubt.
Things that are objects for doubt are, in fact, doubt itself, because they serve as the cause for the repeated arising of doubt. In that regard, improper attention—
In one who frequently engages [in such things], doubt arises. Therefore he said:

“Bhikkhus, there are states that are the basis for doubt. The frequent application of improper attention to them—this is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen doubt, or for the increase and expansion of arisen doubt.”
Furthermore, the abandoning of doubt occurs through wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) toward wholesome and other such phenomena.
Therefore, it was said: "Bhikkhus, there are wholesome and unwholesome phenomena; blameworthy and blameless phenomena; phenomena to be cultivated and not to be cultivated;
inferior and superior phenomena; dark and bright phenomena with their counterparts. Therein, there is frequent application of wise attention."
“This nutriment leads to the non-arising of unarisen doubt, or to the abandoning of arisen doubt.
Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of doubt:
erudition, inquisitiveness, knowledge of the Vinaya, abundance of resolute conviction, friendship with the virtuous, and appropriate discourse. Also, by way of erudition...
For indeed, doubt is abandoned even by one who learns one or—peyyāla—up to five Nikāyas according to the text and according to the meaning;
even by one who is frequently engaged in inquiry regarding phenomena classified as wholesome and so forth with reference to the Three Jewels; even by one who has attained mastery over the Vinaya;
and even by one who possesses abundant resolve characterized by faith that is firmly settled upon the Three Jewels.
Doubt is abandoned even by one who serves a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitta) such as the Elder Vakkali, who is resolute in faith;
it is also abandoned through appropriate talk concerning the qualities of the Three Jewels while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore it is said:
"Six things lead to the abandoning of doubt."
And herein, regarding these hindrances which have been abandoned by way of suppression through those various states as previously described:

first, the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) is abandoned absolutely by the path of Arahantship; likewise, the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor (*thinamiddha-nīvaraṇa*) and the hindrance of restlessness (*uddhacca-nīvaraṇa*) [are abandoned].
However, the hindrance of ill-will (*byāpāda-nīvaraṇa*) and the hindrance of worry-and-regret (*kukkucca-nīvaraṇa*) are abandoned by the path of Non-returning (*anāgāmi-magga*).
The hindrance of doubt is abandoned once and for all by the path of stream-entry.
Therefore, in order to show the factors conducive to their abandonment in that manner, the passage beginning with "vigor has been aroused" was undertaken.

Or rather, this very abandonment of the hindrances such as covetousness, as previously described, [is achieved] because one who is lazy due to deficient vigor, and one whose mindfulness is unestablished...
It is never possible for one who is unmindful, whose body is agitated due to a lack of tranquility, and whose mind is distracted due to a lack of concentration, to produce even that [first stage];

how much less the other? Therefore, in order to show the way of practice by which the disappearance and abandonment of covetousness and the rest become possible, the passage beginning with "vigor is aroused" was undertaken. Its meaning is as follows:
It is said that for the abandoning of those hindrances— or for the purpose of completely cutting off all defiled states—
energy has been undertaken, exerted, and set in motion without slackening. And because it is thus undertaken, it does not fall into despondency midway.
"Established mindfulness is unconfused": not only is energy established, but mindfulness also becomes established by way of being directed toward the object;
and because it is thus established, it is "unconfused" due to its capacity to remember what was done long ago and spoken long ago.
"Tranquil": through the subsiding of bodily and mental agitation, his body also becomes tranquil.

In this context, because when the mental body (*nāmakāya*) is calmed, his physical body (*rūpakāya*) is likewise calmed, it is therefore stated, "the body is calmed," without distinguishing between "mental body" and "physical body.
"Unagitated" means that due to that very state of calm, he is free from agitation;
what is meant is that he is devoid of distress. "The mind is concentrated, one-pointed"—his mind, too, is thus.
It is rightly placed, well-established, as if fixed; and precisely because it is concentrated (*samāhita*), it is one-pointed, immovable, unwavering, and unshakable.
Up to this point, the preliminary practice for the paths of *jhāna* has been explained. Therefore, he said:
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has become thus is called ardent, ashamed, constantly and continuously energetic, and resolute.
The meaning of this has already been explained above.

Regarding the verses: *yataṃ care* means one should walk with restraint; even while engaging in movement such as walking meditation (*caṅkama*), one should act with mindfulness so that unarisen [defilements] do not arise... [and so forth].

The meaning is that, by means of the right effort (*sammappadhāna*) described in the passage beginning, “one generates desire and exerts oneself for the non-arising of evil, unwholesome states,” one should strive, struggle,
and exert oneself so that unwholesome states are abandoned and wholesome states reach the perfection of their development; this is the method.
He should know this as well. Some, however, explain the meaning of "yata" as "saṃyata" (restrained). "Should stand" means he should stand, should maintain his posture.
"Should sit" means he should sit down. "Should lie down" means he should recline.

"Stretching out what is restrained" means that being one who possesses the aforementioned energy, while restraining—meaning controlling—the hands, feet, and so forth which ought to be stretched out, he should stretch them out.
The intention is that one should abandon negligence in all respects.
Now, in order to show the practice by which one who practices becomes "restrained" (*yata*) or "striving with restraint" (*yatamāna*), the passage beginning with "above" (*uddham*) was spoken.
Therein, "above" (*uddham*) means upwards. "Across" (*tiriyam*) means across, that is, on all sides by way of the eastern direction and so forth.

"In all directions" is the meaning. "Below" means downward. "As far as the course of the world" means wherever there is the occurrence of the world consisting of the various formations of sentient beings; the meaning is "in all those places.

By this much, he shows the object of the knowledge of comprehension (*sammasana-ñāṇa*) by including it without remainder. "Having thoroughly examined" means having correctly examined by way of reason and method, that is, by way of impermanence and so forth.
"Vipassaka" means one who sees clearly. "Of phenomena" (dhammānaṃ) means of those things empty of a self. "Of aggregates" (khandhānaṃ) means of the five aggregates, beginning with form.
"Arising and passing away" (udayabbayaṃ) means both arising and falling away. This is what is meant:

in all the world comprised by the three dimensions—above, across, and below—of all things classified as the five aggregates of clinging, which are differentiated by distinctions such as the past and so forth...

One would be a contemplator and observer by means of the knowledge of arising and passing away—attained through the comprehension of the impermanence and other characteristics of material and immaterial phenomena—in twenty-five modes regarding arising, and in twenty-five modes regarding passing away.
"Proper conduct regarding mental serenity" (*cetosamatha-sāmīci*) refers to the absolute pacification of the defilements of the mind; thus, it is termed "mental serenity."
The purification of knowledge and vision is the practice appropriate to the Noble Path.
"One who trains" means one who is practicing, cultivating, and generating a succession of knowledges. "Always" means at all times, both by night and by day.
"Mindful" means acting with mindfulness endowed with the four kinds of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*). "Constantly resolute" means being resolute at all times.
"Because his mind is directed toward Nibbāna": the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas and others, say, declare, and speak of such a bhikkhu in this way.
The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the twelfth sutta is finished.

13. Commentary on the Lokasutta (Sutta 112) In the thirteenth [sutta], "the world" (*loka*) refers to that which is subject to breaking up and disintegrating. In terms of meaning, the first two Noble Truths [were discussed] previously, but here it should be understood as the Noble Truth of Suffering (*dukkha*).
This consists of the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*), the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāraloka*), and the world of space (*okāsaloka*).

It has already been explained above according to its divisions and its essential nature. Furthermore, the world is manifold in terms of the aggregates (*khandha*), the world-systems (*loka*), and so forth. As it is said: "The world:

the world of aggregates, the world of elements (*dhātu*), the world of bases (*āyatana*), the world of misfortune and existence, the world of the origin of misfortune, the world of prosperity and existence, the world of the origin of prosperity.
One world: all beings subsist by nutriment. Two..."
The worlds consist of name and form; the three worlds are the three feelings; the four worlds are the four nutriments; the five worlds are the five aggregates of clinging;
the six worlds are the six internal sense bases; the seven worlds are the seven stations of consciousness;
the eight worlds are the eight worldly conditions; the nine worlds are the nine abodes of beings; the ten worlds are the ten sense bases; [the twelve worlds are] the twelve...
"The worlds are the twelve sense-bases; the eighteen worlds are the eighteen elements.
Thus, although the world is analyzed in many ways, it is all subsumed and converges within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānakkhandhā*).
And the aggregates of clinging are the Noble Truth of Suffering: "Birth is suffering... [and so on] ...in short, the five aggregates of clinging are also suffering."
“Suffering. Therefore it was said: “In terms of meaning, the first two Noble Truths [are dealt with] previously; however, here the Noble Truth of Suffering is to be understood.
But is it not the case that the sense of “breaking up and falling apart” occurs without distinction in all five aggregates?
True, it does occur. However, that which is apprehended as “not breaking up” is not so; it breaks up in every respect.

"It disintegrates, therefore it is the world"—thus it should be understood that the word "world" (*loka*) is conventionally established specifically for the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*).
Therefore, "the world" is simply the Noble Truth of Suffering (*dukkha-ariyasacca*).
Although the meaning of the term "Tathāgata" has been analyzed in detail through various methods in the *Tathāgata-sutta* cited below, [it is not repeated here].
Nevertheless, this exposition of the meaning is given by way of a commentary on the meaning of the text:

"Abhisambuddho" (fully awakened) refers, first of all, without distinction, to the various categories such as latent tendencies (*āsaya*), underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), conduct (*carita*), and inclination (*adhimutti*); or to the classification of wholesome and unwholesome states, etc.;

or to the classification of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) according to its measure, shape, and so forth. Or, specifically, it refers to one who has fully awakened to the fact that "this person has an inclination toward eternalism," and so on.

By means of his own uniquely distinguished knowledge— such as "this is the tendency toward annihilationism" and so forth, and "the earth element has the characteristic of hardness, the water element has the characteristic of trickling" and so forth— he has awakened to, known,
and made manifest for himself each and every meaning exactly as it is to be understood,
correctly and without error; thus he is "Abhisambuddha" (fully awakened).

"In the world" means from the world as previously described. "Dissociated" means unattached; the meaning is that he is completely liberated from it because all fetters connected to it have been thoroughly cut off. "The origin of the world," according to the method of the Suttas, is craving;

however, according to the method of the Abhidhamma, it consists of one thousand five hundred defilements together with the volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*). "Abandoned" [refers to its abandonment] at the Seat of Enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
By means of the knowledge of the path to arahantship, it is abandoned along with its latent tendencies through the mode of total eradication. "The cessation of the world" is Nibbāna.
"Realized" means it has been made personally manifest. "The practice leading to the cessation of the world" is the Noble Eightfold Path, which comprises the three aggregates beginning with virtue;
for that indeed goes to, or attains, the cessation of the world, which is Nibbāna, for that purpose.
And because it is practiced by the noble ones (*ariya*), it is called "the practice leading to the cessation of the world.

To this extent, the meaning of "Tathāgata" is shown as follows: he is a Tathāgata because he has fully awakened to the *tathā* (suchness) and has gone according to reality (*yāthāvato gata*). For the Four Noble Truths are indeed called *tathā*. As it is said in detail:
"Monks, these four are *tathā*, not otherwise, not different. Which four? 'This is suffering,' monks—this is *tatha*, this is not otherwise, this is not different," and so forth.
Furthermore, he is a *tathāgata* because he has gone (*gata*) to suchness (*tathā*); he is a *tathāgata* because he has gone to what is real (*tathaṃ*).

"Gone" means understood, transcended, attained, and practiced. This is what is meant: because the Blessed One has gone to and understood all the world through the full comprehension of its investigation as it truly is (*tathā*), without error, therefore the world has been fully awakened to by the *Tathāgata*; thus he is a *tathāgata*.

He has gone (gata) to suchness (tathā) by means of the full understanding of abandonment regarding the origin of the world; thus he is a Tathāgata. He has gone to and attained suchness by means of the realization of the cessation of the world;
thus he is a Tathāgata. He has gone upon and entered the path leading to the cessation of the world, which is such and non-erroneous;
thus he is a Tathāgata. In this way, the meaning of this passage should be understood as illustrating the Blessed One’s state of being a Tathāgata.
Thus, having manifested his own state as a Tathāgata by way of the full awakening to the Four Truths, the Blessed One now spoke the passage beginning with “Bhikkhus, that which...
in order to demonstrate it also by way of the full awakening to seeing and so forth therein. In the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated:
“Having declared his own Buddhahood by means of the four truths,” and so on. This [refers] to the words *tathāgata* and *buddha*.
This was stated in order to show that there is no difference in meaning [between the terms]. For it is precisely in this way that the text proceeds.

In this context, "seen" refers to the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*). "Hear"d refers to the sense-sphere of sound (*saddāyatana*). "Sensed" refers to the sense-spheres of odor, taste, and the tangible, because they are to be grasped by reaching them.
"Cognized" refers to mental objects such as pleasure, pain, and so forth. "Attained" refers to having sought after...
Or having sought after the bowl. "Sought after" means that which has been sought, whether the bowl has been reached or not reached.
"Mentally traversed" means mentally wandered over. But of what was it mentally traversed?

It should be connected as: "of the world with its devas... [omission] ...of the world with its devas and humans. In this context, "together with the devas" means *sadevaka*; "of that world with its devas."
The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
Here, by the expression "together with devas" (sadevaka), the inclusion of the gods of the five sense-sphere realms (pañca-kāmāvacara-deva) is to be understood;

by the expression "together with Māras" (samāraka), the inclusion of the gods of the sixth sense-sphere realm is to be understood; by the expression "together with Brahmās" (sabrahmaka), the inclusion of the Brahmās such as those belonging to the Brahmakāyika realm is to be understood; and by the expression "together with recluses and brahmins" (sassamaṇabrāhmaṇi).
The inclusion of both those ascetics and brahmins who are adversaries of the Dispensation and those ascetics and brahmins who have stilled evil and cast out evil;
the inclusion of the world of beings by means of the word "people" (*pajā*); and the inclusion of conventional gods and the rest of humanity by means of the phrase "together with gods and men.

Thus, it should be understood that here the world of beings is included by three terms along with the gods, Māras, and Brahmās, while the world of beings is also included by two terms through the category of "people."
Another method: by the inclusion of "together with devas," the world of the immaterial-sphere devas is included; by the term "together with Māras," the world of the six sense-sphere devas;

by the term "together with Brahmas," the world of the material-sphere Brahmas; and by the phrase "together with recluses and brahmins," etc., the rest of the world of beings along with conventional devas is included.
Furthermore, here, by the term "together with devas," from the perspective of the highest limit, the entire sphere of the world is indicated.

When the Blessed One’s state of having attained full enlightenment was proclaimed, there might be those who think: "Māra is indeed of great power, the lord of the six sense-sphere realms, and a wielder of authority;

but Brahmā is even more powerful than he, for he radiates light with his ten fingers throughout ten thousand world-systems and experiences the bliss of the attainment of the highest meditative absorption. And there are many other ascetics and brahmins..."
“Those possessing psychic power, those with the divine eye, and those who know the minds of others—beings of great majesty—are found to exist.
And this body of beings is infinite and immeasurable; is it the case that the Blessed One has fully awakened to the domain of all these without exception?
To dispel their doubt, the Blessed One said, “Of the world together with its devas,” and so forth.
But the Ancients said: “Of the world with its devas” includes the remainder of the world together with the devas;
“with Māra” includes the remainder of the world together with Māra; “with Brahmā” includes the remainder of the world together with the Brahmas.
Thus, having included all beings subject to the three realms of existence within these three terms, he further encompasses them with two more terms:
He said, "together with the generation of recluses and brahmins, with gods and humans. Thus, by these five phrases, he encompasses all beings as delimited by the three aggregates.
By the words "which has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata," this is what he shows: that which [exists] in immeasurable world-systems...
In this world with its devas, when a visible object such as "blue" or "yellow" comes within the range of the eye-door, the Tathāgata has thus fully awakened to it all:
"At this very moment, having seen this particular visible object, this being has become glad, dejected, or neutral. Likewise, regarding that which [occurs] in immeasurable...
In the world-systems of this world together with its devas, sound-objects such as "the sound of drums" and "the sound of kettledrums" come into the range of the ear-door;
odor-objects such as "the scent of roots" and "the scent of bark" come into the range of the nose-door;
and taste-objects such as "the taste of roots" and "the taste of trunks" come into the range of the tongue-door.
“Hard,” “soft,” and so forth—this tactile object (*phoṭṭhabba*), which is divided into the earth element, the fire element, and the air element, comes into the range of the body door;

and [the Tathāgata knows] all this, such as: “At this very moment, having touched such a tactile object, this being has become glad, or dejected, or neutral”—all this is thus perfectly awakened by the Tathāgata.
Likewise, whatever object of a mental phenomenon— such as pleasure and so forth— arises within the mind-door for this world with its devas across immeasurable world-systems,
such that [the Tathāgata knows]: "At this very moment, having cognized this particular mental object,
this being has become joyful, dejected, or neutral"— all of that is thus fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.
Thus, there is nothing in this world with its devas that has been seen, heard, sensed, or cognized by this person which has not also been seen, heard, sensed, or cognized by the Tathāgata.
Yet, among these great masses of people, there is that which is not attained even after searching; there is that which is not attained even without searching;
there is that which is attained after searching; and there is that which is attained without searching.
There is even what has been attained. For the Tathāgata, there is nothing whatsoever that is not attained or not personally realized through his knowledge.

Therefore, whatever form-object exists within the range of the eye-door of the immeasurable beings in the immeasurable world-systems, the Blessed One knows and sees it all in every aspect. By knowing thus—

And by him, having seen that [form]—either by way of the desirable and undesirable, or by way of the terms available among the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—it has been analyzed according to many names and thirteen sections in such a manner as:
"What is that form which is the form-base (*rūpāyatana*)? It is that form derived from the four great elements which is visible and impinging, blue, yellow," and so forth.
When analyzed by way of the fifty-two methods, it remains exactly so; there is nothing false.
This same method applies to sounds and other objects that enter the range of the ear-door and the other sense-doors.

Therefore, he is called the "Tathāgata" because he has gone (gata) exactly as the world has gone (tathā). Thus, he is the Tathāgata because he has gone in the very same way as that which the world has gone.
It is so called. However, in the Pāḷi it is stated as "abhisambuddha" (fully awakened), which has the same meaning as the word *tathāgata*.
By this, the sense that he is a "Tathāgata" because he sees things as they truly are (*tathādassibhāva*) is demonstrated. For this was said by the General of the Dhamma:
"There is nothing here in this world that he has not seen..."
And furthermore, that which is unknown and ought to be known—
he has directly realized all that is to be understood;
therefore, the Tathāgata possesses the universal eye.
It is also said by the Blessed One in the Suttanta:

"Bhikkhus, whatever in this world with its devas... among the generation with its devas and humans, has been seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or pondered by the mind—that I know; that I have directly realized."
"That was known by the Tathāgata; that the Tathāgata did not dwell upon.

And, monks, on the night when the Tathāgata fully awakens to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment—that full-moon night of Visākha—on that very night, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), upon the invincible throne (aparājita-pallaṅka), [attained it] in the sense of having come to suchness (tathā-āgata).
Seated there, having crushed the heads of the three Māras and because there is nothing higher than this, he attains unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-sammāsambodhi*)— namely,
omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) together with the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*).
And on the very same night, the full-moon day of the month of Visākha, at Upavattana in Kusinārā, he passes away into the Nibbāna-element without remainder (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*).
He attains final nibbāna through the element of nibbāna without residue remaining in the Sāla Grove of the Mallas, between the twin Sāla trees.
Regarding the phrase "in the interval between these":

it refers to the period measuring forty-five years in the interval between these two states of nibbāna—with residue remaining and without residue remaining—whether during the first enlightenment, the middle enlightenment, or the final enlightenment.

Whatever Dhamma he speaks—distinguished as Sutta, Geyya, and so forth—he utters by way of pointing out, he proclaims by way of indicating, and he demonstrates by way of further demonstration. All that is exactly so;
thus, all the ninefold word of the Buddha (navāṅga buddhavacana) taught therein, beginning with Sutta and Geyya, is irreproachable in both meaning and phrasing, neither deficient nor redundant.
It is complete in all its aspects, crushing the intoxication of lust... [and so on] ...crushing the intoxication of delusion; therein there is not even a hair’s breadth of error.

It remains exactly as it was spoken for the sake of that purpose—just like something marked with a single seal, measured by a single reed, or weighed on a single scale—because it accomplishes that goal exclusively and not otherwise.
Therefore, it is suchness (*tathaṃ*), not-untruth (*avitathaṃ*), and not-otherwise (*anaññathaṃ*). By this, he shows that he is the "Tathāgata" because of speaking suchness (*tathāvāditāya*).
This word *gata* has the sense of "speaking" (*gada*), having changed the letter *da* to *ta*; therefore, the meaning is "one who speaks suchness" (*tathaṃ gadati*), thus a "Tathāgata.
Alternatively, *āgada* is "speaking," meaning "speech. He is one whose speech (*āgado*) is such (*tatho*), i.e., non-perverted; [this is the meaning] when the letter *da* [is changed to *ta*].
By adding the letter *ta*, the word is thus established here as *tathāgata*.
Regarding the phrase "one who acts as he speaks": when the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma to others, saying, "These things are unwholesome, blameworthy, censured by the wise;
when fully undertaken and practiced, they lead to harm and suffering," [he is one who acts as he speaks].
He himself abandoned those states entirely. But as for those states which the Blessed One declares, saying, "These states are wholesome, blameless, praised by the wise;

when fully undertaken and practiced, they lead to welfare and happiness," he himself dwelt having entered upon them entirely. Therefore, it should be understood that the Blessed One is one who acts exactly as he speaks.
"One who acts as he speaks" means that the Blessed One himself is one who acts accordingly because he has practiced rightly by way of the perfect fulfillment of virtue and the other factors.
Likewise, he is "one who speaks as he acts" because, through his teaching of the Dhamma, he establishes others in those very same qualities.
Indeed, for the Blessed One, the body conforms to speech, and speech conforms to the body. Therefore, he is one who speaks as he acts, and one who acts as he speaks.
And it is so. For one who has become thus, his body proceeds in the same manner as his speech;
and his speech proceeds in the same manner as his body—this is the meaning.
"The Conqueror, unconquered" means that from the peak of existence above down to the Avīci hell below, and across the intermediate directions, [he is unsurpassed].

In immeasurable world-systems, the Blessed One surpasses all beings by virtue of his moral conduct, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; there is no equal or measure for him.
He is peerless, equal to the unequaled, matchless, incomparable, without a rival, unmeasured, immeasurable, unsurpassed—the King of Dharma, the god beyond gods.
He is the supreme among the Sakkas and the supreme among the Brahmas. For that very reason, he is "unconquered" (*anabhibhūto*), because he himself is not overcome by anyone.
*Aññadatthu* is a particle used in the sense of emphasis. He is "all-seeing" (*daso*) because he sees whatever is knowable (*neyya*) as clearly as an amala fruit on the palm of his hand.
