He is "the one who leads" (*netā*) because, through the correct awakening to the inclinations (*āsaya*) and other factors of beings, and through the bestowing of benefit and so forth, he brings them to the transformation of their state.

Because he exercises mastery over the mental states (*saṅkhāra*) through the power of having practiced them perfectly in every way, he brings the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the mind under his control;
thus, he is "one who wields mastery" (*vasavattī*). To this extent, the Blessed One demonstrates his state as a *Tathāgata* in the sense of being "overpowering.

In this regard, the derivation of the word should be understood as follows: it is like a medicine (*agada*); for what is this? It is both the splendor of his teaching and the accumulation of his merit.
For this very reason, this Exalted One, like a physician with a divine antidote overcoming snakes, overcomes all those of other doctrines as well as the world with its devas.

Thus, because his charm of teaching and his accumulation of merit are a true, unerring antidote (*agada*) in the overcoming of the entire world, one should understand him as the *Tathāgata*, having changed the letter *da* to *ta*. By that—
It is said: “In the world with its devas, bhikkhus... [and so on] ...he is a wielder of power; therefore he is called the Tathāgata.
In the verses, “having directly known the entire world” means having understood the dwelling of the world within the three realms.
“According to reality in the entire world” means that whatever is to be known within that dwelling of the world in the three realms, all of it is according to reality, unerring.
Having known [this]. "Detached from the entire world" means that through the complete abandonment of the four bonds (*yoga*), he is detached from and liberated from the whole world.
"Without attachment" means that in the entire world he is without attachment—without the attachments of craving and views—and is devoid of those attachments.
"Overcoming all" means having overcome all objects such as form, the entire range of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), and all Māras.
"Steadfast. "The Wise One" (*dhīra*) means one endowed with steadfastness (*dhiti*).

"Liberator from all bonds" means he stands having liberated [others] from all bonds such as the bodily bond of covetousness (*abhijjhā-kāya-gantha*); he is called "liberator from all bonds" because he liberates those to be trained within their own mental continuums through the excellence of his own teaching.
"Phuṭṭhāssa" means "it has been touched by him. This genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental; the meaning is "touched by this [person]. "Supreme" (*paramā*)...
“Peace” (*santi*) refers to *nibbāna*. For that [peace] has been touched by that touch of knowledge. Therefore it was said: “*Nibbāna* is fearless from every side” (*akutobhaya*).
Alternatively, “supreme peace” (*paramā santi*) means the highest peace. What is that? *Nibbāna*.
Since there is no fear from any quarter whatsoever in *nibbāna*, it is therefore called “fearless from every side.”
"Anīgho" means free from suffering. "Sabbakammakkhayaṃ patto" means he has reached the destruction, the end, and the absolute non-existence of all kamma.
"Vimutto upadhisaṅkhaye" means he is liberated by the liberation of fruition which takes as its object Nibbāna—known as the destruction of the acquisitions (upadhi).
"Esa so" means this is he. "Sīho anuttaro" [is so called] in the sense of enduring all dangers.
In the sense of slaying the defilements (*kilesa*), the Tathāgata is called the "unsurpassed lion. "Brahmā" means the supreme. "Wheel" (*cakra*) means the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*).
"He set it in motion" means he turned it with its three revolutions and twelve aspects.

"Thus" (*iti*) means having known the qualities of the Tathāgata in this way. "Having gathered together" (*saṅgamma*) means having come together. "They pay homage to him" (*taṃ namassanti*) means to him...
Gods and humans, having gone to the Tathāgata for refuge, pay him homage. He is "Great" because he is endowed with great qualities such as virtue (sīla) and the rest;

he is "Free from Timidity" by virtue of his possession of the four grounds of self-confidence (vesārajja). Now, in order to show that which they proclaim while paying homage, the words beginning with "Tamed" (danta) are spoken.
Their meaning is already evident.

Thus, in this Chapter of Fours, it should be understood that the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is explained in the sixth and seventh suttas; the turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭa*) is explained in the first, second, third, twelfth, and thirteenth; and in the remaining suttas, both the round and the turning away are explained.
The commentary on the thirteenth sutta is finished.
Thus ends [the section] of the *Paramatthadīpanī*.
The commentary on the Catukkanipāta (Section of Fours) of the Itivuttaka within the Khuddakanikāya-ṭīkā is finished.
Concluding Remarks.
And at this point—
by the Lord of Dhamma, who brings light to the world through the Dhamma,
who knows the Dhammas that are to be awakened, and who understands the method of teaching.
Based on various occasions, the Great Seer, seeking the welfare of the entire world,
taught these two hundred and ten discourses in the *Itivuttaka*, categorized by their divisions beginning with the single verse.
By means of this classification of "Thus it was said" (Itivuttaka), the great seers—
those who had attained mastery of the six supernormal powers, who were proficient in the analytical knowledges,
and who were formerly the upholders of the Dispensation and the compilers of the Dhamma— recited [the scriptures].
To elucidate its meaning, I have undertaken this commentary on the sense,
relying upon the method of the ancient commentaries.
Therein, the ultimate meanings within the Suttantas are presented as appropriate.
The *Pakāsanā*, titled *Paramatthadīpanī*,
has reached its completion by way of recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*) from the thirty-eight-fold measure of the Pāḷi, through unconfused analysis.
Thus, by compiling this, whatever merit has been attained by me—
by the power of that merit, having plunged into the teaching of the Lord of the World through the practice of purity in virtue and the rest— may [all beings attain liberation].
May all living beings partake in the essence of liberation.
May the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One endure for a long time in the world;
may all living beings always have reverence for it.
"May the Lord of the World, the King of Devas, rain down in due season;
may he, devoted to the True Dhamma, rule the world by means of the Dhamma alone.
Thus was it composed by the teacher Dhammapāla, a resident of the Badaratittha Monastery.
The commentary on the Itivuttaka is completed.
